Consumer Protection Law — Law No. 92-117 of December 7, 1992

Enacted: December 7, 1992 | In force: 1993 | Amended: 2009, 2015
Protects consumers against defective goods, unfair commercial practices, misleading advertising, and price manipulation. Establishes the right to information, right to safety, and right to redress. Regulates consumer contracts including distance contracts and credit. Creates the National Council for Consumer Protection.
CommercialCivil

Law No. 98-40 of June 2, 1998Sales Techniques and Commercial Advertising

Enacted: June 2, 1998 (JORT No. 44, June 2, 1998) | In force: 1998
Tunisia's dedicated statute governing sales promotion techniques and commercial advertising, distinct from — and more detailed than — the general "misleading advertising" language in the Consumer Protection Law (No. 92-117) above. Chapter 1 defines the regulated actors (merchant, consumer, advertiser, product). Chapter 2 governs price-reduction sales (soldes/liquidations): a genuine reduction must be measured against the lowest price charged in the prior three months, restricts promotional sales during the 40 days preceding the two statutory seasonal-sales periods, and requires prior declaration to the Ministry of Commerce. Chapter 3 regulates off-premises (door-to-door) and distance selling. Chapter 4 requires advertisers to be able to substantiate the truthfulness of any factual claim and prohibits misleading advertising. Chapter 5 sets fines of 500–10,000 dinars for violations. (Added Run 163) A wholly new standalone entry, previously undocumented across 162 prior runs despite the Consumer Protection Law's overlapping general language; verified via jurisitetunisie.com's full-text database, cross-confirmed by the JORT n°44 filename on pist.tn (Tunisia's official scientific/technical information portal, which mirrors JORT issues). No amendment to this 1998 law was found in this run's research; comparative-advertising and pyramid-scheme provisions, if any, were not located within this specific text and may fall under Competition Law (No. 2015-36) instead.
CommercialCivil

Draft Law No. 113/2020 (adopted by Council of Ministers, never promulgated)Consumer Credit & Household Over-indebtedness

Adopted by Council of Ministers: December 2020 | Status: Never promulgated; revived debate 2026
Tunisia has no dedicated statute defining household over-indebtedness or regulating consumer-credit affordability; a bill (referenced in secondary sources as "Loi n° 113/2020") addressing both was approved by the Council of Ministers in December 2020 but was never submitted to, or adopted by, parliament, leaving a persistent legal vacuum — no over-indebtedness observatory and no statutory debt-to-income caps. Correction: credit-bureau infrastructure specifically is no longer entirely absent — see the separate Credit Reporting (Credit Bureau) Decree-Law entry below, a narrower licensing framework that does not itself address affordability caps or over-indebtedness. Household debt reached an estimated TND 32.2 billion in 2024 (91% bank-issued, 9% microfinance), with a household debt-service burden reported to have risen from 107% to 171% of disposable income between 2014 and 2024. In March 2026 the Institut Arabe des Chefs d'Entreprises (IACE) published a policy note ("Le surendettement des ménages : une urgence nationale") renewing calls to promulgate the dormant bill and proposing debt-to-income caps (40% for consumer credit, 50% for mortgage credit) plus governorate-level over-indebtedness commissions offering a 7-year repayment plan, partial debt write-off with reintegration commitments, or full write-off paired with a 3-year credit ban. As of mid-2026 no such law had been enacted. Note: the "113/2020" bill number is drawn from secondary press/policy sources, not independently verified against a primary JORT or ARP record.

Decree-Law No. 2022-2 of January 4, 2022Credit Reporting (Credit Bureau) Licensing

Enacted: January 4, 2022 | Published: JORT N°2, January 5, 2022 | BCT implementing circular: No. 2022-09 of October 25, 2022
Creates a licensing ("agrément") regime, under Central Bank of Tunisia (BCT) supervision, for private "sociétés d'information sur le crédit" (credit-reporting companies/credit bureaus) — a narrower measure than, and distinct from, the still-unenacted household over-indebtedness bill above; it does not itself impose affordability caps or debt-to-income limits. Article 7 licensing criteria cover shareholder quality, technical/IT capacity, management fitness, governance, and personal-data-protection compliance (cross-referencing Law No. 2004-63). One firm, MITIGAN CIB, was initially licensed, but the BCT withdrew its agrément on March 17, 2026 for failing to launch operations within the required timeframe — leaving Tunisia with no operating licensed credit bureau as of mid-2026 despite the legal framework being in force since 2022.

Law No. 98-4 of February 2, 1998Debt-Recovery Companies

Enacted: February 2, 1998 | Amended: Law No. 2001-91 of August 7, 2001; Law No. 2003-42 of June 9, 2003
Regulates "sociétés de recouvrement de créances" (third-party debt-collection companies), setting minimum capital, licensing conditions, and permissible collection practices; Law No. 2001-91 and Law No. 2003-42 subsequently amended aspects of the regime. Actual debt-collection litigation runs through ordinary civil process under the Code of Obligations and Contracts and Code of Civil and Commercial Procedure. Separately, Tunisia's Commercial Code criminalizes issuing a bad cheque (see Law No. 2024-41 above), which Human Rights Watch's June 10, 2024 report "No Way Out: Debt Imprisonment in Tunisia" documented as a de facto debt-imprisonment regime — citing official figures of 496 people imprisoned for unpaid cheques and business-association estimates as high as ~7,200, and arguing the practice is inconsistent with ICCPR Article 11's prohibition on imprisonment for inability to fulfill a contractual obligation.

Competition and Prices Law — Law No. 2015-36 of September 15, 2015

Enacted: September 15, 2015 | In force: 2015 | Replaced: Law No. 91-64
Governs competition policy, prohibits anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position, and anti-competitive mergers. Establishes the Competition Council (Conseil de la Concurrence) as independent regulatory authority. Regulates prices for essential goods and services. Pending reform: the Competition Council's president announced in April 2025 a planned "radical revision" of the law to align it with COMESA competition standards. Refinement (Run 526): that revision effort in fact took the concrete form of a member's bill (proposition de loi n°6-2025) proposing to toughen the law's sanctions against anti-competitive and unfair-competition practices, heard alongside a companion e-commerce/online-platform bill by the ARP's Industry, Trade, Natural Resources, Energy and Environment Committee on April 15–16, 2025 (L'Économiste Maghrébin, WebManagerCenter, Managers.tn) — correcting the prior "no bill text yet before the ARP" characterization. No further committee action, vote, or plenary scheduling has been reported since that April 2025 hearing; still not enacted. Enforcement (added Run 141): the Conseil de la Concurrence issued three separate decisions dated December 31, 2025 (reported January 7–8, 2026) fining companies a combined TND 4.2 million under this Law's Article 5 anti-competitive-practices provisions: TND 1.2 million against a pharmaceutical-sector company, TND 2.5 million combined against companies in the smartphone market, and TND 0.5 million combined against packaging-sector companies — a distinct, dated enforcement action under the currently-enacted law, separate from the still-pending COMESA-alignment revision above.

Ministry of Commerce Price-Cap Decisions — Bottled Water & Poultry

Entered into force: August 19, 2026 | Poultry caps stated to run August 19 – September 19, 2026 | No decision number or JORT reference published
Two ministerial decisions of the Ministry of Commerce and Export Development, issued under the price-regulation powers of the Competition and Prices Law (Law No. 2015-36) above and framed as anti-speculation measures amid summer supply crises. Administrative/regulatory implementing measures rather than new primary legislation. Correction (Run 1036): this entry previously described the bottled-water measure as "a 15-millime-per-bottle margin cap." That is wrong, and the error is traceable: La Presse's August 19, 2026 write-up rendered the figure as 15 millimes where every other outlet reporting the same decision — Business News the same day among them — gives a 15% gross profit margin, applied separately at the wholesale and the retail stage and computed on the net invoice purchase price. A percentage margin is also the only reading consistent with the decision's companion element, a schedule of maximum retail prices by bottle size, which a flat per-bottle margin would make redundant. The millime figure is recorded here as a source error rather than silently dropped, so a future run does not reintroduce it from the same article. Bottled mineral water: margins capped at 15% wholesale and 15% retail on net purchase price; maximum retail prices fixed at 600 millimes (0.5 L), 800 millimes (1 L), 850 millimes (1.5 L) and 950 millimes (2 L); operators must sell through organised, traceable distribution circuits, be tax-compliant, and produce invoices on inspection, with violations prosecuted under the price and competition legislation. Poultry: live chicken capped at 5,300 millimes/kg; ready-to-cook chicken at 7,900 millimes/kg at the slaughterhouse and 8,950 millimes/kg at retail, the latter raised from a previous 8,500; operators are obliged to maintain regular market supply, respect the legal traceability of distribution channels, and keep cut-chicken marketing to reasonable proportions. On the poultry measure's duration, a widely-repeated "capped until the end of September" formulation comes from a Business News headline and is loose: reporting of the ministry communiqué gives a precise one-month window — "entre en vigueur à partir de ce mercredi, 19 août et s'étalera jusqu'au 19 septembre 2026" (Tunisie Tribune, August 20, 2026, corroborated by African Manager). The caps therefore lapse September 19, not September 30, absent renewal. Note the direction of travel differs between the two: the water decision lowers effective prices by capping margins, while the poultry decision raises the permitted retail ceiling — both are supply-stabilisation measures, not uniformly consumer-price-reducing ones. Confirmed via Business News, La Presse de Tunisie and Tunisie Tribune (August 19–20, 2026). Open item carried forward: neither decision has a published decision number or JORT reference; both were announced by ministry communiqué and are known only through press reporting, so the underlying instruments remain uncited. Update (Run 1042): re-checked against Business News, La Presse, Tunisie Tribune and African Manager; no outlet cites a decision or arrêté number for either measure, consistent with these being administrative price-regulation communiqués issued directly by the Ministry rather than instruments routed through JORT publication — JORT issue N°84 (due August 21, 2026) had not yet been indexed with retrievable contents as of this run, so it could not be checked as a possible source for either number; still open pending either a citable JORT reference or confirmation that none exists. (Added Run 1026; corrected and expanded Run 1036.)

Law No. 94-89 of July 26, 1994Financial Leasing Law

Enacted: July 26, 1994 | In force: 1994
Regulates financial leasing (crédit-bail / ijar) of movable and immovable assets. Defines the leasing contract, rights and obligations of lessor and lessee, and end-of-term purchase options. Financial leasing companies must be licensed by the BCT. Key instrument for SME financing in Tunisia.
CommercialFinancial

Law No. 88-92 of August 2, 1988, as amended by Law No. 95-87 of October 30, 1995 (Run 146 correction)SICAR Law

Base law enacted: August 2, 1988 | SICAR-specific amendment: October 30, 1995 | Further amendment: 1992
Run 146 correction: prior runs cited only "Law No. 95-87 of October 30, 1995" as if it were the foundational statute; independent verification against jurisitetunisie.com and the CMF's own official reference PDF confirms the actual framework-creating law is Law No. 88-92 of August 2, 1988 "sur les sociétés d'investissement," which repealed Law No. 59-29 and created Tunisia's investment-company regime (SICAV — variable-capital, and SICAF — fixed-capital), laying the initial groundwork for venture capital. Law No. 95-87 (following an intermediate 1992 amendment) is the amendment that specifically developed and refined the SICAR (Société d'Investissement à Capital Risque) sub-category for venture-capital financing of SMEs at various growth stages — a real but distinct legislative act from the 1988 base law, not a standalone "SICAR Law" in its own right. SICARs invest in the capital of SMEs and startups and benefit from significant tax advantages: contributions to SICARs are deductible from taxable income, and SICARs are exempt from capital-gains tax on their principal-activity dispositions where at least 80% of resources are invested within the second year following each capital release. Regulated by the CMF (Financial Market Council).

Enacted: October 8, 1996 | In force: 1996
Regulates commercial agency agreements (contrats de représentation commerciale). Defines the rights and obligations of commercial agents (independent representatives). Provides mandatory compensation to agents on termination (indemnité de clientèle). Applied in cross-border distribution and agency arrangements.

Law No. 2020-37 of August 6, 2020 (Run 103 correction)Crowdfunding Law

Adopted by ARP: July 21, 2020 (127–0–0) | Enacted/published: August 6, 2020 | Implementing decrees: Nos. 2022-765 & 2022-766 of October 19, 2022
Run 103 correction: prior runs cited this statute as "Decree-Law No. 2020-170 of November 10, 2020" — no such decree-law could be independently verified in any source searched (CMF, WebManagerCenter, ilBoursa), and it appears to have been a fabricated citation. The verified statute, adopted by the Assembly of the Representatives of the People on July 21, 2020 and published in JORT on August 6, 2020, is Law No. 2020-37, establishing Tunisia's legal framework for crowdfunding (financement participatif) across three models — loan-based, securities/equity investment (limited to SARLs and SAs), and donation-based — through platforms that must be Tunisian-registered joint-stock companies, with projects restricted to those carried out in Tunisia. Regulatory oversight is split among the CMF (securities/equity crowdfunding), the BCT (loan-based crowdfunding), and the Microfinance Control Authority. Implementing decrees were delayed roughly two years, finally issued as Decree No. 2022-765 (crowdfunding in securities investment) and Decree No. 2022-766 (crowdfunding lending), both of October 19, 2022. Enables startups under the Startup Act to raise equity via registered platforms.

Law No. 2008-66 of October 20, 2008Factoring (Affacturage)

Enacted: October 20, 2008 | In force: January 2009
Establishes the legal framework for factoring operations (affacturage) in Tunisia. Authorizes banks and specialized financial institutions licensed by the Banque Centrale de Tunisie to provide factoring services — the purchase of trade receivables from commercial enterprises at a discount. Regulates the assignment of receivables to the factor, notification obligations to debtors, and the recourse/non-recourse models. Facilitates access to working capital for Tunisian exporters and domestic suppliers.

  • Art. 13–18: Rights of the factor against debtor and seller
  • Art. 19–22: Recourse factoring vs. non-recourse factoring

Law No. 2009-69 of August 12, 2009Commerce de Distribution & Franchise Regulation (Run 81 addition)

Enacted: August 12, 2009 | Published: JORT N°65, August 14, 2009 | Implementing decree: Décret n° 2010-1501 of June 21, 2010
A wholly new standalone entry, confirmed via direct reading of the primary text hosted by jurisitetunisie.com and a Ministry of Commerce document. Tunisia's general framework statute for the retail/distribution sector, regulating large-surface retail authorizations, commercial-zoning requirements, and — the aspect most relevant to cross-border business — franchise contracts. Article 14 defines the franchise contract; Article 15 (not Article 14, a common misattribution in secondary sources) imposes a mandatory pre-contractual disclosure document at least 20 days before signature, with nullity as the sanction for non-compliance. No statutory anti-competitive-clause restriction was found within Articles 14–17 of the base law itself; that restriction, where reported, appears to stem from the implementing decree or a separate competition-law order rather than the 2009-69 text directly, and is flagged here as unconfirmed at the statutory level.

Chambers of Commerce and Industry Law — Law No. 2006-75 of November 30, 2006Loi relative aux Chambres de Commerce et d'Industrie

Enacted: November 30, 2006 | Replaces: Law No. 88-43 of May 19, 1988 (as amended by Law No. 92-112) | Organization and operation: Decree No. 2013-1331 of March 7, 2013 | In force
The statute of Tunisia's chambers of commerce and industry, previously uncovered here despite entries on the Commercial Code, the National Business Register and the distribution trade. The CCIs are public establishments, not private trade associations — the classification that explains both their supervision by the Minister of Commerce and the fact that their board elections are regulated rather than internal. The law sets their territorial districts and regional structure, their composition and board elections, and their supervisory relationship to the ministry. Their functions are threefold: consultative towards the public authorities, administrative — notably the delivery of commercial documents and certificates of origin, which gives them a practical gatekeeping role in the export chain governed by the Foreign Trade Law and the preferential-origin regimes documented in this artifact's international section — and economic promotion. (Added Run 1036.)

Foreign Trade Law — Law No. 94-41 of March 7, 1994Loi relative au Commerce Extérieur

Adopted by the Chamber of Deputies: February 22, 1994 | Promulgated: March 7, 1994 | Published: JORT n° 19 of March 8, 1994, pp. 403–406 | In force: July 1, 1994 | 40 articles in 5 chapters | Still in force
The framework statute liberalising Tunisian import and export trade, uncovered here despite entries on customs, competition and exchange control. Verified by direct reading of the JORT facsimile hosted by the Central Bank of Tunisia. Article 2 states the governing principle — "Les importations et les exportations de produits sont libres à l'exception des produits assujettis aux restrictions prévues par la loi" — reversing the prior authorisation-based system, whose principal instrument, Décret-loi No. 85-11 of September 27, 1985 on import trade, Article 40 repeals along with Article 41 of the Code des changes et du commerce extérieur annexed to Law No. 76-18 of January 21, 1976, Law No. 66-1 of January 28, 1966 and Law No. 88-9 of February 23, 1988. Chapter III (Arts. 12–33) is a WTO-accession-era anti-dumping and countervailing-duty code, giving Tunisia a full trade-remedy procedure with petition, investigation, provisional measures, undertakings and review. A correction of a recurring secondary-source error: several summaries state that Law No. 2019-47 of May 29, 2019 amended Law No. 94-41. It did not — Article 5 of Law No. 2019-47 amends Law No. 94-42 on sociétés de commerce international, a different statute printed in the same JORT issue (pp. 406 ff.). No law amending Law No. 94-41 itself was located, though a negative of that kind cannot be certified; what has actually evolved is the implementing decrees. A complementary statute, Law No. 98-106 of December 18, 1998 on import safeguard measures and prior import surveillance, sits alongside the anti-dumping chapter and is distinct from it (medium confidence, secondary-sourced). Still cited as the operative legal basis in the Ministry of Commerce's Manuel des procédures du commerce extérieur (2022 edition).
Key provisions
  • Art. 2: freedom of import and export is the principle, restrictions the exception
  • Art. 3: excluded goods are those touching sécurité, ordre public, hygiène, santé, morale, protection of fauna and flora, and cultural heritage; the list is fixed by Décret No. 94-1742 of August 29, 1994 (modified by Décret No. 2000-1803 of July 31, 2000)
  • Art. 4: save occasional non-commercial operations, import and export are reserved to persons whose activity involves using, producing or selling the goods and who operate lawfully in Tunisia; Art. 5: excluded products move only under authorisations issued by the Minister of Commerce
  • Art. 6: operational modalities fixed by Décret No. 94-1743 of August 29, 1994 (modified by Décret No. 2000-244, Décret No. 2006-2619 of October 2, 2006 and Décret No. 2014-3487 of September 18, 2014); Art. 7: operations subject to exchange-law settlement procedures
  • Arts. 8–11 (technical control): imported products may be subjected to control of conformity with national technical standards and regulations or international standards, or with particular contractual specifications so long as these do not conflict with national or international standards or the consumer's interest; the symmetrical rule applies to exports, adding conformity with the importing country's specifications; modalities and accredited bodies fixed by Décret No. 94-1744 of August 29, 1994 (completed by Décret No. 99-1233 of May 31, 1999, modified by Décret No. 2010-1684 of July 5, 2010), with the list of controlled products fixed by arrêté of the Minister of Commerce
  • Arts. 12–13: defines the unfair practice as dumped or subsidised imports causing or threatening material injury or materially retarding the establishment of a domestic industry, and defines dumping and subsidy
  • Art. 14: a countervailing duty may be imposed, capped at the dumping margin or subsidy amount, established by arrêté of the Minister of Finance on the Commerce Minister's proposal and recovered like customs duties; Art. 15: a provisional duty via guarantee, valid 4 months and extendable by 2; Art. 16: retroactive imposition possible within 90 days of the customs declaration; Art. 18: an additional duty where the exporter absorbs the duty
  • Arts. 20–23: written petition to the Commerce Ministry, opening of the investigation announced in the JORT, questionnaires returned within 30 days extendable by 15, and on-the-spot verification including abroad with the exporter's and authorities' agreement
  • Arts. 24–26: confidentiality, non-confidential summaries and professional secrecy under Art. 254 of the Penal Code; Art. 29: once the investigation is announced, prospective importers must notify quantities and values before customs clearance; Arts. 30–31: termination, including by acceptance of price or subsidy undertakings
  • Arts. 32–33: review no earlier than one year after imposition, with refund if duties are revised downward
  • Arts. 34–35: creates the Conseil National du Commerce Extérieur, advising on export-promotion strategy and trade policy, monitoring anti-dumping and subsidy measures and trade flows, and setting the national fairs and exhibitions programme and its budget
  • Arts. 36–38: breaches of Arts. 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 38 repressed under customs, tax, exchange, economic-control, technical-control, hygiene, health and safety legislation; non-conforming imports are liable to refoulement (Art. 37); infringements recorded by procès-verbaux of economic-control inspectors and duly mandated agents
CommercialInternational

Import Safeguard Measures Law — Law No. 98-106 of December 18, 1998Loi relative aux Mesures de Sauvegarde à l'Importation — الإجراءات الوقائية عند التوريد

Adopted by the Chamber of Deputies: November 24, 1998 | Promulgated: December 18, 1998 | Published: JORT n° 102 of Tuesday, December 22, 1998, pp. 2451–2454 | 32 articles | No amending instrument located | In force and actively applied through 2022
A subject area identified as missing at Run 1035 and written up here from the JORT original. Tunisia's trade-remedy law comes in two distinct statutes, and this artifact previously documented neither as such: this law covers safeguards — protection against surges of fairly-traded imports — while Law No. 99-9 of February 13, 1999 covers unfair practices, dumping and subsidies. The two are frequently conflated. Article 1 anchors the regime explicitly in Article XIX of GATT 1994 and the WTO Agreement on Safeguards, ratified by Law No. 95-06 of January 23, 1995 — this is WTO-accession implementing legislation, and its architecture follows the Agreement closely. It does not amend the Foreign Trade Law but sits alongside it: Law No. 94-41 establishes freedom of import and export as the principle, and this law is the derogation from that freedom. Implementing texts cite both. Notably, no décret d'application exists — implementation is at arrêté level, principally the Minister of Commerce's arrêté of August 12, 2004 on prior-surveillance procedures (JORT n° 68 of August 24, 2004), taken expressly under Art. 30. (Added Run 1036.)
Key provisions
  • Art. 2 (definitions): serious injury is "une dégradation générale notable de la situation d'une branche de production nationale"; a threat of serious injury must rest on facts, not mere allegation, conjecture or remote possibility
  • Arts. 4–5 (initiation): on application by the domestic industry or trade associations to the Minister responsible for trade, or ex officio by the Minister on sufficient evidence
  • Art. 6: preliminary examination within one month; if evidence suffices, the Minister authorises the investigation, publishes notice in the JORT, and notifies the WTO Committee on Safeguards
  • Art. 15: investigation runs nine months, extendable by two in exceptional circumstances; on completion the Minister informs the Conseil National du Commerce Extérieur, whose opinion precedes any measure (Art. 16)
  • Art. 17: de minimis exemption for developing-country WTO Members — 3% individually, 9% collectively
  • Art. 18 (form of measures): safeguards may take the form of quantitative restrictions or tariff increases only
  • Art. 22 (provisional measures): tariff increases only, in critical circumstances, after the Council's opinion and with prior WTO notification; Arts. 23–24 require refund of provisional duties if no injury is found
  • Art. 26 (duration): total application including any provisional measure ≤ 4 years; provisional measures ≤ 200 days; extendable after fresh investigation to a maximum of 10 years; Art. 27 requires progressive liberalisation and mid-term review beyond three years; Art. 28 imposes a re-application cooling-off period
  • Art. 30: imports may be placed under surveillance préalable where import trends threaten injury — operationalised by the August 12, 2004 arrêté, which requires a fiche d'information to the Minister before bank domiciliation of the import, for a renewable six-month period
  • Art. 31: special agricultural safeguard under Art. 5 of the WTO Agreement on Agriculture — per the 2005 WTO Trade Policy Review, never invoked
Investigations actually opened under this law, each verified in the JORT, showing a statute used sparingly but genuinely: two investigations announced June 16, 2006 (JORT n° 48 — product names not recoverable, that issue being image-only in the archive); enamels (n° 75, September 17, 2013); MDF wood-fibre panels and glass bottles (n° 79, September 30, 2014); ceramic tiles (n° 56, July 14, 2015); the minibus industry (n° 90, October 1, 2021, petitioner SETCAR); and iron or non-alloy steel wire for furniture springs (n° 80, July 19, 2022). For context, the WTO's 2005 Trade Policy Review recorded that Tunisia had to that point applied no safeguard, anti-dumping or countervailing measure at all. Update (Run 1042): the June 2006 pair is independently corroborated at the WTO level — a WTO Secretariat statistical note of November 29, 2006 confirms Tunisia initiated exactly two safeguard investigations in the January–October 2006 window, consistent with the two June 16, 2006 JORT n° 48 notices — but the product names remain unrecoverable from any source reachable this run; the WTO notification symbols for the 2014 pair (MDF panels and glass bottles) are G/SG/N/6/TUN/3 and /4, which would place the 2006 pair at /1 and /2, but no text of those two earlier notifications could be located to confirm the product descriptions. This stays an open item. Separately, no amending instrument to this 1998 law itself has been found in any source through 2022 (Ministry of Commerce, customs authority, and WTO Trade Policy Review material, plus investigation notices as recent as the 2021 minibus and 2022 steel-wire cases, all cite the original 1998 text without amendment) — treated as confirmed unamended rather than merely unconfirmed.
CommercialCustomsAdministrative

Defence Against Unfair Import Practices — Law No. 99-9 of February 13, 1999Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Duties

Published: JORT n° 15 of February 19, 1999, from p. 279 | Implementing decree: Décret No. 2000-477 of February 21, 2000 (JORT n° 18 of March 3, 2000, p. 577), replacing Décret No. 94-1745 of August 29, 1994 | In force
The companion trade-remedy statute to the safeguards law above, and the instrument that supplies Tunisia's dedicated anti-dumping and countervailing-duty regime. Article 1 states its object as defining the rules applicable to unfair import practices and the conditions under which they are neutralised; Article 2 defines the droit antidumping as the duty applied to remedy injury to a domestic industry caused by dumped imports, and the droit compensateur as its counterpart for subsidised imports. A refinement to this artifact's existing account: the Foreign Trade Law entry describes Chapter III of Law No. 94-41 (Arts. 12–33) as a WTO-accession-era anti-dumping and countervailing-duty code. That remains accurate as to the 1994 text, but the operative modern regime is this 1999 statute with its 2000 implementing decree, which replaced the pre-WTO Décret No. 94-1745 — itself preceded by Décret No. 93-695 of April 5, 1993 instituting a countervailing duty. Procedure, per the WTO's 2005 Trade Policy Review: complaint by producers representing at least 50% of production, or exceptionally ex officio; a normal timeline of 12 to 18 months; provisional duties by decree after a minimum 60-day period; price undertakings available; and definitive duties lapsing after five years absent review. (Added Run 1036.)
CommercialCustoms

Alcohol Taxation and Licensing RegimeLoi n°74-101 · Décret n°97-1368 · Décret n°94-492

Régie Nationale des Alcools founding law: December 25, 1974 (Art. 43, 1975 Finance Law) | Consumption-tax implementing decree: Décret n°97-1368 of July 24, 1997 | Establishment-classification decree: Décret n°94-492 of February 28, 1994, as modified by Décret n°2000-821 of April 17, 2000 (JORT n°33)
A genuine, previously undocumented gap: this run's targeted search found no standalone alcohol-regulation entry in the artifact despite two prior runs (1045, 1049) recording a "gap check" conclusion that the area was "already comprehensively documented" — no such entry could in fact be located, so that earlier conclusion appears to have been mistaken, and is corrected here rather than repeated. Tunisia has no single consolidated alcohol code; the regime is assembled from a state production monopoly, an excise/consumption-tax decree, and municipal licensing rules. Production and commercialization of ethyl alcohol is assigned to the state-owned Régie Nationale des Alcools, created by Loi n°74-101 of December 25, 1974 (Art. 43 of that year's Finance Law) — confirmed by direct retrieval of the Régie's own scanned founding-law text (regiedesalcools.com.tn/images/loi_creation.pdf). That same text's Art. 44 states the Régie took over "le monopole des alcools prévu par le décret du 20 Novembre 1927 et les textes qui l'ont modifié" — identifying a Protectorate-era 1927 decree, not a 1959 text, as the monopoly's original legal basis; that 1927 decree's own citation number has not yet been independently located and is an open item. Décret n°97-1368 of July 24, 1997 applies the "droit de consommation" (excise duty) framework of Law No. 88-62 of June 2, 1988 specifically to beers, wines, alcoholic beverages, and spirits (customs headings 22.03–22.08): it designates manufacturers/bottlers/packagers as taxpayers, sets differentiated rates for "classified" versus "unclassified" wine, and requires pre-activity declarations, bonded warehousing, and denaturation procedures for industrial/cosmetic/pharmaceutical alcohol. Separately, on-premises drinking establishments (débits de boissons) are classified and licensed under Décret n°94-492 of February 28, 1994 (JORT n°33), as modified by Décret n°2000-821 of April 17, 2000, feeding into the annual municipal licensing fee under the Local Taxes Law. Rates have shifted over time: the tax on strong-alcohol imports/manufacture was cut from 650% to 50% by the 2016 Finance Law, and Article 62 of the 2023 Finance Law added a 5% advance-payment obligation on sales by alcohol manufacturers/bottlers. Market production is dominated by SFBT (Société Frigorifique et Brasserie de Tunis), maker of Celtia beer. A companion state fiscal-monopoly instrument to the RNTA tobacco/matches monopoly immediately below and the Promosport gambling/lottery monopoly, illustrating the same recurring Tunisian regulatory pattern of colonial-era-rooted state monopolies over vice/excise goods. Confirmed via direct WebFetch of regiedesalcools.com.tn's own founding-law PDF (now reachable after returning HTTP 503 across several recent runs) for the 74-101/1927-decree citations; the Décret n°94-492/2000-821 establishment-classification citation and the 88-62/97-1368 consumption-tax framework rest on secondary press/legal-portal sourcing and were not independently re-verified against primary JORT text this run. (Added Run 1059.)

Law No. 64-57 of December 28, 1964Régie Nationale des Tabacs et des Allumettes (RNTA)

Enacted: December 28, 1964 | Predecessor entity (French-protectorate tobacco régie): founded 1891 | Merged with Manufacture de Tabac de Kairouan (MTK): 1981
A genuine, previously undocumented gap identified this run: this artifact's Tobacco Control Law (98-17) covers only the public-health regulation of tobacco (advertising bans, smoke-free places, minors' access) and had no companion entry for the separate statute governing tobacco's production and distribution. Law No. 64-57 establishes the Régie Nationale des Tabacs et des Allumettes (RNTA) as a public establishment with industrial and commercial character (établissement public à caractère industriel et commercial), endowed with civil personality and financial autonomy, under the supervisory authority of the Ministry of Finance, holding Tunisia's state fiscal monopoly on the manufacturing and marketing of tobacco products and matches, extended in practice to playing cards and hunting powder. The RNTA absorbed the Manufacture de Tabac de Kairouan (MTK, founded 1981) into a combined production structure. A companion state-monopoly instrument to the already-documented Promosport gambling/lottery monopoly under Decree-Laws No. 74-20/74-21 of 1974, illustrating a recurring Tunisian regulatory pattern of state fiscal monopolies over vice/excise goods predating the post-1987 economic liberalization era. Confirmed via the RNTA's own official institutional-history page (rnta.tn), which quotes the law's own establishing language verbatim; cross-checked against independent encyclopedic sources, which corroborate the 1891/1964/1981 institutional timeline though without citing the law number themselves. (Added Run 1049.)

Labor Code — Law No. 66-27 of April 30, 1966Majallat Al-Shughl

Enacted: April 30, 1966 | In force: May 1966 | Amended: 1994, 1996, 2006, 2007, 2011, 2017
The primary statute governing employment relationships in Tunisia. Covers individual employment contracts, conditions of work, wages, termination, workplace safety, collective bargaining, and trade unions. Applies to the private sector; public servants are governed by the General Statute of Civil Servants. Implements ILO core labor conventions (Tunisia has ratified 62 ILO conventions).
Key provisions
  • Art. 6: Employment contract — types (fixed-term, indefinite-term, project-based)
  • Art. 14–22: Trial period (période d'essai)
  • Art. 23–35: Obligations of employer and employee
  • Art. 40: Minimum wage (SMIG/SMAG) — set by decree
  • Art. 73–83: Annual paid leave — minimum 1 day per month (18 days/year)
  • Art. 90–100: Work hours — 48 hours/week maximum (40 hours in industry)
  • Art. 120: Dismissal — requires just cause; procedural requirements for economic dismissal
  • Art. 123: Severance pay for unfair dismissal
  • Art. 152: Trade union rights; freedom of association
  • Art. 155: Right to strike (with pre-notice requirements)
  • Art. 193–200: Labor inspectorate powers
  • Art. 230–240: Occupational health and safety requirements

Law No. 2025-9 of May 21, 2025Employment Reform Law

Enacted: May 21, 2025 | Published: JORT May 23, 2025
Landmark reform overhauling Tunisia's employment framework. Three pillars: (1) Indefinite employment contracts (CDI) are the statutory default; CDDs (fixed-term contracts) permitted only in three circumstances: temporary workload increase, replacement of absent worker, and seasonal work; any non-compliant CDD is void and automatically converted to CDI with full seniority. (2) Prohibition of labor subcontracting — workers supplied via subcontracting arrangements are deemed permanent employees of the beneficiary company; employers have 3 months to regularize. (3) Criminal penalty of TND 10,000 fine for engaging prohibited subcontracting. Contested by employer federations; supported by UGTT. Update (Run 1001): Nawaat's August 2026 institutional reporting places this law among several enacted-but-not-implemented statutes lacking implementing decrees — see the new Government–Parliament Institutional Standoff entry under Constitutional Law.
Labor

Law No. 2025-18 of December 22, 2025Public-Sector Recruitment of Long-Term Unemployed Graduates

Adopted by ARP: December 16, 2025 (92 for, 4 abstentions, 1 against) | Published: JORT No. 2025-153, December 23, 2025 | In force: December 23, 2025
An 8-article member's bill (sponsored by the "Pour que le peuple triomphe" parliamentary bloc) creating an exceptional mechanism for public-sector and civil-service recruitment of higher-education graduates in long-term unemployment, applied alongside the General Statute of Civil Servants above. Priority is given to candidates over 40 and to those whose diploma is 10+ years old, limited to one member per family, via a dedicated digital application platform. Excludes candidates who previously benefited from a regularization program, who had continuous social-security affiliation, who held a tax ID in the prior year, or who hold loans exceeding TND 40,000. Recruitment is staged in waves over up to 3 years; Finance Law 2026 (Law No. 2025-17) Art. 57 allocates budget for a first tranche of roughly 3,000 graduates. Status as of July 2026: implementing decrees remain unpublished; affected graduates staged protests (Siliana, reported July 1, 2026; a further protest planned for Tunis on July 8, 2026) demanding their publication. Update (Run 73): protest organizers put the affected pool at roughly 60,000 over-40 graduates out of some 137,000–140,000 unemployed higher-education graduates nationally, and specify three demands for the July 8 protest — publication of the implementing decrees, the promised digital application platform's launch, and a public implementation timetable (webdo.tn, directinfo.webmanagercenter.com, July 1, 2026). Update (Run 167): the July 8, 2026 protest occurred as planned — dozens of graduates demonstrated near Place de la Kasbah in Tunis renewing the same three demands — with the implementing decrees and digital platform still unpublished as of that date (webdo.tn, July 8, 2026). Update (Run 201): escalating beyond street protest, 52 ARP deputies sent a formal petition to the Head of Government on July 9, 2026 — over seven months after JORT publication — demanding the same three items: publication of the implementing decrees, launch of the digital application platform, and a public recruitment timetable (La Presse, July 9, 2026). Update (Run 916): still no implementing decrees or digital platform as of mid-August 2026, now nearly eight months after JORT publication; on August 12, 2026, unemployed-graduate coordinations from all 24 governorates gathered at Tunis's Municipal Théâtre municipal to renew the demand, stating they refuse to let "la loi n°18" remain "un texte adopté, mais dépourvu d'effets concrets" (leconomistemaghrebin.com, August 12, 2026). Kapitalis's August 13, 2026 follow-up reported no substantive government response and cited authorities restricting some national/regional protest gatherings, which organizers characterize as infringing constitutional free-assembly rights; the same report placed Q1 2026 graduate unemployment at 24.2% (up from 22.5% in Q4 2025), with a pronounced gender gap (32% for women vs. 14.2% for men) forming the backdrop to the mobilization. No new legal text, decree, or ARP action beyond the July 9 deputies' petition has been identified.
LaborAdministrative

Decrees No. 2026-63 through 2026-69 of April 30, 2026Public & Private Sector Wage Increase Package 2026–2028

Published: JORT No. 44, April 30, 2026 | Implements: Finance Law 2026 (Law No. 2025-17), Art. 15 | Effective: retroactive to January 1, 2026 | Covers: 2026–2028
A seven-decree package implementing Finance Law 2026 Art. 15 and Labor Code Art. 40, staging wage and pension increases across the entire public and private sectors over three years (2026–2028). Update (Run 38): previously this entry documented only the SMIG/SMAG/collective-agreement decrees (66–68); the package's other four decrees, covering the civil service, public enterprises, and the judiciary, are now added. Decree No. 2026-63 sets the raise program for agents of the state, local authorities, and administrative public establishments (fonctionnaires). Decree No. 2026-64 covers employees of public enterprises and establishments governed by special statutes or establishment-level collective agreements, staging monthly increases of TND 120 (cadres), TND 100–105 (supervisory/maîtrise), and TND 90 (execution-grade) across 2026–2028. Decree No. 2026-65 raises the "prime de magistrature" by TND 120/year (2026–2028) for judges of the judicial order, the Administrative Court, and the Court of Accounts, also extended to their retirement pensions. Decree No. 2026-66 sets the guaranteed agricultural minimum wage (SMAG) for workers 18 and over at TND 21.336/day in 2026, rising to TND 22.400 (2027) and TND 23.520 (2028), plus a technical-skill premium for specialized agricultural workers. Decree No. 2026-67 sets the guaranteed inter-professional minimum wage (SMIG) for non-agricultural sectors at TND 554.736/month (48-hour regime) or TND 470.251/month (40-hour regime) in 2026, rising in stages to TND 611.520 / TND 517.571 by 2028. Decree No. 2026-68 mandates an annual 5% increase in base salaries plus transport and attendance allowances for non-agricultural sectors covered by sectoral collective bargaining agreements, with monthly increases of roughly TND 36–46 for line workers, ~TND 53 for supervisory staff, and ~TND 69 for management-grade employees in 2026. Decree No. 2026-69 sets smaller, separately staged increases (roughly TND 30–39/month execution-grade, TND 44 maîtrise, TND 58–64 cadres in 2026, rising through 2028) for non-agricultural Labor Code employees covered by neither an enterprise-specific statute nor a sectoral collective agreement. A further schedule of monthly increases (TND 90–120, staged by category A1/A2/A3/B and phased through 2027–2028) applies to specified "sensitive" public-service corps, including health professionals (physicians, dentists, pharmacists, veterinarians), oversight/control bodies, scientific researchers, university academic staff, social-service personnel, and labor inspectors. Across all seven decrees, the increases extend to retirement pensions, are non-cumulative with certain pre-existing allowances, are excluded from year-end/performance-bonus calculations, and remain subject to standard social-security contributions; non-compliance with the SMIG/SMAG minimums is subject to the penalties under Art. 3 of the Labor Code Law of April 30, 1966.

Circular No. 11 of the Head of Government, August 11, 2025End of Trade-Union Secondment

Issued: August 11, 2025 (effective same day) | Reported: August 14, 2025
A circular from the Head of Government (then Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri) to all ministers and secretaries of state cancelling, effective August 11, 2025, all standing authorizations for "détachement syndical" — the practice of seconding civil servants to work full-time for trade-union structures while remaining on the public payroll. Ministries were instructed to compile lists of seconded agents, recall them to their original posts, and pursue "appropriate administrative and judicial procedures" against those who refuse. UGTT deputy secretary-general Sami Tahri called the measure "a political gesture" — arguing union secondment had "practically disappeared since 2022" — intended to "incite a war against union rights" rather than address a live administrative problem; some press subsequently referred to the instrument as "Decree No. 20," though the underlying text is a head-of-government circular, not a numbered decree. Confirmed via two independent French-language reports (webdo.tn and WebManagerCenter, both dated August 14, 2025) that agree on the August 11 effective date. Contemporaneous with, but legally distinct from, the Finance Law 2026 Art. 15 wage-setting-by-decree mechanism above, which separately bypassed UGTT's traditional role in tripartite wage negotiation — together read by UGTT and independent commentators as a broader narrowing of the union's institutional role in 2025–2026.

Law No. 2024-44 of August 12, 2024Maternity and Paternity Leave Reform

Adopted by ARP: July 31, 2024 (111-1-4) | Published: JORT No. 2024-099, August 12, 2024
Restructures maternity and paternity leave across the public and private sectors. Expands paternity leave from the prior baseline of 1 day (private sector, Labor Code) / 2 days (civil servants) to 7 days at full pay — extended to 10 days for multiple births or a newborn with disability, prematurity, or a congenital condition requiring care, plus 3 additional days in the event of stillbirth; must be taken within 30 days of the birth. Restructures maternity leave into a prenatal component (up to 15 days in the final month, on medical order) and a postnatal component extended from 30 to 90 days (120 days for complicated or multiple births).

Law No. 93-10 of February 17, 1993 (as amended)Vocational Training Law

Enacted: February 17, 1993 | In force: 1993 | Amended: multiple times
Framework law governing vocational and professional training in Tunisia. Creates the National Agency for Vocational Training (ATFP — Agence Tunisienne de la Formation Professionnelle). Establishes the national apprenticeship system, certification standards, and quality assurance for vocational qualifications. Employers must contribute 1% of payroll to the Vocational Training Fund (TFP).

Digital Platform ("Gig-Economy") Workers — Regulatory Vacuum (Run 99 addition)

UGTT study launched: June 2025 | Findings presented: June 29, 2026
A genuine legislative gap, previously undocumented despite 98 prior research runs: Tunisia has no law, decree, or Labor Code amendment specifically classifying or regulating digital-platform ("gig-economy") workers — the general Labor Code (No. 66-27, above) applies loosely at best, since most platform workers are treated as independent contractors rather than employees. A UGTT research-department study, launched June 2025 and presented June 29, 2026, found roughly 60,000 workers across four categories (commercial order delivery, pharmacy/medicine delivery, home care/caregiving, and motorcycle passenger transport) operating in what it called the "parallel economy," entirely outside any legal framework: 98% lack any social coverage, 60% of delivery workers are denied all insurance, and 75% suffer irregular income. UGTT's recommendations: integrate platform workers into the CNSS social-security regime, mandate clear written contracts defining the parties' relationship, create professional/union representation mechanisms, provide occupational health and safety training, and establish a national database of platform workers. The union also invoked newly-adopted ILO Convention No. 193 on decent work in the platform economy (see the International Law & Treaties section's companion entry) as a reference framework. No Tunisian bill or draft text addressing platform work has been filed with the ARP as of this run; corroborated across Business News, L'Économiste Maghrébin, WebManagerCenter, La Presse de Tunisie, Gnet News, and allAfrica, all dated June 29–30, 2026. Update (Run 378): the government moved from documenting the gap to publicly proposing to close it: Minister of Social Affairs Issam Lahmar, opening a July 14, 2026 workshop on new forms of employment and decent work, called for adapting several Labor Code provisions to establish a balanced framework covering digital-platform work, and for deepened tripartite consultation toward an inclusive national approach (La Presse de Tunisie, July 14, 2026). UGTT responded on July 17, 2026 by demanding formal, mandatory inclusion of its social-protection and informal-sector department in the technical committees that will draft the resulting sectoral bills, specifically naming delivery workers' (livreurs) and ride-hailing drivers' (chauffeurs) legal status as the priority to address within the Labor Code revision (La Presse de Tunisie and allAfrica, both July 17, 2026). Still no bill text has been filed with the ARP on gig/delivery-platform work specifically — see the separate, already-filed freelance/digital-economy self-employment bill below, which addresses a related but distinct category of independent digital workers. Update (Run 438): Minister Lahmar advanced from the July 14 workshop's general call to a concrete two-bill framing: opening the 8th Arab Conference on Pensions and Social Insurance in Tunis (July 20–22, 2026), he announced that two draft laws are nearing finalization as part of a broader social-security/protection-system overhaul — one dedicated to regulating private-sector telework, the other specifically to the digital "platform economy," intended to give new forms of employment a legal framework, support the underlying economic activity, and extend social protection to the workers concerned (Business News and La Presse de Tunisie, both July 20, 2026; corroborated by allAfrica same-day). Still pre-filing — neither bill had been transmitted to the ARP as of this update. Update (Run 826): Minister Lahmar reframed the effort on August 6, 2026 as part of a broader new Labor Code overhaul — rather than solely the two standalone telework/platform-economy bills described above — adding occupational health and safety modernization as a third pillar alongside telework (now specified to cover data protection, employer-provided equipment, and a right to disconnect) and platform-economy gig-worker status, with explicit reference to aligning Tunisian labor law with ILO norms (webdo.tn, August 7, 2026, reporting the minister's August 6 statement). Still no bill text filed with the ARP as of this update. Update (Run 1003): the government moved from ministerial statements to formal action — on August 18, 2026 it decided to immediately begin drafting the implementing texts for a structural reform of the social-security system, covering a revision of pension regimes, expanded social coverage, and digital transformation of social and health services, framed as reconciling the financial equilibrium of the social-security funds with social justice while adapting to demographic, labor-market, and platform-economy change (La Presse de Tunisie and Business News, both August 18, 2026). Still pre-bill — no draft text published or ARP filing identified as of this update — but this marks the reform's first concrete drafting mandate rather than a further announcement.

Freelance Work & Digital-Economy Self-Employment Bill (Proposition de loi)

Filed at the ARP: June 9, 2026 (Proposition de loi n°36/2026, 11 deputies) | Transmitted to Finance & Budget Committee: June 22, 2026 | Status: committee examination, not yet enacted
A member's bill (proposition de loi n°36/2026) filed with the Assembly of the Representatives of the People on June 9, 2026 by 11 deputies, creating for the first time a dedicated legal framework for independent ("freelance") workers operating in Tunisia's digital economy, distinct from the gig/delivery-platform gap tracked in the companion entry above. Structured in six substantive chapters plus a seventh on transitional provisions. Chapter I sets general provisions and defines the bill's core concepts: independent/freelance work, the legal status of the freelance worker, electronic-payment platforms, and dedicated bank accounts for freelance-related transactions. A further chapter sets out state obligations to support independent workers, including facilitating access to the global digital-services market and to electronic payment for cross-border freelance income (Business News, June 16, 2026). The transitional-provisions chapter establishes a phase-in period of not less than five years, during which caps on certain electronic-payment and funds-transfer operations, together with security and financial-verification (anti-money-laundering/KYC-style) procedures, apply on a graduated basis to manage the sector's controlled integration into the formal economy — addressing long-standing complaints from Tunisian freelancers about restricted access to international payment platforms (PayPal, Payoneer, and similar services) and the foreign-currency repatriation rules under the Foreign Exchange Code (see that entry). Update (Run 861): the bill was transmitted to the ARP's Finance and Budget Committee on June 22, 2026, moving it past the pre-committee stage; an August 10, 2026 explainer round (Business News, Le Courrier de l'Atlas) put concrete figures to the previously-vague transitional-cap language for the first time — a proposed 15% withholding on withdrawals from the freelance-designated account and a monthly ceiling reported at USD 5,000, with automatic conversion of received funds to Tunisian dinars — while noting the calculation basis, collection mechanism, and interaction with other taxes/contributions remain undefined and that "the debate cannot limit itself to the figure of 15%." Still at committee-examination stage as of this update; no vote or hearing date reported (Business News, June 16 and August 10, 2026; Le Courrier de l'Atlas, August 10, 2026; Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, June 16, 2026).

Overseas Recruitment & Placement Bureau Reform Bill (draft, strengthening the 2010 framework)

Ministry draft announced: April 21, 2025 (targeting May 2025 submission to the Presidency of Government) | Still unenacted, re-confirmed to the ARP plenary: April 10, 2026 | Status: drafted, not yet formally filed as a numbered ARP bill
A wholly new standalone entry — a lead first surfaced (via a stale-dated April 2025 article) and correctly set aside as out-of-scope at Run 948, but now independently re-confirmed as a genuinely still-live, currently-reported pending reform via an April 10, 2026 update, one year later, showing it remains unenacted. The Ministry of Vocational Training and Employment announced in April 2025 a draft law strengthening the existing 2010 legal framework governing private overseas-placement/recruitment bureaus (the agencies that place Tunisians in jobs abroad), in response to a wave of fraud complaints involving fake foreign work contracts exchanged for money — described by officials as tantamount to "véritables opérations de traite d'êtres humains" (real human-trafficking operations). As drafted, the bill would: create a dedicated control and inspection body to monitor licensed placement companies and detect unlicensed operators; require a clear mediation contract between job seekers and approved companies; empower the Minister of Employment to order immediate closure of unlicensed structures, including online-only operations; set prison sentences of up to five years and fines of TND 10,000–20,000 for conducting unlicensed overseas recruitment (whether through shell companies, the internet, or social media); and separately fine media outlets and online platforms TND 5,000 for publishing foreign job offers from unauthorized entities. The Ministry originally targeted submission to the Presidency of Government by May 2025, but as of a same-day April 10, 2026 report (webdo.tn, allAfrica), the draft had not yet been formally filed. Minister Riadh Chaoued confirmed to the ARP plenary on April 10, 2026 that legislative strengthening remained under active development, citing 71–72 complaints filed against unauthorized placement structures during 2025 alone (figures vary slightly between the April 2025 and April 2026 reports) and confirming continued inter-ministerial coordination with the Interior Ministry and the State's General Litigation Office. No bill number, ARP committee referral, or JORT publication has been located as of this pass. Confirmed via La Presse de Tunisie (April 15 and 20, 2025; April 10, 2026), webdo.tn (April 21, 2025), and allAfrica (April 22, 2025), cross-checked against each other; the April 2026 confirmation was independently verified via direct WebFetch of the April 10, 2026 La Presse article.

Law No. 85-78 of August 5, 1985 — General Statute of Agents of Offices, EPIC and Wholly State-Owned CompaniesStatut Général des Agents des Offices, des Établissements Publics à Caractère Industriel et Commercial et des Sociétés à Capital Entièrement Public

Adopted in the Chamber of Deputies sitting of July 30, 1985 | Signed at Palais de Skanès: August 5, 1985 (Habib Bourguiba) | Published: JORT n° 58, issue dated August 9–13, 1985, pp. 1011–1017 | 78 articles in 8 titles | Repeals Law No. 68-13 of June 3, 1968 | In force
The employment statute for the commercial and industrial half of the Tunisian public sector — a substantial gap alongside the Labor Code and the General Statute of Civil Servants already documented. Law No. 83-112 of December 12, 1983 governs the State, local authorities and administrative public establishments; Law No. 85-78 governs the offices, EPIC and companies whose capital is held directly and wholly by the State or local public authorities — STEG, SONEDE, CPG, the Office des Terres Domaniales and their peers. The single most consequential difference between the two regimes is Article 3: under Law No. 85-78 the Labor Code applies residually, in everything not contrary to the statute, so these agents are simultaneously statutory and, subsidiarily, employees; agents under Law No. 83-112 sit outside the Labor Code entirely. The second structural difference is delegation: Law No. 85-78 is a short framework that pushes almost all operational detail down to statuts particuliers approved by décret for each establishment (Art. 1), and allows partly-public companies whose agents were covered at entry into force to opt into the conventions collectives regime instead, with the collective-agreement regime applying by default if no choice is reported within a year (Art. 2). Verified from the JORT scan obtained through the ARP parliamentary archive. Three citation errors are corrected here. (i) The ARP archive catalogue record dates the law to 4 أوت 1985; the JORT text itself reads August 5 — the neighbouring transport law on the same page is the one dated August 4, and the catalogue entry is a cataloguing error. (ii) At least one secondary source gives the number as "Law No. 85-87"; the number is 85-78. (iii) Decree preambles use two title variants; the JORT wording is الجماعات العمومية المحلية — collectivités publiques locales. Still operative: it is recited in the visas of instruments as recent as Décret No. 2023-518 of July 6, 2023 and Décret No. 2024-170 of March 22, 2024, each citing it "ensemble les textes qui l'ont modifiée ou complétée." Those amending texts — Law No. 99-28 of April 3, 1999, Law No. 2003-21 of March 17, 2003 and, per secondary sources, Law No. 2007-69 of December 27, 2007 — could not be read this run, so the article-level detail below reflects the original 1985 text and should be checked against a consolidated version before being relied upon.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1: applies to agents employed on a permanent basis by offices, EPIC and companies whose capital is held directly and wholly by the State or local public authorities, with each establishment's detailed rules set by a statut particulier approved by décret
  • Art. 3: the Code du travail applies to these agents in everything not contrary to this law — the defining difference from the civil-service statute
  • Arts. 5–7: prohibition on any remunerated private professional activity (derogations by décret) and on holding, directly or through intermediaries, interests in an enterprise under the establishment's control where those interests compromise functional independence; a spouse's remunerated professional activity must be declared
  • Art. 9: a statutory list of ten fautes graves, including obstructing or paralysing the establishment's normal functioning, abuse of position or excès de pouvoir, obtaining material benefits linked to the establishment's operations, using entrusted funds or objects for personal or third-party benefit, attending work drunk, and continuous unjustified absence exceeding three consecutive days
  • Arts. 11–13: where a third party sues, the establishment bears the damages unless a personal fault separable from the function is imputable to the agent, and it must protect the agent against threats and assaults suffered by reason of the function, being subrogated in their rights; the personal file may not contain any indication of political, philosophical, religious or trade-union opinions
  • Arts. 14–16: each establishment creates one or more commissions consultatives paritaires, competent for titularisation, notation, échelon advancement, promotion, compulsory transfers involving a change of residence, and discipline — chaired by management and composed on a parity basis of appointed establishment representatives and elected agent representatives
  • Arts. 18–19: recruitment conditions include Tunisian nationality, civil rights and good conduct "excluding any political, religious or trade-union consideration," a regular position under conscription law and fitness for the functions; the concours is the principal method, with recruitment following the jury's ranked merit list
  • Art. 20 (the quota architecture): up to 50% of posts filled by external competition, the balance split 40% internal competition and 10% direct appointment by selection among agents of the immediately lower category with at least five years' actual service — a route an agent may use only once in a career in the same establishment, with one promotion table per year per category; statuts particuliers may derogate from these ratios
  • Art. 23: probation of one year, extendable by a maximum of six months, with a report every six months notified to the agent; probation counts towards seniority once tenured, and tenure is automatic if no decision is taken within eighteen months of recruitment
  • Art. 28: promotion by professional worth assessed on the average of the last three years' marks, actual seniority in the immediately lower grade (minimum three years) and training acquired in the post, by registration on a tableau d'avancement au mérite, ties broken by general seniority, then age, then family responsibilities
  • Art. 30 (the disciplinary scale, no cumulation permitted): first degree — rappel à l'ordre, avertissement, blâme without entry in the file, blâme with entry, suspension of up to three days; second degree — mutation d'office without change of residence, suspension of more than three days up to one month, delay in échelon advancement of three months to one year, suspension of one to two months, demotion in échelon, grade or category, mutation d'office with change of residence, and révocation without loss of retirement-pension entitlement
  • Arts. 31–38: first-degree sanctions are imposed without consulting the commission, on the written report of the head of service and after written observations; before any second-degree sanction the agent must be given access to the personal file including the case file, past marks and prior sanctions; rights of defence include copies of the evidence, witnesses and assistance by a person of choice, with written summons at least fifteen days before the hearing; the council must give a reasoned opinion within one month (two with a supplementary inquiry), and the authority may not aggravate the sanction proposed by a majority of members
  • Arts. 39–42: révocation without file access or council consultation where a final judgment has been rendered for rebellion, impersonation of a public official, an offence against morals, forgery, theft, breach of trust, false accusation, an offence against State security, or an offence committed by reason of the job; mise à pied conservatoire must be definitively settled within two months, failing which full salary is recovered, and where the fault is a délit or crime — notably bribery, embezzlement of public funds, forgery or disclosure of professional secrets — the matter must be referred immediately to the public prosecutor; sanctions are effaced automatically after two years (first degree) and four years (second degree) absent a further sanction
  • Arts. 43 & 59–61: four positions — activité, détachement, disponibilité and sous les drapeaux; disponibilité of right on request covers one year renewable once for serious illness of a spouse, ascendant or descendant, three years renewable once for research or studies of general interest, two years renewable twice for a working woman raising a child under six or a child with a disability requiring continuous care, and up to five years for personal reasons; special disponibilité covers a spouse's transfer or posting abroad and five years renewable for an agent elected to the Chamber of Deputies, with mandatory reintegration and pension continuity
  • Arts. 67–70 & 75–77: definitive cessation results from accepted resignation, éviction, révocation or retirement (and equally from loss of Tunisian nationality or civil rights, or failure to return from disponibilité); acceptance of a resignation is irrevocable and does not bar disciplinary proceedings for facts discovered afterwards; salary is payable after work performed and fixed by the statuts particuliers and by décret; temporary agents hold priority for permanent recruitment at equal merit, and foreign agents are engaged on a one-year renewable contract approved in advance by the supervisory authority
Run 1036 update — the substance of the 1999, 2003 and 2007 amendments, previously an acknowledged gap. Run 1035 obtained only the original 1985 text and left the amendment content open. All three are now identified from the JORT. (1) Law No. 99-28 of April 3, 1999 (JORT n° 28 of April 6, 1999) is not a targeted amendment but a wholesale overhaul, repealing and replacing some forty provisions across Arts. 1–73. Its most consequential changes: Art. 1 (new) widens the statute's scope to add companies with public participation that already applied a statut particulier to their staff; Arts. 5, 8 and 9 (new) rebuild duties and disciplinary liability around the tableau de classification des emplois, the procedures manual and the job description, and enumerate the fautes graves — among them obtaining improper advantages, misuse of entrusted funds, drunkenness at work, and unjustified absence exceeding three consecutive days including two working days; Art. 13 (new) governs the individual personnel file and provides that "in no case" may it record the agent's political, philosophical or religious opinions or trade-union membership; and Arts. 14–15 (new) make commissions administratives paritaires mandatory in every enterprise, with an enumerated competence covering tenure, advancement, promotion, disputes over professional marks, compulsory transfer involving a change of residence, resignation, revocation, serious professional insufficiency and discipline, composed on a parity basis of enterprise-designated and agent-elected members. (2) Law No. 2003-21 of March 17, 2003 (JORT n° 22 of March 18, 2003) adds Arts. 53 bis, ter, quater and quinto, creating leave to start a business — up to one year, renewable once, granted by decree, with social cover maintained but salary, advancement and promotion lost, and a more generous variant in zones de développement régional carrying social cover and half salary; it bars any activity other than the one for which leave was granted, on pain of immediate termination and repayment, and gives a right to reinstatement in the original collège even in supernumerary position, provided reinstatement is requested by registered letter at least one month before expiry. Its civil-service twin is Law No. 2003-20 of the same date. (3) The 2007 amendment is Article 35 of Law No. 2007-69 of December 27, 2007 on economic initiative — not a standalone amending law, which is why it is easily missed. It extends the business-creation leave in regional development zones from a maximum of two years to three, adds the takeover of an ailing enterprise under Law No. 95-34 as a qualifying ground, and lengthens the half-salary entitlement in those zones to the first two years with social cover for three. Art. 34 of the same law makes the parallel changes to Arts. 50 bis and 50 quater of Law No. 83-112 for civil servants.

🏛️ Administrative Law

Administrative Court Law — Law No. 72-40 of June 1, 1972

Enacted: June 1, 1972 | In force: 1972 | Amended: multiple times
Establishes the Administrative Court (Tribunal Administratif) as the supreme administrative jurisdiction. Has jurisdiction over disputes between citizens and public bodies, annulment of illegal administrative acts, and administrative contracts. Also serves as the Supreme Audit Institution reviewing public accounts. Organized into chambers; appeals go to Administrative Court plenary.
Administrative

Local Government Code — Law No. 2018-29 of May 9, 2018Majallat Al-Jama'aat Al-Mahaliyya

Enacted: May 9, 2018 | In force: May 2018 | Implements: 2014 Constitution Chapter VII
Comprehensive decentralization legislation replacing the previous municipalities law. Organizes three levels of local government: municipalities (balladiyyat), regions (wilayat), and districts (aqalim). Establishes directly-elected municipal councils with legislative powers in local matters. Introduces participatory budgeting and citizens' right to petition. Implemented after 2018 municipal elections. Superseded in part: Organic Law No. 2025-4 of March 12, 2025 (JORT No. 30, March 13, 2025; adopted by the ARP February 27, 2025, 109–2–4) repealed this code's region and district provisions (and Organic Law No. 89-11 of February 4, 1989 on regional councils), replacing the elected-region model with local, regional, and district councils organized by decree, and transferring former regional councils' assets and holdings to the State for governors to administer. The 2018 code's municipal-level provisions remain in force; local council elections continue to be organized under Decree-Law No. 2023-10 of March 8, 2023 (see the CNRD entry in Constitutional Law).
Key provisions
  • Three levels: municipality, region (governorate), district
  • Directly elected councils at all three levels
  • Fiscal autonomy — own revenue sources and transfers from central budget
  • Participatory democracy mechanisms (citizen petitions, public consultation)
  • Gender parity requirement for municipal council lists
  • Youth quota (minimum 1/3 of each list under 35)
Administrative

Public Procurement Decree — Decree No. 2014-1039 of March 13, 2014

Enacted: March 13, 2014 | In force: 2014 | Amended: 2022
Governs all public procurement by state entities, public establishments, and local authorities. Establishes competitive bidding requirements, transparency obligations, evaluation criteria, and remedies for tenderers. Creates the National Commission for Public Procurement Investigations (HAICOP). Sets thresholds for direct award, restricted tendering, and open tendering. Pending reform (added Run 122): Head of Government Sarra Zaâfrani Zenzri presided over a Council of Ministers session on November 22, 2025 devoted to overhauling the public-procurement system, described in a January 3, 2026 report as "one of the most important legislative reforms currently under examination" for its expected effect on investment and competition; as of this run the reform remains at the policy-objective stage, with no decree or bill number yet filed to amend or replace Decree No. 2014-1039.
Administrative

Access to Information Decree — Decree-Law No. 2011-41 of May 26, 2011

Enacted: May 26, 2011 | In force: 2011 | Strengthened by 2016 Organic Law
Grants citizens the right to access information held by public bodies. Establishes a 20-day response deadline for requests. Replaced in part by the more comprehensive Organic Law No. 2016-22 of March 24, 2016, which created an independent Access to Information Commission (IVD predecessor).

Law No. 99-32 of April 13, 1999National Statistics System (Run 81 addition)

Enacted: April 13, 1999 | Published: JORT | In force: 1999
A wholly new standalone entry — despite 80 prior research runs, no dedicated entry existed for the statute organizing Tunisia's official statistics. Confirmed via direct reading of the law's full 29-article primary text (hosted by the National Institute of Statistics, ins.tn) cross-checked against legislation-securite.tn. Establishes the "Système National de la Statistique" (Art. 12), comprising the National Statistics Council (CNS), the National Institute of Statistics (INS) as the system's central executive body (Art. 18–19), other public statistical bodies, and statistical-training institutions. Article 3 guarantees the system's structures scientific/methodological independence and impartiality in their statistical work, and Article 5 imposes a 60-year confidentiality rule on individual survey data collected under the law.

Law No. 82-85 of December 2, 1982Engineers Profession Organization

Enacted: December 2, 1982, ratifying Decree-Law No. 82-12 of October 21, 1982 | Amended: Law No. 97-41 of June 9, 1997
Creates the Ordre des Ingénieurs Tunisiens (OIT) and restricts legal use of the professional title "ingénieur" — and provision of engineering services under that title — to persons registered on the Order's roll; an engineering diploma alone does not confer the right to use the title. OIT's missions include upholding professional honor and ethics and advising on national engineering-workforce planning. A reform petition to modernize OIT governance was reported circulating among engineers as of late 2025, with no bill filed with the ARP as of this run. (Run 90 addition)
