Administrative Mediator — Law No. 93-51 of May 3, 1993Médiateur Administratif (Run 179 addition)

Institution created: Decree No. 92-2143 of December 10, 1992 | Legal framework: Law No. 93-51 of May 3, 1993 | Amended: Law No. 2000-16 of February 7, 2000; Law No. 2002-21 of February 14, 2002 | Attributions/organization decree: Decree No. 96-1126 of June 15, 1996
A wholly new standalone entry — despite 178 prior research runs across this section, no dedicated entry existed for Tunisia's ombudsman-equivalent institution. The Médiateur Administratif ("Administrative Mediator") was created by Decree No. 92-2143 of December 10, 1992 and given its operating legal framework by Law No. 93-51 of May 3, 1993, later extended by Law No. 2000-16 of February 7, 2000 and Law No. 2002-21 of February 14, 2002; Decree No. 96-1126 of June 15, 1996 (superseding the 1992 decree's own provisions) fixes the institution's attributions and its administrative/financial organization. Appointed by decree for a renewable five-year term, the Mediator examines individual and corporate complaints against state services, local authorities, public establishments, and public enterprises, and — per the law's own independence guarantee — "receives no instructions from any public authority" while examining a request. The Mediator directs the institution and administers its own budget, which attaches to the general state budget but falls under the Presidency's direct authority; regional mediation offices were added following the 2000 amendment to extend the service nationwide. Recommendations issued are non-binding, distinct from the judicially enforceable rulings of the Administrative Court (Law No. 72-40, above). Tunisia's Administrative Mediator is a member of the Association des Ombudsmans et Médiateurs de la Francophonie (AOMF). Confirmed via legislation-securite.tn's primary-text reproductions of Law No. 93-51 and Decree No. 96-1126, and the AOMF's institutional profile of Tunisia.
Administrative

Proposition de Loi Organique (unnumbered, ~10 deputies)Administrative Transparency & Anti-Lobbying Bill (Run 284 addition)

Reported: July 10, 2026 | Status: recently submitted to ARP Commission de la Législation Générale | Not yet numbered | Not yet enacted
A deputy-initiated organic bill of 19 articles, carried by a group reported as around ten deputies, aimed at curbing "powerful lobbies" and administrative non-compliance/evasion by public officials. Per a July 10, 2026 La Presse editorial ("Quand la justice retrouve ses clés") and a July 11, 2026 allAfrica republication, the text introduces prison sentences of up to three years and increased, "finally dissuasive" fines, and imposes a transparency obligation on administrations via mandatory annual reports, framed by the source as a first step toward institutional accountability. Caveat: neither article named the bill's official title, an assigned proposition/projet de loi number, or the sponsoring deputies, and a direct fetch of the La Presse source (its primary framing is a broader opinion piece on judicial enforcement) likewise did not surface these details — this entry is added on the strength of the specific, dated (July 10–11, 2026), multi-outlet-corroborated factual claims (19 articles, ~10 deputies, 3-year maximum prison term, annual-report transparency mechanism) while the bill's formal identifiers remain unconfirmed and are a priority to pin down in a subsequent run. Distinct from the unrelated, already-documented Public Procurement reform (still at the policy-objective stage, no bill filed) and the Tax Adviser organic bill (proposition n° 2023-013) above.

Decree No. 2014-4030 of October 3, 2014Code of Conduct and Ethics of the Public Agent (Code de Conduite et de Déontologie de l'Agent Public)

Enacted: October 3, 2014 | In force | Template for sector-specific codes, e.g. Decree No. 2023-240 of March 16, 2023 (FSI code of conduct)
The general ethics instrument binding every public agent in Tunisia, and the missing middle term between this artifact's asset-declaration and whistleblower-protection entries: those two texts address disclosure and reporting, while this decree states the underlying duties whose breach the other two are meant to surface. It binds public agents of every category and grade across central, regional and local State services, local authorities, and public establishments and enterprises. Its enforcement hook is deliberately simple — each agent signs a register on recruitment acknowledging receipt of the code, which forecloses the "I was unaware of the rule" defence in later disciplinary proceedings. Substantively it imposes duties of integrity, neutrality, impartiality and confidentiality, requires declaration of conflicts of interest, prohibits the acceptance of gifts, and obliges agents to report corruption. The governance state-secretariat services monitor its application and may update it. It has since served as the model for sector-specific codes, most visibly the internal security forces' own code of conduct approved by Decree No. 2023-240 of March 16, 2023. (Added Run 1036.)
AdministrativeAnti-Corruption

Mosques Law — Law No. 88-34 of May 3, 1988, and the Mosque-Personnel RegimeRégime des Mosquées et Statut des Cadres Mosquéens

Framework statute: Law No. 88-34 of May 3, 1988 | Personnel regime: Décret gouvernemental No. 2019-1228 of December 24, 2019 | Social coverage: Décret gouvernemental No. 2020-762 (CNRPS affiliation from January 1, 2020) | Appointment conditions: Circulaire No. 2014-15 of the Ministry of Religious Affairs | In force
An entirely uncovered subject area until this run: the administrative law of religious institutions and their personnel. This artifact documented habous (waqf) endowments and the heritage protection of mosque buildings, but never the statute governing mosques as institutions or the legal position of the people who staff them. The framework text is the 1988 mosques law, which places mosques under the supervision of the Ministry of Religious Affairs. Citation discrepancy resolved (Run 1037): Tunisian legal databases (Marsad/majles.marsad.tn, CAWTAR) give the statute as Law No. 88-34 of May 3, 1988, while French- and Arabic-language press covering the current reform bill repeatedly cite "Law No. 88-33 / القانون عدد 33 لسنة 1988". Marsad's own legislative-tracking record for a 2020 amendment proposal (n°99/2020) names its base text explicitly as "loi relative aux mosquées n°34 de 1988 du 03 mai 1988" — a primary legislative-tracker record, not a secondary summary, confirming 88-34. The press's "88-33" almost certainly comes from confusion with the similarly-numbered Law No. 88-32/33 of May 3, 1988 on political parties, enacted the same day — an easy mix-up between two same-day, adjacently-numbered 1988 statutes on unrelated subjects.

The legally consequential layer is subordinate, not statutory. Décret gouvernemental No. 2019-1228 of December 24, 2019 is the operative text governing khatibs (preachers), imams of the five daily prayers, muezzins and mosque maintenance staff: it fixes their missions, rights, duties and remuneration and governs their appointment, activity and dismissal. Its defining feature is negative — it confirms that these functions are not grades under a statut particulier, so those holding them cannot obtain civil-service promotion or integration into the general statute of civil servants. Pay is set at the guaranteed minimum wage for full-time personnel working 48 hours a week who have no other fixed income and draw no public or private pension; a person may hold up to three posts, with posts beyond the first generating indemnities of roughly 50–130 dinars. Discipline is aligned with the sanctions applicable to temporary public-sector agents under Law No. 83-112. Social protection arrived separately and later: Décret gouvernemental No. 2020-762 affiliated full-time mosque personnel to the CNRPS from January 1, 2020 under Law No. 85-12 on civil and military pensions. Décret No. 2012-1710 on the working hours of State agents is expressly inapplicable to them, a special work regime reflecting prayer-time duties. The net effect is a workforce performing permanent public-facing functions under decree-level regulation rather than statute — the gap the pending bill below is intended to close. (Added Run 1036.)
AdministrativeLaborSocial

Proposition de Loi No. 78/2025Statut des Cadres des Mosquées — Basic Statute for Mosque Personnel

Filed: July 4, 2025 | Referred to committee: July 10, 2025 (ARP Bureau, under Art. 123 of the Rules of Procedure) | Committee hearings: April 2026 (file opened), June 8, 2026 (bill's initiators), further hearing with the Ministry of Finance on cost | Status: first reading in committee — not adopted, not withdrawn, no plenary scheduled
A private members' bill (proposition, not a government projet) that would replace the decree-level regime described in the entry above with a dedicated statute for mosque personnel. Sponsored by a cross-bloc group of deputies drawn from Al-Ahrar (Les Libres), Ligne Nationale Souveraine, Voix de la République, Honnêteté et Travail, Nationaux Indépendants and non-affiliated members; individual signatories are not listed on the ARP record. Before the Commission de l'organisation de l'administration, du développement, de la digitalisation, de la gouvernance et de la lutte contre la corruption, where as of September 2025 it was one of 37 legislative initiatives queued. Twelve articles in five chapters (general provisions; recruitment and training; rights and duties; breaches and penalties; transitional and final provisions). Worth noting for classification purposes: the bill is framed by its defenders as social legislation rather than religious — deputy Youssef Tarchoun has publicly argued "the mosque personnel bill is social, not religious" — and its substance bears that out, being concerned with pay, pensions and career structure rather than doctrine. No movement in the August 14–20, 2026 window, parliament being in recess since July 29, 2026. (Added Run 1036.)
Key provisions
  • Legal status: creates a sui generis unified statut particulier for imams, khatibs, muezzins and mosque caretakers performing permanent religious functions in State-supervised mosques — it does not integrate them into the general civil service as titular fonctionnaires; the accessible texts avoid that word
  • Pay: a fixed monthly salary replacing the current indemnity-based arrangement
  • Social protection: insurance, healthcare and retirement coverage, plus annual leave and sick leave
  • Career: advancement, bonuses, and mandatory continuing training in fiqh, Islamic sciences, religious discourse, law and religious administration
  • Recruitment: Tunisian nationality, good conduct, at least a baccalauréat (religious/sharia training preferred), and success in written and oral examinations run by the Ministry of Religious Affairs
  • Duties: respect for the Constitution, political and partisan neutrality, promotion of moderate religious discourse, and a prohibition on using the pulpit for non-religious purposes
  • Discipline: sanctions graduating from warning to dismissal for incitement to hatred, politicisation of the mosque, and administrative violations
  • Transitional: obliges the State to regularise the situation of all serving mosque personnel within a maximum of two years from entry into force

💰 Tax & Fiscal Law

Income Tax Code — Law No. 89-114 of December 30, 1989Code de l'Impôt sur le Revenu des Personnes Physiques et l'Impôt sur les Sociétés

Enacted: December 30, 1989 | In force: January 1, 1990 | Amended: annually in Finance Laws
Governs personal income tax (IRPP) and corporate income tax (IS) in Tunisia. Personal income tax is progressive with rates from 0% to 35%. Corporate income tax standard rate is 15%, with higher rates for banks and telecoms (35%) and reduced rates for SMEs and certain sectors. Amended annually through the Finance Law. Digital fiscal cash-register mandate (added Run 280): a Ministerial Order of October 14, 2025, implementing CIRPP/IS Art. 59 ter, phases in mandatory digital cash registers ("caisses enregistreuses numériques") for on-site food/beverage-consumption businesses (restaurants, cafés, tea rooms, fast food), defined as any establishment selling prepared food or drink for consumption on the premises. Phase 1 (November 1, 2025): classified tourist restaurants and 2nd/3rd-category cafés. Phase 2 (July 1, 2026): extended to all other legal entities (companies) in the sector. Phase 3 (July 1, 2027): extends to real-regime individual taxpayers filing monthly returns. Phase 4 (July 1, 2028): extends to remaining individual operators. Distinct from the Finance Law 2026 Art. 56 e-invoicing mandate (see below), which governs invoice issuance rather than point-of-sale transaction recording; confirmed via La Presse, Tunisie Numérique, Le Temps News, and L'Economiste Maghrébin, cross-checked against each other.
Key rates (as of 2024)
  • Personal income tax: 0% up to 5,000 TND, 26% bracket, 35% top rate
  • Corporate income tax: 15% standard rate
  • Banks, financial institutions, telecoms: 35%
  • SMEs: reduced rate of 10% (conditions apply)
  • Withholding tax on dividends: 10%
  • Capital gains tax: included in income tax
TaxAmended

VAT Code — Law No. 88-61 of June 2, 1988Code de la Taxe sur la Valeur Ajoutée

Enacted: June 2, 1988 | In force: January 1, 1989 | Amended: annually
Establishes value-added tax in Tunisia. Standard rate 19%; reduced rates of 13% (certain services) and 7% (basic goods, agricultural products). Exports are zero-rated. Registration required for businesses with turnover exceeding 100,000 TND/year (services) or 200,000 TND (goods).

Tax Procedures Code — Law No. 2000-82 of August 9, 2000Code des Droits et Procédures Fiscaux

Enacted: August 9, 2000 | In force: 2001 | Amended: annually
Unifies and governs all tax administration procedures including filing obligations, tax audits, assessment, payment, penalties, and dispute resolution. Establishes taxpayers' rights during tax audits. Provides for administrative appeals before tax committees and judicial appeals before administrative courts.
Tax

Customs Code — Law No. 2008-77 of December 22, 2008

Enacted: December 22, 2008 | In force: 2009 | Replaced: 1955 Customs Code
Governs importation, exportation, transit, and customs duties. Establishes the legal framework for customs declarations, inspections, duty rates, and customs offenses. Aligns Tunisia's customs procedures with international standards (WCO Revised Kyoto Convention). Governs free zones and customs warehouses.

Enacted: February 3, 1997 | In force: 1997 | Amended: multiple times
Regulates taxes and fees collected by municipalities including property taxes (TFP — taxe foncière sur les propriétés bâties et non bâties), tourism taxes, advertising taxes, and local business taxes (TCL — taxe sur les établissements à caractère industriel, commercial ou professionnel).

Code of Registration and Stamp Duties — Law No. 93-53 of May 17, 1993Code des Droits d'Enregistrement et de Timbre

Promulgated: May 17, 1993 | Amended annually by successive finance laws (consolidated Ministry of Finance editions through 2025) | In force
The largest remaining gap in this artifact's tax coverage, closed this run. The reference already documented income tax, corporate tax, VAT, customs, local taxes and tax procedure — but not the code that governs registration and stamp duties, which is the tax layer most citizens and businesses actually meet, since it attaches to the act rather than to income. It is the fiscal counterpart to several entries elsewhere in this artifact: property transfers registered under the land registration regime, company formation documents under the Companies Code, and above all successions and donations, whose tax treatment sits here rather than in the Code of Personal Status that governs the underlying inheritance shares — a division of labour between the two codes worth stating explicitly, because succession law and succession taxation are routinely conflated. (Added Run 1036.)
Key provisions
  • Part I — registration duties: which acts and transfers are subject to compulsory registration, the time limits for doing so, and the basis and rates for fixed, proportional and progressive duties
  • A dedicated section on donations and successions, including exemptions for certain legacies
  • Part II — stamp duties on documents, invoices and administrative formalities
  • Penalties for late registration or failure to register
  • Interaction with real-property transfers registered under the land-registration regime, making registration duty a practical gatekeeper to valid title transfer
  • Rates and exemptions are revised annually through the finance laws, so the operative figures must always be read against the current year's Finance Law rather than the 1993 base text
TaxCivilLand

Decree-Law No. 2022-79 of December 22, 2022Finance Law 2023

Enacted: December 22, 2022 | Published: JORT No. 141, December 23, 2022 | In force: January 1, 2023
Annual budget law, exceptionally issued as a presidential decree-law rather than an ordinary parliamentary statute because the Assembly of People's Representatives had not yet resumed full legislative activity following the December 2022 legislative elections. Set state expenditure at approximately TND 54 billion against TND 46.4 billion in revenue (deficit of approximately TND 7.5 billion). Introduced a real-estate wealth tax on individuals' property holdings worth TND 3 million or more, and temporary customs/VAT relief on EV charging equipment.

Law No. 2023-13 of December 11, 2023Finance Law 2024

Adopted by ARP: December 10, 2023 (116 for, 4 against, 26 abstentions) | Enacted: December 11, 2023 | Published: JORT, December 12, 2023 | Fiscal year: 2024
First annual Finance Law passed by the elected Assembly of People's Representatives since 2021. Key changes: Corporate Income Tax (CIT) increased from 15% to 20% for general companies effective January 1, 2024. Bank and insurance company CIT rate increased from 35% to 40%. New 2% conjunctural contribution on FY2023 taxable income for companies with turnover ≥ TND 20 million. Standard deduction for rental income raised from 20% to 25%. New 4-year CIT/IRPP exemption for enterprises filing investment declarations in 2024–2025. Raised import duties on solar panels from 10% to 30% effective January 1, 2025.

Law No. 2024-48 of December 9, 2024Finance Law 2025

Adopted by ARP/CNRD: December 2 & 4, 2024 | Enacted: December 9, 2024 | Published: JORT No. 149, December 10, 2024 | Fiscal year: 2025
Key measures: VAT reduced to 7% (from 13%) on low-voltage electricity for domestic consumers using ≤300 kWh/month. New conjunctural budget contribution (2% on FY2024 taxable income) for large companies (turnover ≥ TND 20M). Additional tax incentives for R&D-intensive companies. Community enterprises exempt from VAT under new suspension regime. Reinforces tax inspection powers for real estate valuations. Raises low pensions to TND 260 with roughly 7–7.5% increases for retirees, plus income-tax relief for pensioners, and begins phasing in mandatory electronic invoicing for an expanded range of service providers.

Law No. 2025-17 of December 12, 2025Finance Law 2026

Adopted: ARP December 4, 2025 (89 for/23 against/12 abstain); Council of Regions and Districts December 7, 2025 | Published: JORT No. 148, December 12, 2025 | Fiscal year: 2026
State budget sets revenues at TND 52.56 billion and expenditures at TND 63.575 billion, with tax receipts of TND 47.773 billion as the dominant funding source. Key measures: Art. 88 establishes a new annual "wealth tax" (impôt sur la fortune) on Tunisian-resident individuals' worldwide net patrimony (non-residents taxed only on Tunisian-situs assets, subject to double-tax treaties), at 0.5% on net wealth between TND 3–5 million and 1% above TND 5 million, assessed as of January 1 each year including minor children's assets held in trust; exempts the taxpayer's principal residence, professional assets recorded on a business balance sheet, home-savings and investment-savings accounts, life insurance/capitalization contracts, and non-utility vehicles rated ≤12 fiscal horsepower; declared electronically by end of June each year, first applying to the 2026 tax year; implementing guidance issued via Note Commune n°13 (DGELF, June 11, 2026) and n°15. Art. 56 expands mandatory e-invoicing from goods transactions to the entire services sector (~380,000 professionals affected), effective January 1, 2026 — invoices must be issued through the "El Fatoora" platform operated by Tunisie TradeNet (TTN) in the standardized TEIF/XML format and bear a qualified electronic signature issued by TunTrust/ANCE; penalties run 100–500 TND per invoice (capped at 50,000 TND/year) for invoices wrongly issued outside the electronic system where e-invoicing is mandatory, and 250–10,000 TND (doubled for repeat offenses) for non-compliant electronic invoices; Art. 55 "voiture pour chaque famille" (added Run 674): adopted as a standalone floor amendment on November 29, 2025 by a 131–2–1 vote (ahead of the law's own December 4, 2025 final passage), Art. 55 creates a one-time-per-family customs-duty exemption letting each Tunisia-resident family import or locally purchase, tax-free, a single passenger vehicle (new, or used and no more than eight years old); the benefit is non-combinable with the separate "voiture populaire" (popular car) fiscal regime and the vehicle cannot be resold within five years of acquisition. As of this run (August 1, 2026), the measure remains enacted but publicly acknowledged by the Finance Ministry as practically inapplicable eight months on: financing-source rules (whether via emigrants' foreign-currency remittances/donations or the existing tourist currency allowance), beneficiary-registration procedures, and priority criteria all remain undefined, alongside unresolved concern over the impact on Tunisia's foreign-currency reserves — corroborated across La Presse de Tunisie (November 29, 2025 and August 1, 2026 reports), webdo.tn, Le Quotidien, ilBoursa, Le Courrier de l'Atlas, and Business News (July 31, 2026), which independently agree on the article number, vote count, and eligibility conditions. state-subsidized interest bonuses (up to 3 points) on investment credits taken out in 2026–2027; salary and pension increases staged across 2026–2028 by decree; VAT exemption on packaging inputs for locally produced olive oil; VAT reduced to 7% on EV charging equipment and lithium battery manufacturing inputs; Art. 135 (added Run 130) authorizes farmers to import, possess, and use drones for agricultural purposes (field surveillance, irrigation optimization, phytosanitary treatment) — adopted as an additional article by ARP vote of 60–29–14 on December 4, 2025; see the Civil Aviation Code entry for the separate, still-pending general civil-drone regulatory framework. A parliamentary amendment adopted December 2, 2025 (69–17–17) additionally authorizes Tunisian residents to open and hold foreign-currency bank accounts for the first time — see Exchange Control Law entry. Tunisian financial-press sources (ilBoursa, InFirst Auditors) also report that the FY2024–2025 "conjunctural contribution" of 4% on taxable profit — previously limited to banks, financial establishments, and insurers (see the Finance Law 2024 entry) — was made permanent under this law and extended to telecommunications network operators and automobile dealers/concessionaires; this extension is corroborated by two independent secondary sources but the specific implementing article number could not be confirmed against a primary JORT text during this research pass, so it is noted here with that caveat. Art. 83 (added Run 109): revises tax and customs advantages for Tunisians residing abroad (TRE) — full customs-duty exemption on electric and plug-in-hybrid vehicle imports (VAT reduced to 7%, customs-service fees to 3%), a once-per-five-years equipment/materials import benefit (plus a separate single-truck allowance under tariff heading 8704) for TRE-backed investment, extension, or participation projects in Tunisia, and exemption from filing a Tunisian tax return for TRE who present a foreign tax-residency certificate — corroborated across Managers.tn, Tunisie Numérique, La Presse de Tunisie, and InFirst Auditors' commentary on the law; see also the National Council for Tunisians Residing Abroad entry (Nationality section). Pending amendment (added Run 118): the law's core assumptions have been overtaken by an oil-price shock — the budget was set on a reference Brent price of USD 63.3/barrel, versus actual prices approaching USD 110/barrel by June 2026 (each additional dollar costing roughly TND 160 million; a financing gap estimated at TND 5–8 billion by year-end). ARP Finance and Budget Commission president Maher Ktari stated on radio June 9, 2026 that recourse to a "loi de finances rectificative" (or, per some economists' competing proposal, a more flexible scenario-based "loi de finances d'urgence") in September or October 2026 is now "inevitable," while criticizing the Finance Ministry for not yet engaging the commission on the amendment's substance; a ministerial meeting to examine the discrepancy was scheduled for July 2026. No amending bill text had been filed with the ARP as of this run — corroborated across La Presse/allAfrica, Business News, Kapitalis, Tustex, and webdo, but treat as a forecast/committee-pressure signal, not yet a pending bill with a registry number. Update (Run 544): a July 25, 2026 La Presse report narrows the timeline first flagged at Run 118 — Ktari (also transliterated "El Kattari") stated the reference oil price had by then been exceeded by over USD 100/barrel (rather than the roughly USD 110/barrel figure cited in June), that each additional dollar per barrel now adds an estimated TND 164 million to compensation-fund expenditure (versus the TND ~160 million figure previously on file), and that a "loi de finances complémentaire" for 2026 could specifically be submitted to the ARP in October 2026 — narrower than the earlier "September or October" framing — with an urgent year-end financing need estimated at TND 5 billion. Still no bill text filed with the ARP as of this update; the underlying forecast is unchanged in substance, only refined in figures and timing. Also effective January 1, 2026 (added Run 120): this law repealed Article 45 of the Finance Law 2019 (Law No. 2018-56 of December 27, 2018), which had capped cash payments at TND 5,000 — payments above that threshold are again permitted — and introduced a new TND 230 registration tax on donation contracts (donations) between spouses, ascendants, and descendants. Tax amnesty (added Run 127): Art. 69 establishes a 2026 tax-debt regularization mechanism, operationalized by Tax Administration Circular No. 4/2026 ("JIBAYA"): control penalties, late-payment penalties, and prosecution fees are waived for taxpayers who settle principal tax debt (in full or via an installment plan) with the tax authority by June 30, 2026, and separately for unfiled, omitted, or rectificative declarations and unregistered acts/contracts subject to registration duties (Fiscal Procedures Code Arts. 81, 82 & 85) relating to obligations due before October 31, 2025, if regularized by September 30, 2026. Art. 36 implementing decree (added Run 327): a joint order of the Ministers of Social Affairs, Health, and Finance, published in JORT on or around July 14, 2026, sets the conditions and procedure for the monthly TND 130 allowance under Art. 36 for people with xeroderma pigmentosum ("enfants de la lune") toward the cost of UV-protection equipment (sun-filtering products, protective clothing), and a parallel monthly allowance for gluten-intolerant/celiac patients from low-income families toward the cost of gluten-free food products; both require an application with supporting medical documentation, reviewed by a dedicated medical commission — corroborated by La Presse de Tunisie, Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, and allAfrica (all July 14–15, 2026); the exact JORT issue number was not independently confirmed across these sources and is therefore omitted rather than guessed. Large-holdings restructuring fund (added Run 407): the law also creates a dedicated 2026-budget financing line for restructuring large agricultural exploitations exceeding 1,000 hectares, funded from revenue generated by regularizing previously undeclared agricultural wells (a measure carried over from the Finance Law 2025); however, the article number is disputed between the two independent sources found — Tunisie Numérique cites Art. 138 and frames it as an Office des Terres Domaniales fund targeting state-owned ("domanial") parcels in Sfax, Siliana, Béja, and Jendouba, while CKF's professional tax commentary cites Art. 97 and frames it more generally as covering "exploitations agricoles internationales" without naming specific governorates or the Office des Terres Domaniales. Both sources agree on the >1,000-hectare threshold and the restructuring purpose; neither could be cross-checked against primary JORT text during this pass, so the article number and precise scope are flagged here as unresolved rather than asserted, pending a future run's access to the primary text. Art. 107 implementation gap (added Run 655): Art. 107 provides for the regularization/integration of substitute teachers and instructors ("enseignants et instituteurs suppléants") who worked before 2006 and 2008, intended to be operationalized via Decree No. 21 of 2025 on the integration of substitute staff in primary, secondary, and tertiary education. Responding July 31, 2026 to a written parliamentary question from Deputy Fathi Mechri asking why this category's regularization had stalled, the Ministry of Education acknowledged the impasse: roughly 500 pre-2006/2008 substitute teachers were never entered into the ministry's own personnel database, which excluded them from Decree No. 21's integration mechanism entirely; the ministry stated it is now "conducting consultations" to identify the affected cases and regularize their status, without committing to a timeline. Confirmed via Tunisie Tribune and Business News, both July 31, 2026, cross-checked against each other; no implementing measure or revised timetable had been reported as of this run. Art. 115 SME-promoter regularization and Art. 23 employment-fund financing line (added Run 813): two further additional-article measures, absent from this entry despite predating it, were located during a fresh article-by-article audit. Art. 115, adopted December 4, 2025 by a 55–29–12 floor vote, regularizes the situation of small/medium-enterprise promoters who benefited from the Fonds de Développement et de Décentralisation Industrielle (Industrial Development and Decentralization Fund) more than 15 years ago without having sold their companies (applies to both new promoters and existing Fund beneficiaries): it waives penalties accrued since release of the fund contribution, conditional on the managing investment companies having exhausted legal disposal procedures; allows capital repayment over up to seven years, at 3% interest for new promoters or Central Bank tender-offer rates for existing ones; and sets December 31, 2026 as the final deadline for regularization requests. Art. 23 separately mobilizes a TND 15 million preferential-rate financing line from the Fonds National de l'Emploi (National Employment Fund), channeled through the Banque Tunisienne de Solidarité, prioritizing less-developed regions. Corroborated across Entreprises Magazine, African Manager, and domiciliation.tn, which independently agree on the article numbers, vote count, and eligibility terms. Art. 44 earmarked-external-loan projects (added Run 1012): Art. 44 suspends VAT, customs duties, consumption tax, and state-fund contributions on goods, services, and works purchased for development projects (infrastructure such as bridges, dams, roads, and hospitals, plus equipment acquisition, but not operational expenses like raw materials) financed by a foreign donation or an "earmarked external loan" under an international-cooperation agreement — extending to loans a customs/VAT-suspension regime previously available only to grant-financed projects. Eligible beneficiaries are state departments, local authorities (newly added for 2026), public institutions/state-owned enterprises, and management groups in public-interest industrial zones; each procurement contract requires prior VAT-suspension certification from the competent tax authority before purchase, applies to contracts concluded from January 1, 2026, with flexible transitional arrangements for contracts already underway. Clarified by DGELF Note Commune n°9 of 2026 (General Directorate of Tax Studies and Legislation), alongside the already-documented Note Commune n°13/n°15 (wealth tax) above — confirmed via Tunisie Numérique's dedicated explainer, cross-checked against the article's own donation/loan eligibility conditions. Arts. 46–47 low-emission vehicle & lithium-battery package (added Run 1032): this entry previously carried only an unattributed one-clause summary ("VAT reduced to 7% on EV charging equipment and lithium battery manufacturing inputs") with no article numbers or conditions; an article-by-article audit this run resolved both to specific provisions and recovered the eligibility thresholds that clause omitted. Art. 47 exempts plug-in-hybrid (PHEV) and fully-electric passenger vehicles outright from the consumption tax and from customs duties, and reduces their VAT to 7% (from the 19% standard rate). Critically — and absent from the prior summary — classic non-plug-in hybrids (HEV) do not receive the same treatment: they get only a 50% consumption-tax reduction, and only where the engine is petrol ≤1,700 cm³ or a goods-transport utility engine ≤2,100 cm³; above those displacements, or outside those engine types, HEVs are taxed as ordinary thermal vehicles at 19% VAT and standard customs duties. Art. 47 further cuts by 50% the taxes due on first registration in Tunisia of hybrid and electric vehicles, and the annual circulation tax (vignette) on fully-electric cars and motorcycles; used-vehicle transactions are excluded. EV charging-station equipment is set at a reduced 10% customs duty and 7% VAT. All Art. 47 benefits run through December 31, 2028. Art. 46 supports local battery manufacturing: industrial firms producing lithium batteries receive full customs-duty exemption and 7% VAT on imported components and raw materials, across seven specified tariff codes covering battery cells, connectors, and Battery Management System (BMS) electronics. A third element is reported by only one source (finco.tn), which attributes to Art. 45 an Energy Transition Fund mechanism subsidizing up to 3 percentage points of loan interest — conditional on the lending bank's margin not exceeding 3.5% — on Banque Tunisienne de Solidarité (BTS) financing for electric-vehicle purchases by taxi operators and driving schools, over 2026–2028; that article attribution is recorded here with the caveat that it could not be independently corroborated this run, consistent with this entry's existing practice for the Art. 97-vs-138 and 4%-conjunctural-contribution attributions above. Confirmed via finco.tn and WebManagerCenter (March 26, 2026), which independently agree on Arts. 46–47's substance, the rate structure, the cm³ thresholds, and the December 31, 2028 sunset; DGELF issued a general note setting out the package's application modalities. Distinct from — and separately combinable-or-not with — the Art. 83 TRE vehicle-import advantages and the Art. 55 "voiture pour chaque famille" exemption already documented above, which target importer status rather than powertrain type. A widely-reported "50,000 electric vehicles and 5,000 charging points by 2030" figure (webdo.tn) is a stated government policy target, not a statutory provision of this law, and is noted here as context rather than cited as enacted text.

Draft Finance Law 2027 (PLF 2027)Budget-Preparation Social Dialogue

Finance Ministry invited UGTT contribution: reported May 15, 2026 | UGTT transmitted formal proposals: ~July 1–2, 2026 | Ministry's registry office declined to formally receive the document: reported July 2–4, 2026 | First restricted ministerial council on PLF 2027 orientations: August 4, 2026
Tunisia's 2027 budget law remains at the pre-draft stage — no PLF 2027 bill text has been circulated publicly as of this pass, a genuine gap distinct from the still-pending Finance Law 2026 amendment discussed above. The Finance Ministry invited UGTT to contribute proposals for the 2027 budget in mid-May 2026; UGTT Secretary-General Slaheddine Selmi called the invitation a positive step but was explicitly skeptical it signaled a genuine return of social dialogue after months of rupture between the union and government (echoing his stance already documented in the Judicial Statute entry's ONAT-related coverage). UGTT's proposals, formally transmitted in early July 2026, include raising the fully tax-exempt income threshold from TND 5,000 to TND 7,000, revising the IRPP income-tax brackets to ease pressure on the upper-middle class, increasing public investment, rebalancing debt policy, and reviving budget-related social dialogue; the union separately criticized an "austerity orientation" it said risked public-service quality and cautioned against curbs on professional promotions. In early July 2026, the Ministry of Finance's own registry office declined to formally receive UGTT's proposal document, which Selmi characterized as a setback for recognition of the union's role as a social partner. No PLF 2027 draft text, committee referral, or vote had occurred as of this pass. (Added Run 481.) (Run 635 update): a second, parliamentary-committee-level track has separately begun alongside the government/UGTT dialogue above — per late-July 2026 reporting, ARP Finance and Budget Committee chair Maher Ktari had correspondence sent to the Assembly's Bureau proposing that parliamentary blocs be invited to submit preliminary article proposals for inclusion in the PLF 2027 text, ahead of any formal government bill. This remains a preparatory, pre-drafting step — no bill text, committee referral, or vote — consistent with this entry's existing "pre-draft, social-dialogue stage" characterization; the two tracks (executive/UGTT and now ARP-committee-level) have not yet been reported as converging on a single text. (Run 742 update): on August 4, 2026, the executive advanced to a third, government-internal track: Prime Minister Sarra Zaâfrani Zenzri presided over a first restricted ministerial council ("conseil ministériel restreint") dedicated to PLF 2027, at which Finance Minister Mechket Slama Khaldi presented a progress report on 2026 budget execution and the macroeconomic assumptions for 2027; the council set the draft's "grandes orientations" (major orientations) — consolidating food, water, energy, and pharmaceutical-supply sovereignty against external price volatility; strengthening social protection and reforming healthcare/social-protection systems and public-enterprise governance; reviving public and private investment, formalizing the informal sector, and prioritizing job creation for university graduates; and accelerating digital transition and renewable-energy deployment — explicitly framed as implementing the 2026–2030 Development Plan; confirmed via Business News and La Presse de Tunisie, cross-checked against each other. This remains an orientations-setting stage, not a bill text: no article numbers, committee referral, or vote yet exist, so the entry's "pre-draft" characterization is updated to reflect this newest step rather than superseded by it. (Run 1024 update): on August 19, 2026, the full Council of Ministers reviewed the 2027 budget project directly (a step beyond the August 4 restricted ministerial council), with officials citing 2.4% GDP growth for the first half of 2026 (attributed to cereals, olive oil, tourism, and the mechanical/electrical industries), unemployment easing from 15.3% to 14.9%, inflation described as "controlled," and foreign-currency reserves described as "satisfactory"; Zaâfrani Zenzri called for accelerating finalization of the budget project by prioritizing initiatives according to maturity and socio-economic impact. Still no specific tax measures, expenditure figures, or article-level detail disclosed, and no draft text yet filed with the ARP. Confirmed via L'Économiste Maghrébin (August 19, 2026). (Run 1033 update): this session's independent sweep corroborated the August 19 session across three further sources — Kapitalis/Anbaa Tounes, Tunis Now, and the Presidency of the Government's own pm.gov.tn conseils-ministériels listing — upgrading it from the single-sourced status above, and sharpened two points. First, terminology: the session's formal object as stated in the Arabic record was the projet de Budget Économique 2027 (مشروع الميزان الاقتصادي لسنة 2027) — the annual economic budget, a macroeconomic planning and forecasting instrument that accompanies and precedes the finance bill, rather than the PLF 2027 itself; the two are related but formally distinct documents, and earlier reporting (and this entry's own prior wording) conflated them. Second, figures: the growth data presented were more granular than the 2.4% half-year figure recorded above — GDP grew 2.3% year-on-year in Q2 2026 and 1.4% quarter-on-quarter, aggregating to the 2.4% H1 2026 figure already on file. The council stressed alignment of the economic budget with the 2026–2030 Development Plan and with the forthcoming 2027 finance and budget bills. This remains an orientations-and-forecasting stage: still no PLF 2027 bill text, article numbers, committee referral, or vote.

🏦 Financial & Banking Law

Banking Law — Law No. 2016-48 of July 11, 2016

Enacted: July 11, 2016 | In force: 2016 | Replaced: Law No. 2001-65
Regulates credit institutions, banking activities, and financial services in Tunisia. Establishes licensing requirements for banks and microfinance institutions. Strengthens the supervisory powers of the Central Bank of Tunisia (BCT). Introduces new categories of banking licenses and regulates Islamic banking activities.
Key provisions
  • Licensing: exclusive reserve of banking activities for licensed credit institutions
  • Capital requirements: minimum TND 25 million for universal banks
  • Supervision: BCT has powers to inspect, sanction, and revoke licenses
  • Islamic banking: participatory banks regulated under specific provisions
  • Deposit guarantee: Art. 149 creates the Fonds de Garantie des Dépôts Bancaires (FGDB)
  • Resolution: framework for failing banks established
Financial

Central Bank Law — Law No. 2016-35 of April 25, 2016

Enacted: April 25, 2016 | In force: 2016 | Replaced: Law No. 58-90 (1958) | Amended: 2024, 2026
Establishes the Banque Centrale de Tunisie (BCT) as an independent institution responsible for monetary policy, exchange rate management, payment systems oversight, and banking supervision. Grants operational independence to the BCT Governor. Article 25 originally prohibited direct central bank financing of the state budget deficit. This prohibition was exceptionally suspended by Law No. 2024-10 of February 7, 2024 (JORT No. 2024-021, adopted by the ARP 92 votes to 41), authorizing the BCT to lend the Treasury up to TND 7,000 million, interest-free, repayable over 10 years with a 3-year grace period, to help cover the 2024 budget deficit — a measure Carnegie Endowment and TIMEP analyses describe as eroding central bank independence. Update (Run 40): Finance Law 2026 Art. 12 authorizes a further, separate interest-free BCT advance to the Treasury of up to TND 11,000 million (up from TND 7,000 million in 2024/2025). Independent of fiscal financing, the BCT cut its policy rate in three steps from 8% to 7% between late 2025 and March 2026 (held at 7% at its March 30, 2026 meeting); a March 26, 2026 circular (No. 2026-4) newly restricts bank financing of "non-priority" imports, generally requiring 100% importer-funded deposits; and in January 2026 the BCT granted OFT Tunisie (Ooredoo's fintech arm) a definitive payment-institution license (JORT No. 65/2026). Update (Run 191): on July 7–8, 2026 the BCT signed an expanded balance-of-payments support facility with the Arab Monetary Fund worth US$312 million (76.7 billion Arab accounting dinars), disbursed in three tranches over a seven-year maturity (La Presse de Tunisie, Tustex). Update (Run 706): the BCT's Board of Directors held its policy rate at 7% for a second consecutive meeting on July 29, 2026, citing persistent underlying-inflation risk and a widening current-account deficit driven by the energy import bill — confirmed via La Presse de Tunisie, Kapitalis, Managers.tn, businessnews.com.tn, L'Économiste Maghrébin, webdo.tn, and Challenges.tn, all independently reporting the same figure and rationale. Update (Run 760): two further BCT circulars, previously undocumented, extend the same sub-decree regulatory layer as the March 2026 non-priority-imports circular above. Circular No. 2026-02 of January 23, 2026 tightens AML/CFT obligations on licensed manual currency exchange bureaus: systematic client and beneficial-owner identification (even for small transactions), ten-year record retention, sanctions-list screening, a designated CTAF correspondent for suspicious-activity reports filed via the goAML platform, and disciplinary sanctions up to permanent authorization withdrawal for non-compliance (confirmed via Business News, Managers.tn, Tustex, and La Presse de Tunisie). Circular No. 2026-05 of April 24, 2026 sets the operating conditions and a 25-institution roster for the Plateforme Électronique Unique des Chèques (unified electronic check platform), the centralized clearance system underpinning the 2024 bad-cheque reform's digital-verification mechanism (confirmed via Managers.tn, La Presse de Tunisie, and allAfrica). A third, later BCT circular (July 21, 2026, on school-registration digital-payment readiness for banks, payment institutions, and La Poste) was investigated but not added: two independent sources (Managers.tn, THD.tn) confirm its date, addressees, and content, but neither reports its circular number, so it is withheld pending a citable number rather than risk an unverified reference. Update (Run 992): a fourth, earlier BCT circular in this same numbering sequence, previously undocumented, was found while re-checking BCT circular coverage: Circular No. 2026-3 of January 29, 2026 sets prudential conditions on bank and financial-establishment dividend distributions from FY2025 profits — a 35% payout cap for institutions holding a solvency ratio at least 2.5 points above the regulatory minimum, a higher cap available only with an additional 2.5-point Tier 1 buffer and prior BCT authorization, and mandatory prior BCT authorization for any institution that failed capital-adequacy standards at FY2025 year-end or drew auditor reservations on its financial statements, with authorization requests due at least fifteen days before the institution's ordinary general assembly (confirmed via Managers.tn, cross-checked against the BCT's own sequential circular numbering alongside No. 2026-02, No. 2026-4, and No. 2026-05 already on file). Update (Run 1005): a fifth BCT circular in this sequence, previously undocumented, was found while re-sweeping BCT circular activity: Circular No. 2026-132 of May 5, 2026 creates "TUNPAY," a mandatory unified national visual label/certification for mobile electronic wallets, imposed on all licensed mobile-payment issuers (banks, La Poste Tunisienne, and non-bank payment establishments), developed jointly with Société Monétique Tunisie (SMT), which manages Tunisia's national mobile-payment switching infrastructure — intended to unify the fragmented mobile-wallet ecosystem's visual identity and signal BCT-validated security wherever the mark appears, amid continued growth in Tunisian digital payments (BCT Bulletin No. 16: 477,000 active e-wallets in Q1 2026, up 67.1% year-on-year) (confirmed via La Presse de Tunisie, Business News, Challenges.tn, Managers.tn, Gnet News, and allAfrica, all independently reporting the same circular number and date). Update (Run 1006): a sixth BCT circular in this sequence, previously undocumented, was found while re-sweeping BCT circular activity: Circular No. 2026-7 of August 18, 2026 revises, for the first time since 1987, the per-hectare bank-financing ceilings and repayment deadlines for seasonal credits to cereal and forage-crop growers (amending Circular No. 47 of December 23, 1987), differentiating by crop, agro-climatic zone, and irrigation status: hard wheat/soft wheat/legumes at TND 1,415/ha (first rainfed zone), TND 1,175/ha (second rainfed zone), or TND 1,930/ha (irrigated), all due August 31; barley at TND 940/ha (first rainfed zone), TND 890/ha (second rainfed zone), or TND 350/ha (third rainfed zone), also due August 31; and forage crops at TND 1,030/ha (winter, rainfed, due August 31) or TND 1,260/ha (summer, irrigated, due September 30) — these are maximum thresholds of bank intervention, with final loan amounts still set per bank assessment of planted area, farm size, and projected yields. Distinct from the separate agricultural-debt regularization law (Law No. 2026-5), which reschedules existing non-performing loans rather than setting new seasonal-credit ceilings. Confirmed via Le Temps News/L'Économiste Maghrébin and La Presse de Tunisie (both August 18, 2026), cross-checked against each other.

Enacted: March 9, 1992 (JORT No. 17 of March 17, 1992) | In force: 1992 | Amended: 1997, 2002, 2008, 2014
Governs all insurance and reinsurance activities in Tunisia. (Added Run 139) Distinct from that pending cap-raising bill, the underlying Fonds de Garantie des Victimes des Accidents de la Circulation (Traffic Accident Victims Guarantee Fund) — created within this Code (Title V, Ch. III, Arts. 172–176, added by Law No. 2005-86 of August 15, 2005) to compensate accident victims or heirs when the at-fault driver is unknown, uninsured, or coverage is void/suspended — was itself restructured by Article 18 of Finance Law 2025 (Law No. 2024-48): effective January 1, 2025, Insurance Code Arts. 172 and 174–176 were repealed and the fund was converted into a special Treasury account administered by the ministry overseeing state domains, funded by a 0.2% levy on insurers' net motor-liability premiums plus a 2% levy on insureds' premiums (collected monthly alongside the unified insurance tax), with continuing subrogation rights against at-fault parties. Deposit Guarantee Fund — Art. 149 of Law No. 2016-48 of July 11, 2016Fonds de Garantie des Dépôts Bancaires (FGDB) (Run 172 correction)

Founding law: July 11, 2016 (Art. 149) | Implementing decree: No. 2017-268 of February 1, 2017 | Replaced: Law No. 2006-19 of May 2, 2006
Correction: this entry previously cited the fund's 2006 predecessor (Law No. 2006-19, "FGTD," TND 20,000 cap) as still governing; independent verification against the fund's own official site (fgdb.gov.tn) confirms the deposit-guarantee scheme was re-created under Article 149 of the 2016 Banking Law, not merely amended, as the Fonds de Garantie des Dépôts Bancaires (FGDB) — a public-interest establishment with legal personality, capitalized at TND 5 million and jointly subscribed by the Tunisian State and the Central Bank (BCT). Administered under BCT supervision; covers savings banks and electronic-money institutions per the 2016 Banking Law's broadened scope.

Law No. 76-18 of January 21, 1976 (as amended by Finance Law 2026)Exchange Control Law

Enacted: January 21, 1976 | Amended: multiple times, most recently Finance Law 2026 (Dec. 2025)
Governs foreign exchange transactions, capital movements, and currency restrictions; historically prohibited Tunisian residents from holding foreign currency. A parliamentary amendment to the 2026 Finance Law, adopted December 2, 2025 (69 for/17 against/17 abstain) — after a near-identical proposal was narrowly rejected in November 2024 (51 against/48 for) — for the first time authorizes resident individuals and businesses to open and fund foreign-currency bank accounts, ending a 50-year-old restriction. This 2025 amendment is a stopgap pending the wholesale replacement of the 1976 law by the new Foreign Exchange Code (Draft Law 115/2025) — see separate entry.

Draft Law No. 115/2025 (pending)New Foreign Exchange Code (Code des Changes)

Registered with ARP: 2025 | Finance & Budget Committee hearings: ~90% complete as of June 17, 2026 | Committee article-by-article vote scheduled: first post-recess session, October 2026 | Status: not enacted as of August 20, 2026
Comprehensive replacement of the 1976 Exchange Control Law and its implementing decrees — the first wholesale rewrite of Tunisia's foreign-exchange regime in 50 years, composed of 91 articles. Would broaden the definition of foreign exchange operations, formally recognize crypto-assets, create a new "licensed exchange operator" status, authorize private exchange offices for the first time, enable a regulated framework for international digital payment platforms, and guarantee immediate and unrestricted repatriation of profits, dividends, and asset-sale proceeds. The Finance and Budget Committee has held extensive hearings (including with CONECT, which submitted 41 proposed amendments, plus the Ministry of Finance and the Directorate General of Customs) and as of mid-June 2026 was weighing whether to proceed to a committee vote without the Central Bank of Tunisia's opinion, after the BCT failed to respond to repeated hearing requests. Update (Run 36): that posture has since softened rather than hardened — a June 23, 2026 report on the committee's continuing work (alongside separate STEG financing-agreement hearings) has Ktari instead calling continued BCT consultation "essential" before final adoption, with the BCT still not having formally responded as of that date; the committee's earlier openness to voting around the BCT's silence should therefore be read as superseded by this more recent, more cautious stance, not as the operative plan. Economists heard by the committee estimated the reform could add 1–1.5 percentage points to GDP growth. Committee chair Maher Ktari has reiterated parliament's aim to pass the bill before the summer 2026 recess, with additional listening sessions continuing into late June before transmission to plenary — the committee also heard the Chamber of Commerce (mixed chambers) on May 14, 2026. However, a July 1, 2026 report on the separate Development Plan debate notes MPs were still publicly urging "acceleration" of this Code's adoption that same day, indicating the bill had not yet passed and Ktari's summer-recess target should be treated as unconfirmed rather than on track. A related but separate track — Bill No. 58/2025 on amnesty for past exchange violations (see entry below) — was sent back to committee in April 2026 with reporting suggesting the two efforts are being harmonized rather than passed separately. Update (Run 70): a July 3, 2026 IACE report named this reform Tunisia's single highest enactment priority among sixteen pending economic reforms, arguing the underlying 1976 exchange-control framework is obsolete against digital-economy payment flows and contemporary cross-border finance; unlike the Investment, Water, Environment, and Hydrocarbons codes IACE separately flagged as stalled pre-ARP transmission (see those entries), this Code is already before the Finance and Budget Committee, so IACE's "priority" framing here concerns urgency of a floor vote rather than executive-stage delay. Update (Run 1034): the summer-recess target flagged above as "unconfirmed" is now definitively missed, and the committee has set a concrete post-recess plan. On July 23, 2026, committee chair Maher Ktari publicly rejected a proposal to defer the Code to January 2027, saying officials had already assured parliament the bill would be before it in January 2026 and that "waiting another year is unreasonable" since "state credibility requires honoring commitments made by the executive"; he announced that the Finance and Budget Committee's first session after the parliamentary recess, in October 2026, will be devoted to the Foreign Exchange Code, and that it will proceed to article-by-article committee voting with or without the Central Bank's opinion — "if we receive the Central Bank's response, excellent, but if not, we will proceed to vote on the Foreign Exchange Code article-by-article within the committee." This restores the vote-around-BCT-silence posture that the Run 36 update had recorded as softened, and should be read as superseding it. On August 6, 2026, Ktari escalated further, stating the bill had by then been blocked for roughly eight months solely because the BCT governor had not transmitted the committee's repeatedly-requested observations, that "communication with parliament is mandatory given the code's critical importance to the national economy," and appealing directly to President Kaïs Saïed to intervene with the governor. Both statements verified by direct fetch of the Tunisie Numérique (Arabic) reports of July 23 and August 6, 2026, with the article-by-article-voting posture independently corroborated by African Manager and Kashf Media. No committee vote, plenary transmission, or BCT response had occurred as of August 20, 2026, with the ARP in recess since its fourth ordinary session closed July 29, 2026.

Bill No. 58/2025 (pending)Regularization ("Amnesty") of Past Exchange-Control Violations

Filed: late May 2025 (Independent National Bloc) | Plenary examination: April 14, 2026 | Sent back to Finance Committee: April 14, 2026 (54 for / 3 against / 2 abstain) | Status: not yet enacted as of July 2026
Distinct from the wholesale Foreign Exchange Code rewrite (Draft Law No. 115/2025, above), this narrower bill would let residents holding undeclared foreign-currency assets or funds held abroad regularize their situation through repatriation and a sworn declaration, in exchange for a one-off "liberatory contribution": reported rates of 15% of value for foreign real estate/financial assets, and 7% of the dinar-equivalent for repatriated sums (reduced to 4% if fully converted to dinars). Payment would extinguish both the underlying exchange-control and tax violations. Brought to a plenary vote on April 14, 2026 after a first committee pass, but following hours of debate and a wave of proposed amendments, deputies voted 54–3–2 to send the text back to the Finance Committee for further work rather than adopting or rejecting it outright — some press coverage described this as the amnesty being "postponed indefinitely," though the bill was not formally withdrawn or defeated. Critics (including deputy Abderrazak Houas) argued the draft was insufficiently rigorous on the source-of-funds and money-laundering questions raised by an amnesty of this kind. Reporting since December 2025 indicates the Finance Committee is now working to harmonize this amnesty mechanism with the broader Foreign Exchange Code reform and Tunisia's anti-money-laundering framework rather than advancing it as a standalone text — watch the Foreign Exchange Code entry above for developments, as the two efforts may ultimately merge.

Draft Law No. 023/2024 (pending)Combating Financial Exclusion

Filed by the Presidency of the Republic: March 6, 2024 | Referred to Finance & Budget Committee: March 7, 2024 | Committee hearing: June 26, 2026 | Status: not yet enacted as of July 2, 2026
A government-drafted bill to overhaul Tunisia's financial-inclusion framework, developed as the legislative centerpiece of the National Financial Inclusion Strategy. Motivated by a Ministry of Finance diagnosis showing only around 60% of Tunisians over 18 interact with a bank or postal financial institution at all, with far lower uptake of modern financial services (roughly 17% use non-cash payment methods, 3% use mobile financial services, under 2% hold voluntary insurance). Structured around four axes: expanding access to and use of financial services; consolidating sectoral oversight; consumer protection and financial-literacy promotion; and rationalizing financial flows. Correction (Run 43): the "n° 38/2026 and n° 39/2026" numbering attributed to this bill in a prior run was in error — those numbers in fact belong to the unrelated STEG IBRD loan-guarantee bills approved by the same committee two days after this bill's hearing (see standalone entry above). This bill's number is confirmed via the ARP's own official bill registry (arp.tn/loi/project/4016) as Draft Law No. 023/2024 ("مشروع قانون عدد 023 لسنة 2024 يتعلّق بمكافحة الإقصاء المالي"), filed by the Presidency of the Republic on March 6, 2024 and pending in committee since March 7, 2024 — the June 26, 2026 session was a committee hearing on this long-pending 2024 bill, not a newly filed 2026 text. The Finance and Budget Committee hearing was chaired by committee president Maher Ktari with vice-president Dhafer Sghiri and deputies including Amal Moueddeb, Mohamed Ben Hassine, Mustapha Boubakri, and Mohamed Zied El Maher, with officials from the Ministry of Finance, the Microfinance Supervision Authority, and the General Insurance Committee. A central sticking point has been a proposed "banque postale" (postal bank) — now identified as a related but formally separate proposition de loi, n° 82/2025, filed by 21 deputies, which would offer expanded banking-type services through La Poste Tunisienne's network under Central Bank of Tunisia supervision without converting La Poste into a full bank; on June 28, 2026 the Ministry of Finance publicly "temporized" on this specific proposal, describing it as a "strategic option" requiring further legal and economic study and broader stakeholder consensus. Distinct from the pre-existing Microfinance Law (2011) and Banking Law (2016), which the bill would supplement rather than replace. Not yet put to a committee vote or enacted as of this update.

Law No. 2005-96 of October 18, 2005Strengthening the Security of Financial Relations (Sécurité des Relations Financières)

Enacted: October 18, 2005 | Amends: Law No. 94-117, the Companies Code and related texts | Further amended by Law No. 2019-47 | In force as amended
Tunisia's corporate-governance and audit-integrity statute, referenced in this artifact only as one of the laws amending the Financial Market Law and never documented in its own right. It is the country's response to the early-2000s international accounting scandals, and it operates on three fronts. First, audit: it extends the mandatory appointment of a commissaire aux comptes to a wider class of commercial companies and imposes rotation and independence rules, complementing the chartered accountants and accounting profession entries. Second, periodic disclosure: listed issuers must file semi-annual interim financial statements together with the full auditor's report with the CMF within two months of the half-year end, and publish them in the CMF bulletin and a Tunis daily. Third, related-party dealings and audit committees: it strengthens disclosure of related-party transactions and the requirement for a permanent audit committee. It is widely criticised for lacking a dedicated enforcement body — a recurring pattern in Tunisian financial regulation, where obligations are stated in statute while supervision rests on the CMF's general powers. (Added Run 1036.)

Law No. 88-108 of August 18, 1988Chartered Accountants (Experts Comptables) (Run 54 addition)

Enacted: August 18, 1988 | Published: JORT No. 56, August 26, 1988 | Superseded: Law No. 82-62 of June 30, 1982
"Portant refonte de la législation relative à la profession d'expert comptable" — creates the Ordre des Experts Comptables de Tunisie (OECT) as a body with legal personality, under Ministry of Finance supervision. Defines the "expert comptable" profession: organizing, verifying, and certifying company accounts, and — subject to conditions — acting as statutory auditor (commissaire aux comptes) referenced in the Companies Code entry above. Sets diploma/qualification requirements for admission to the Order and its disciplinary framework. Law No. 2002-16 of February 4, 2002Accounting Profession (Compagnie des Comptables de Tunisie) (Run 54 addition)

Enacted: February 4, 2002 | Amended: Law No. 2004-88 of December 31, 2004 (Art. 28 transitional registration deadlines)
"Portant organisation de la profession des comptables" — creates the Compagnie des Comptables de Tunisie, a distinct civil-law professional body (Art. 4) for non-expert accountants performing bookkeeping and general accounting services, who may also perform statutory-auditor functions for commercial companies under specified conditions. Complements, without merging into, the chartered-accountants' Order (OECT, Law No. 88-108, above). Wholly absent from this artifact despite 53 prior research runs.

Draft Text No. 113/2020 (unpromulgated)Household Over-Indebtedness (Surendettement) (Run 83 addition)

Adopted in principle: Council of Ministers, December 2020 | Status: still unpromulgated as of March 2026 (5+ years)
A wholly new standalone gap identified via a March 2026 IACE report ("Le surendettement des ménages : une urgence nationale," March 27, 2026) and corroborated by L'Economiste Maghrébin and WebManagerCenter (both March 27–28, 2026): Tunisia has no legal definition of household over-indebtedness, no dedicated observatory, no centralized credit bureau, and no specialized adjudication commission, despite household debt reaching roughly TND 32 billion — described as a "critical over-indebtedness threshold." Draft text n°113/2020, adopted in principle by a Council of Ministers in December 2020, would define over-indebtedness as the debtor's manifest inability to honor non-professional debts within a reasonable time, coupled with a good-faith criterion, but remains unpromulgated more than five years later. IACE's 2026 proposal builds on this dormant text with binding prudential debt-to-income ratio caps (40% for consumer credit, 50% for mortgage credit), a per-governorate over-indebtedness commission offering a seven-year recovery plan, partial debt write-off with a reinsertion commitment, or total write-off with a three-year credit ban, plus a national observatory (TND 500,000 first-year budget) and a centralized credit bureau (TND 7 million over three years, funded 50% BCT / 30% international donors / 20% banking sector). None of this has reached the ARP as a filed bill as of this run — the gap is the absence of any consumer-over-indebtedness framework, not a pending-bill status to track under the standard watchlist.
FinancialSocialDraft

Decree No. 2026-148Conditions for "Crédits d'Honneur" (Honor Loans) (Run 547 addition; sharpened Run 569)

Dated: July 23, 2026 | Published: JORT, July 2026 | Legal basis: Article 412 ter (new) of the Commercial Code
Implementing decree fixing the conditions and criteria for granting small, interest-free "crédit d'honneur" financing under Article 412 ter of the Commercial Code, which requires each bank to open a dedicated "compte de la ligne de financement d'honneur" funded from a share of its profits. Ceilings are tiered by beneficiary rather than a flat cap: TND 5,000 for individuals, TND 10,000 for micro-project holders, and TND 25,000 for SMEs and community-based societies (sociétés communautaires) — micro-projects defined as total investment not exceeding TND 150,000, SMEs as TND 150,000–15 million. Loans are interest-free and require no collateral/guarantees, carry a maximum 2-year repayment term with an optional grace period of up to 6 months, and banks must process applications within 10 business banking days and give written reasons for any rejection. At least 50% of each bank's available honor-financing funds must go to SMEs and community societies. Bank auditors (commissaires aux comptes) must file an annual compliance report with the Ministry of Finance and the Central Bank of Tunisia within 3 months, with BCT holding enforcement authority. Complements the pre-existing Microfinance Law (2011) framework by creating a bank-funded, guarantee-free small-credit channel rather than relying solely on licensed microfinance institutions. A wholly new gap identified via a July 25, 2026 La Presse de Tunisie report and independently corroborated by Business News and allAfrica the same day; no prior run had captured Article 412 ter or its implementing decree. (Run 569 update, July 27, 2026) A same-day Managers.tn JORT recap supplied the tiered ceilings, processing deadline, grace period, 50% SME/community-society set-aside, and auditor-reporting mechanics above, replacing the earlier flat-TND-25,000 approximation. (Run 636 update, July 31, 2026): per a July 30, 2026 Business News report, fiscal expert Mohamed Salah Ayari estimates the resulting bank-funded envelope could reach approximately TND 120 million, based on banks' 2025 profits and the 8%-of-profits allocation rule — the first aggregate sizing estimate found for this financing line; also independently reconfirmed (Business News, La Presse de Tunisie, allAfrica, Réalités Magazine, webdo, all July 30, 2026) that the repayment term is 2 years with up to a 6-month grace period, as already stated above — a separate July-30 search snippet suggesting a contradictory "6-year" repayment term in decree Article 3 did not survive verification against these direct outlet reports and is not corroborated by any primary source.

Law No. 99-64 of July 15, 1999Repression of Usury / Excessive Interest Rates (Run 669 addition)

Enacted: July 15, 1999 | Implementing decree: No. 2000-462 of February 21, 2000 | Latest rate order: JORT of July 31, 2026 (H2 2026)
A wholly new gap identified this run: despite the crédit d'honneur decree above and multiple bank-financing entries across this artifact citing semi-annual BCT interest-rate ceilings, the underlying statute creating that mechanism had never itself been documented. Article 1 defines an "excessive interest rate" loan as any conventional loan whose effective global rate exceeds, at the time granted, the prior semester's average effective rate charged by banks/financial institutions for the same category of credit by more than one-fifth (20%). The Central Bank of Tunisia (BCT) computes that average effective rate every six months per credit category; the Finance Minister then publishes the resulting excessive-rate ceilings in JORT for application the following semester. The order published in JORT on July 31, 2026 set the H2 2026 thresholds: consumer credit at an 11.23% average / 13.47% excessive-rate ceiling, and movable/immovable leasing at 13.37% average / 16.04% ceiling — directly relevant to this artifact's own Financial Leasing Law entry, which has never cited a specific rate figure. Confirmed via Jurisite Tunisie's hosted text of the law and Business News's July 31, 2026 rate-order report, cross-checked against each other. A 2017 reform bill (Projet de loi n°39/2017, tracked by Marsad/Al Bawsala) proposed decriminalizing the offense (a doubled fine replacing imprisonment), letting government decree set the excess margin per financing category, and adapting the law to Islamic-finance products — but does not appear to have been enacted: Article 5's original criminal penalty below remains the operative sanction as of this run.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1: an excessive-interest loan is one exceeding, by more than one-fifth, the prior semester's BCT-computed average effective rate for the same category of credit
  • BCT sets the average effective rate semi-annually per credit category; the Finance Minister publishes the resulting excessive-rate ceilings in JORT for the following semester
  • Art. 5: banks/financial establishments granting an excessive-rate loan face 6 months' imprisonment and a fine of TND 3,000–10,000, or either penalty alone
  • Implementing Decree No. 2000-462 of February 21, 2000 sets the calculation methodology and credit-category breakdown
  • A 2017 reform bill (decriminalization, decree-set margins, Islamic-finance adaptation) does not appear to have been enacted
