Code des Organismes de Placement Collectif — Law No. 2001-83 of July 24, 2001Collective Investment Schemes (OPCVM, SICAV, FCP, FCPR, FIS)

Enacted: July 24, 2001 | Adopted by the Chamber of Deputies: July 10, 2001 | Published: JORT n° 59 of July 24, 2001, pp. 1790–1796 | In force, extensively amended
A subject-matter gap closed this run: the artifact documented the Financial Market Law and the microfinance and leasing regimes, but had no entry for the statute governing Tunisia's collective investment vehicles — the legal form through which most retail and institutional savings are pooled. The Code des organismes de placement collectif (COPC) is a single code covering all such vehicles. Its introductory article defines "organismes de placement collectif" as comprising (a) OPCVM — the SICAV (an open-ended investment company) and the FCP (a contractual fund) — and (b) fonds communs de créances, the securitisation vehicle documented in its own entry below. Structure: Titre I (Arts. 2–34) OPCVM; Titre II (Arts. 35–48) FCC; Titre III (Arts. 49–56) common and penal provisions. Article 2 of the promulgating law repealed and replaced Titre II of Law No. 88-92 of August 2, 1988 (sociétés d'investissement) and Titre I of Law No. 92-107 of November 16, 1992, and Article 3 rewrote Articles 1 and 2 of Law No. 88-92. Confirmed by direct reading of JurisiteTunisie's full text cross-checked against the Conseil du Marché Financier's own consolidated French edition. Data-quality note: the CMF's consolidated PDF is internally inconsistent on one amendment, citing in one footnote "la loi n° 2019-4 du 29 mai 2019" and elsewhere "loi n° 2019-47 du 29 mai 2019, art. 17"; the correct number is Law No. 2019-47 of May 29, 2019, verified against the official text hosted by IGPPP (JORT n° 47 of June 11, 2019, p. 1644), whose Articles 16–17 amend the COPC. "2019-4" is a typographical error in the CMF edition and should not be propagated. In force as of this run and listed on the CMF's current Textes de référence page; no repeal or recodification located.
Key provisions
  • Art. 2: a SICAV is a société anonyme whose sole object is managing a securities portfolio, its resources limited to its own funds
  • Art. 3: SICAV minimum capital 1,000,000 TND at formation; capital always equals net asset value less distributable sums; a 500,000 TND floor below which redemptions are barred; mandatory dissolution if capital stays below 1,000,000 TND for 90 days
  • Arts. 10 & 12: the FCP is a co-ownership without legal personality (indivision and société en participation rules disapplied), requiring 100,000 TND raised at formation
  • Art. 25: subscriptions and redemptions at the valeur liquidative (net assets ÷ units), plus or minus entry and exit commissions; Art. 26: distributing OPCVM must pay distributable sums within 5 months of year-end
  • Art. 28: assets must be held by a single depositary (a bank or a legal person on a list fixed by arrêté of the Minister of Finance); the manager and depositary functions cannot be combined, and the depositary remains liable even where it sub-delegates custody
  • Art. 29: concentration ratios — no more than 10% of a single class of securities of one issuer, and no more than 10% of assets in securities issued or guaranteed by one issuer (State, local-authority and State-guaranteed paper excepted)
  • Art. 31: a société de gestion must be an SA whose sole object is managing OPCVM portfolios, with capital ≥ 100,000 TND and permanently ≥ 0.5% of assets under management until capital reaches 500,000 TND
  • Arts. 32–33: CMF agrément required to constitute or liquidate an OPCVM and to constitute a management company; the CMF must decide within 3 months; agrément withdrawn if unused for 12 months
  • Art. 51: the statutory auditor must be an expert-comptable on the OECT roll, appointed for 3 financial years, with a direct whistle-blowing duty to the CMF; the CMF may bar a defaulting auditor for up to 3 years or permanently, with appeal to the Tunis Court of Appeal within 20 days
  • Arts. 53–56: criminal penalties (imprisonment and fines) for the code's principal breaches
  • Amendment chain: Law No. 2005-58 of July 18, 2005 (fonds d'amorçage); Law No. 2005-96 of October 18, 2005; Law No. 2005-105 of December 19, 2005 (inserting Chapitre II bis on fonds communs de placement à risque, Art. 22 bis et seq.); Law No. 2008-78 of December 22, 2008; Decree-Law No. 2011-99 of October 21, 2011 (rewriting Arts. 22 bis and 22 quater, adding Arts. 22 quinquies to 22 octodecies, including the "agrément allégé"); Law No. 2019-47 of May 29, 2019, Arts. 16–17 (rewriting Art. 22 ter and adding Art. 22 novodecies creating the fonds d'investissement spécialisés for "investisseurs avertis")
  • Implementing texts: Décret No. 2001-2278 of September 25, 2001 (applying Arts. 15, 29, 35, 36 and 37); Décrets No. 2012-890 and 2012-891 of July 24, 2012; Décret No. 2012-2945 of November 27, 2012; BCT Circulaire No. 2021-09 of December 30, 2021 (foreign-currency subscription by resident "investisseurs avertis")
Run 1036 update — citation verified, prior run confirmed exactly. The reference recorded at Run 1035 as needing verification is correct as it stood: JORT n° 59 of Tuesday, July 24, 2001 (144th year), the law and the annexed Code running pp. 1790–1796 (p. 1797 begins the following section). Verified against the JORT facsimile. Recorded here because a confirmed citation is as useful to a future run as a corrected one, and saves the check being repeated.
FinancialCommercial

Securitisation — Fonds Communs de Créances (COPC Titre II, Arts. 35–48)Titrisation: the Tunisian Securitisation Regime

Statutory basis: Law No. 2001-83 of July 24, 2001 (Code des organismes de placement collectif), Titre II | Implementing: Décret No. 2001-2278 of September 25, 2001, as amended by Décret No. 2006-1248 of May 2, 2006 | In force; effectively dormant in practice
Tunisia has no separate securitisation statute. The entire regime is Titre II of the Code des organismes de placement collectif, Articles 35 to 48, which creates the fonds commun de créances (FCC) as a bankruptcy-remote co-ownership vehicle. It is documented here as its own entry because securitisation is a distinct legal subject from collective portfolio management, and because two persistent errors circulate about it. First correction: there is no "2017 securitisation reform law." No securitisation reform statute has been enacted in 2017 or since; the 2017 texts in this space are Décrets gouvernementaux No. 2017-1332 and No. 2017-1333 of December 6, 2017 (JORT n° 99 of December 12, 2017), which govern the constitution, early liquidation and management of a fonds commun de sukuk under the Sukuk Law — a different vehicle under a different statute, and the likely origin of the confusion. Second correction: Tunisia has no covered-bond regime. A dedicated search across the CMF's reference-text lists, the BVMT, the BCT, the Commercial Companies Code bond chapter and Laws No. 92-107 and No. 2000-35, in French and Arabic (السندات العقارية), found no "obligations foncières" statute; the CMF's bond-related reference text is Décret No. 2005-3018 of November 21, 2005 (Art. 329 CSC, emprunts obligataires), governing ordinary unsecured corporate bonds. Recorded here explicitly so future runs do not add an entry for a covered-bond law that does not exist. Practical state of the regime: only two FCCs have ever been created in Tunisia — BIAT CREDIMMO 1 and 2, roughly 50 MTND each, in 2005–2006 — with nothing since, and the Article 35 decree that would designate non-bank originators was never issued, so the eligible-originator pool remains confined to banks. That assessment is sourced to Habib Chebbi (CEO, Tunisie Titrisation), "L'indispensable réforme de la loi sur la Titrisation," Leaders, July 13, 2017 — a single expert source, flagged as such, though consistent with the absence of any other FCC filing on the CMF's site.
Key provisions
  • Art. 35: an FCC is a co-ownership whose sole object is acquiring performing ("saines") receivables held by banks — or by other bodies to be designated by decree, a decree never issued — financed by a single issuance of units; credit enhancement is limited to four listed techniques (over-collateralisation; subordinated units, which natural persons and OPCVM may not hold; a bank or insurance guarantee; adequate security attached to the receivables)
  • Art. 36: no legal personality; co-ownership and société en participation rules disapplied; the fund may not acquire receivables after issuance and may not borrow
  • Art. 37: units are valeurs mobilières, may carry different rights to principal and interest, and are not redeemable at the holder's request; the minimum unit denomination is set by decree
  • Art. 38: true sale by a simple acte de cession de créances (bordereau) with prescribed mentions — effective and opposable to third parties on delivery of the bordereau, automatically transferring all accessory security without further formality
  • Art. 39: the fund may not resell acquired receivables except on liquidation, once residual assets fall below 10% of the initial issue, and may not pledge them
  • Art. 40: mandatory rating by a specialised agency on a Finance Ministry list (after CMF opinion), annexed to the prospectus, with published ongoing monitoring
  • Art. 41: démarchage (cold-selling) of FCC units is prohibited
  • Art. 42: the originator remains servicer by convention; servicing may be transferred to another bank, with notification to debtors
  • Art. 44: the manager must be an SA with FCC management as its sole object, capital ≥ 100,000 TND and ≥ 0.5% of assets managed (falling away above 500,000 TND); the depositary must be a bank or a listed Tunisian legal entity and may be the originator itself
  • Art. 45: CMF approval for constitution, early liquidation and for the management company; the CMF must decide within 3 months
  • Arts. 46–48: semi-annual asset inventory within 6 weeks; auditor duties; liquidation within 6 months of the last receivable's extinction; criminal conviction of managers or depositary officers terminates their functions ipso jure
FinancialCommercial

Islamic Banking Regime — Law No. 2016-48 of July 11, 2016, Arts. 4, 11–16, 22–23, 54, 75–76 & 150Opérations Bancaires Islamiques

Statutory basis: Banking Law No. 2016-48 of July 11, 2016 | Adopted by the ARP: June 9, 2016 | Published: JORT n° 58 of July 15, 2016, pp. 2195–2229 | Repeals Law No. 2001-65 (Art. 198) | In force
A structural gap in this artifact's coverage: the Banking Law entry documented the general credit-institution regime but not the Islamic-banking provisions embedded in it, and no entry anywhere described how Sharia-compliant banking is authorised in Tunisia. There is no dedicated Islamic banking statute. That is a deliberate design choice rather than a gap in Tunisian law: Law No. 2016-48 integrates Islamic banking into the ordinary licensing perimeter instead of creating a parallel regime, listing "les opérations bancaires islamiques" at Article 4 as one of the six categories of banking operations. Verified by direct reading of the JORT text hosted by the CMF. The most consequential — and most frequently misreported — feature is the permissive Sharia-governance rule: Article 54 provides that an institution "peut créer" a comité de contrôle de conformité des normes bancaires islamiques, in contrast to the takaful regime, where Article 206 of the Insurance Code says the insurer must constitute one (see the Takaful entry). Under Law No. 2016-48 a Sharia board is therefore not a statutory precondition to carrying on Islamic banking; the composition and reporting rules of Article 54 bind only institutions that create one. That reading rests on the French JORT text; the Arabic original governs, and this point is flagged for confirmation against the Arabic before it is relied upon. The same asymmetry runs to windows: Article 22 permits a conventional bank to conduct Islamic banking operations subject to BCT authorisation and financial, accounting and administrative separation, whereas Article 202 of the Insurance Code bars any cumulation of conventional and takaful business in the same entity outright. Institutions: the Fonds de Garantie des Dépôts Bancaires' official Liste des banques adhérentes au titre de l'année 2025 carries an explicit "BANQUES ISLAMIQUES" heading listing exactly three of its 28 member banks — Wifak International Bank, Banque Zitouna and Al Baraka Bank Tunisia. No Islamic window of a conventional bank appears in that list.
Key provisions
  • Art. 4: "les opérations bancaires islamiques" are one of the six categories of banking operations — the load-bearing provision making Islamic banking an ordinary banking activity rather than a separate licence class
  • Art. 11: defines them as banking operations giving rise to no receipt or payment of interest in deposit-taking, placement, financing and investment, in conformity with Islamic banking norms; charges the BCT with controlling conformity against the international standards practised in the field; enumerates Mourabaha, Ijara with purchase option, Moudaraba, Moucharaka, Istisna'a, Salam and investment deposits; the BCT Governor fixes these operations and their terms by circulaire
  • Art. 12 (Mourabaha): cost-plus sale with declared cost and profit margin, the bank acquiring from a third party at the orderer's request and reselling at cost plus a pre-agreed margin
  • Art. 13 (Ijara with purchase option): the bank acquires and owns the asset, leases it for professional use for a fixed term, and must grant the client an option to acquire during or at the end of the lease; Law No. 94-89 on leasing applies subsidiarily
  • Art. 14 (Istisna'a): manufacture-financing sale with the bank as intermediary between Mostasni'i and Sani'i, on the express condition that neither contract may be made dependent on the other
  • Art. 15 (Salam): forward purchase of tangible movables against full spot cash payment, the bank being required to resell the goods within the fixed period
  • Art. 16 (investment deposits): sums placed under a Moudaraba or Wakala contract, restricted or unrestricted — "La banque ne garantit aucune perte de l'investissement" except on proven negligence or breach of contract, so investment-account holders bear investment risk
  • Art. 22: a bank or financial institution proposing to carry on Islamic banking operations must apply to the BCT with a business plan and a description of its financial, accounting and administrative separation arrangements; institutions already licensed before entry into force are grandfathered
  • Art. 23 §2: carves the acquisition and holding of movable and immovable property necessary for Islamic banking operations out of the general activity restriction, conditional on onward transfer to clients within a reasonable period — without which Mourabaha, Ijara and Istisna'a would breach the object clause
  • Art. 54: an institution may create a comité de contrôle de conformité des normes bancaires islamiques attached to the board — at least three members of Tunisian nationality, appointed by the general meeting for a 3-year term renewable once, no member sitting on more than one such committee, every appointment notified to the BCT without delay; its annual report goes to the board with copies to the BCT and to the general meeting at least one month before it is held; the institution must then appoint an auditeur des opérations bancaires islamiques acting as committee secretary; members are bound by professional secrecy under Art. 254 of the Penal Code
  • Art. 75 §2: the general participation limits do not apply to financings in the form of Moucharaka, provided the contract stipulates an undertaking to retrocede within five years
  • Art. 76: a bank licensed for Islamic banking must keep client accounts so as to separate investment-deposit accounts from other deposit categories, and must periodically inform investment-deposit holders of the nature of the investment operations, their participation share, and the profit-sharing and loss-contribution arrangements
  • Art. 150 §3: the Fonds de Garantie des Dépôts Bancaires must allocate a separate special account to banks carrying on Islamic banking exclusively (and to non-resident banks)
  • Not verified this run: the BCT circulaire contemplated by Art. 11 fixing the operations and their terms — its number and date could not be located and should be chased on bct.gov.tn
Run 1036 update — the Art. 11 circular is identified, and the Art. 54 Arabic question is answered. The circular required by Article 11 is Circulaire aux banques et aux établissements financiers No. 2019-08 of October 14, 2019 (Définition des opérations bancaires islamiques et fixation des modalités et conditions de leur exercice), reproduced in the BCT's Réglementation bancaire — Recueil de textes. Its lateness is itself the notable fact: Art. 11 gave the Governor a maximum of two months from the law's entry into force, a deadline that expired in September 2016 — the circular arrived more than three years late. Its content runs to four titles: commercial financing (Mourabaha, Ijara with purchase option, Salam with parallel Salam, Istisna'a with second Istisna'a, whose exposure may never exceed the first); participatory financing (Moucharaka, Moudharaba); investment deposits under Moudharaba or Wakala, where returns follow investment results and the bank must disclose whether it acts as Mudharib or Wakil, state its investment policy and risk rate before each operation, and report to investment-account holders every six months; and general provisions requiring prior notification to the BCT of any new Islamic product, with a BCT right to object by reasoned decision within ten working days, and mandatory compliance with international standards, AAOIFI's in particular, so far as they do not conflict with Tunisian law. On Article 54, the answer is yes: the provision is permissive in the Arabic original exactly as in the French. The Arabic reads للبنك أو للمؤسسة المالية … أن تحدث هيئة — the standard facultative formula, the precise counterpart of peut créer. The contrast is visible inside the same article, where the drafter switches to the mandatory ويتعيّن على البنك أو المؤسسة المالية for the duties that are obligatory: notifying the BCT of appointments, appointing a Sharia auditor, and the annual report. So the optionality of the Sharia board is deliberate and identical in both language versions — a point of substance, not a translation artefact. A further finding: Art. 54 was constitutionally challenged before the Instance provisoire de contrôle de la constitutionnalité des projets de loi, on the ground that a Sharia-compliance body is "religious par excellence" and breaches Arts. 2 and 50 of the Constitution on the civil character of the State, and on the procedure by which the amendment was adopted. The Instance rejected both grounds (decision taken at Bardo, July 2, 2016, presided by Khaled Ayari; published in Arabic in the same JORT n° 58 of July 15, 2016).
Financial

Law No. 2013-30 of July 30, 2013 — Islamic SukukSukuk Islamiques

Adopted by the Assemblée Nationale Constituante: July 17, 2013 | Promulgated: July 30, 2013 (Moncef Marzouki) | Published: JORT n° 62 of August 2, 2013, pp. 2300–2302 | 29 articles in 5 chapters | In force; no sovereign issue completed
The statute creating Tunisia's sukuk framework, absent from this artifact until now despite several entries touching Islamic finance (the ITFC Mourabaha guarantee bills in Public Finance, and the Islamic banking regime above). Verified by direct reading of the official French text hosted by the Conseil du Marché Financier, cross-checked against legislation.tn's record (JORT 2013-062). Article 1 defines sukuk as negotiable instruments representing equal undivided shares in the ownership of assets, usufruct, services or rights — existing or to be created — or a mix of assets, usufruct, services, currencies and receivables from the subscription proceeds, issued under a contract conforming to Sharia standards and based on profit-and-loss sharing; Article 2 makes them valeurs mobilières within the meaning of Article 1 of Law No. 2000-35 of March 21, 2000. The law is unusual in the region for placing the Sharia board on a statutory footing with binding decisions (Art. 29) and, for State and local-authority issues, appointment by the Ministry of Finance itself (Art. 28). Implementation lag: the enabling decrees arrived four to five years after the statute — Décrets gouvernementaux No. 2017-1332 and No. 2017-1333 of December 6, 2017 (JORT n° 99 of December 12, 2017) for the constitution, early liquidation and management of a fonds commun de sukuk, and Décret gouvernemental No. 2018-579 of June 22, 2018 (JORT n° 53 of July 3, 2018) for private-sector issuers. No sovereign sukuk has been completed. Successive finance laws have authorised recourse to the instrument — Law No. 2025-17 of December 12, 2025 (Finance Law 2026) sets the ceiling for State guarantees for loans or sukuk issues at TND 7,000,000,000 for 2026 — but reporting through 2025 consistently states that Tunisia has never completed a sovereign issue, with Banque Zitouna working with Islamic Development Bank support on a structuring model to unblock the first one. That negative finding rests on secondary sources only and is recorded as such; whether any corporate sukuk has been issued under the law, and whether a sovereign issue occurred in the first half of 2026, remain unverified. A related but distinct statute is Law No. 2013-48 of December 9, 2013 on Islamic investment funds.
Key provisions
  • Art. 3: issuable in dinars or foreign currency, subject to exchange regulation (see the Exchange Control Law)
  • Art. 5: the permitted issuers are exhaustive — (i) the State; (ii) public establishments and enterprises and local authorities; (iii) private-sector enterprises, under conditions fixed by decree (Décret gouvernemental No. 2018-579 of June 22, 2018)
  • Art. 6: sukuk issued or guaranteed by the State on international markets are carved out of Arts. 8–24, so the fonds-commun machinery does not apply to sovereign international issues
  • Art. 7: State-issued or State-guaranteed sukuk must be authorised by the finance law, each issue ratified before the proceeds are used; issues by public establishments, public enterprises and local authorities are authorised by the Ministry of Finance
  • Art. 8: subscription is called through a document d'émission de sukuk signed by the issuer's legal representative and bearing the Sharia supervisory committee's approval, with mandatory contents including the issuance contracts, total amount and nominal value, estimated rate of return, nature of any guarantee, detailed use of proceeds, an economic and social feasibility statement, negotiability and redemption terms, and the party to which ownership of the underlying assets is transferred; Art. 9: a document missing any Art. 8 item is null
  • Arts. 10–13: issuance is carried out through a fonds commun de sukuk unless the Sharia committee considers it unnecessary; FCS units are themselves sukuk; the fund is a co-ownership with no legal personality, indivision and société en participation rules disapplied, and no partition may be provoked
  • Arts. 14 & 18: CMF agrément required for constitution and early liquidation of an FCS and for the management activity (Décrets gouvernementaux No. 2017-1332 and No. 2017-1333 of December 6, 2017)
  • Art. 17: the management company must be an SA with management of the FCS as sole object, charged with protecting holders' rights, managing the project per the issuance document and publishing an information bulletin; Art. 19: it may not incur debt for the fund nor mortgage its assets
  • Art. 21: the depositary must be a bank — the text still cross-refers to Law No. 2001-65 of July 10, 2001, repealed by Art. 198 of Law No. 2016-48; the reference was never updated
  • Art. 22: management company and depositary individually or jointly liable; a court may revoke their directors on a holder's application and appoint a provisional administrator
  • Arts. 25–26: negotiability and redemption after closing of subscription, in conformity with Sharia rules on assets, receivables, currency and exchange; listed and traded on the BVMT under Law No. 94-117, with foreign-currency sukuk able to trade on foreign exchanges
  • Arts. 27–29: each issuer appoints a comité de contrôle charaïque for fatwa and Sharia audit; for State-issued or State-guaranteed sukuk and local-authority issues the committee is appointed by the Ministry of Finance (Art. 28); its decisions "ont un effet obligatoire" (Art. 29); members serve three years renewable once and are bound by professional secrecy under Art. 254 of the Penal Code
Run 1036 update — the open question is answered: yes, a corporate sukuk has been issued in Tunisia. Run 1035 left open "whether any corporate sukuk has ever been issued in Tunisia." One documented issuance exists: « SUKUK ZITOUNA TAMKEEN 2023 », recorded in the JORT's Annonces Légales n° 152 of December 29, 2023, pp. 2946–2951, issued without recourse to public offering. Issuer: Zitouna Tamkeen, an Islamic microfinance institution governed by Decree-Law No. 2011-117, capital 31,000,000 TND. Terms as printed: 6,000,000 dinars, 60,000 sak of 100 dinars, seven years in fine, registered form, contract type Wakala Bil Istithmar, subscription December 25–29, 2023, four subscribing companies of the MAJDA Tunisia group, expected profit rate 10.65%, redemption on the basis of التنضيض الحكمي (constructive liquidation), proceeds to reinforce the issuer's complementary own funds. Authorised by an AGO of December 11, 2023 for up to 10 million dinars over three years, with Sharia Committee approval of November 13, 2023 and the statutory auditor's attestation under Art. 8 of this law dated November 14, 2023. Structurally important: the issue was made directly by the company under Décret gouvernemental No. 2018-579 of June 22, 2018 (issuance of sukuk for private-sector institutions, taken under Art. 5 of this law) — not through a fonds commun des sukuk. Three negatives are logged with it, so future runs need not re-search them: no other sukuk issuance appears anywhere in the JORT archive; no fonds commun des sukuk and no sukuk-fund management company appear ever to have been licensed, despite the 2017 décrets creating the regime; and no sovereign sukuk has been issued. On the two 2017 texts Run 1035 referred to: Décret No. 2017-1332 governs licensing and early liquidation of the sukuk fund and the issuance mechanics (CMF visa on the prospectus, availability of the prospectus and règlement intérieur before subscription, notification of amounts subscribed within two weeks), and Décret No. 2017-1333 licenses the fund's management company; both were published in JORT n° 99 of December 12, 2017.

Code de Prestation des Services Financiers aux Non-Résidents — Law No. 2009-64 of August 12, 2009Non-Resident (Offshore) Financial Services Regime

Enacted: August 12, 2009 | 147 articles in 6 titles | Repeals Law No. 85-108 of December 6, 1985 | Amended: 2010, 2012, 2013, 2018 | In force | JORT issue reference: unverified
The statute governing Tunisia's non-resident ("offshore") financial sector, complementing the Free Zones Law and the offshore companies framework already documented for the industrial and commercial sectors — the financial-sector equivalent had never been covered. It replaced the 1985 offshore banking regime wholesale: Article 2 of the promulgating law repeals Law No. 85-108 of December 6, 1985, giving existing non-resident banks two years to meet the new capital requirement, and Article 4 substitutes the term "établissements de crédit non résidents exerçant dans le cadre du code de prestation des services aux non résidents" for the old "organismes financiers et bancaires travaillant essentiellement avec les non résidents" throughout Tunisian law. The most consequential development since enactment is the loss of the sector's headline tax advantage, a change that post-dates most published descriptions of the regime and is therefore recorded here in detail. Article 143's first paragraph — the 10% corporate income tax on profits from operations with non-residents — was abrogated by Article 39-1 of the Finance Law 2019 (Law No. 2018-56 of December 27, 2018), with Article 142 abrogated by Article 39-3 of the same law; this was verified directly against the official text of Law No. 2018-56 (JORT n° 104 of December 28, 2018, p. 4540). Entities in activity at December 31, 2018 kept the old regime until December 31, 2020 under Article 41-1. The consequence is that for financial years from 2021, non-resident financial service providers are taxed under ordinary corporate-tax rules — reported as the 35% band of Article 49 of the Income Tax Code covering banks and financial institutions, a rate taken from secondary tax-practice sources and flagged as not independently verified against the code text. The exchange-control freedoms of Title VI survive intact. The JORT issue number and date for Law No. 2009-64 itself could not be confirmed from any primary source (legislation.tn returned HTTP 503 throughout this run's checks) and is recorded as an open citation gap.
Key provisions
  • Arts. 1–2: governs the supply of financial products and services to non-residents within the meaning of exchange legislation, by non-resident providers, who may serve residents only in the cases the code allows
  • Art. 60: non-resident credit institutions comprise non-resident banks and non-resident financial institutions; only non-resident banks may take deposits from the public, and those licensed as banks are deemed to make an appel public à l'épargne (the text still cites the repealed Law No. 2001-65 rather than Law No. 2016-48)
  • Art. 72: prior agrément required, assessed on the business programme, means, quality of direct and indirect capital providers, and honourability and experience of directors and the internal-control officer — with a "four-eyes" rule requiring effective direction by at least two persons; the BCT and/or CMF must decide within a maximum of three months from a complete file
  • Art. 74: minimum capital, fully paid up at incorporation and subscribed in convertible foreign currency — non-resident bank 25 million TND equivalent; non-resident financial institution 10 million TND; non-resident investment firm 7.5 million TND; non-resident portfolio management company 250,000 TND; foreign-headquartered institutions operating through branches must allocate an equivalent dotation
  • Art. 138: no repatriation obligation for income and proceeds abroad, and full exchange freedom for operations with non-residents; Art. 140: settlements in Tunisia must pass through comptes étrangers en dinars convertibles, with a dinar cash float permitted for current administrative expenses
  • Art. 143 (as amended): the 10% corporate-tax paragraph abrogated by Finance Law 2019, Art. 39-1; surviving benefits for operations with non-residents are fixed-duty registration of deeds (except acquisitions of Tunisian real estate), exemption from tax on income generated by foreign-currency deposits made in Tunisia, no withholding on interest on foreign-currency borrowings from non-residents not established in Tunisia, and exemption from the taxe de formation professionnelle and the FOPROLOS contribution pro rata to non-resident turnover
  • Art. 145 (as amended by the Complementary Finance Law 2012, Law No. 2012-1 of May 16, 2012, Arts. 58-1 and 58-2): suspension of import duties and turnover taxes on equipment, broadened to local acquisitions of equipment and services from VAT-registered suppliers; onward sale in Tunisia triggers the duties and taxes
  • Art. 146: foreign-national staff holding non-resident status at recruitment are exempt from IRPP on salaries paid by the non-resident entity, replaced by a flat 20% fiscal contribution on total gross remuneration including bonuses and benefits in kind; duty-free import of personal effects and one passenger car per employee; an option, exercisable before recruitment, for a non-Tunisian social-security regime, in which case no Tunisian contributions are due by employee or employer
  • Art. 147: the fiscal, exchange and customs regime may be extended by convention (Minister of Finance, after BCT, Comité Général des Assurances or CMF opinion, ratified by decree) to insurance and reinsurance of risks not required to be covered in Tunisia, participations in projects, representation offices, and similar financial activities
  • Amendment chain: Law No. 2010-58 of December 17, 2010 (Finance Law 2011, extending the grandfathered Law 85-108 exemptions to December 31, 2011); Law No. 2012-1 of May 16, 2012; Law No. 2013-54 of December 30, 2013 (Finance Law 2014, abrogating the TCL exemption at Art. 50-4); Law No. 2018-56 of December 27, 2018 (Finance Law 2019)
Run 1036 update — citation gap closed. Published in JORT n° 65 of August 14, 2009, the law beginning at p. 2316 and the annexed Code running to p. 2338 (Law No. 2009-65 starts on p. 2339). Adopted by the Chamber of Deputies on July 21, 2009 and the Chamber of Councillors on July 30, 2009. Art. 2 repeals Law No. 85-108 of December 6, 1985, the former offshore-banking law, subject to the transitional provisions of Art. 3.

Central Securities Depository & Dematerialisation — Law No. 94-117, Arts. 77–80, and Law No. 2000-35 of March 21, 2000Tunisie Clearing (formerly STICODEVAM), Book-Entry Securities and Settlement Finality

Depository basis: Law No. 94-117 of November 14, 1994, JORT n° 90 of November 15, 1994, p. 1850 | Dematerialisation: Law No. 2000-35 of March 21, 2000 | Operating framework: Arrêté of the Minister of Finance of January 12, 2016, JORT n° 6 of January 19, 2016, p. 150 | In force
The post-trade infrastructure layer of Tunisian securities law, previously undocumented here although the Financial Market Law entry covers the market's regulatory architecture. There is no separate CSD statute: the depository rests on four articles of Law No. 94-117 (Titre III, Chapitre 3, "De la société de dépôt, de compensation et de règlement"), verified from the JORT facsimile hosted by the Ministry of Justice, with the operative detail living in a CMF règlement. The company was incorporated on December 28, 1993 as STICODEVAM and confirmed in existence by the 1994 law; no legal instrument or firm date was located for the rename to Tunisie Clearing, which should be treated as a corporate name change rather than a statutory event until evidence emerges. Dematerialisation is a distinct statute, Law No. 2000-35 of March 21, 2000 (6 articles), which abolished bearer securities in Tunisia on a hard two-year deadline: Article 4 provides that holders of pre-existing bearer securities who fail to present them within two years lose the exercise of their rights, with unclaimed rights sold and the proceeds consigned. The current operating framework is the CMF règlement on the dépositaire central approved by arrêté of the Minister of Finance of January 12, 2016 (47 articles, signed by Finance Minister Slim Chaker), with Tunisie Clearing's own operating rules reported as entering into force July 1, 2016. A caveat worth recording: settlement finality and irrevocability rest on that règlement, not on primary legislation — Tunisia has no statutory settlement-finality act equivalent to the EU Settlement Finality Directive, so the insolvency-law override question is not addressed at statutory level. That observation is this artifact's reading of the instruments consulted rather than a sourced assertion, and is flagged accordingly.
Key provisions
  • Law 94-117 Art. 77: stockbrokers must constitute, as an SA, a single société interprofessionnelle de dépôt, de compensation et de règlement de titres, its capital openable to Finance-Minister-approved bodies and its statutes approved by the Minister — the source of the monopoly, since the law contemplates one interprofessional company rather than a licensing regime open to competitors
  • Law 94-117 Art. 78: the depository may receive securities on deposit by contract and keeps accounts for the issuer, the owner and the broker, recording both deposited securities and securities physically held by owners, and registering pledges, oppositions and other charges; Arts. 689–697 of the Commercial Code (deposit) apply; it also clears and settles exchange transactions
  • Law 94-117 Art. 79: issuers must deposit listed securities as a single collective certificate representing the admitted quantity
  • Law 94-117 Art. 80: a selling broker must have the securities in its depository account before the sell order is executed (pre-positioning)
  • Law 2000-35 Art. 2: securities are dematerialised, represented by book entry with the issuer or an approved intermediary, and transfer by account-to-account movement, the account keeper issuing a holding certificate
  • Law 2000-35 Art. 3: all securities issued in Tunisia under Tunisian law must be registered (nominatives) and held in accounts — for non-APE companies, exclusively by the issuer
  • Law 2000-35 Art. 4: phase-in of 1 year for issuers and 2 years for holders of pre-existing bearer securities, after which holders lose the exercise of their rights unless presented, with unclaimed rights sold and proceeds consigned; Art. 5: on an account-keeper's cessation or bankruptcy, owners may transfer to another intermediary or the issuer and may claim shortfalls from the trustee under Art. 497 of the Commercial Code
  • CMF règlement Art. 4: the depository's missions are centralised safekeeping as guarantor of issue integrity and organising the circulation of securities in the settlement/delivery system
  • CMF règlement Arts. 18.1–18.3: only securities negotiable on an organised market may be admitted, securities traded on the BVMT electronic system must be admitted, and Treasury bills and State bond issues are admitted de plein droit
  • CMF règlement Arts. 28.1 & 30.1: delivery-versus-payment in central bank money — delivery occurs only on BCT confirmation that the corresponding payment has been made, each participant settling via a cash account at the BCT; Arts. 33.5–33.6: no partial delivery, participant securities positions being only credit or nil after each settlement session
  • CMF règlement Arts. 35–36: instructions become irrevocable once the depository transmits payment instructions to the BCT (or, for free-of-payment instructions, once it updates participants' securities balances), and "le règlement définitif intervient dès la mise à jour des soldes de comptes en valeurs mobilières des participants par le Dépositaire Central des Titres"
  • Implementing texts: Décret No. 2001-2728 of November 20, 2001 as amended by Décret No. 2005-3144 of December 6, 2005 (registration conditions and approved account-keepers); CMF règlement on the keeping and administration of securities accounts, visa arrêté of August 28, 2006. Law No. 94-117 has been amended by Law No. 99-92 of August 17, 1999, Law No. 2005-96 of October 18, 2005, Law No. 2009-64 of August 12, 2009 and Law No. 2019-47 of May 29, 2019; Arts. 77–80 carry no "(nouveau)" marking and appear unamended
Run 1036 update — the rename gap is closed, and the answer is that there was no legal instrument. This entry previously recorded that "no legal instrument or firm date was located for the rename to Tunisie Clearing." The question is now settled from the primary record, and the finding is a negative one worth stating precisely: the rename was effected by a purely corporate act, not by statute, decree or CMF règlement — a resolution of STICODEVAM's assemblée générale extraordinaire of Tuesday, October 21, 2014, registered October 22, 2014, filed at the Tunis Court of First Instance October 27, 2014, and taking effect November 14, 2014. The source is the company's own legal announcement in the JORT's Annonces Légales, Réglementaires et Judiciaires n° 135 of November 11, 2014, p. 4594 (the notice spells the old name "STICODEAM," a typo in the original). The earlier suspicion recorded here — that this should be treated as a corporate name change rather than a statutory event — is therefore confirmed rather than merely retained. A structural confirmation sits in the governing règlement itself: it is drafted generically throughout as le Dépositaire Central des Titres and never uses the name "Tunisie Clearing", precisely because the corporate name is fixed by no legal text. Founding: the company was created December 28, 1993 as STICODEVAM and therefore pre-dates its own statutory basis — it was constituted as a company first, and Law No. 94-117 then made it compulsory and defined its remit (CMF, Les chambres de compensation, June 2025). Shareholders are the stockbrokers and certain commercial banks, participating in equal parts. Capital: 4,414,635 TND as at 2014, raised by 916,245 TND to 5,330,880 TND by the EGM of May 21, 2015 (Annonces Légales n° 76 of June 25, 2015). Two loose ends logged rather than smoothed: the commercial-register number is B163781996, whose "1996" cannot be reconciled with a 1993 constitution; and no arrêté approving STICODEVAM's statutes was ever found despite Art. 77 al. 2 of Law 94-117 requiring Minister of Finance approval — such approvals appear simply not to be published. Implementing decree for dematerialisation: Décret No. 2001-2728 of November 20, 2001, amended by Décret No. 2005-3144 of December 6, 2005. On supervision, there is no separate BCT licensing; the règlement instead embeds the depository in the central bank's payment infrastructure, cash legs settling in central-bank money on accounts held at the BCT. Run 1038 update — capital advanced past the 2015 figure. Independently corroborated by African Manager and the state news agency TAP: at an extraordinary general assembly of May 19, 2022, Tunisie Clearing's capital was raised from 10,560,000 TND to 10,562,380 TND, a technical adjustment to preserve shareholder equality following the merger by absorption of Biat Capital into Tunisie Valeurs (an ordinary general assembly the same day approved a 1,740,000 TND dividend distribution, 60,000 TND per shareholder). This confirms capital rose materially between the 2015 figure recorded above (5,330,880 TND) and 2022, but the intervening increases were not traced and 10,562,380 TND is itself a 2022 figure, not verified as still current in 2026 — the exact capital today and the full shareholder list remain open.

Intermédiaires en Bourse — Law No. 94-117, Arts. 55–62, and Décret No. 99-2478 of November 1, 1999Stockbrokers: Licensing, Capital and Client-Asset Segregation

Statutory basis: Law No. 94-117 of November 14, 1994, JORT n° 90 of November 15, 1994 | Implementing statute: Décret No. 99-2478 of November 1, 1999 (90 articles), as amended by Décret No. 2007-1678 of July 5, 2007 | In force | JORT references for both décrets: unverified
The licensing and conduct regime for Tunisia's securities intermediaries — the profession through which all exchange transactions must pass — previously uncovered here. It is a two-layer regime: Articles 55 to 62 of the Financial Market Law set the principles, and Décret No. 99-2478 of November 1, 1999, adopted on the basis of Article 58, supplies 90 articles of operational detail. No later replacement décret was located. The regime's centre of gravity is client-asset segregation, which is unusually explicit for the region: Article 79 of the décret states flatly that "l'intermédiaire en bourse ne doit pas utiliser les titres et les fonds de ses clients pour son propre compte," Article 56 (as amended in 2007) requires a bank compte professionnel reserved exclusively to client cash, and Article 75 gives client orders absolute priority over those of the broker, its managers and its staff. Two data-quality points are recorded rather than resolved. First, headcount: the CMF's Intervenants sur le marché financier page lists 19 licensed intermédiaires en bourse, while the Association des Intermédiaires en Bourse shows 24–25 adherent institutions; the two figures are not comparable, because the AIB count mixes brokers with sociétés de gestion, and neither is treated here as superseding the other. Second, stale cross-references: Articles 5 and 84 of the décret still cite Law No. 2001-65 on credit institutions, repealed by Article 198 of Law No. 2016-48, and the references have not been updated in the CMF and BVMT consolidated texts — a trap for anyone reading the décret in isolation.
Key provisions
  • Law 94-117 Art. 55: brokers hold the exclusive right to negotiate and register securities and financial products on the BVMT; the activity must be exercised permanently and is incompatible with any other professional activity
  • Law 94-117 Arts. 57 & 59–62: licensed by the CMF after the opinion of the AIB, brokers must be of Tunisian nationality (natural persons or specialised SA); they are liable to clients for delivery and payment of what they buy and sell, bound by professional secrecy and a duty to put the client's interest first, obliged to belong to the AIB, and covered by a compulsory fonds de garantie clientèle for non-commercial risks
  • Décret Art. 2: contrepartie, market-making and underwriting are reserved to specialised SA brokers; Art. 4: no broker may hold, directly or indirectly, more than 30% of another broking SA
  • Décret Art. 3: minimum paid-up capital 1,000,000 TND for negotiation, registration, advice, démarchage, portfolio management and portage — rising to 3,000,000 TND where the broker is also licensed for contrepartie, market-making or underwriting
  • Décret Arts. 7–17: a two-stage licence (agrément de principe then agrément définitif) with 3-month then 2-month CMF review and a 6-month window (extendable by 3) to file the second file; the licence is personal, non-transferable and non-assignable (Art. 15), and business may not start without proof of participation in the BVMT and depository capital and membership of the fonds de garantie de marché, the fonds de garantie clientèle and the AIB (Art. 16)
  • Décret Arts. 22–25: suspension and withdrawal grounds include 12 months' non-use of the licence, 6 months' inactivity, or 4 months' continuous breach of a prudential rule; on withdrawal, bankruptcy, incapacity or death the CMF appoints another broker to run off the book (Art. 24)
  • Décret Art. 49: at least one account per client recording all cash and securities, with a unique client identifier disclosable only to the CMF; deposited securities governed by Arts. 689–697 of the Commercial Code; the broker may hold funds only in connection with its licensed activities
  • Décret Arts. 56–57 & 71: a bank compte professionnel reserved exclusively to client cash; sums held are deemed demand deposits; accounting segregation between holdings held for contrepartie, underwriting, market-making, portage and ordinary proprietary holdings
  • Décret Arts. 75 & 79: client orders always take priority over the broker's own and those of its managers and staff, and the broker may not use client securities or funds for its own account
  • Décret Arts. 55 & 62: on transfer of an account to another broker, a contradictory stock-take and procès-verbal, cash returned directly to the client and securities transferred within 3 trading days; a compulsory insurance policy against loss, theft and destruction of client funds, proof filed with the CMF on the first business day of each year
  • Décret Arts. 86, 86 bis and 86 ter: a mandatory CMF-approved responsable du contrôle (compliance officer) reporting semi-annually to the board and to the CMF
  • Décret Arts. 87–88: permanent net own funds at least equal to those required to cover the risks in the broker's portfolio, at risk weights fixed by CMF décision générale; any shortfall must be notified to the CMF the next business day and cured within 48 hours
  • Décret Arts. 84–85: credit institutions carrying on démarchage, third-party portfolio management, securities account-keeping and order collection are subject to an enumerated list of the décret's conduct and segregation articles under CMF supervision, must segregate these activities from the rest of the bank, and must appoint a CMF interlocutor
Run 1036 update — both citation gaps closed, and Décret No. 2007-1678 identified. Décret No. 99-2478 of November 1, 1999 (portant statut des intermédiaires en bourse, 90 articles) was published in JORT n° 93 of Friday, November 19, 1999, 142nd year, pp. 2442–2450, taken under Art. 58 of Law No. 94-117; its Art. 89 repeals the arrêté du ministre du plan et des finances of January 18, 1990. Décret No. 2007-1678 of July 5, 2007 — whose subject Run 1035 could not identify — is precisely an amending text to the above: modifiant et complétant le décret n° 99-2478, published in JORT n° 56 of Friday, July 13, 2007, 150th year, pp. 2366–2369. It rewrote or amended a long list of articles (1, 2, 4, 12, 24, 30, 32, 33, 36, 41, 43, 45, 48, 55, 57, 61, 63, 74 among others) and inserted new Arts. 36 bis and 48 bis. A note on the archive for future runs: the 1999 issue's PDF uses a shifted font encoding, so its text is recoverable only by low-level extraction, not ordinary copy-paste.

Law No. 2014-47 of July 24, 2014 — Takaful Insurance (Insurance Code, Titre VII, Arts. 201–217)Assurance Takaful

Enacted: July 24, 2014 | Amends and completes the Insurance Code (Law No. 92-24 of March 9, 1992, JORT n° 17 of March 17, 1992, p. 314) | Adds Titre VII, Arts. 201–217, in 5 chapters | In force | JORT issue reference: unverified
Tunisia's Sharia-compliant insurance regime, absent from this artifact although the Insurance Code entry has always been present. A date correction: this law is commonly cited as an August 2014 text; the Insurance Code's own official footnote in the Imprimerie Officielle consolidated edition reads "Le titre VII a été ajouté par art. premier de la loi n° 2014-47 du 24 juillet 2014" — July 24, not August. Beyond adding Title VII, the 2014 law amended three existing articles: Article 50 ter (extending fit-and-proper notification to comités de supervision sharaïque), Article 88 §1 (penalty for non-communication of documents) and Article 58 (adding the Article 212 provision d'équilibrage to the solvency margin). Firms already writing takaful at publication had six months, extendable by six, to comply. The regime's defining structural choice is the outright ban on windows: Article 202 bars any cumulation of conventional and takaful business in the same entity, and Article 204 extends the ban to agents, so Tunisia permits only the subsidiary model. That is a clean contrast with the Islamic banking regime, where Article 22 of Law No. 2016-48 permits a conventional bank to conduct Islamic banking operations subject to BCT authorisation and internal separation — and where the Sharia board is merely permitted rather than, as here at Article 206, required. Market: three licensed takaful operators, all supervised by the Comité Général des Assurances — Zitouna Takaful, El Amana Takaful and At-Takafulia — per the FTUSA's L'Assurance tunisienne en 2024 (published December 2, 2025); no dedicated retakaful company was found. Zitouna Takaful's audited 2024 statements show a combined balance-sheet total of 417.7 MTND, Wakala commissions of 26.53 MTND and Moudharaba commissions of 5.29 MTND, and no qard hassan granted as at December 31, 2024. The applied remuneration rates for FY2024 were Wakala 28% and Moudharaba 25%; a reported 25% statutory cap on the Moudharaba rate could not be verified against the text of the implementing arrêté and is not asserted here.
Key provisions
  • Art. 201: takaful is a contractual regime of mutual assistance in which contributions are paid as a donation; the contributions form the fonds des adhérents, dedicated to claims payment and "totalement séparé des comptes de l'entreprise d'assurance Takaful", the operator managing and investing it against a commission per Sharia norms
  • Art. 202: takaful firms take one of the corporate forms of Art. 53, with no cumulation of conventional and takaful business in the same entity; Art. 204 extends the ban to agents; Art. 203: portfolio transfer, merger or absorption only to or by another takaful firm, with Finance Minister approval on the CGA's report
  • Art. 205: Wakala for underwriting, Moudharaba for investment management as defined in the Code of Obligations and Contracts — the Wakala commission computed on contributions, the Moudharaba commission as a percentage of investment income, both rates stated in the conditions particulières, with the calculation basis set by arrêté of the Minister of Finance (arrêté of March 15, 2022)
  • Arts. 206–208: a comité de supervision sharaïque is mandatory — three members appointed by the general meeting for a 3-year term renewable twice, with conflict-of-interest declarations and no more than two takaful Sharia boards per person; its decisions are binding on the firm (Art. 207); it reports annually to the board with a copy to the CGA by July 31; Art. 208 additionally requires an internal auditeur sharaïque
  • Art. 209: strict account separation — one account for shareholders' capital investments and one, or several by branch, for the fonds des adhérents; Art. 210: participants' fund assets invested per a Finance Minister asset list and with the Sharia board's authorisation
  • Art. 211: the firm must distribute the underwriting surplus to participants by a method it sets after the Sharia board's opinion — surplus being net contributions plus investment income and other income, less claims paid, technical provisions, reserves, shareholder remuneration and other fund expenses; shareholders may take no profit out of the participants'-fund surplus
  • Art. 212: at least 30% of annual surplus is retained as a provision d'équilibrage des pourcentages d'indemnisation to cover future deficits, the levy stopping once the provision reaches 50% of the current year's net contributions
  • Arts. 213–214 (qard hassan): the operator bears no participants'-fund risk unless the loss stems from its own breach, but on fund insolvency it must grant an interest-free loan — only after retakaful treaties and the Art. 212 provision are exhausted — repaid out of future surplus before reconstituting the Art. 212 provisions, and capped at the operator's total equity
  • Art. 215: seven mandatory contract clauses — Sharia-compliance undertaking, contribution as donation, total account separation, management models, investment policy, surplus-distribution method, and the qard hassan undertaking
  • Art. 216: cession only to takaful or retakaful reinsurers, with conventional reinsurance permitted only where retakaful capacity is insufficient or the cover does not exist, minimising the cession rate and period, and after Sharia board approval; Art. 217: the rest of the Insurance Code applies residually
  • Implementing and related texts: Arrêté of the Minister of Finance of March 15, 2022 (Wakala calculation basis and Moudharaba rate under Art. 205); Règlement CGA No. 01/2022 of June 24, 2022 on financial and accounting management of takaful companies; the takaful tax regime was specified in the Finance Law 2020 (Law No. 2019-78 of December 23, 2019, JORT n° 104 of December 27, 2019)
Run 1036 update — citation gap closed, and the date conflict dissolved rather than decided. The apparent dispute between a "July 24, 2014" and an "August 2014" date turns out not to be a conflict at all: both are right, and they describe different things. The law is dated July 24, 2014, and it was published in a combined triple issue — JORT n° 60-61-62, covering July 25, July 29 and August 1, 2014, 157th year — which is where the August dating in secondary sources comes from. The text runs pp. 1913–1916 (Law No. 2014-48 begins on p. 1916). A further precision: the law's official title makes no mention of takaful — it is simply Loi n° 2014-47 du 24 juillet 2014, amendant et complétant le code des assurances; the takaful content sits in the inserted Titre VII (Arts. 201–217). Art. 2 replaces a provision on directors' competence and Art. 3 adds a further takaful provision. Transitional rule: insurers already writing takaful had six months, extendable by six more on reasoned request with the Minister of Finance's agreement. Adopted by the National Constituent Assembly on July 14, 2014.
Financial

📈 Investment & Business Environment

Investment Law — Law No. 2016-71 of September 30, 2016

Enacted: September 30, 2016 | In force: April 2017 | Replaced: Investment Code of 1993
Tunisia's primary investment statute, replacing the 1993 Investment Code. Applies to both domestic and foreign investment. Guarantees freedom of investment, equal treatment of foreign and domestic investors, protection against expropriation (with compensation), and transfer of profits and capital. Establishes the Investment Authority (FIPA — Foreign Investment Promotion Agency) and the Investment Development Agency (IDI). Creates investment incentives including tax benefits for priority sectors and regions. Implementing update: Décret n° 2024-182 of April 4, 2024 (JORT No. 2024-047) amended the executive regulation on financial incentives, Décret gouvernemental n° 2017-389 of March 9, 2017 — not the 2016 law itself — setting a 2-year deadline from the investment declaration certificate date to submit incentive claims with a feasibility study, requiring exceptional deadline-extension requests to be filed 6 months before expiry, and clarifying which agricultural services (milk collection, grain storage, seed conditioning, hay storage) qualify for regional-development incentives.
Key provisions
  • Freedom of establishment for foreign investors (with exceptions in certain sectors)
  • Art. 7: Equal treatment of foreign investors
  • Art. 21–25: Protection against nationalization and expropriation
  • Art. 26: Freedom to transfer capital, profits, and salaries of foreign staff
  • Incentive framework: preferential tax rates for investment in priority sectors
  • Regional development incentives for investments in interior regions
  • Foreign ownership: up to 100% in most sectors; limited in certain strategic sectors
  • Single window (guichet unique) for investment approvals
CommercialFinancial

Free Zones Law — Law No. 92-81 of August 3, 1992

Enacted: August 3, 1992 | In force: 1993 | Amended: 2007, 2009, 2019
Creates special economic zones (free zones) offering customs and tax advantages for export-oriented businesses. Free zone companies are exempt from import duties, VAT on local purchases, and income tax for initial periods. Currently active free zones include Bizerte Economic Activity Park. Requires minimum 70% export of production.
CommercialTax

Startup Act — Law No. 2018-20 of April 17, 2018

Enacted: April 17, 2018 | In force: August 2018
Innovative legislation creating a special legal and fiscal framework for innovative startups. Eligible startups receive a "Startup" label granting advantages including: salary coverage for founders for 1 year, exemption from employer social security contributions for 3 years, preferential tax treatment, facilitated foreign currency access, and streamlined administrative procedures. One of Africa's first dedicated startup laws.
Key provisions
  • "Startup" label granted by the Startup Tunisia Committee
  • Founder salary covered by the state for up to 1 year
  • 3-year exemption from employer social security contributions
  • 5-year corporate tax holiday
  • Foreign currency account allowed for startups
  • Fast-track work permits for foreign talent
  • Crowdfunding and convertible notes facilitated

Arbitration Code — Law No. 93-42 of April 26, 1993

Enacted: April 26, 1993 | In force: 1993
Governs domestic and international commercial arbitration in Tunisia. Based on the UNCITRAL Model Law. Provides for arbitration agreements, constitution of tribunals, conduct of proceedings, and recognition and enforcement of awards. Tunisia ratified the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards in 1967.

Law No. 2015-49 of November 27, 2015Public-Private Partnership Law

Enacted: November 27, 2015 | In force: 2015
Creates the legal framework for PPP contracts between the state and private operators. Defines PPP modalities: concessions, affermage (lease-operate), and BOT contracts. Establishes the General Committee for Public-Private Partnerships under the Ministry of Finance. Requires competitive tendering and feasibility studies. Enables private participation in infrastructure (ports, airports, highways, water, energy).

Law No. 92-81 and Investment CodeOffshore (Totally Exporting) Companies Framework

Established: 1992 | Updated: Investment Code 2016
Regime for 100% export-oriented foreign investment: exemption from all customs duties, exemption from VAT on purchases, tax holiday for first 10 years, then 50% reduction. Must export ≥70% of production. May employ up to 30% of workforce from Tunisia. Separately regulated from free zones; offshore companies may locate anywhere in Tunisia.

Decree-Law No. 2022-15 (as substantially amended by Decree-Law No. 2025-3 of October 3, 2025)Sociétés Communautaires (Community Enterprises)

Original framework: 2022 | Major reform: Decree-Law No. 2025-3, published JORT October 3, 2025
Part of President Kais Saied's "new social project" economic program, this framework creates a distinct legal form — the "community enterprise" — intended as a third pillar of the economy alongside the public and private sectors, oriented toward participatory local and regional economic development. Decree-Law 2025-3 substantially overhauled the original 2022 framework: it distinguishes "local" community enterprises (participants from a single delegation, minimum 10 members) from "regional" ones (participants from multiple delegations within a governorate, minimum 15 members); sets minimum capital at TND 5,000 (local) and TND 10,000 (regional); grants a 10-year total exemption from taxes and duties from formation, VAT suspension on certain operations, preferential bank-loan interest rates, National Guarantee Fund coverage for financing, and priority long-term leasing (up to 40 years, with a 5-year rent exemption) of state-owned agricultural and non-agricultural land; creates a National Register of Community Enterprises conferring legal personality and a unique identifier; and sets governing-board composition at 3–10 members elected for renewable 3-year terms with conflict-of-interest rules. The Finance Law 2025 separately extended VAT-suspension treatment to community enterprises (see Finance Law 2025 entry). (Run 181 addition, corroborated and refined Run 196): a concrete application of this land-leasing mechanism was reported July 6, 2026 — the state released state-owned ("domanial") agricultural land to newly-formed community enterprises, an executive/administrative allocation carried out under this existing decree-law framework rather than a new legislative act. Independently corroborated by a second source (businessnews.com.tn, July 6, 2026), which specifies the allocation as 38 state farms totaling 17,014 hectares, earmarked for priority lease under a November 4, 2025 joint ministerial order implementing this decree-law's land-leasing provisions — resolving Run 181's "single-sourced pending further corroboration" caveat.
CommercialTax

Law No. 89-9 of February 1, 1989Public Enterprises & Privatization Framework

Enacted: February 1, 1989 | Amended: Laws No. 94-102, 96-74, 99-38, 2001-33, 2006-36
Tunisia's foundational statute governing state holdings ("participations"), public enterprises (wholly state-owned companies, and those where the state, local authorities, or public establishments jointly or individually hold over 50%), and public establishments. Defines the legal mechanisms for restructuring these entities — including share sales or exchanges, mergers, divisions, and asset sales — providing the general framework that enables privatization (transfer of state-owned shareholdings to the private sector). Privatization decisions are administered by CAREPP (Commission d'Assainissement et de Restructuration des Entreprises à Participation Publique), created under this law and detailed by Decree No. 97-410. Distinct from the narrower 2011 Confiscation Law entry above, which targets only assets seized from Ben Ali-clan associates via the separate Tunisian Confiscation Commission/Privatisation Authority.
CommercialFinancial

Draft Investment Code Reform Bill (pending)Proposed Overhaul of Law No. 2016-71

Approved in principle: Restricted Ministerial Council, December 31, 2025 | Under committee review: ARP Strategic Planning Commission (article-by-article vote stage) | Status: not enacted as of July 1, 2026
A government-sponsored bill to revise the 2016 Investment Law, launched at a Conseil ministériel restreint on December 31, 2025 and alongside the related Foreign Exchange Code reform (Draft 115/2025), as part of a broader push to modernize Tunisia's business and capital-flow environment. As of late May 2026, the ARP Strategic Planning Commission — chaired by Saber Jelassi — had moved to article-by-article voting after incorporating several amendments, following expert hearings and consultations with business organizations (Conect, Utica, Utap). Goals reported by officials and business groups include streamlining incentive eligibility, easing the single-window approval process, and aligning investment guarantees with the liberalized exchange regime. Reporting as of late June 2026 describes the amended text replacing the current prior-authorization regime with a prior-declaration principle for most investments, coupled with a positive (tacit-approval) administrative-silence rule under strict response deadlines for the administration, plus a proposed "licence premium" fast-track status to attract larger investors; this description was independently repeated by officials at the 22nd Tunisia Investment Forum (June 25–26, 2026), a second source corroborating the reform direction — but none of these provisions could be confirmed against a primary committee text as of this update, so they remain noted as reported reform direction rather than settled article language. Update (Run 38): Tunisian financial press (Tustex, late May/early June 2026) explicitly frames the reform as tied to the 2026–2030 National Development Plan's investment targets, citing a 3.3% GDP growth objective for 2026 specifically and an approximately TND 29.9 billion total public-and-private investment target for the year — figures presented alongside, not yet reconciled against, the Development Plan bill's own five-year targets documented in that entry's standalone card. As of July 1, 2026 the 2016 Investment Law remains unchanged and fully in force; the reform bill had not yet reached a plenary vote. Tracking note: a follow-up search also surfaced a separate, MP-initiated proposition n°26/2024 amending the 2016 law under the same Strategic Planning Commission, distinct from the government-driven track described above; it remains unclear from open sources whether these are the same initiative described differently or two parallel bills before the same commission — flagged for clarification in a future run rather than merged into a single narrative here. Update (Run 70): a July 3, 2026 IACE report ("cartographie" of Tunisia's pending economic-code reforms), independently corroborated by African Manager, La Presse de Tunisie, and Tustex, offers a partial resolution of that ambiguity: it classifies the Investment Code among five priority reforms — alongside the Water, Environment, and Hydrocarbons codes — that are "technically finalized and validated by the Council of Ministers but never transmitted to the ARP," attributing the bottleneck to unfinished interministerial arbitration and sectoral resistance rather than to parliamentary delay. Read together with the ARP Strategic Planning Commission's own article-by-article voting activity documented above, this suggests the government-driven track (approved in principle December 31, 2025) may be the one still stalled pre-transmission, while the committee voting already underway concerns the separate MP-initiated proposition n°26/2024 — a plausible but not yet independently confirmed reconciliation of the two tracks. IACE separately named the Investment Code one of its top three enactment priorities for the remainder of 2026, citing a decline in the overall investment rate from 19.3% of GDP (2016) to 16% (2024) and average FDI inflows down 25% (US$728M/year in 2019–2023 vs. US$974M/year in 2014–2018), and recommended a Prime Ministry-based coordination unit with binding milestones to move all sixteen tracked reforms forward. Update (Run 586): a July 4, 2026 La Presse de Tunisie piece ("Créer une entreprise en 24 heures, l'une des principales mesures de la réforme du Code de l'investissement"), framing the reform within the 2026–2030 Development Plan's business-climate agenda, adds previously-uncaptured concrete detail: a headline target of capping business-registration time at 24 hours ("standards internationaux"); a planned national digital single-window investor portal interconnected with public administrative systems to digitize authorization procedures; and digitalization/interconnection of land-registry services with a unified property database for investment-ready land, alongside the already-documented incentive-eligibility, single-window, and exchange-regime-alignment goals. These figures come from secondary press coverage of the Plan rather than a primary committee text, consistent with this entry's existing sourcing caveat, and do not resolve the still-open question of which of the two parallel tracks (government-driven vs. MP-initiated proposition n°26/2024) they attach to.
CommercialFinancial

Law No. 2020-30 of June 30, 2020Social and Solidarity Economy Law (Run 81 addition)

Enacted: June 30, 2020 | Published: JORT N°63, July 3, 2020 (pp. 1399–1403)
A wholly new standalone entry — this artifact's own Run 4 changelog previously described this law as "already implied elsewhere," but a full-text search confirmed no standalone citation for it actually existed; only the distinct 2025 "sociétés communautaires" decree-law (see above) was documented. Confirmed via direct reading of the scanned Journal Officiel text (JORT N°63, hosted by ILO NATLEX). The first framework law of its kind in the Maghreb (Morocco and Algeria had no equivalent text at the time of enactment, per leaders.com.tn), giving legal status and a governance structure to the "économie sociale et solidaire." Article 2 defines the sector as an economic model of social-purpose activities whose primary goal is not profit distribution; Article 3 lists covered entity types — cooperatives, agricultural/fisheries development groups, mutual associations, microfinance associations, mutual insurance companies, Decree-Law 2011-88 associations conducting social-purpose economic activity, and certain qualifying companies/economic-interest groupings. Creates a Conseil supérieur de l'économie sociale et solidaire (Art. 7) and an Instance tunisienne de l'économie sociale et solidaire (Art. 8). Secondary sourcing indicates the law remained largely unimplemented roughly ten months after passage pending its application decrees — an implementation gap, not a citation issue.
