💡 Intellectual Property Law

Law No. 2009-33 of June 23, 2009Literary and Artistic Property (Copyright)

Enacted: June 23, 2009 | In force: 2009 | Replaced: Law No. 94-36
Governs copyright and related rights in Tunisia. Protects literary, artistic, and musical works, software, databases, and audiovisual productions. Protection term: author's life + 70 years. Covers moral rights (inalienable) and economic rights (transferable). Aligns with WIPO Copyright Treaty and TRIPS Agreement obligations. Enforced by the Tunisian Copyright Protection Office (OTPDA). Pending reform: Bill Proposal No. 2024-47, amending and supplementing the copyright framework to address digital-era exploitation of works, is under review by the ARP's Rights and Freedoms Committee; a June 24, 2026 parliamentary study day examined the draft's likely impact on the protection regime. Not yet enacted as of July 2026.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–10: Scope — literary, artistic, musical, audiovisual, photographic works; software
  • Art. 15: Moral rights (right of integrity, right of attribution) — inalienable and perpetual
  • Art. 16–22: Economic rights — reproduction, distribution, public performance
  • Art. 24: Duration — life of author + 70 years
  • Art. 45–55: Related rights for performers, producers, broadcasters
  • Art. 60–75: Exceptions and limitations (private use, education, libraries)
  • Art. 87–100: Civil and criminal remedies for infringement
IP

Law No. 2000-84 of August 24, 2000Patents (Brevets d'Invention) (Run 1034 correction)

Enacted: August 24, 2000 | Published: JORT No. 68, August 25, 2000 | Repealed: Décret of December 26, 1888 on patents (Art. 102) | No amending law identified
Scope corrected (Run 1034): this entry previously described Law No. 2000-84 as a single omnibus "Industrial Property (Patents, Trademarks, Designs)" statute covering patents, trademarks, geographical indications, industrial designs, and utility models. That is inaccurate: Tunisia has no consolidated industrial-property code, and Law No. 2000-84 governs patents only. Trademarks, industrial designs, integrated-circuit topographies, and geographical indications each sit in their own separate statutes, now documented as distinct entries below. The prior entry's design term ("5 years, renewable up to 4 times, 25 years total") described the EU Community-design regime, not Tunisian law, and has been replaced by the actual Art. 10 term in the Industrial Designs entry.

Law No. 2000-84 sets patentability on the classic three criteria (Arts. 2–3): novelty, inventive activity, and industrial application. Excluded from patentability are discoveries and mathematical methods, schemes and rules for intellectual activity, games or economic activity, computer programs, ornamental creations, presentations of information, therapeutic/surgical/diagnostic methods practised on humans or animals, naturally occurring living substances, and (Art. 3) plant varieties, animal races, and essentially biological processes for producing plants or animals. Protection runs 20 years from the filing date (Art. 36). Filing, examination, and the registre national des brevets are administered by INNORPI (Art. 37). The law contains dedicated chapters on compulsory licences, licences of right, and customs border measures. Penalties (Art. 83): fines of TND 5,000–50,000, rising on recidivism to 1–6 months' imprisonment plus a doubled fine; falsely claiming patent status is punished by TND 1,000–5,000 (Art. 90). Implementing decrees: Décret No. 2001-328 of January 23, 2001 (national patent register), Décret No. 2001-836 of April 10, 2001 (fees), and Décret No. 2001-2750 of November 26, 2001 (sharing of exploitation proceeds for public-sector inventors). Tunisia is party to the Paris Convention and acceded to the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) on September 10, 2001, in force for Tunisia December 10, 2001 (with a declaration under PCT Art. 64(5)); accession to the Budapest Treaty on the deposit of micro-organisms was ratified by Décret No. 2003-2420 of November 24, 2003. Verified against WIPO Lex and JurisiteTunisie; no law amending 2000-84 was located, though this is an inference from WIPO Lex's silence rather than positive proof.
Key provisions
  • Arts. 2–3: Patentability — novelty, inventive activity, industrial application; statutory exclusions incl. software, therapeutic methods, plant varieties and animal races
  • Art. 36: Term — 20 years from the filing date
  • Art. 37: INNORPI maintains the national patent register
  • Compulsory licences and licences of right; customs border-measures chapter
  • Art. 83: Fines TND 5,000–50,000; recidivism 1–6 months' imprisonment + doubled fine
  • Art. 90: False claim of patent status — TND 1,000–5,000
  • Art. 102: Repeals the Décret of December 26, 1888 on patents
IP

Law No. 2001-36 of April 17, 2001 (as amended by Law No. 2007-50 of July 23, 2007)Trademarks — Marks of Manufacture, Trade and Service (Run 1034 addition)

Enacted: April 17, 2001 | Amended: Law No. 2007-50 of July 23, 2007 (JORT No. 60, July 27, 2007) | Structure: 69 articles in 9 chapters
A wholly new standalone entry closing a long-standing misattribution — Tunisian trademark law was previously folded into this artifact's Law No. 2000-84 entry, which in fact governs patents only. Loi n° 2001-36 relative à la protection des marques de fabrique, de commerce et de services is the governing statute, drafted closely on Book VII of the French Intellectual Property Code. Art. 2 defines a protectable mark as any visible sign capable of distinguishing a natural or legal person's goods or services — denominations, figurative signs including designs and colours, and sound signs. Registration confers property in the mark for the designated goods and services for a renewable ten-year term (Art. 6: "pour une période de dix ans indéfiniment renouvelable"), renewed by written declaration provided the sign is unmodified and the specification not extended. INNORPI operates the national trademark register and the official bulletin; third parties may oppose within two months of publication of the application (Art. 11). Foreign applicants neither established nor domiciled in Tunisia benefit from the law on condition of a home-country filing and reciprocal protection of Tunisian marks. Chapter 7 (Arts. 56–65) provides customs border measures against counterfeit-marked imports; Arts. 66–67 govern collective marks.

The 2007 amendment (Law No. 2007-50) is the only substantive amendment to any of Tunisia's four core industrial-property statutes. It replaces Art. 51 — raising the infringement fine to TND 10,000–50,000 for breaches of Arts. 22–23 or importation of counterfeit-marked goods — and inserts Arts. 52 bis through 52 nonies, building an enforcement apparatus that the 2001 text lacked: designated enforcement agents (judicial police, economic-control, veterinary and medical inspectors, customs officers), provisional seizure, powers of entry and sampling, laboratory analysis, formal procès-verbaux, and penalties of TND 5,000–20,000 and/or imprisonment for obstructing agents (Art. 52 octies). Procedure is now governed by Décret gouvernemental No. 2015-303 of June 1, 2015, which replaced Décret No. 2001-1603 and, significantly, provides for electronic filing and for international designations under the Madrid Protocol — Tunisia deposited its Madrid Protocol accession July 16, 2013, in force October 16, 2013 (Madrid Notification No. 201). Verified against WIPO Lex (ref TN014), the PIST scientific-information portal, and INNORPI's published text; the JORT issue number for the 2001 law itself could not be confirmed, as INNORPI's site returned HTTP 503 throughout.
Key provisions
  • Art. 2: Protectable subject matter — visible signs (denominations, figurative signs, colours, sound signs)
  • Art. 6: Ten-year term, indefinitely renewable
  • Art. 11: Two-month opposition window after publication
  • Arts. 22–23: Acts constituting infringement
  • Art. 51 (as replaced 2007): Fine TND 10,000–50,000
  • Arts. 52 bis–nonies (added 2007): Enforcement agents, seizure, entry, sampling, analysis; TND 5,000–20,000 and/or imprisonment for obstruction
  • Art. 53: Recidivism — 1–6 months' imprisonment + doubled fine; Art. 55: confiscation and destruction
  • Arts. 56–65: Customs border measures | Arts. 66–67: Collective marks

Law No. 2001-21 of February 6, 2001Industrial Designs and Models (Dessins et Modèles Industriels) (Run 1034 addition)

Enacted: February 6, 2001 | Published: JORT No. 12, February 9, 2001, pp. 257–261 | No amending law identified
A wholly new standalone entry, and the counterpart to a correction made this run: Law No. 2001-21 is the industrial-designs statute, not the integrated-circuit statute this artifact previously attributed to that number (see the corrected Integrated-Circuit Topographies entry below). The two laws were adopted the same day and published consecutively in the same gazette issue, which is the likely origin of the confusion. Art. 2 protects any new design, new plastic form, or industrial object distinguished from its like by a distinctive configuration conferring novelty or an external appearance of its own; where an object is simultaneously a protectable design and a patentable invention whose novelty elements are inseparable, patent law applies alone. The term is unusual and expressly elective: Art. 10 provides that protection lasts, at the applicant's choice, five, ten, or a maximum of fifteen years ("de cinq, dix ou quinze années au maximum"), renewable within the final six months up to that fifteen-year ceiling — not the "5 years renewable four times to 25 years" figure this artifact previously carried, which described the EU Community-design regime. Registration at INNORPI proceeds without prior examination of ownership or novelty (Art. 11), with publication within nine months (Art. 15), deferrable by twelve months on request and payment. Penalties (Art. 24): fines of TND 5,000–50,000, and TND 1,000–5,000 for falsely declaring a design registered; prosecution requires a complaint by the injured party. Art. 25 sets recidivism at 1–6 months' imprisonment plus a doubled fine; Art. 26 provides for confiscation of manufacturing instruments; Art. 28 for saisie-description (provisional description and seizure); Art. 29 for a three-year limitation period. Chapter V provides customs border measures. Implementing texts: Décret No. 2001-1604 of July 11, 2001; Décret No. 2001-1985 of August 27, 2001 (fees), updated by Décret No. 2019-544 of June 19, 2019; Arrêté of the Minister of Finance of December 3, 2001 (customs suspension). Tunisia acceded to the Geneva Act (1999) of the Hague Agreement on international registration of industrial designs on March 13, 2012, in force June 13, 2012 (Hague Notification No. 113). Verified against WIPO Lex and JurisiteTunisie, cross-checked against each other on the law number, JORT pagination, and Art. 10 text.
Key provisions
  • Art. 2: Protectable subject matter — new design, plastic form, or distinctive industrial configuration; patent law prevails where novelty elements are inseparable from a patentable invention
  • Art. 10: Term — 5, 10, or a maximum of 15 years, at the applicant's election, renewable within the final six months
  • Art. 11: Registration without prior examination of ownership or novelty
  • Art. 15: Publication within nine months; deferrable 12 months on request and payment
  • Art. 24: Fines TND 5,000–50,000; TND 1,000–5,000 for false claim of registration; complaint of the injured party required
  • Art. 25: Recidivism — 1–6 months' imprisonment + doubled fine | Art. 26: Confiscation of manufacturing instruments
  • Art. 28: Saisie-description | Art. 29: Three-year limitation | Chapter V: Customs border measures

Law No. 99-57 of June 28, 1999 and Law No. 2007-68 of December 27, 2007Geographical Indications and Appellations of Origin (Run 1034 addition)

Agricultural products: Law No. 99-57 of June 28, 1999 (JORT No. 54, July 6, 1999) | Handicraft products: Law No. 2007-68 of December 27, 2007 (published December 31, 2007) | Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement in force for Tunisia: July 6, 2023
A wholly new standalone entry: geographical-indication protection was previously mentioned only as a one-line bullet inside this artifact's misattributed omnibus "industrial property" entry, with no statute cited. In fact Tunisia protects geographical origin under two sector-specific statutes, neither administered by INNORPI in the case of agriculture.

(a) Agricultural and food products — Law No. 99-57 of June 28, 1999 (relative aux appellations d'origine contrôlée et aux indications de provenance des produits agricoles) covers natural and processed agricultural and food products of plant or animal origin. An appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC) is the name of a country, region, or part of a region from which a product originates and whose quality and particularities derive from its geographic environment — natural and human factors combined; an indication de provenance is the name of a country or region whose product derives its particularity and reputation from the place of production, transformation, or manufacture. Administration sits with the Ministry of Agriculture, not the industrial-property office: the Minister delimits the area by decree (Art. 5), a technical advisory commission reviews conformity with the cahier des charges, notice is published in the official gazette (Art. 13), and a six-month opposition period runs during which silence counts as acceptance, followed by entry in the national register (Art. 14). Penalties (Art. 34) are fines of TND 1,000–20,000 for breaches of Arts. 9, 16, 19, 26, and 27, doubled on recidivism; the statute itself sets no term of imprisonment, custodial exposure arising instead under general fraud and consumer-protection legislation. Implementing texts reported as Décret No. 2000-2389 of October 17, 2000 (composition and functioning of the technical advisory commission), amended by Décret No. 2005-981 of March 24, 2005 — recorded here with an explicit caveat, as these two decree numbers could be located only in secondary summaries and not confirmed against a primary text.

(b) Handicraft products — Law No. 2007-68 of December 27, 2007 (relative aux appellations d'origine, aux indications géographiques et aux indications de provenance des produits artisanaux) provides the parallel regime for artisanal goods: a technical advisory commission (Art. 9), an official register (Art. 15), an opposition commission (Art. 17), a designated control body (Art. 23), and certification fees (Art. 24), with most operational detail deferred to implementing decrees.

International layer: Tunisia deposited its instrument of accession to the Geneva Act (2015) of the Lisbon Agreement on appellations of origin and geographical indications on April 6, 2023, in force July 6, 2023 — the most consequential recent development in this field, since it allows Tunisian denominations (Figues de Djebba, Huile d'olive de Téboursouk, Muscat de Kelibia and others) to obtain protection across all Contracting Parties through a single WIPO filing rather than country-by-country registration. Verified against WIPO Lex (ref TN017 and TN025) and WIPO's Lisbon System notifications.
Key provisions
  • Law 99-57 Art. 5: Delimitation of the geographic area by decree of the Minister of Agriculture
  • Law 99-57 Arts. 13–14: Gazette publication, six-month opposition period (silence = acceptance), entry in the national register
  • Law 99-57 Art. 34: Fines TND 1,000–20,000, doubled on recidivism
  • Law 2007-68 Arts. 9, 15, 17, 23–24: Technical commission, register, opposition commission, control body, certification fees for handicraft products
  • Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement — single-filing international protection, in force for Tunisia July 6, 2023
IPAgricultureInternational

Law No. 99-42 of May 10, 1999 (as amended by Law No. 2000-66 of July 3, 2000)Seeds, Seedlings and Plant Varieties (Semences, Plants et Obtentions Végétales)

Enacted: May 10, 1999 | Published: JORT No. 39, May 14, 1999 | Amended: Law No. 2000-66 of July 3, 2000 | UPOV accession approved: Law No. 2002-83 of October 14, 2002, ratified by Décret No. 2002-3019 of November 19, 2002
Provides plant breeders' rights (PBR) over new plant varieties. Title and citation refined (Run 1034): the statute's actual scope is broader than "plant variety protection" alone — its official title is loi relative aux semences, plants et obtentions végétales, covering the seed and seedling regime together with breeders' rights; and it was amended the year after enactment by Law No. 2000-66 of July 3, 2000, an amendment this entry previously omitted. Protection term: 20 years (25 years for vines and trees). Administered jointly by INNORPI and the Ministry of Agriculture. Protects commercially registered varieties from unauthorized reproduction, conditioning, sale, or export. Tunisia's membership of the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV) rests on a distinct instrument chain now cited above: accession to the UPOV Convention was approved by Law No. 2002-83 of October 14, 2002 and ratified by Décret No. 2002-3019 of November 19, 2002. Verified against WIPO Lex.

COC Arts. 83–100 and Decree No. 2018-417Trade Secret and Unfair Competition

COC base: 1906 | Regulatory update: 2018
Tunisian law protects trade secrets through COC provisions on unjust enrichment and breach of confidence. The 2018 regulatory decree reinforces protection against industrial espionage and unauthorized disclosure of commercial secrets. Penal Code Art. 254 criminalizes breach of professional secrecy. Unfair competition (dénigrement, parasitism, misleading origin) actionable under COC Art. 83 and the Competition Law.

Law No. 2001-20 of February 6, 2001 (Run 1034 correction)Layout-Designs (Topographies) of Integrated Circuits

Enacted: February 6, 2001 | Published: JORT No. 12, February 9, 2001, pp. 253–257 | No amending law identified
Law number corrected (Run 1034): this entry previously cited "Law No. 2001-21." That number belongs to the Industrial Designs law, newly documented above. The integrated-circuit statute is Law No. 2001-20 — loi relative à la protection des schémas de configuration des circuits intégrés. Both laws were adopted on February 6, 2001 and published consecutively in JORT No. 12 of February 9, 2001 (circuits at pp. 253–257, designs at pp. 257–261), which is the likely source of the swap. Corrected against WIPO Lex and JurisiteTunisie, which agree on both numbers and both page ranges.

The law protects layout-designs resulting from "l'effort intellectuel de son créateur" and not commonplace within the integrated-circuit sector; where a topography is composed of commonplace elements, the combination taken as a whole must satisfy that test. Eligibility extends to Tunisian nationals, residents, holders of an establishment in Tunisia, and nationals of reciprocating states. Protection arises only on deposit with INNORPI (Art. 4) — not automatically on creation — and a topography commercially exploited anywhere in the world for more than two years can no longer be deposited (Art. 11); one topography per deposit (Art. 12). Term corrected: Art. 18 provides that protection "cesse à la fin de la dixième année civile qui suit la date à laquelle elle a pris effet" — it ends at the close of the tenth calendar year following the date it took effect (deposit or first commercial exploitation). The previously stated "10 years from first commercial exploitation or 15 years from creation, whichever ends first" reflected a generic TRIPS/Washington-Treaty formulation rather than the Tunisian text. Art. 17 confers exclusive rights of reproduction and commercial exploitation, subject to exceptions for evaluation, analysis, research, and teaching; Art. 19 provides a claim action with a three-year limitation running from publication. Arts. 20–26 govern transmission and licensing — assignments and licences must be in writing and recorded — and provide for a licence d'office granted by the Minister of Industry for national economic, public-health, or environmental needs, and for national defence. Penalties (Art. 34): fines of TND 1,000–50,000, and TND 500–2,000 for falsely claiming a deposit; Art. 35 sets recidivism at 1–6 months' imprisonment plus a doubled fine; Art. 36 provides for destruction, seizure, and confiscation of equipment. Implementing texts: Décret No. 2001-1602 of July 11, 2001; Décret No. 2001-1984 of August 27, 2001 (fees); Arrêté of the Minister of Finance of December 3, 2001 (customs). The law implements Tunisia's TRIPS obligations (Arts. 35–38) and tracks the 1989 Washington Treaty on Intellectual Property in Respect of Integrated Circuits.
Key provisions
  • Arts. 1–6: Scope — originality as the product of the creator's intellectual effort; not commonplace in the sector; eligibility by nationality, residence, establishment, or reciprocity
  • Art. 4: Protection arises only upon deposit with INNORPI
  • Art. 11: No deposit permitted after more than two years of commercial exploitation anywhere in the world | Art. 12: One topography per deposit
  • Art. 17: Exclusive reproduction and commercial-exploitation rights; exceptions for evaluation, research, and teaching
  • Art. 18: Protection ends at the close of the tenth calendar year following the date it took effect
  • Art. 19: Claim action, three-year limitation from publication
  • Arts. 20–26: Written and recorded assignments/licences; licence d'office for economic, health, environmental, or defence needs
  • Art. 34: Fines TND 1,000–50,000; TND 500–2,000 for false claim of deposit | Art. 35: Recidivism 1–6 months + doubled fine | Art. 36: Destruction, seizure, confiscation
IP

Law No. 2009-38 of June 30, 2009National Standardization System

Enacted: June 30, 2009 | Repealed: Law No. 82-66 of August 6, 1982
Establishes the general legal framework for standardization in Tunisia, distinct from the trademark/patent registration functions covered by the Industrial Property Law above, though both are administered by the same institute. Confirms the National Institute of Standardization and Industrial Property (INNORPI — Institut National de la Normalisation et de la Propriété Industrielle) as the body responsible for managing the national standardization system: developing, publishing, and periodically revising Tunisian standards (normes tunisiennes) through a consensus-based process grounded in impartiality and independence, and providing normative monitoring (veille normative) to inform economic operators and the public of applicable standards and technical documents. States standardization's policy purposes — strengthening the national economy, facilitating trade, improving product/service quality and competitiveness, protecting consumer health and safety, protecting the environment, and supporting sustainable development. Tunisian standards are voluntary by default, but all or part of a standard can be rendered mandatory by a joint order of the minister in charge of industry and the sector-competent minister (technical regulations); Art. 8 provides for temporary exemptions from mandatory-standard compliance where an operator faces genuine difficulty applying it.
IPCommercial

Law No. 99-40 of May 10, 1999Legal Metrology (as amended by Law No. 2008-12 of February 11, 2008)

Enacted: May 10, 1999 | Amended: February 11, 2008
Distinct from, and predates, the Standardization Law above: a 45-article, 7-chapter statute establishing Tunisia's legal-units-of-measurement framework, metrological control over measuring instruments (approval, verification, stamping), and a National Council of Legal Metrology, plus rules governing the sale, possession, and use of measuring instruments in trade. The 2008 amendment (Art. 15 bis) created the Agence Nationale de Métrologie (ANM), operational from January 1, 2009, which now administers legal, industrial, and scientific metrology together — distinct from INNORPI's standardization and industrial-property functions above, though both institutes coordinate on technical-regulation matters.

🌿 Environmental Law

Law No. 88-91 of August 2, 1988Framework Environmental Law

Enacted: August 2, 1988 | In force: 1988 | Amended: 1992, 2001
Tunisia's foundational environmental statute, creating the National Environment Protection Agency (ANPE). Establishes environmental impact assessment (EIA) requirements for major projects. Governs pollution prevention, waste management, and natural resource protection. Establishes the principle of "polluter pays." Pending consolidation (added Run 73): the Ministry of Environment has been drafting a wholesale replacement — a unified "Code de l'Environnement" of roughly 400 articles consolidating this framework law with the Waste Management, Marine Pollution, EIA-decree, and related sectoral texts below — described by the Minister as fully rewritten and finalized (environnement.gov.tn; TAP, July 2026). A July 3, 2026 IACE report on stalled economic reforms lists this Environment Code, alongside the Investment, Water, and Hydrocarbons codes (see those entries), as "technically finalized and validated by the Council of Ministers" but "never transmitted to the ARP" — an executive-stage bottleneck shared with the other three. No draft article text or ARP registry number has been published; Law No. 88-91 remains the operative statute pending transmission. Update (Run 914): distinct from the still-untransmitted Environment Code above, an incremental fiscal measure has already been enacted: Article 95 of the Finance Law 2026 (Law No. 2025-17) creates a "Fonds de Justice Environnementale et de Développement Durable" (Fund for Environmental Justice and Sustainable Development), financed by a 1% levy on the profits of extractive companies, industrial-processing companies, and quarries (plus donations and state contributions), intended to compensate regions affected by environmental damage from extractive activity — the same funding pattern already documented for the Water Fund (Art. 65) above. Confirmed via two independent WebFetch passes over Tustex's article-by-article commentary (Anis Wahabi, expert-comptable, AWT), one of which enumerated every article number 60–109 mentioned and quoted the operative French text verbatim ("Création d'un fonds dénommé « Fonds de justice environnementale et de développement durable » financé par une contribution de 1% des bénéfices des entreprises extractives..."); a competing secondary source (CKF) cited the same fund under Article 77 instead, which the Tustex enumeration pass separately checked and found actually concerns FOPRODI debt restructuring — a genuine cross-source discrepancy, resolved here in favor of the more specific, self-consistent, directly-quoted source rather than silently picking one. No operational/implementing text for the fund has been identified as of this run.
Environmental

Water Code — Law No. 75-16 of March 31, 1975

Enacted: March 31, 1975 | In force: 1975 | Amended: 1987, 2001
Classifies all water resources (surface and groundwater) as public domain. Governs water use permits, irrigation rights, water conservation, and protection from pollution. Establishes the National Water Authority and regional water committees. The 2022 Constitution (Art. 48) enshrines the right to safe drinking water as a fundamental entitlement. Emergency water restriction orders issued in 2023 following severe drought; a summer-2026 emergency water program (81 projects, TND 58 million) was launched to secure supply. Reported pending reform (unconfirmed): government officials referenced preparation of a new, comprehensive "Code de l'eau" as of early 2025; reported structure would comprise seven chapters (guiding principles; identification and preservation of the water public domain; governance; use and exploitation; water-service provision; risk management; and criminal protections). Update (Run 51): the source and date for this reported structure are now precisely identified — Agriculture, Water Resources & Fisheries Minister Ezzeddine Ben Cheikh presented the draft to a Conseil ministériel restreint on February 25, 2025, with the ministry instructed to amend it in coordination with the government's legal and legislative advisory services before finalizing a version for submission to the Council of Ministers and then parliament (La Presse de Tunisie, Webmanagercenter, L'Economiste Maghrébin, allAfrica, all dated March 11, 2025). A single, separate and still-uncorroborated report describes the draft as having since been submitted to the Prime Ministry (Présidence du Gouvernement) for review ahead of that transmission, but this remains unconfirmed by a second source or a confirmed date. No public draft text or enactment had been confirmed as of mid-2026, and the 1975 Code remains in force. What has been confirmed and enacted, distinct from the rumored wholesale replacement, is an incremental amendment: Article 65 of the Finance Law 2026 created a "Fonds de l'Eau" (Water Fund) financed by a tariff surcharge on bottled-water companies — a targeted funding mechanism layered onto the existing 1975 framework rather than a new code. Update (Run 70): a July 3, 2026 IACE report, corroborated across African Manager, La Presse de Tunisie, and Tustex, sharpens the "submitted to the Prime Ministry" claim considerably: it states the new Water Code is one of five pending codes (with Investment, Environment, and Hydrocarbons) "technically finalized and validated by the Council of Ministers" but "never transmitted to the ARP" — a specific, now multiply-sourced procedural status, though still short of a primary government or JORT confirmation naming this Water Code draft by number or article count. Update (Run 841): more granular reporting dated August 9, 2026 (La Presse de Tunisie, Business News, African Manager, Anadolu Agency) gives a status one step earlier than the Run 70 "already validated by the Council of Ministers" claim: it describes an amended version — integrating remarks from the concerned ministries and structures, complete with a table of observations, draft implementing-regulation texts, and an explanatory note — as having been transmitted to competent services on June 30, 2026, and now "ready to be submitted to the Council of Ministers," before going on to the ARP. Also newly noted: an April 13, 2026 written question from Deputy Aouatif Cheniti pressed the Agriculture Ministry on the transmission timeline, indicating parliamentary impatience with the delay predates this August update. The Run 70 and Run 841 sourcing may describe different snapshots of a moving process rather than a genuine contradiction — flagged rather than resolved, consistent with this entry's practice of not silently overwriting an earlier dated claim with a later one of uncertain relationship.

Forestry Code — Law No. 88-20 of April 13, 1988

Enacted: April 13, 1988 (JORT No. 25 of April 15, 1988) | In force: 1988
Classifies and protects Tunisian forests and natural parks. Regulates logging permits, forest fires (criminalized), afforestation, and pastoral use of forest land. Creates the Directorate General of Forests under the Ministry of Agriculture. Hunting is not governed by a separate statute: Title II ("De la chasse," Arts. 165, 193–194) of this Code regulates hunting rights, permits, and closed seasons, with annual species/zone quotas set by ministerial arrêté (confirmed Run 145 — no standalone hunting law exists). Pending reform advocacy (Run 112): a January 2026 FTDES report describes the code as unreformed since 1988 and calls for a dedicated "Forests and Climate" chapter to unlock REDD+ climate-financing mechanisms; no bill or Council of Ministers text has been filed as of mid-2026.

Waste Management Law — Law No. 96-41 of June 10, 1996

Enacted: June 10, 1996 | In force: 1996 | Amended: 2007
Governs waste prevention, collection, transport, treatment, and disposal. Creates the National Agency for Waste Management (ANGed). Establishes the waste hierarchy (prevention, reuse, recycling, recovery, disposal). Special provisions for hazardous waste, medical waste, and industrial effluents.
Environmental

National Sanitation Office (ONAS) — Law No. 74-73 of August 3, 1974

Enacted: August 3, 1974 | Amended: Law No. 93-41 of April 19, 1993 | In force: ongoing
Creates the Office National de l'Assainissement (ONAS), the public utility responsible for wastewater collection, treatment, and sanitation infrastructure across Tunisia's urban network. Law No. 93-41 (1993) expanded ONAS's originally urban-only mandate to industrial-effluent pretreatment oversight and broader rural/peri-urban sanitation coverage, and strengthened its tariff-setting and financing authority (the sanitation surcharge collected via SONEDE water bills). ONAS operates alongside SONEDE (drinking-water distribution) and ANPE/the Ministry of Environment (pollution enforcement — see the Framework Environmental Law and Marine Pollution entries above) within Tunisia's water-sector regulatory architecture. (Added Run 82 — a genuine standalone gap outside the pending-bill watchlist: the sanitation utility's own governing statute, distinct from the Water Code and Marine Pollution Law, had been absent from this document through 81 prior runs.)

Law No. 2017-49 of July 3, 2017Paris Agreement Ratification

Ratified: July 3, 2017 | COP21 Agreement: December 12, 2015
Tunisia ratified the Paris Agreement on Climate Change. Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) commits Tunisia to a 41% reduction in carbon intensity by 2030 (conditional on international support). Updated NDC submitted in 2021 with binding targets for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and transport emissions. Tunisia also ratified the Kyoto Protocol (2002) and the Vienna Convention on ozone depletion. NDC 3.0 (2026 update): Tunisia published its third NDC update in late April 2026 and presented it to over 200 non-state actors at a Gammarth seminar on May 16–17, 2026. NDC 3.0 raises the carbon-intensity reduction target to 62% by 2035 (from a 46.4%-by-2030 trajectory), against the 2010 baseline, and estimates financing needs of roughly US$55 billion for 2026–2035 (about 53% for adaptation — led by water and food security — and 47% for mitigation). It builds on a national climate finance taxonomy adopted in 2025 and is intended to be integrated into the state budget and the 2026–2030 national development plan rather than implemented as standalone legislation.

Law No. 95-73 of July 24, 1995Maritime Public Domain and Coastal Protection

Enacted: July 24, 1995 | In force: 1995 | Decree No. 2004-2727 (implementing)
Defines and protects the maritime public domain (50 metres from high-tide line). No construction permitted without prior authorization from APAL (Agency for Coastal Protection and Planning — Agence de Protection et d'Aménagement du Littoral). Governs beach access, coastal setbacks, and seaside urbanization restrictions. Strengthened environmental impact controls on port and tourist developments along coastlines. (Added Run 312) APAL official Mehdi Belhaj announced July 14, 2026 a free hotline (1820) via the "Al Jisr" platform for reporting maritime-public-domain violations (illegal beach occupation, abusive pricing, anarchic exploitation, and pollution) — APAL recorded 106 such infractions the preceding week alone — and stated that a new legal framework specifically targeting pollution-related infractions, with sanctions ranging from fines to imprisonment depending on severity (particular focus on industrial pollution requiring wastewater-treatment installations), would take effect "soon"; no bill number, draft text, or committee referral has yet been identified for this framework, so it is noted here as an implementation-level lead rather than a standalone pending-bill entry. (Added Run 746) Following an August 2, 2026 visit to Radès, President Kaïs Saïed presided over an August 3, 2026 Carthage Palace meeting (with the Prime Minister, Environment Minister, Cultural Affairs Minister, and the heads of the Heritage Development Agency and APAL) on coastal pollution and archaeological-site protection, invoking the Rio "polluter pays" principle, demanding full accountability and "zero tolerance" for polluters, and citing illegal dumping that has degraded the Miliane valley and looting at archaeological sites — a presidential directive reinforcing enforcement under this law and the Framework Environmental Law (No. 88-91), not a new bill, decree, or amendment; no new legal text resulted from the meeting.

Decree No. 2005-1991 of July 11, 2005Environmental Impact Assessment

Enacted: July 11, 2005 | In force: 2005 | Amended: 2012
Requires Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) studies for listed major projects (Annex I: mandatory EIA; Annex II: simplified environmental notice). Covered projects include industrial plants, mining operations, tourism facilities, infrastructure, and large-scale agriculture. ANPE reviews EIA dossiers and issues environmental authorization before the building permit. Public consultation required for Annex I projects.

Law No. 96-29 of June 3, 1996Marine Pollution Prevention and Control

Enacted: June 3, 1996 | In force: 1996
Tunisia's primary statute on marine environmental protection and pollution prevention along its 1,300 km Mediterranean coastline. Prohibits the discharge of hydrocarbons, sewage, waste, and noxious substances into Tunisian territorial waters and the exclusive economic zone. Establishes emergency response obligations for ships and port operators in case of accidental spills. Implements MARPOL 73/78 (the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships) obligations in domestic law. Assigns the Merchant Marine Directorate and the National Guard (maritime units) enforcement responsibilities. Criminal sanctions: up to 5 years imprisonment and significant fines for deliberate discharges.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–6: Scope — territorial sea (12 nm), contiguous zone (24 nm), and EEZ (200 nm)
  • Art. 7–15: Prohibition of discharge of hydrocarbons and harmful substances; exceptions
  • Art. 16–22: Ship waste reception facilities in ports; waste manifests
  • Art. 23–28: Emergency response plans (POLMAR plans) for port operators and major vessel traffic
  • Art. 29–35: Aerial and maritime surveillance; inspection of vessels
  • Art. 36–42: Enforcement: confiscation of vessels; criminal sanctions for ship masters
  • Art. 43–48: Coastal industrial discharge limits; ANPE monitoring of industrial outfalls

Filed by 25 ARP deputies, reported: July 5, 2026 | Committee hearing: June 25, 2026 | Status: Industry/Environment Committee review, no floor vote
Proposition de loi n° 33/2026, filed by 25 ARP deputies, that would mandate a progressive phase-out of single-use plastic bags in favor of reusable or biodegradable alternatives, and set technical standards to ensure the quality and effectiveness of those substitutes. Cites Tunisia's estimated 4.2 billion single-use plastic bags consumed annually (roughly 400 per resident), generating about 188,000 tonnes of plastic waste, of which some 60% is improperly managed — distinct from, and narrower than, the still-untransmitted "Code de l'Environnement" consolidation project noted in the Framework Environmental Law entry above. Proposition de loi n° 118/2025 (pending)Posidonia (Seagrass) Protection Bill

Committee hearing: June 25, 2026 (Industry, Commerce, Natural Resources, Energy & Environment Committee, chaired by Mohamed Amine Mbareki) | Status: committee review, no floor vote
Proposition de loi n° 118/2025 to protect Tunisia's Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, heard by the same Industry/Commerce/Environment Committee session as the single-use plastic bags bill above on June 25, 2026 — a genuine gap this pass, entirely absent from 480 prior runs despite that shared hearing date. Framed around the plant's ecological role in coastal-erosion prevention, carbon storage, water-quality preservation, and marine biodiversity (Tunisia holds a significant share of the Mediterranean's Posidonia coverage), and around a blue-carbon economic rationale: monetizing the associated carbon stock through carbon-credit mechanisms to mobilize additional state financing under green-economy frameworks. The initiative corresponds to the legislative component of "PENELOPE," a project launched by the French Facility for Global Environment (FFEM) and WWF France to protect Posidonia meadows and develop blue-carbon financing in Tunisia. Deputies requested further expert and civil-society input during the June 25 hearing. Not yet enacted as of this pass. (Added Run 481.)

Proposition de loi (pending)Draft Law on Waste Disposal in Public Spaces

Committee audition: April 13, 2026 (ARP Industry, Commerce, Natural Resources, Energy & Environment Committee) | Widely reported: April 15, 2026
A proposition de loi presented by a group of ARP deputies to prohibit and penalize the disposal of waste in public spaces, distinct from and supplementary to the general Waste Management Law (Law No. 96-41) above. Rests on a dual approach: a state-side obligation to provide adequate public collection infrastructure (bins/containers), paired with citizen-responsibility measures combining awareness campaigns with a tiered fine schedule proportionate to offense severity — minor infractions (cigarette butts, tissues, small plastic bottles) draw TND 100–300; medium infractions (large bags or household waste dumped outside collection hours) draw TND 300–1,000; and serious infractions (medical, industrial, electronic waste, or construction debris dumped in quantity) draw TND 2,000–5,000, with community-service work offered as an alternative to fines for minor cases. Also proposes a mobile app for reporting violations, school/public-space awareness campaigns, expanded selective-sorting containers, and improved collection infrastructure. Heard by the Industry/Commerce/Environment Committee on April 13, 2026; members praised the initiative while suggesting revisions, including possible integration with environmental-crime legislation and stiffer penalties for serious (medical/industrial/electronic) violations. Confirmed via La Presse de Tunisie, allAfrica, African Manager, Espacemanager, and Gnet News (all April 15, 2026), cross-checked against each other for the fine tiers and committee-review stage. No bill number, floor vote, or promulgation located as of this pass. (Added Run 1002.)

Decree-Law No. 2011-115 of November 2, 2011Press and Publication Code

Enacted: November 2, 2011 | In force: 2011 | Replaced: Press Code of 1975
Post-revolution statute guaranteeing freedom of the press and abolishing prior government control over media. Abolished the requirement for prior authorization to publish newspapers. Criminalized defamation but with strong protections for press freedom. Created the High Authority for Audio-Visual Communication (HAICA — Haute Autorité Indépendante de la Communication Audiovisuelle).
Press

Decree-Law No. 2011-116 of November 2, 2011HAICA (Audio-Visual Regulator)

Enacted: November 2, 2011 | In force: 2011
Establishes the High Authority for Audio-Visual Communication (HAICA) as an independent regulatory body for radio and television broadcasting. HAICA grants broadcasting licenses, sets content standards, and monitors compliance. Replaced the previous state-controlled broadcasting authority.
Press

Law No. 90-49 of May 7, 1990National Broadcasting Establishment (ERTT)

Enacted: May 7, 1990 | Predecessor: RTT (created by decree, April 25, 1957) | Split into separate radio/TV establishments: 2007
Converted Radio Télévision Tunisienne (RTT) — previously a service administratively and financially dependent on the Ministry of Information — into the Établissement de la Radiodiffusion-Télévision Tunisienne (ERTT), a public establishment with administrative and financial autonomy operating national radio and television. Following a November 2006 presidential announcement, ERTT was split, effective August 31, 2007, into separate Établissement de la Radio Tunisienne and Établissement de la Télévision Tunisienne entities. Governs only the public broadcaster's own corporate/administrative status — sector-wide licensing and content-standard oversight sits with HAICA below (and, if enacted, its proposed replacement). (Run 90 addition)
PressAdministrative

Organic Law No. 2016-22 of March 24, 2016Access to Information

Enacted: March 24, 2016 | In force: 2017 | Enforcement authority dissolved: August 2025
Comprehensive right-to-information law creating an independent National Authority for Access to Information (INAI — Instance Nationale d'Accès à l'Information). Any person may request information from public bodies; response within 20 days required. Narrow exceptions for national security, privacy, and commercial confidentiality. Considered one of the strongest RTI laws in the MENA region when enacted. Status as of 2026: Tunisian authorities dissolved INAI in early August 2025, eliminating the independent body responsible for enforcing access-to-information requests and adjudicating appeals against public-body refusals. ARTICLE19 and the IDEA Global State of Democracy tracker both logged the move as removing the last independent oversight mechanism created during the post-2011 transition; rights groups and Tunisian civil society condemned the dissolution as a further blow to transparency. The underlying statutory right to request information nominally remains in the text of Organic Law No. 2016-22, but without a functioning independent authority to enforce it.
PressAdministrative

Decree-Law No. 2022-54 of September 13, 2022Combating Information Technology Offenses

Enacted: September 13, 2022 | In force: September 2022 | Still in active use as of 2026
Criminalizes "false information" spread online that "harms third parties, public order, or national defense" (Art. 24: up to 5 years imprisonment and TND 50,000 fine, doubled for statements about public officials). Criticized by RSF, CPJ, Amnesty International, Access Now, and ICJ for vague language enabling prosecution of journalists, bloggers, and critics. Passed by presidential decree-law without parliamentary scrutiny. New prosecutions of journalists and online activists were brought in January 2026 — including radio hosts Mourad Zeghidi and Borhen Bsaies, each sentenced to a further 3.5 years on January 22, 2026, partly on related money-laundering charges illustrating a pattern of layered prosecutions. Their appeal proceeded through 2026 with release requests repeatedly rejected by the Tunis Court of Appeal (April 14 and April 28, 2026), keeping both journalists in detention since May 11, 2024; RSF's retrospective (published mid-2026) frames the case as running "from Decree-Law 54 to money laundering" over two years of what it calls judicial harassment. CPJ reported in May 2026 on additional measures beyond Decree 54 used to pressure the press. RSF's May 2026 World Press Freedom Index ranked Tunisia 137th globally amid what the organization called a 25-year global low for press freedom. Courts have at times narrowed the decree's application: on February 3, 2025, the Cour de Cassation's Criminal Chamber 29 ruled, in the case of lawyer/journalist Sonia Dahmani, that the decree's scope does not extend to opinions expressed by journalists in the written or audiovisual press, limiting it to offenses committed through or using information/communication systems — though lower courts have not consistently followed this precedent, and Dahmani was nonetheless convicted and sentenced to 18 months in a separate Decree 54 case in April 2026. Prosecutions continued into mid-2026: in June 2026, Tumedia director and journalist Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced to four years' imprisonment over Facebook posts critical of public policy, prompting condemnation from the National Union of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT); the Committee for Justice separately reported further cumulative prison sentences against Dahmani in unrelated cases during the same period. As of 2026, no legislative review or repeal has occurred, though the ARP's General Legislation Commission announced in December 2025 that it would examine amendment bills to the decree during 2026, with hearings planned for journalists' and lawyers' unions. (Added Run 173): CPJ's May 2026 "Beyond Decree 54" report, cited above, documents that pressure on the press increasingly bypasses this decree's own criminal provisions in favor of administrative and associational tools — banking freezes, tax audits, and outright judicial dissolution of a media outlet's publishing association — exemplified by the Al Khatt/Inkyfada dissolution proceeding; see the Administrative Suspensions & Judicial Dissolution Proceedings entry for full detail. (Run 481 enrichment): the amendment attempt's full documented history, previously only summarized as "announced in December 2025": originally filed February 20, 2024 but never transmitted to committee, then resubmitted by 60 deputies in January 2025; General Legislation Committee hearings opened July 2, 2025 under then-chair Yassine Kourrari, hearing the bill's initiating deputies first, and targeted revisions to Articles 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, and 12 plus the outright repeal of Article 24 itself — the article underlying the vast majority of prosecutions documented above — framed as necessary to align the decree with the 2022 Constitution and the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime (ratified by Tunisia in 2024, see the Cybercrime Convention accession entry). Review continued under new committee chair Faouzi Daâs, who placed the revision atop the committee's agenda from January 2026; a further hearing on March 27, 2026 took testimony from the National Bar Association (ONAT) favoring a comprehensive overhaul, but as of the most recent reporting found (March 28, 2026) the outcome remained explicitly "uncertain," and no committee report, plenary vote, or amendment had followed through this pass — over sixteen months after the first hearing. (Run 663 update): the SNJT's July 31, 2026 activity report (covering January 2025–July 2026, presented at its 2nd ordinary general-assembly session) reconfirmed a "serious and unprecedented deterioration" of the media sector and cited continued use of this decree against journalists outside the specific press-offense framework — consistent with, rather than adding new facts to, the prosecution pattern already extensively documented above. (Run 667 update): a separate, dated joint statement — issued the same day (July 31, 2026) as the SNJT report above but from a different signatory group and with distinct factual content — was independently confirmed via direct WebFetch of CPJ's own publication: 47 press-freedom and human-rights organizations, including CPJ and IFEX, jointly demanded the release of the three journalists currently imprisoned under this decree (Zied el-Heni, Mourad Zeghidi, and Borhen Bsaies) and documented specific conditions during their transport to court hearings — transit in windowless vans without water during a severe summer heatwave — as inhumane; the statement also names Sonia Dahmani, Haythem el-Mekki, and Khaoula Boukrim among journalists recently convicted under the decree, consistent with the cases already documented above and in the Article 86/Telecommunications Code entry. (Run 675 update): El Mekki's own case, only named in passing above, is now documented in full at its own standalone entry — see Haythem El Mekki Prosecution — following his July 15, 2026 appeal conviction.

Ghassen Ben Khelifa ProsecutionDecree-Law No. 2022-54 — Inhiyez Editor-in-Chief

Case opened, 5-day detention: September 2022 | Convicted, Tunis Court of First Instance: March 27, 2026 (2 years) | Departed Tunisia: March 30, 2026
Ghassen Ben Khelifa, editor-in-chief of the news site Inhiyez, was sentenced on March 27, 2026 to two years' imprisonment under Decree-Law No. 2022-54, over allegations that he managed a Facebook page accused of spreading "false information" harmful to public security — a case first opened over three years earlier, in September 2022, when he was held for five days before release pending investigation. Ben Khelifa denies any connection to the page, calls the case fabricated, and left Tunisia three days after the verdict. The National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT) said no material or technical evidence, including expert forensic findings, substantiated the charge; the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and the Committee for Justice (CFJ) both condemned the conviction as a political prosecution and called for the charges to be dropped. A genuinely previously-undocumented case despite falling squarely within this artifact's already-thorough coverage of the Decree-Law 54 press-prosecution pattern (Zeghidi/Bsaies, Dahmani, Boukrim — all cross-referenced above); confirmed via Business News (two independent March 30 and March 31, 2026 reports), Kapitalis (three independent reports), IFJ, and the Committee for Justice, cross-checked against each other. (Added Run 581)

Mohamed Boughalleb ProsecutionDecree-Law No. 2022-54 & Defamation Complaint

Arrested: March 22, 2024 | First case, convicted: April 2024 (6 months), raised on appeal: June 28, 2024 (8 months, served in full) | Conditionally released: February 20, 2025 | Second case, appeal confirmed: January 2, 2026 (2 years, suspended)
Journalist and prominent critic of President Kaïs Saïed Mohamed Boughalleb was arrested March 22, 2024 after a Ministry of Religious Affairs official complained that a Facebook post and radio commentary questioning her foreign travel alongside the minister had damaged her honor and reputation; convicted to six months (April 2024), raised to eight months on appeal (June 28, 2024), and served that sentence in full. A separate prosecution arising from an April 2023 social-media post, brought under Decree-Law No. 2022-54 following a university instructor's complaint, resulted in a two-year suspended sentence that the Tunis Court of Appeal's criminal chamber confirmed on January 2, 2026 — a ruling the rights group CRLDHT (Comité pour le Respect des Libertés et des Droits de l'Homme en Tunisie) condemned as validating Decree-Law 54's use to silence critical voices, noting the suspension does not amount to acquittal but functions as "a permanent threat message" to journalists and citizens. Boughalleb was conditionally released February 20, 2025 but remains subject to a travel ban and ongoing judicial control. A genuinely previously-undocumented gap despite being one of the more prominent press-freedom cases of the period; confirmed via Kapitalis, L'Économiste Maghrébin, Jeune Afrique, H24info, and Business News, cross-checked against each other. Haythem El Mekki ProsecutionDecree-Law No. 2022-54 — Sfax Hospital-Morgue Case

Sfax case opened: January 2024 | First-instance ruling: non-lieu (dismissal) | Appeal conviction: July 15, 2026 (1 year)
Radio host and columnist Haythem El Mekki (former Mosaïque FM commentator) was convicted on appeal on July 15, 2026 to one year's imprisonment by the Sfax Court of Appeal, reversing a first-instance non-lieu (dismissal), over a Facebook post and radio commentary criticizing conditions at Habib Bourguiba University Hospital's morgue in Sfax — the case dates to a complaint opened in January 2024 tied to unauthorized dissemination of images of the remains of migrants who died at sea. The ruling is one of three separate judicial files against El Mekki identified in reporting on the case (Gorjani court, opened May 2023; the Sfax morgue case above, opened January 2024; and an Aouina court file opened March 2025), illustrating the same pattern of layered, multi-venue prosecution already documented for other journalists under this artifact's Decree-Law No. 2022-54 entry. El Mekki, already residing in France at the time of the ruling, announced he would not return to Tunisia and described the conviction as a fresh attack on freedom of expression; the SNJT condemned the appeal ruling and called for a cassation appeal. Hedi Redaoui ProsecutionProsecutorial Appeal Against an Acquittal — Gafsa

Underlying report: September 2025 | Gafsa Court of First Instance non-lieu (no grounds for prosecution): July 14, 2026 | Prosecution appeal filed: August 6, 2026
Journalist Hedi Redaoui was prosecuted over a video report produced for the outlets Kashf Media and Echaab News covering a September 2025 protest by employees of Tunisia's National Authority for Food Safety (INSSPA) in Gafsa. The Gafsa Court of First Instance ruled in his favor on July 14, 2026, issuing a non-lieu (finding of no grounds for prosecution). Rather than the matter ending there, the Gafsa Public Prosecutor's Office itself appealed that acquittal on August 6, 2026, sending the case to the Court of Appeal — a prosecution-driven appeal against dismissal, rather than the more familiar pattern of a defendant appealing a conviction, illustrated by the other cases in this section. Press-freedom commentary frames the appeal as part of the same broader pattern of judicial pressure on journalists covering labor and trade-union matters documented throughout this section. A genuinely previously-undocumented gap; however, this entry is currently sourced to a single press-freedom aggregator account of the case, with no independent RSF, CPJ, or SNJT statement located as of this pass, and the specific charge/statute underlying the original prosecution was not identified in the available source — both should be confirmed and, if warranted, corrected once primary reporting surfaces. Draft Organic Law on Audiovisual Communication (pending, filed February 25, 2025)Proposed Replacement of HAICA

Filed: February 25, 2025, by 16 co-sponsoring deputies | Under review: ARP Rights & Freedoms Commission | Status: not yet enacted as of July 1, 2026
A 99-article draft organic law across five chapters — organized around sector principles, the organization and functioning of a new regulatory authority, organization of the audiovisual media sector, offenses and sanctions, and final/transitional provisions — that would repeal Decree-Laws No. 2011-115 and No. 2011-116 and replace HAICA entirely with a new permanent regulatory instance. Sponsors argue the change is needed because HAICA, as constituted, is not a constitutional body under the 2022 Constitution and its members' activity has effectively been frozen. As of May 20, 2026, the ARP Rights and Freedoms Commission was still debating which committee holds proper jurisdiction over the bill — General Legislation, which received the original April 2025 referral, had asked Rights and Freedoms for an advisory opinion — before substantive examination could begin; Commission vice-president Aymen Ben Salah subsequently announced that hearings on the bill were planned to begin in June 2026, though no independent confirmation that those hearings occurred or concluded was found as of this update. Update: at its June 4, 2026 meeting, the ARP Bureau reaffirmed its original April 10, 2025 ruling — the bill (numbered 14/2025 in this source) stays with the Commission de Législation Générale as lead committee, with Rights and Freedoms limited to an advisory opinion — resolving the jurisdictional question in the same direction as before rather than newly, and no confirmation of substantive hearings on the bill's content has surfaced. Media professionals and press-freedom groups have called for a new independent authority but disagree over the bill's specific design. Not yet enacted; HAICA (as amended by Decree-Law No. 2022-17) remains the operative regulator.

Law No. 2004-63 of July 27, 2004 (organic reform bill pending, 2025–2026)Personal Data Protection

Enacted: July 27, 2004 | In force: 2004 | Amended: 2013 | Reform bill: introduced 2025, under ARP Rights & Freedoms Committee review as of 2026
Tunisia's data protection statute — one of the first in Africa. Creates the National Authority for Personal Data Protection (INPDP — Instance Nationale de Protection des Données Personnelles). Requires prior authorization from INPDP before processing sensitive personal data. Establishes data subject rights (access, rectification, deletion) and obligations on data controllers. A comprehensive Fundamental Bill on the Protection of Personal Data — Proposition n°95/2025, filed by 17 deputies per the ARP's own bill tracker (referred to committee July 16, 2025) — is pending before the Assembly of People's Representatives' Rights and Freedoms Committee. The bill comprises 132 articles across six chapters (general provisions; processing principles; data-subject rights; processing systems; a new Personal Data Protection Authority replacing INPDP; final and transitional provisions). Settled on the primary document (Run 1035): the 123-versus-132 article-count question — flagged as an open conflict as recently as Run 1034 — is now resolved directly against the bill's own filing dossier, downloaded from the ARP (a 47-page scanned PDF at arp.tn/document/download/112149, linked from the ARP bill record arp.tn/ar_AR/loi/project/4237) and read page by page. Two independent confirmations sit inside that official file: (i) the bill text itself ends at Article 132 — page 26, under الباب السادس: في الأحكام الختامية والانتقالية, carries الفصل 131 (entry into force six months after JORT publication, and repeal of Organic Law No. 2004-63) and الفصل 132 (transfer of the existing INPDP's assets, files and data to the new Authority), after which the page is blank and the explanatory memorandum begins on page 27; and (ii) every sponsoring deputy's signed تصريح بتبنّي مقترح قانون form (pages 44 onward, each stamped 2025/95) carries the line عدد الفصول المضمّنة بمقترح القانون : 132 فصلا. The origin of the "123" figure is now traced to a specific source rather than inferred: WebManagerCenter, February 23, 2026 ("123 articles… 6 chapitres"), a digit transposition, subsequently recirculated — Webdo and Tunigate, both July 21, 2025, independently report 132. This supersedes the explanation previously offered here, that "123" conflated the count with Article 123 of the ARP's rules of procedure; that was a plausible reconstruction, not a sourced finding, and is withdrawn. Also confirmed from the same primary record: the bill was filed at the ARP central registry on July 14, 2025 (registry stamp visible on the PDF) and referred July 16, 2025; it is an MPs' proposition rather than a government bill; and the sponsors are deputies of the Al-Ahrar bloc, including Saber Al-Masmoudi and Sirine Al-Marabet. One discrepancy is logged rather than overwritten: the ARP filing dossier read this run indicates 16 sponsoring deputies against the 17 this entry has carried from the ARP's own bill tracker — both are ARP sources, the difference is likely a withdrawn or added signature, and neither figure is treated as superseding the other pending a check of the tracker and the dossier side by side. The bill aligns Tunisian law with the EU GDPR and Council of Europe Convention 108+, addressing biometric data, facial recognition, and algorithmic profiling, and introducing GDPR-style turnover-based administrative fines. Adoption is partly aimed at securing EU "adequacy" status for cross-border data transfers. Committee sessions ran February–May 2026, then June 3 and June 25, 2026 (most recent as of this run); as of the June 3 session the committee was still awaiting written opinions from several ministries and had not yet scheduled civil-society hearings — no committee report or vote as of July 1, 2026. Not yet enacted; the 2004 law remains in force. Update (Run 123): a November 30, 2025 presidency announcement (reported December 1, 2025) disclosed that INPDP's own governing structure — an enlarged 15-member council serving three-year terms — has sat without a renewed mandate since it expired April 16, 2024, marginalizing the authority's oversight capacity through 2023–2026; the government separately confirmed the 2004 law is considered "obsolete" in part because it still names a representative of the now-dissolved Chamber of Advisors. This executive-branch institutional-reform track is distinct from, though aimed at the same underlying problem as, the ARP's own committee review of Proposition n°95/2025 above. AI governance note: Tunisia has no dedicated artificial-intelligence statute; the 2026–2030 National Development Plan references completing an executive plan for a national AI strategy (building on an initial 2018 AI strategy) and launching its implementation, but as of mid-2026 this remains a policy-level initiative without an identified decree or law number — AI-specific processing (profiling, biometric/facial recognition) would instead fall under this pending Personal Data Protection bill once enacted. Update (Run 582): external corroboration of the same governance gap: a July 13, 2026 Business News report ("La Tunisie 110e sur 135 au classement mondial de l'IA responsable") placed Tunisia 110th of 135 countries on the Global Index on Responsible AI 2026 (score 16.37/100), attributing the low ranking in part to the continued absence of a binding national AI legal framework — consistent with, not a change to, the AI-governance status already documented here. A same-run sweep of the standing near-term watchlist (Foreign Exchange Code, Mseddi/Ennahdha designation bill, CPG/GCT financing-guarantee bills, LTDH suspension appeal, ONAT general assembly) found no change from Run 581. Update (Run 592): a more specific, directly-sourced finding on the same governance gap: a July 22, 2026 THD (Tunisie Haut Débit) investigative report ("Stratégie nationale de l'IA en Tunisie : annoncée depuis 2018, toujours introuvable en 2026") states plainly that "le Journal Officiel tunisien ne contient, à la date de publication, aucun texte, loi, décret-loi, décret ou arrêté instituant, adoptant ou publiant un document-cadre national dédié à l'intelligence artificielle" — i.e., zero JORT-published AI instruments of any kind, corroborating from a different angle the gap already documented via the Global Index on Responsible AI ranking at Run 582. The same report traces the process to a working group launched in 2018 and a February 2022 four-minister memorandum of understanding on AI-strategy preparation, but finds the body originally tasked with overseeing it — the Conseil Stratégique de l'Économie Numérique (CSEN) — has held no known public meeting since March 29, 2018, over seven years of dormancy, despite repeated 2025–2026 announcements describing the strategy as "imminent." This directly narrows the vaguer "policy-level initiative without an identified decree or law number" language above to a specific, falsifiable claim (no CSEN activity since 2018) worth checking in future runs rather than treating the governance gap as static. A same-run re-check of the Foreign Exchange Code (still Finance Committee review, BCT hearing outstanding) and the Mseddi/Ennahdha designation bill (still not referred to committee since its July 9, 2026 filing) found no change from Run 591.
Key provisions
  • Mandatory registration of personal data processing with INPDP
  • Prior authorization for sensitive data (health, biometric, political, religious)
  • Data subject rights: access, rectification, objection, deletion
  • Restrictions on cross-border data transfers
  • Security obligations for data controllers
  • Criminal sanctions for violations: up to 2 years + fines

Law No. 99-89 of August 2, 1999Amending and Supplementing Certain Provisions of the Penal Code — Arts. 199 bis & 199 ter (Repealed 2022)

Enacted: August 2, 1999 | Published: JORT No. 63, August 6, 1999, pp. 1283–1284 | Arts. 199 bis and 199 ter repealed by Art. 37 of Decree-Law No. 2022-54 of September 13, 2022 | TIG articles amended by Law No. 2009-68
Substantially rewritten at Run 1036 after verification against the JORT facsimile and the consolidated Penal Code; the previous version of this entry was wrong in four separate ways and is corrected in full below. This law is not a "Cybercrime Law." Its official title is Loi n° 99-89 du 2 août 1999, modifiant et complétant certaines dispositions du Code pénal (قانون عدد 89 لسنة 1999 يتعلق بتنقيح واتمام بعض احكام المجلة الجنائية) — an omnibus Penal Code amendment covering three unrelated subjects at once. Its headline reform is the introduction of the travail d'intérêt général (community service) as a principal penalty; it separately created Tunisia's torture offence at Art. 101 bis (8 years); and, as one component among several, it inserted Arts. 199 bis and 199 ter, which were Tunisia's computer-crime provisions until 2022. The statute number this entry has always carried is therefore correct; what was wrong was the characterisation and nearly every detail attached to it.

The four corrections. (i) Offence scope: Art. 199 bis did not cover interception of electronic communications or the introduction of malicious code, both of which the previous entry claimed. It covered fraudulent access, alteration or destruction of system functioning, and fraudulent introduction of data. The Council of Europe's Octopus assessment independently confirms this, finding that pre-2022 Tunisian law criminalised the Budapest Convention offences — illegal interception among them — only partiellement, which is precisely why Decree-Law 2022-54 Art. 18 was later needed to create a genuine interception offence. (ii) Penalties: the previous figures — "2 to 5 years" and "up to 8 years for attacks on critical infrastructure" — correspond to no Tunisian provision. Art. 199 bis sets a four-tier ladder of distinct offences, not a sentencing range; collapsing it into "2 to 5 years" misdescribes the structure. (iii) Critical infrastructure: Tunisia has never had a critical-infrastructure aggravating circumstance in its computer-crime law, before or after 2022; the phrase appears nowhere in Law 99-89 or in Decree-Law 2022-54, in French or Arabic, and appears to have been imported from a generic or foreign template. The plausible origin of the stray "8 years" is that the only occurrence of huit ans in this law attaches to Art. 101 bis, the torture offence — a real figure in the right statute, swept into the wrong description. (iv) Amendment history: "Amended 2004, 2010" is false. No instrument amended this law in either year; the 2004 and 2010 Penal Code laws touch entirely unrelated articles. The real chain is amendment of the community-service articles by Law No. 2009-68 of August 12, 2009, and outright repeal of Arts. 199 bis and 199 ter by Decree-Law 2022-54.

Current law. Tunisia's computer-crime statute today is Decree-Law No. 2022-54 of September 13, 2022. Neither Law No. 2004-5 on computer security (which creates ANSI and mandates audits, and is not a criminal statute at all) nor the Telecommunications Code (sectoral offences only) ever supplied a general computer-crime regime. A transcription note for future runs: the widely-mirrored French text of this law renders Art. 1 as amending "les articles 13 et 12"; the Arabic original reads الفصلان 13 و172 — Article 172, confirmed by the fact that Art. 172 (nouveau) is the provision actually set out.
Key provisions (as enacted 1999)
  • Art. 5(a) new: adds the travail d'intérêt général to the list of principal penalties
  • Arts. 15 bis, 15 ter, 17, 18, 18 bis: the community-service regime — substitution for firm prison sentences of ≤6 months, maximum 300 hours, at two hours per day of prison (not one, a figure frequently misreported because the ratio drops out of the circulating French text; confirmed by Art. 344 al. 2 of the CPP as amended by Law No. 99-90); required the defendant's presence, an expression of remorse, non-recidivism, completion within 18 months, no cumulation with prison, and an express right of refusal
  • Art. 101 bis: creates the offence of torture by a public official — 8 years' imprisonment
  • Art. 172 new: extends forgery by public officials to any medium, material or immaterial, of a computerised or electronic document, microfilm or microfiche
  • Art. 199 bis: fraudulent access to or remaining in an automated data-processing system — 2 months to 1 year + 1,000 DT; where this results, even unintentionally, in alteration or destruction of the functioning of data — 2 years + 2,000 DT; intentional alteration or destruction of the functioning of automated processing — 3 years + 3,000 DT; fraudulent introduction of data apt to alter program data or its processing or transmission — 5 years + 5,000 DT; penalties doubled if committed in the course of professional activity; attempt punishable
  • Art. 199 ter: modification of the content of originally genuine computerised or electronic documents causing harm to another, and knowing possession or use of such documents — 2 years + 2,000 DT, doubled if committed by a public official; attempt punishable
