Telecommunications Code — Law No. 2001-1 of January 15, 2001

Enacted: January 15, 2001 | In force: 2001 | Amended: 2002, 2008, 2013
Liberalizes the telecommunications sector and establishes the independent regulator (INT — Instance Nationale des Télécommunications). Governs licensing of operators, frequency management, interconnection, universal service obligations, and quality standards. Opened mobile and internet markets to competition. Article 86 — criminalizing "knowingly harming others or disturbing their peace" via public telecommunications networks, up to 2 years' imprisonment — has been repeatedly used against journalists and commentators alongside Decree-Law No. 2022-54 (see Criminal Law section). Update (Run 63): journalist Zied El Heni was sentenced to one year in prison under Article 86 on May 7, 2026 (arrested April 24, 2026 after sharing a social-media post criticizing the treatment of journalist Khalifa Guesmi); the Tunis Court of Appeal confirmed the sentence on June 26, 2026. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), the International Federation of Journalists, and the Committee for Justice condemned the ruling as an abusive use of the telecom-harassment provision to suppress press criticism. Update (Run 182): former deputy Rached Khiari was also convicted under Article 86, over a Facebook publication alleging "disclosure of confidential documents"; his first-instance 8-month sentence was reduced to 6 months on appeal by the Tunis Court of Appeal's correctional chamber on April 10, 2026. Rights group CFJ (Committee for Justice) condemned the sentence as political and separately raised concern for Khiari's health, reporting he had been released from an earlier detention in grave condition with chest tumors and alleging inadequate medical care while detained (CFJ, Kapitalis, L'Économiste Maghrébin). Update (Run 240): Zied El Heni faces a second, legally distinct prosecution — not under Article 86 but under the Anti-Terrorism Law (Organic Law No. 2015-26, see Countering Terrorism entry above), before the specialized anti-terrorism chamber rather than an ordinary correctional court. The case (the "affaire Ounissi") originates from his journalistic verification of information later used to summon him before the anti-terrorism unit as early as March 2024. A hearing was held July 10, 2026 without El Heni, his family, or his defense counsel being informed and without his transfer to court, drawing condemnation from his support committee and press-freedom advocates over the denial of basic defense-rights guarantees (businessnews.com.tn, July 10, 2026). No verdict has been reported as of this run. Update (Run 260): the case's namesake, Mondher Ounissi (Ennahdha's former interim party president), has his own parallel proceeding before the same specialized anti-terrorism chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance, over the online circulation of audio recordings attributed to him discussing a meeting with businessmen and alleged Ennahdha-linked financial violations — the underlying facts El Heni is accused of having journalistically verified. On July 11, 2026, the chamber rejected Ounissi's release request and postponed his case to September 25, 2026 (Kapitalis, Business News, July 11, 2026). No verdict has been reported for either defendant as of this run. Update (Run 338): journalist and radio chronicler Haythem El Mekki, previously cleared by a first-instance non-lieu (dismissal), had that dismissal reversed by the Sfax Court of Appeal on July 15, 2026, which convicted him and imposed a one-year prison sentence under this Article 86, over a January 2024 Facebook post criticizing internal conditions at Sfax's Habib Bourguiba University Hospital (whose administration filed the original complaint). Proceedings had initially been opened under Decree-Law No. 2022-54 before the conviction was ultimately entered under Article 86 instead — the same charge-substitution pattern already documented above for El Heni and Khiari. The SNJT (National Union of Tunisian Journalists) condemned the ruling and announced it would pursue a cassation appeal. Independently corroborated by Kapitalis, Business News, L'Économiste Maghrébin, webdo.tn, and Gnet News (all July 15, 2026). Update (Run 393): a distinct, older case became public July 17, 2026: journalist Hamza Belloumi and journalist Insaf Boughdiri (former editor-in-chief of the political program "Le Huitième Jour"/Al Hiwar Ettounsi) were convicted in absentia by the Tunis Court of Appeal in June 2026 to one year's imprisonment plus an 8,000-dinar fine each, in a prosecution dating to a May 2015 complaint by then-president Moncef Marzouki over a video segment aired on their program that was later shown to have been edited to falsely suggest he called for violence. The investigating judge at the Manouba tribunal had already rejected the plaintiff's "criminal conspiracy" (association de malfaiteurs) theory against the pair (and co-defendants Sofiène Ben Hamida and Noureddine Ben Ticha), characterizing the facts instead as professional misconduct without intent to defame; a Manouba first-instance default judgment in 2024 imposed only a fine, before the prosecution's appeal produced the harsher June 2026 custodial sentence, which the SNJT's July 18, 2026 statement links to the broader pattern of Article 86 prosecutions documented above for El Heni, Khiari, and El Mekki. Both defendants say they were never notified of any hearing at either instance and so could not exercise their right to defense; they have filed opposition, with a hearing before the Tunis Court of Appeal set for July 21, 2026 — outcome not yet known as of this run. Independently corroborated by Business News (three separate pieces), Kapitalis, Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, La Presse de Tunisie, Réalités Magazine, and allAfrica. Update (Run 463): that July 21, 2026 opposition hearing concluded — the Tunis Court of Appeal's correctional chamber accepted the opposition, annulled the in-absentia judgment against both journalists, and referred the case back for a full new examination on the merits, with the next hearing set for December 2, 2026. Corroborated by La Presse, Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, and Kapitalis (all July 21–22, 2026). Update (Run 517): a further case surfaced by the same SNJT July 18, 2026 statement, though on a materially different footing from the cases above: journalist and former HAICA council member Hichem Snoussi was convicted in absentia by the Tunis Court of First Instance to six months' imprisonment, in a case tied to a complaint filed years earlier by Nessma TV founder Nabil Karoui over statements Snoussi made — while serving on HAICA — about Nessma's ownership structure and the identity of its owners. Unlike the El Heni, Khiari, El Mekki, and Belloumi/Boughdiri cases above, no source found specifies the particular statute underlying the conviction (Article 86 is not independently confirmed for this case, only inferred from the pattern), so it is noted here as a related but not confirmed-identical charge. As with Belloumi/Boughdiri, Snoussi says he was not properly notified of the proceedings; he has since filed an opposition, with a new hearing set for October 2026. Sourced solely to Business News' July 18, 2026 report of Snoussi's own public statement — a second independent outlet was searched for but not found, so this is flagged as single-source pending future corroboration, consistent with this artifact's practice for time-sensitive same-day findings. Update (Run 631) — corroborated, SNJT statement content added: the SNJT issued a further, dedicated statement of solidarity on July 29, 2026 (rather than merely the July 18 statement grouping Snoussi with other cases), independently reported by both Kapitalis ("Le SNJT solidaire avec Hichem Snoussi condamné à six mois de prison") and Réalités Magazine ("Hichem Snoussi condamné à 6 mois de prison: le SNJT s'exprime") — resolving the single-source flag standing since Run 517 with two further, mutually-corroborating domestic outlets. Both confirm the six-month sentence, the 2019 Nessma-ownership-disclosure basis, and the accepted opposition/October 2026 rehearing date exactly as already documented, and add the union's substantive position: the SNJT called the conviction "surprising," argued that ownership information about influential media outlets concerns the public interest and media-transparency principles, and called for a stronger legislative framework guaranteeing media transparency, pluralism, and the public's right to information — while reaffirming support for Snoussi. No new procedural development (verdict, appeal outcome) was reported beyond what Run 517 already captured. Update (Run 1073): a further Article 86 case surfaced this run: Seifeddine Arfaoui, a 23-year-old activist with the opposition Nafas movement, was arrested following a Nafas-organized protest against President Kaïs Saïed's government in Tunis on August 20, 2026, after being filmed leading protest chants with a megaphone; reporting attributes the charge to slogans deemed offensive to the head of state. The Tunis Court of First Instance's Public Prosecutor issued a mandat de dépôt (detention order) against him on August 24, 2026 under this Article 86, with a hearing before the Tunis summer criminal chamber scheduled for August 27, 2026 and a maximum exposure of two years' imprisonment. The Nafas movement publicly called for his release, framing the arrest as a restriction on protest speech, and deputy Mohamed Abbou separately raised public questions about the circumstances of the arrest. This is reported as the second Nafas-affiliated Article 86 prosecution, following journalist Zied El Heni's own arrest documented above — El Heni is likewise associated with the Nafas movement in this later reporting, a detail not previously cross-referenced in this entry. Confirmed via Kapitalis (August 22 and 25, 2026) and Business News (August 22 and 24, 2026), cross-checked against each other; the August 27, 2026 hearing's outcome is an open item for a future run. Update (Run 1088): the hearing before the Tunis summer criminal chamber took place as scheduled on August 27, 2026; no verdict, remand decision, or further postponement had been reported by any outlet checked (Kapitalis, Business News) as of this run's cutoff, consistent with same-day reporting lag rather than any indication the hearing did not occur — still an open item for a future run.

Postal Code — Law No. 98-38 of June 2, 1998

Enacted: June 2, 1998 | Published: JORT N°44, June 2, 1998 | Amended: Law No. 2007-40
Sets the conditions for exercising postal activity in Tunisia and guarantees public access to basic postal services while protecting correspondence confidentiality. Governs licensing of postal operators — including the state operator, Office National des Postes (La Poste Tunisienne) — prohibited items, and sanctions for postal offenses. Unlike the telecommunications sector's independent regulator (INT), no standalone postal-sector regulatory authority has been identified; oversight remains with the Ministry of Communication Technologies and La Poste Tunisienne itself.
DigitalAdministrative

Draft "Code du Numérique" (Digital Code)Proposed Replacement of the 2001 Telecommunications Code

Ministerial draft publicly discussed 2025–2026 | Not yet submitted to the ARP as of July 2026
A comprehensive ~258-article draft code, prepared under the Ministry of Communication Technologies, intended to entirely replace the Telecommunications Code (Law No. 2001-1 of January 15, 2001). As publicly previewed by the Ministry, the draft would deregulate market entry for mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs), internet service providers, and data-center/cloud operators; impose "dig-once" shared-infrastructure obligations on network buildout; and restrict formal licensing requirements to genuinely scarce resources (radio spectrum, submarine-cable landing rights, satellite orbital slots), removing licensing for activities not dependent on such resources. It is also intended to consolidate cybersecurity, data-hosting, and digital-services rules currently scattered across the ICT Security Law, cybersecurity decree-laws, and sector-specific texts. The existing Cybercrime Law (Law No. 99-89) is expressly described by commentators as pre-dating this effort. As of July 2026 the draft remains a ministerial/preparatory text and has not been formally tabled before the Assembly of People's Representatives; the 2001 Telecommunications Code remains in force. Update (Run 66): within the existing (unamended) 2001 Code, the government nonetheless completed a full 5G rollout: a roadmap was approved and a licensing committee formed on June 13, 2024, licensing conventions were signed with Tunisie Telecom, Ooredoo, and Orange on November 30, 2024, and amending decrees granting each operator 5 MHz (700 MHz band) and 100 MHz (3.5 GHz band) for 15-year terms were published in JORT No. 8 of January 23, 2025; commercial 5G launched February 14, 2025.

Starlink / Satellite Internet Authorization (pending)

SpaceX request filed: January 2023 | Pilot test: Tunis, Ariana, Gabès (late 2023) | INT feasibility study: March–May 2025 | Status: unauthorized as of mid-2026 (Run 66 addition)
A wholly new standalone entry: Tunisia has neither authorized nor banned SpaceX's Starlink satellite-internet service, leaving a multi-year regulatory process stalled under the existing Telecommunications Code. Following SpaceX's January 2023 authorization request and a three-month pilot in Tunis, Ariana, and Gabès, the national regulator (INT — Instance Nationale des Télécommunications) issued a call for proposals in March 2025 for a feasibility study on satellite very-high-speed internet access, publishing results around May 5–6, 2025 reportedly recommending licensing of at least two LEO satellite operators under 5-year terms. As of early-to-mid 2026, Starlink's own coverage map lists Tunisia as "available from 2026" and takes refundable pre-order deposits, but no commercial license had been granted; the reported sticking point is INT's demand for local ground-station/national IP routing versus SpaceX's standard direct-to-gateway model. The long-pending "Code du Numérique" (see entry above) would eventually restrict licensing specifically to scarce resources including satellite orbital slots, potentially reshaping this process once enacted.

Law No. 2004-5 of February 3, 2004 & Decree No. 2015-1032ICT Security and National Cybersecurity Agency

Law: February 3, 2004 | ANSI Decree: August 4, 2015
The 2004 ICT Security Law mandates security audits and certification for sensitive IT systems connected to public networks. Decree No. 2015-1032 created the National Cybersecurity Agency of Tunisia (ANSI — Agence Nationale de la Sécurité Informatique), responsible for cybersecurity policy, incident response (CERT-TN), and certification of secure IT systems for public entities and critical infrastructure operators.

BCT Circular, May 2018 (exact number unconfirmed — see note)Cryptocurrency Regulatory Ban

Issued: May 2018 (widely reported, exact date unconfirmed) | Status: In force as of August 2026
The Central Bank of Tunisia explicitly banned all cryptocurrency transactions (purchase, holding, trading, mining, exchange) via a May 2018 circular, per consistent secondary-source reporting (ilBoursa, Coinfomania, Wikicrypto, and others). Violations subject to Exchange Control Law penalties. Despite a 2021 Finance Minister statement favoring decriminalization and a 2022 parliamentary proposal, no legislation has been enacted to legalize cryptocurrencies as of 2026. The BCT maintains a blockchain research sandbox (Digital Dinar experiments) separate from the ban. (Run 1045 correction: this entry previously cited "Circular No. 2018-02 (January 25, 2018)." Direct verification against the Conseil Bancaire et Financier's own BCT-circular index (cbf.org.tn) found Circular 2018-02 is actually dated March 16, 2018 — not January 25 — and its title gives no indication of crypto/virtual-currency subject matter, making it an unlikely match. The same index shows Circular 2018-05 (to banks, Arabic-only, dated May 29, 2018) as the closer date match to press reporting, but its content could not be independently confirmed this run (PDF access blocked). The exact circular number for this ban therefore remains an open item pending direct confirmation of a circular's text.)

BCT Fintech Regulatory Sandbox — Circular No. 2020-03

Established: 2020 | Operative: 2020–present
The Central Bank of Tunisia established a regulatory sandbox for fintech innovations including mobile payments, digital wallets, peer-to-peer lending platforms, and open banking services. Applications reviewed by BCT's Innovation Committee. Sandbox participants may test services for up to 24 months before full licensing requirements apply. Part of BCT's Digital Finance Strategy 2025 targeting financial inclusion and payment modernization. (Run 188 addition): a concrete, well-corroborated licensing outcome under this framework: on February 18, 2026, Ooredoo Fintech Tunisie obtained a full BCT agrément (regulatory approval, distinct from mere sandbox admission) to launch "walletii by Ooredoo," a digital wallet offering bill payment, money transfer, and cash withdrawal, drawing on Ooredoo Fintech International's existing operations in Qatar, Oman, and the Maldives (La Presse de Tunisie, Business News, Managers.tn, Leaders.com.tn, and five further independent outlets, all February 17–18, 2026).

Law No. 2000-83 of August 9, 2000Electronic Commerce and Digital Signatures

Enacted: August 9, 2000 | In force: 2000 | Amended: 2004
First statute to legally recognize electronic contracts and digital signatures in Tunisia. Establishes the legal equivalence of electronic documents and handwritten signatures. Governs online commercial transactions, electronic payment, and online offers. Establishes the legal framework for certification authorities issuing digital certificates. Proposition de loi n° 42/2024Regulation of Online Commerce & Social Media Marketing (Pending)

Deposited: May 2024, by 88 co-sponsoring deputies | ARP committee sessions through June 2026, examination ongoing | Status: not enacted as of July 1, 2026
A 49-article member's bill, deposited May 2024 by 88 co-sponsoring deputies, under review by the ARP's Committee on Administrative Organization, Development, Digitalization, Governance and Anti-Corruption, aimed at regulating commercial sales and marketing conducted through social media platforms (Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, etc.), a fast-growing informal segment of Tunisia's e-commerce sector. As proposed, it would require online sellers to obtain a "cahier des charges" (specifications file) from the Ministry of Commerce before operating, include a dedicated chapter on consumer-rights and personal-data protection (barring non-disclosure of a seller's identity, phone contacts, licenses, or commercial-registry details), and grant buyers a three-day right of withdrawal (droit de rétractation) to exchange or obtain a refund without justification. The Ministry of Commerce submitted written observations arguing that existing commercial law already partly covers online sales and separately announced its own e-commerce development strategy running through 2030, while the committee weighed whether to replace the mandatory cahier des charges with a simpler electronic declaration system. Correction: examination was not finalized on June 2, 2026 as previously tracked — reporting instead indicates the committee decided to form a dedicated working group at the end of an early-June session, suggesting unresolved points on the cahier-des-charges-vs-declaration debate remained open; the exact date of that session was not clearly confirmed in available sources. Update (Run 39): a June 24, 2026 WebManagerCenter piece characterized the working group's text as having reached a "near-final" shape, but this is a single secondary source rather than a confirmed committee vote or report, so it should be read as directional progress, not resolution of the underlying cahier-des-charges-vs-declaration question. Distinct from, and would supplement, the 2000 Electronic Commerce Law above, which does not address social-media-specific sales. Not yet adopted.

Law No. 2000-57 of June 13, 2000Electronic Signatures and Certification Authorities

Enacted: June 13, 2000 | In force: 2000 | Complemented by: Decree No. 2000-2333
Establishes the legal framework for electronic signature services in Tunisia, predating the more general e-commerce law. Creates the Agence Nationale de Certification Électronique (ANCE — now part of the ANSI framework) as the root certification authority. Defines qualified electronic signatures, simple electronic signatures, and their respective legal values. Authorizes accredited certification service providers (PSC — prestataires de services de certification) to issue digital certificates. The implementing decree sets technical standards (PKI architecture, key lengths, certificate validity periods).
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–4: Definitions of electronic signature; equivalence with handwritten signature when qualified
  • Art. 5–9: Requirements for qualified electronic signatures (linked to signatory, capable of identifying signatory, created by controlled means)
  • Art. 10–14: Obligations of certification service providers; liability for certificate errors
  • Art. 15–18: Accreditation of PSCs by ANCE; ongoing audit requirements
  • Art. 19–22: Certificate suspension and revocation procedures
  • Art. 23–27: Penal sanctions for fraudulent use of certificates

Decree-Law No. 2023-17 of March 11, 2023National Cybersecurity Framework & Cloud Computing Regulation

Enacted: March 11, 2023 | In force: March 2023 | Implementing decrees: 2024
Landmark post-2022 cybersecurity decree establishing a comprehensive national framework for cloud computing services and digital infrastructure security. As part of this decree, the National Agency for Computer Security (ANSI, created by Law No. 2004-5) was renamed the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCS — Agence Nationale de la Cybersécurité). Mandates data localization requirements for "sensitive" public sector data (health, judicial, financial records must be stored on servers in Tunisia or in countries with adequate protection levels). Creates a licensing regime for cloud service providers operating for Tunisian public entities, including "secure" software/equipment labels and G-cloud/N-cloud labels for cloud providers. Strengthens the mandatory cybersecurity audit regime for critical infrastructure operators (energy, water, finance, telecom). Assigns ANCS enhanced enforcement powers including the ability to issue binding orders to address critical vulnerabilities. (Run 293 note): a separate, more comprehensive pending bill, Proposition de loi n° 2024-36, was under ARP committee examination as of early 2026 and would create a new National Cybersecurity Authority structure alongside this decree-law's existing ANCS framework — its relationship to (replacement of, or supplement to) this decree-law remains unclarified in available sources.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–6: Definitions — cloud computing, critical information infrastructure, sensitive data
  • Art. 7–14: Data localization obligations for public entities; list of sensitive data categories
  • Art. 15–22: Licensing of cloud service providers (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) for public sector use
  • Art. 23–30: Mandatory security audits for critical infrastructure operators (minimum annual frequency)
  • Art. 31–38: ANSI enforcement powers; right to issue binding security directives
  • Art. 39–45: Incident reporting obligations (critical incidents: 4-hour notification to ANSI/CERT-TN)
  • Art. 46–52: Sanctions: up to 500,000 TND administrative fines + criminal penalties

Organic Law No. 2024-22 of March 11, 2024Biometric National Identity Card

Adopted by ARP: March 6, 2024 (107–3–4) | Published: JORT, March 11, 2024 | Amends: Law No. 93-27 of March 22, 1993
Modifies and supplements the 1993 national identity card law to make a biometric, chip-based national ID card mandatory for citizens from age 15 (permitted with parental authorization from age 12). The chip embeds fingerprints, photograph, and encrypted personal data with access-logging safeguards; the reform also removes the profession field, adds a sex/gender data field, and eliminates the card's prior fixed expiration date. A companion statute of the same date, Organic Law No. 2024-23, separately establishes the biometric passport. Distinct from "e-Houwiya" (Mobile ID), an administrative digital-identity service launched by the Ministry of Communication Technologies in August 2022 (via Circulaire n°16 of August 3, 2022) that complements, rather than replaces, the physical biometric card created by this law.

Enacted: February 6, 2024 | Instrument deposited: March 8, 2024
Approves Tunisia's accession to the Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest Convention, 2001), making Tunisia the 70th state party. Proposition de loi n° 2024-36Comprehensive Cybersecurity Framework (Pending)

Deposited: April 30, 2024 | ARP General Legislation Commission examination began: January 25, 2026 (minister hearings January 29, 2026) | Status: not enacted as of July 14, 2026
A member's bill (proposition de loi, as distinct from a government-initiated projet de loi) proposing a standalone, more comprehensive statutory cybersecurity framework than the existing Decree-Law No. 2023-17. As drafted, it would define "cybersecurity," "cyber threats," and "critical infrastructure"; require public entities and critical-infrastructure operators to adopt security policies and undergo regular audits; create a dedicated National Cybersecurity Authority together with a Strategic Cybersecurity Committee and a Crisis Management Committee (a more elaborate institutional structure than ANCS's existing mandate under Decree-Law No. 2023-17); impose security and incident-notification duties on telecom operators, ISPs, and digital service providers; mandate domestic hosting of sensitive data; and set administrative fines of 20,000–60,000 TND for violations (distinct from, and lower than, Decree-Law No. 2023-17's own 500,000 TND ceiling). The ARP's General Legislation Commission examined the bill starting January 25, 2026, hearing Communication Technologies Minister Nizar Ben Neji on January 29, 2026, alongside representatives of the Foreign Affairs and Interior ministries; no committee vote, floor debate, or JORT publication has been reported as of this run's cutoff, and its relationship to (replacement of, or supplement to) Decree-Law No. 2023-17 has not been clarified in any source reviewed. Also related to a separately reported, still-unconfirmed effort to reform Decree-Law No. 2022-54 on offenses involving information and communication systems. (Run 299 update): a direct WebFetch of legislation-securite.tn's own tracking page for this bill found its cross-reference field explicitly reads "Aucun texte n'est lié à ce texte" (no text is linked to this one) — meaning the tracking database itself records no formal linkage to Decree-Law No. 2023-17 or any other instrument. This clarifies, but does not fully resolve, the open question: the two texts appear to be tracked as legally independent rather than as amendment/replacement pairs, though this says nothing about whether the bill's own explanatory memorandum (not sighted) addresses the overlap in its stated legislative intent.

National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (announced April 2018, still not formally adopted as of August 2026)

First announced: April 2018 | Inter-ministerial MOU on drafting the strategy: February 19, 2022 | Main axes presented to a PM-chaired restricted ministerial council: August 15, 2026 | Status: no binding text published as of Run 968 (August 16, 2026)
Distinct from the still-pending Personal Data Protection organic bill (which separately addresses AI-driven profiling/automated decision-making) and from the draft Digital Code, this is Tunisia's long-promised freestanding national AI governance framework. First announced by the Ministry of Communication Technologies in April 2018, it was followed by a February 19, 2022 memorandum of understanding signed by four ministers committing to prepare a strategy document and implementation plan, and by repeated 2025–2026 government statements describing finalization as "imminent" (including a November 5, 2025 La Presse report on the ministry "preparing" the strategy). Despite this eight-year track record of announcements, a dedicated JORT-index search found no law, decree-law, decree, or ministerial order instituting, adopting, or publishing any national AI framework document as of this run — confirmed via a THD (Tunisie Haut Débit) investigative piece published in 2026, which also notes the pre-existing 2013 Conseil stratégique de l'économie numérique (CSEN), nominally responsible for digital-economy strategy oversight, has held no publicly known meeting since 2018. This contrasts with several neighboring and peer states (Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco) that had adopted formal national AI strategies by 2026. Update (Run 968): on August 15, 2026, Minister of Communication Technologies Sofiene Hemissi presented the strategy's main axes — under the explicit "2026–2030" label — to a restricted ministerial council chaired by Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri at the Government Palace, La Kasbah, framing AI as a pillar of economic transformation "respectful of the human, their privacy and constitutional rights" and citing Tunisia's 29th-place global ranking in AI scientific publications; confirmed via Tunisie Numérique and African Manager's coverage of the same session, cross-checked against each other. This partially resolves the Caution for future runs flagged since Run 782 — at least one AI-regulation aggregator site (regulations.ai) claims a 2026–2030 strategy is already "in force" with an established "Conseil National de l'Intelligence Artificielle" chaired by the Head of Government; the "2026–2030" naming is now independently corroborated by this primary ministerial-council presentation, but no decree or JORT text creating a Conseil National de l'Intelligence Artificielle or otherwise formally adopting the strategy as binding was identified this run, so the aggregator's "in force" claim remains uncorroborated and likely premature — this remains presentation of axes, not enactment. Separately, the private business-association Atuge (Tunisian Association of Grandes Écoles alumni) announced August 6, 2026 that it is preparing its own AI-policy white paper to propose national priorities — an advocacy initiative, not a government or legislative act. No enactment to report; tracked here as a standing gap pending a genuine JORT publication or adoption decree.

Public Health Code — Law No. 91-63 of July 29, 1991

Enacted: July 29, 1991 | In force: 1992 | Amended: 1994, 2002, 2008, 2019
Framework law for public health in Tunisia. Covers organization of the health system, health facilities (public and private), medical professions, pharmaceutical activities, and preventive health. Establishes obligations for health establishments and practitioners. Governs mandatory vaccination programs and epidemic disease control.

Pharmacy Law — Law No. 85-91 of September 11, 1985

Enacted: September 11, 1985 | In force: 1986 | Amended: 1992, 2004
Governs pharmaceutical activities including manufacturing, import, distribution, and dispensing of medicines. Requires prior authorization (visa d'exploitation) for drug marketing. Enacted: August 3, 1992 | In force: 1992
Governs mental health care and protection of psychiatric patients' rights. Regulates voluntary and involuntary hospitalization, patient consent, and judicial oversight of psychiatric confinement. Establishes conditions for involuntary placement and patients' right to legal representation.

Organic Law No. 2024-32 of June 19, 2024Patient Rights and Medical Responsibility

Adopted by ARP: June 5, 2024 (108 for) | Enacted: June 19, 2024 | Published: JORT, June 20, 2024
Guarantees patients' rights — including access to emergency care at any public or private facility, information about medical and therapeutic interventions, pain management, and protection of personal health data — and establishes a medical-error compensation framework allowing victims to obtain compensation once damage is established, without waiting for a full criminal investigation. Mandates that healthcare professionals be covered by a compensation fund financed by professional contributions, covering bodily, moral, professional, and aesthetic damage, lost income, and related costs. Originated as a 2019 bill; took five years to pass.

Law No. 91-21 of March 13, 1991 (as amended)Medical Professions Organization

Enacted: March 13, 1991 | In force: 1991 | Amended: 2004
Governs the practice of medicine and regulates the professional orders: Ordre des Médecins, Ordre des Dentistes, and Ordre des Pharmaciens. Sets qualification requirements, ethical rules, and disciplinary procedures. Requires all physicians to register with the Ordre before practicing. Regulates private medical practice licensing, fees, and professional conduct. The 2024 parliament proposed a "brain drain" compensation law requiring doctors trained publicly to pay back if emigrating within 5 years. Update (Run 138): the diploma-equivalence conditions applicable to Tunisian physicians trained abroad — set by a Ministerial Order of October 10, 2023 following consultations begun in 2018 with the Ministry of Health, the medical faculties, and the Ordre des Médecins — already dispense a doctor from the equivalence examination and any supplementary training where they can show at least five years of effective practice following their specialty diploma. The Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research confirmed this in a July 1, 2026 written response published on the ARP's website (following a petition of 100+ signatories from the Association des médecins tunisiens en Allemagne and the Organisation tunisienne des jeunes médecins), and noted the sectoral equivalence commission has already applied the rule to grant equivalences to several Germany-trained physicians after verifying their seniority. A dated clarification of an existing implementing regulation, not a new law.

Presidential Decree No. 2022-318 of April 8, 2022Telemedicine (Run 159 addition)

Enacted: April 8, 2022 | Published: JORT, April 12, 2022 | Legal basis: Law No. 91-21 of March 13, 1991 (Medical Professions Organization, see standalone entry) | Supplemented: Ministerial Orders of June 13, 2024
A wholly new standalone entry, missed by all 158 prior runs despite this project's existing Medical Professions and Patient Rights entries. This 29-article decree establishes Tunisia's first general legal framework for telemedicine, grounded in Law No. 91-21 and the medical/dental/pharmacist codes of ethics. Covers remote consultations, distance screening ("télé-expertise"), medical assistance, tele-coordination between practitioners, electronic prescriptions, and the platforms used to deliver them; requires digital medical reports and e-prescriptions to carry an electronic signature under existing legislation, and permits pharmacists to dispense against e-prescriptions except for Annex B-listed controlled substances and psychotropics. Specialty-specific practice conditions and platform-authorization requirements were left to ministerial order. Two companion Ministerial Orders of the Minister of Health, dated June 13, 2024 (published JORT, June 14, 2024), completed the framework: one fixing the specific conditions for performing telemedicine acts per medical specialty, the other listing the documents/data required to apply for authorization to operate a telemedicine platform or medical-cooperation project. A subsequent restriction limits most remote consultations to patients a physician has already examined in person at least once, with tele-imaging as a notable exception and ministerial-decision-based derogations possible. Distinct from a separate, unrelated French regulatory decree of similar number (2024-164) that a search-engine result initially and incorrectly suggested was Tunisian — verified via direct source fetch to apply only to French teleconsultation companies, and correctly excluded from this entry.

Filed: 2025, supported by 105 deputies | ARP Health Commission hearing: May 5, 2026
A deputy-initiated organic bill (96 articles across 4 titles) that would establish a general statute for health-sector personnel — covering staff assigned to the Ministry of Health's central administration, regional health directorates, and public health establishments — aiming to address structural staffing obstacles and guarantee continuity of care, particularly in Tunisia's interior regions. The ARP's Health, Women's Affairs, Family, Social Affairs, and Persons with Disabilities Commission heard the bill's authors on May 5, 2026. Law No. 2004-71 of August 2, 2004Compulsory Health Insurance (CNAM)

Enacted: August 2, 2004 | In force: 2007 (phased) | Amended: 2014
Creates the National Compulsory Health Insurance Fund (CNAM — Caisse Nationale d'Assurance Maladie), unifying previously fragmented health coverage. Covers all employees and pensioners in public and private sectors. Three coverage regimes: (1) public healthcare network (filière publique); (2) personal physician system (médecin de famille); (3) direct specialist access with reimbursement. Employee contribution: 2.75% of wages; employer contribution: 4% of wages. 2026 liquidity crisis: CNAM entered 2026 with a theoretical accounting surplus of roughly TND 900 million but an acute cash-liquidity shortfall preventing timely payment of pharmacists, physicians, and other private providers. Following talks convened under the Presidency of the Republic, a January 2026 tripartite agreement between the state, CNAM, and pharmacists' representatives guaranteed payment within fixed deadlines and preserved the third-party payer (tiers payant) system. The liquidity crisis persisted into mid-2026: CNAM's accumulated debt to public hospitals was reported at approximately TND 1.95 billion for 2025, contributing to medication shortages and delayed equipment maintenance; a fresh "engagement de paiement" (payment commitment) between CNAM and private pharmacies was reported reached July 1, 2026 to ensure continued medication dispensing, which pharmacists' representatives explicitly described as a provisional stopgap while again demanding durable financing reform. Verification note (updated, Run 30): the July 1, 2026 standoff is now resolved and independently confirmed — Business News (July 1, 2026) reports CNAM reached a payment commitment ("engagement de paiement") with private pharmacies that averted the threatened suspension of tiers-payant prescription processing, closing the unconfirmed hedge carried across Runs 26–29. Pharmacists' representatives nonetheless described the deal as a provisional stopgap pending durable financing reform, consistent with the underlying June 24–30, 2026 standoff (SPOT's threatened suspension over ~TND 80 million in unpaid 2025 claims; the pharmacy "crisis cell" formed June 30) previously documented here. Medical-analysis labs were separately reported to be considering a similar suspension from July 13, 2026. Update (Run 31): at an extraordinary general assembly on June 30, 2026, the private biologists' union voted to proceed with suspending "tiers payant" (third-party payment) with CNAM effective July 13, 2026, over more than seven months of unpaid claims; routine cases for patients registered under the family-doctor (médecin de famille) scheme would remain covered. The suspension had not yet taken effect as of this run and should be watched for confirmation or a last-minute agreement (as occurred with pharmacists on July 1). Update (Run 43): independent reporting confirms the July 1 pharmacist agreement was a narrow, provisional fix rather than a sign of broader resolution — the Ordre des Pharmaciens formed its own separate "cellule de crise" on June 30, 2026 over the continued risk of a renewed rupture with CNAM, indicating the underlying liquidity crisis extends sector-wide (pharmacists and biologists alike) rather than being isolated to the biologists' dispute; as of July 2, 2026 the biologists' July 13 suspension date stood unchanged with no reported negotiated fix. Update (Run 46): the Tunisian Union of Private Biologists confirmed July 1, 2026 that the tiers-payant suspension will proceed as planned on July 13, 2026, covering all analysis categories (ordinary and chronic-illness/APCI forms), citing over seven months of unpaid CNAM claims; patients registered under the family-doctor (médecin de famille) scheme will still receive analyses but must pay upfront and seek reimbursement afterward, while other insured categories lose direct billing entirely at participating private labs. No last-minute agreement had been reported as of this run — unlike the pharmacists' July 1 fix, this dispute reached its deadline unresolved. The Finance Law 2026 includes measures to diversify CNAM's funding sources and revise the social funds' organizational structure, but as of this run a dedicated CNAM structural-reform bill (splitting social-service management from health-insurance management) had still not been filed with the ARP — reporting as of late 2025 described it as "in elaboration" for an "early 2026" submission that has not materialized — so the reform remains at the policy-agreement stage, not yet codified in a standalone statute. Update (Run 69): SPOT (Syndicat des Pharmaciens d'Officine de Tunisie) confirmed July 2, 2026 that the tiers-payant system continues uninterrupted at CNAM-conventioned pharmacies — the pharmacists' track did not follow the biologists' onto a suspension path. At a June 3, 2026 national-council meeting SPOT had already flagged that "most pharmacies face critical financial situations" and could not tolerate further settlement delays; CNAM for its part acknowledged difficulties in honoring prior accords but committed to a "clear agreement for the coming six months" to stabilize the CNAM–pharmacy relationship, with a further meeting between SPOT and CNAM scheduled for mid-July 2026 to be chaired by the Minister of Social Affairs. This is a distinct, still-open track from the private biologists' union's confirmed July 13, 2026 tiers-payant suspension (see the Run 31/46 updates above), which stood unchanged as of this run. Update (Run 255): the July 13, 2026 suspension was called off before taking effect — the Tunisian Union of Private Biologists announced July 10, 2026 that it was suspending its own suspension decision, following a meeting with the Minister of Social Affairs and CNAM officials at which CNAM representatives committed to settling the outstanding debt to private laboratories within an agreed timeframe; the union said it was prioritizing dialogue and "responsibility toward citizens," and tiers-payant billing continues uninterrupted at private labs as of this run (Business News, July 11, 2026). As with the July 1 pharmacist fix, this is a negotiated stopgap rather than the underlying structural-financing reform, which remains uncodified. Update (Run 637) — pharmacists escalate past the July 1 fix, new August 1 suspension threat: the pharmacists' track (previously stable since the Run 69 update) has now itself reached the same brink the biologists faced in July: SPOT (Syndicat des Pharmaciens d'Officine de Tunisie) announced July 16, 2026 that it had engaged judicial proceedings against CNAM and set a final ultimatum of Friday, July 31, 2026 for CNAM to fully regularize its outstanding financial and contractual commitments, failing which SPOT will suspend tiers-payant processing at private pharmacies from August 1, 2026. The trigger is CNAM's non-compliance with the January 15, 2026 tripartite agreement already documented above: at a June 25, 2026 follow-up meeting CNAM had committed to three payment tranches, of which only one was actually disbursed. Reporting as of July 27, 2026 puts CNAM's accumulated debt to pharmacy owners at over TND 180 million (up sharply from the ~TND 80 million figure reported in June), with payment delays now reaching a fixed 180 days; La Presse de Tunisie (July 22, 2026) separately reported both physicians' and pharmacists' representatives denouncing CNAM's governance as defective. A July 27, 2026 Business News report ("les pharmaciens maintiennent leur ultimatum et haussent le ton") confirms SPOT held its position at the deadline rather than softening it, while the same day CNAM reportedly began disbursing roughly one-third of the amount still owed under the January 15 agreement — a partial payment SPOT itself flagged as "pending effective verification and official confirmation," and which it said, even if confirmed, would not resolve its other outstanding demands (cessation of unauthorized deductions, reactivation of the CNAM–pharmacy payment-tracking platform). As of this run — the July 31 deadline itself — no outlet had yet reported whether CNAM met the ultimatum or whether the August 1 suspension will proceed; flagged for confirmation in the next research pass, consistent with this entry's established practice for the biologists' analogous July 13 deadline (Businessnews, African Manager, WebManagerCenter/directinfo, Gnet News, Réalités Magazine, Le Temps News, Tuniscope, all July 16–27, 2026). Update (Run 656) — RESOLVED, no suspension: SPOT announced on the deadline day itself, July 31, 2026, that tiers-payant billing at CNAM-conventioned pharmacies would continue operating normally rather than being suspended on August 1 as threatened, citing "progress made in joint work with the CNAM" and a wish to preserve a constructive climate; the union said it is now seeking a durable, binding ("contraignant") agreement covering continuity of pharmaceutical services, simplified administrative procedures, and patients' uninterrupted access to medication, rather than treating the partial one-third payment flagged as unverified at Run 654 as a final resolution. Source: Business News, "Tiers payant : les pharmaciens tendent la main à la Cnam, dans l'espoir d'un pacte retrouvé" (July 31, 2026). This closes the standing August 1 suspension-outcome watch carried since Run 637 — the fourth negotiated stopgap in this entry's history (after the July 1 pharmacist fix, the called-off July 13 biologist suspension, and the July 27 partial payment) rather than the structural CNAM financing reform, which remains uncodified.
Key provisions
  • Universal coverage for salaried workers and pensioners
  • Three coverage tracks: public network, family doctor, direct specialist access
  • Reimbursement rates: 70–80% of tariff for most services
  • Catastrophic illness: 100% coverage for chronic and severe conditions
  • Low-income beneficiaries covered by AMGP (gratuitous medical assistance)
  • Pharmaceuticals: reimbursed from national essential drugs list
HealthSocial

Law No. 91-22 of March 13, 1991 (amended by Law No. 99-92 of October 25, 1999)Organ Transplantation

Enacted: 1991 | Opt-out amendment: October 25, 1999
Governs organ and tissue transplantation in Tunisia. The 1999 amendment introduced the opt-out (presumed consent) system — all Tunisian citizens are deemed organ donors at death unless they have explicitly registered an objection with the National Transplant Registry. Permits live donation between relatives (kidneys, partial liver). Cadaveric organ procurement coordinated by CNPTO. Prohibits organ trafficking (criminalized under Penal Code); prohibits commercial kidney transplants.
Health

Law No. 91-72 of August 5, 1991 (as amended)Blood Transfusion and Blood Products

Enacted: August 5, 1991 | In force: 1992 | Amended: 2003, 2015
Governs the collection, processing, quality control, storage, and distribution of blood and blood products in Tunisia. Establishes the National Center for Blood Transfusion (CNTS — Centre National de Transfusion Sanguine) as the regulatory and coordinating authority. Mandates voluntary, non-remunerated blood donation; prohibits commercial blood sale. Requires testing of all donated blood for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and malaria (in endemic periods). Blood banks (banques de sang) in hospitals operate under CNTS quality standards.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–6: Voluntary, gratuitous, and anonymous donation as ethical principles
  • Art. 7–14: CNTS mandate; regional blood collection centers
  • Art. 15–20: Mandatory serological screening tests for all donations
  • Art. 21–26: Hospital blood bank licensing; traceability obligations
  • Art. 27–32: Prohibition of commercial blood trade; criminal sanctions
  • 2015 amendment: plasma fractionation framework for locally produced clotting factors
Health

Law No. 98-17 of February 23, 1998Prevention of the Harmful Effects of Smoking

Enacted: February 23, 1998 | Implementing decrees: 98-2248 (Nov. 16, 1998), 2009-2611 (Sept. 14, 2009)
Tunisia's principal tobacco-control statute — forbids smoking in enclosed places of collective use (schools, hospitals, government offices, public transport), prohibits sale of tobacco products to minors under 18, and bans tobacco advertising and sponsorship across audiovisual and print media. Decree No. 98-2248 (as supplemented by Decree No. 2009-2611) specifies the covered "places of collective use" and signage requirements. (Run 90 addition) A ministry-drafted amendment bill to extend the framework to e-cigarettes and other new nicotine products, aimed particularly at protecting minors, was reported under preparation in June 2026 — not yet filed with the ARP as of this run.
Health

Law No. 2015-31 of August 17, 2015Bioethics and Assisted Reproductive Technology

Enacted: August 17, 2015 | In force: January 2016
Tunisia's framework statute on bioethics — one of the most progressive in the Arab world at the time. Regulates medically-assisted reproduction (MAR/ART): in-vitro fertilization (IVF), intra-uterine insemination (IUI), and embryo freezing are permitted for married couples only. Prohibits surrogacy, egg donation to third parties, and post-mortem sperm use. Establishes the National Bioethics Committee (Comité National d'Éthique Médicale — CNEM) as advisory body. Regulates research on human embryos, embryonic stem cells (severely restricted), and pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD permitted for certain hereditary diseases with CNEM authorization).
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–8: Scope and bioethical principles (non-maleficence, dignity, informed consent)
  • Art. 9–20: Permitted ART procedures for infertile married couples; authorized centers
  • Art. 21–28: Prohibition of surrogacy, gamete commerce, and posthumous reproduction
  • Art. 29–36: Embryo research — maximum 14-day rule; prohibition of reproductive cloning
  • Art. 37–42: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) conditions and limits
  • Art. 43–48: CNEM composition and advisory mandate
  • Art. 49–55: Criminal sanctions for violations (up to 5 years + fines)

A wholly new standalone entry — a proposal presented to the ARP Health Committee by Dr. Iman Ben Fredj, president of the National Syndicate of Aesthetic Doctors, with a dual aim: criminalizing the unlicensed practice of aesthetic medicine (reserving it exclusively to qualified doctors) and imposing comprehensive regulation of the import and distribution circuits for injectable cosmetic products, in response to reported cases of unlicensed practitioners and counterfeit injectable products. PCT Circular No. 30/2026 of July 24, 2026Medicine Price Revision(Run 753 addition)

Issued: July 24, 2026 | Issuing body: Pharmacie Centrale de Tunisie (PCT) | Effective: immediately upon publication
A circular issued by the Pharmacie Centrale de Tunisie (PCT) — the state body responsible for importing, warehousing, and distributing medicines under the Pharmacy Law above — titled "Document unique fixant les prix des médicaments en Tunisie" (technical reference DT-TEC-01/02), revising official reference prices for roughly 300–306 human-use pharmaceutical specialties, spanning chronic-disease treatments (hypertension, epilepsy, psoriasis) as well as common analgesics and dermatological products. Reporting on the scale of the revision genuinely conflicts across sources: Business News (August 3, 2026) described individual increases of up to 556% on some products "sans la moindre explication," while an August 4, 2026 communiqué from a bloc of 17 ARP deputies (led by Deputy Thabet El Abed) characterized the circular as having "updated medication codes and revised prices for 12 medicines with slight increases" — both figures are given pending clarification against the PCT's official circular text, which could not be independently located by this run. Drew objection from the pharmacy-owners' union SPOT (Syndicat tunisien des propriétaires de pharmacies privées), which said it received no advance notice and has been excluded from the Commission d'achat des médicaments (CAM) for nearly a year, participating in the medicines-price observatory only by exceptional invitation; the UGTT issued an August 4, 2026 statement demanding cancellation of the increases as a threat to the constitutional right to healthcare, particularly for chronic-disease patients and lower-income households. Confirmed via Réalités Magazine, Business News, La Presse de Tunisie, and African Manager, cross-checked against each other. Illustrates the circular/sub-regulatory layer beneath primary statutes, alongside the head-of-government union-secondment circular in the Labor Law section above.

🎓 Education Law

Education Framework Law — Law No. 2002-80 of July 23, 2002

Enacted: July 23, 2002 | In force: 2002 | Replaced: Law No. 91-65
Framework law organizing the Tunisian national education system. Establishes compulsory schooling for 6–16 year olds. Organizes the three-stage system: basic education (9 years), secondary education (4 years), and higher education. Defines national curriculum objectives, teacher qualifications, and school governance.

Higher Education Law — Law No. 2008-19 of February 25, 2008

Enacted: February 25, 2008 | In force: 2008
Governs universities, higher institutes, and research establishments. Introduces the LMD (Licence–Master–Doctorat) system aligned with the Bologna Process. Regulates accreditation, quality assurance, student rights, and university governance. Establishes the framework for private higher education institutions. Pending reform: a bill filed by 27 deputies to amend Article 15 would replace the current system of elected university presidents with ministry-appointed presidents (capped at two terms); under live parliamentary debate as of February 2026 and opposed by the Federal General Union of Higher Education and Scientific Research (FGESRS). Not yet enacted. (Cross-ref, Run 437) A separate, distinct pending bill targeting the private higher-education sector specifically (rather than public-university governance) is tracked at the Private Higher Education Reform Bill entry below.

Proposition de loi n° 026/2023 (pending)Private Higher Education Reform — Mandatory Permanent Doctoral Faculty

Under Education & Sports Commission review since October 2023 (nine hearing sessions) | Final report submitted to ARP Bureau; awaiting plenary scheduling as of June 18, 2026 | Status: not yet enacted
A member's bill amending Law No. 2000-73 of July 25, 2000 on private higher education institutions, affecting all 85 private higher-education establishments operating in Tunisia as of the 2024–2025 academic year. It would require each institution to employ at least 30% of its teaching staff on permanent contracts, all holding doctoral degrees, with these permanent faculty guaranteed the same salary conditions, minimum pay, and teaching-hour load as their public-sector counterparts, and required to deliver at least half of the course-hours in every degree program offered. Institutions would have two years from the law's publication to comply, after which non-compliant establishments would be barred from enrolling new students and face further unspecified sanctions. Deputy Mounir Kamouni, vice-president of the Education and Sports Commission, confirmed the bill's final report has been transmitted to the ARP Bureau and the commission is now awaiting scheduling of a plenary session. Distinct from the ministry-appointed-university-president reform bill amending the public Higher Education Law above. (Added Run 437, cross-checked against Managers.tn's March 10, 2025 committee-hearing report and Tunisie Numérique's June 18, 2026 status update, which converge on the bill's number, content, and procedural stage.)

Vocational Training Law — Law No. 93-10 of February 17, 1993 (as amended)

Enacted: February 17, 1993 | In force: 1993 | Amended: 2008
Framework law governing vocational and professional training. Creates the National Vocational Training Agency (ATFP — Agence Tunisienne de la Formation Professionnelle). Establishes the national apprenticeship system, certification standards (CAP, BTP, BTS), and quality assurance for vocational qualifications. Law No. 96-6 of February 1, 1996 (amended 2010, 2018)Scientific Research and Technology

Enacted: February 1, 1996 | In force: 1996 | Amended: 2010, 2018
Framework law for scientific research and technological development in Tunisia. Creates the National Research Council (CNR) and sector-based research centers. Proposition de loi n° 15/2026 (pending)National Educational Security ("Sécurité Nationale Éducative")

Filed: February 21, 2026 | Referred to the ARP General Legislation Commission | Status: not yet enacted as of Run 576
A 14-article bill filed by a group of ARP deputies to create a unified legal framework treating schools and their immediate surroundings as a protected space, replacing safeguards currently scattered across the Penal Code and other statutes. Would impose life imprisonment for drug trafficking and sexual crimes against minors committed in or around schools, and 20–30 years' imprisonment for harassment, online grooming, extortion, and recruitment of minors into criminal activity in the same settings. Would create a General Directorate of National Educational Security within the Ministry of the Interior to coordinate security efforts and rapid-intervention mechanisms around schools, and mandate annual national protection strategies covering psychological support, health/social services, digital-risk prevention, and anti-drug initiatives. Sponsors cite the dispersal of existing protections across multiple codes and the absence of a unified safeguard against rising school-based drug trafficking, harassment, and child sexual abuse. (Added Run 576, cross-checked against Tunisie Tribune's and African Manager's independent February 21, 2026 coverage of the same filing, which converge on the bill's number, article count, and provisions.)

Draft Law on Single-Session School Scheduling ("Séance Unique") (pending)

Reported filed: July–August 2025 (exact date, bill number, and sponsor count not stated in located press coverage) | Referred to: ARP Commission of Education and Professional Training | Status: not yet enacted as of Run 762
A 7-article proposition de loi that would replace the traditional two-session (morning and afternoon) public-school day with a single, continuous daily session — capped at 5 hours for primary pupils, and up to 30 hours per week spread over five days for middle- and high-school students — framed by sponsors as reducing school fatigue and safeguarding students' physical and psychological wellbeing while freeing the remainder of the day for extracurricular activity. Would take effect from the school year following JORT publication, phased in progressively over three years with rural and hard-to-reach or disadvantaged regions prioritized first. Distinct from the separate "sécurité nationale éducative" bill and the educator-assault-protection bill below, both of which address school safety rather than scheduling. (Added Run 762, cross-checked against La Presse de Tunisie's July 17, July 21, and August 18, 2025 coverage, African Manager, L'Économiste Maghrébin, and Tunisie Tribune's August 18, 2025 reporting, all converging on the bill's 7-article structure, scheduling terms, and committee referral, though none cites a specific proposition number or exact filing date.)

Joint Ministerial Order (Ministries of Higher Education & Economy)Cahier des Charges for Private Student Residences

Published: JORT n° 75 of July 24, 2026 | Status: in force
A joint ministerial order setting a strict cahier des charges (regulatory specifications) governing the opening and operation of private student residences (foyers universitaires privés / résidences estudiantines privées), exclusively reserving such premises for lodging students enrolled in Tunisia's public and private university circuit and barring any other use of the licensed space. Organized around six pillars covering the full lifecycle of a residence, from initial authorization through ongoing compliance monitoring: (1) authorization conditions requiring investors to furnish proof of property ownership or lease, a technical-compliance certificate issued by a licensed expert, and full insurance coverage for the building and residents; (2) mandatory annexed documents — architectural plans, sanitary/washroom facility detail, internal regulations, and a detailed per-bed tariff grid; (3) background-check requirements (a clean judicial record, bulletin n°3, plus CV and diplomas) for both the investor and residence staff; (4) technical and safety standards for bedrooms and common areas; (5) tariff transparency; and (6) a graduated scale of sanctions for infractions. (Added Run 598, cross-checked against La Presse de Tunisie and allAfrica's independent July 25, 2026 coverage of the same JORT text.)

Decree-Law No. 2024-2 of September 16, 2024Higher Council of Education and Teaching (Conseil Supérieur de l'Éducation et de l'Enseignement) (Added Run 944)

Created: Decree-Law No. 2024-2 of September 16, 2024 | Administrative/financial organization: Decree No. 2025-246 of May 8, 2025 | Governing-board & leadership appointments: Presidential Decrees No. 2026-203 to 2026-205 of August 12, 2026 | Inaugural session: August 17, 2026
A consultative body created by Decree-Law No. 2024-2 of September 16, 2024, following a national education consultation, tasked with evaluating and reforming Tunisia's basic, secondary, and higher education, scientific research, vocational training, and employment-policy systems — distinct from, and consultative to, the sector-specific Education Framework Law and Higher Education Law above. Decree No. 2025-246 of May 8, 2025 subsequently fixed its administrative and financial organization. The Council remained largely dormant at the operational level until President Kaïs Saïed signed three implementing decrees on August 12, 2026, formally standing it up: Presidential Decree No. 2026-203 appoints the seven members of its Haute Instance (Tijani Gmati, Youssef Ben Othmen, Chiraz Stanbouli, Rim Aribi, Kamel Hnid, Mohamed Habib Allani, and Mohamed Seifallah Ben Abderrazak); Presidential Decree No. 2026-204 appoints Mohamed Ali Boughdiri — a former Education Minister abruptly dismissed without public explanation on April 1, 2024 and replaced by Salwa El Abassi — as the Council's Secretary General; and Presidential Decree No. 2026-205 fixes the Council's inaugural session for August 17, 2026. Confirmed via L'Économiste Maghrébin and Business News (both August 14–15, 2026), cross-checked against each other for the decree numbers, dates, and appointee list. Update (Run 970): the inaugural session convened as scheduled on Monday, August 17, 2026, per same-day/eve preview coverage from Business News, La Presse de Tunisie, and RTCI (August 16–17, 2026); no report of the session's substantive proceedings or resolutions had appeared in available sources as of this update, so its content remains a standing gap for a future pass. Update (Run 984): President Kaïs Saïed personally visited the Council's Tunis headquarters that day to mark the official start of its activities, per Réalités Magazine's same-day report — he reviewed the institution's progress and described its role as "central" to improving the performance of the education, teaching, scientific research, and vocational-training systems, but the report describes no concrete policy directive, resolution, or vote adopted at the session itself; the gap is accordingly narrowed (a presidential visit occurred and is now documented) rather than fully closed (the session's substantive agenda, if any, remains unreported).

🤝 Social Security & Protection

CNSS Organic Law — Law No. 60-30 of December 14, 1960 (as amended)

Enacted: 1960 | Extensively amended through 2024
Establishes the National Social Security Fund (Caisse Nationale de Sécurité Sociale — CNSS) for private sector workers. Covers contributory retirement pensions, invalidity, death benefits, occupational hazards, family allowances, and maternity. Employee contribution: 9.18%; Employer contribution: 16.57% of gross wages. A possible CNSS–CNRPS merger into a unified pension fund and a new "Identifiant Social Unique" were repeatedly discussed at ministerial-council level in early 2026 but remained at the study stage, with no bill text. Only a 2024 decree-law amnesty on late-payment penalties (Decree-Law No. 2024-503 of October 24, 2024, extended by Decree No. 2025-259 of May 22, 2025) and routine Finance Law contribution/benefit adjustments have actually been enacted. Two further bills remained under ARP review as of early 2026, neither yet adopted: Proposition de loi No. 16/2026 (filed February 21, 2026), which would let public-sector employees request a one-year (extendable to three, capped at age 70) deferral of retirement by amending Law No. 85-12 on civil/military pensions; and Projet de loi No. 104/2025 (filed January 29, 2026), which would ease early-retirement conditions for private-sector women covered by CNSS by removing the "mother of three children" requirement and setting eligibility at age 50 with at least 80 quarters of contributions. (Cross-ref, Run 115) A third, distinct retirees' bill (Proposition de loi n° 30/2026) targeting the cumul-emploi-retraite ban and retiree tariff benefits is tracked as its own standalone entry below. Update (Run 1017, August 19, 2026): the early-2026 ministerial-council-level CNSS–CNRPS merger discussion escalated into a formally announced, broader "structural" reform: at an August 18, 2026 ministerial working session at the Kasbah, Head of Government Sarra Zaâfrani Zenzri, with Minister of Social Affairs Issam Lahmar presenting a diagnosis of the current pension/social-security/health-coverage regimes, announced the immediate launch of drafting implementing legislative texts across five stated pillars: pension-regime adaptation to demographic and labor-market shifts; coverage expansion to informal-sector, agricultural, maritime, and platform-economy workers via simplified enrollment; closer social-security/health-sector coordination (including pharmaceutical-supply management); accelerated digitalization of social-identification systems and caisse/beneficiary data exchange; and CNSS/CNRPS governance and transparency improvements, to proceed via urgent measures first followed by short/medium/long-term structural changes. L'Économiste Maghrébin (August 19, 2026) was critical of the announcement's lack of concrete detail, noting the government specified no financing mechanism, contribution-rate levels, retirement-age policy, or fund-equilibrium projections. No bill number, draft text, or ARP filing had been identified as of this run. Confirmed via Business News (two August 18, 2026 reports), La Presse de Tunisie, webdo.tn, L'Économiste Maghrébin, Managers.tn, and the Ministry of Social Affairs' own site (social.gov.tn), cross-checked against each other for the meeting date, chair, presenter, and reform pillars. Update (Run 1027, August 20, 2026): the already-tracked Projet de loi No. 104/2025 easing CNSS early-retirement conditions for private-sector women resurfaced in press coverage on August 14, 2026 (La Presse de Tunisie, corroborated by allAfrica, Nessma.tv, Tunisie Numérique, Business News, and Espace Manager), reported this time as a "proposition de loi" driven by a group of roughly 27 deputies with Finance Commission rapporteur Zine Jebali as spokesperson, who wants to remove the "mother of three children" condition entirely and cut the required contribution period from roughly 30 years to 20 years — a figure consistent with, rather than additional to, the 80-quarters (20-year) threshold already on file for the January 2026 bill, so this is treated as continued advocacy for the same measure rather than a second, distinct bill absent a differing bill number. Jebali confirmed it as a parliamentary initiative expected to follow the ordinary legislative process; no committee-hearing date, vote, or bill number distinct from 104/2025 was located. Flagged as an open item for future runs to confirm whether this is formally a renumbered proposition de loi or press shorthand for 104/2025's continued committee life.

Decree-Law No. 2024-4 of October 22, 2024Social Protection for Female Agricultural Workers

Enacted: October 22, 2024 | Published: JORT, October 2024
Establishes a dedicated social protection regime for female agricultural workers (ouvrières agricoles), a category long excluded from effective social security coverage. Covers health insurance, old-age and disability pensions, workplace accident insurance, and maternity benefits, and includes provisions on economic inclusion and transport. Comprises 52 articles across 4 chapters; financed in part through the AMEN Social framework and subsequent Finance Laws.

Social Assistance Program Law — Law No. 2019-49 of June 6, 2019AMEN Social

Enacted: June 6, 2019 | In force: 2020
Creates Tunisia's unified social protection system "AMEN Social" replacing fragmented assistance programs. Provides means-tested direct cash transfers to poor families (National Aid Program — PAN), health coverage for the poor (AMGP), and subsidized access to services. Governed by the Ministry of Social Affairs. The monthly PAN cash-transfer amount, previously set at TND 260 by a decree of July 10, 2024, was raised to TND 280/month by a joint arrêté of the Ministers of Social Affairs and Finance (JORT Issue No. 80, August 7, 2026), which repeals Article 1 of the 2024 decree; the increase applies retroactively from January 1, 2026. Run 1036 verification: the 2026 arrêté's own signature date is August 5, 2026, two days ahead of its August 7 publication; the July 10, 2024 date for the superseded text is confirmed correct against a competing "August 10, 2024" rendering circulating in secondary coverage, which is not supported. Neither arrêté carries a published sequential number — Tunisian joint arrêtés of this kind are cited by date alone — so the "80" appearing in Arabic-language reports is the JORT issue number, not a decision number, and should not be cited as one. Scale of the measure as reported: roughly 260,000 needy families plus some 220,000 low-pension beneficiaries, around one million people in total.

Disability Law — Law No. 2005-83 of August 15, 2005

Enacted: August 15, 2005 | In force: 2005
Framework law for the rights and inclusion of persons with disabilities. Prohibits discrimination in employment, education, and public services. Requires accessibility in public buildings and transportation. Originally established a disability employment quota of 1% in the public sector. Creates the National Bureau of Disabled Persons (ONHA). Amended by Law No. 2016-41 of May 16, 2016: raised the quota to 2% and extended it beyond the public sector — public and private enterprises with 100+ employees must reserve 2% of positions for persons with disabilities, and enterprises with 50–99 employees must reserve at least one position, filled in a statutory priority order (Art. 30), with alternative compliance measures available where direct hiring is not feasible (Art. 31). Finance Law 2026 (Art. 32): created a dedicated Fund for the Promotion of Persons with Disabilities, a special treasury fund managed by the CNSS, financed by a 1% levy on compensation paid out for road accidents, workplace accidents, and occupational diseases (withheld by insurers, mutual funds, the Road Accident Victims Guarantee Fund, CNSS, CNRPS, and the Deposits and Consignments Fund), applicable to payouts made from January 1, 2026 onward regardless of when the underlying accident or judgment occurred; proceeds fund economic, social, cultural, and sports inclusion programs plus training, employment, and entrepreneurship support.

Law No. 85-12 of March 5, 1985Civil and Military Retirement and Survivors' Pension Regime (Public Sector)

Enacted: March 5, 1985 | Amended: Law No. 2019-37 of April 30, 2019 (parametric reform raising retirement age and contribution rates) | Managed by: CNRPS | In force as amended
The public-sector counterpart to the CNSS private-sector regime, and the statute that the public pension reform entry above amends rather than replaces. It applies to all public-sector agents regardless of statute or terms of employment — which is why it reaches groups governed by quite different employment statutes elsewhere in this artifact, including agents of offices and EPIC and, since 2020, mosque personnel. Management is entrusted to the CNRPS. The law fixes conditions of entitlement, contributory periods, pension calculation and retirement age, provides disability pensions, sets the survivor's pension at 75% of the deceased's pension (or of the pension they would have received had they been active at death), and governs cumulation and revalorisation. Its parameters are the subject of the pending retirement bills tracked in the retirees' benefits entry. (Added Run 1036.)

Reformed the public sector pension fund (CNRPS — Caisse Nationale de Retraite et de Prévoyance Sociale). Raised minimum civil service retirement age from 55 to 60. Established the National COVID-19 Solidarity Fund funded by state appropriations and private/diaspora donations. Law No. 2020-19 of April 12, 2020COVID-19 Enabling Act & Related Decree-Laws (Run 44 addition)

Enabling law: April 12, 2020 | Lockdown decree: March 22, 2020 | Lockdown lifted: July 3, 2020
Sits alongside the Solidarity Fund decree above as the rest of Tunisia's pandemic legal architecture, previously undocumented here. Law No. 2020-19 authorized the Head of Government, under Art. 70 of the 2014 Constitution, to issue decree-laws for 2 months to address COVID-19, each subject to later ARP ratification. Under this authority: Decree-Law No. 2020-2 (April 14, 2020) exceptionally suspended Labor Code provisions on dismissals/layoffs for force majeure; Decree-Law No. 2020-8 (April 17, 2020) suspended administrative/judicial procedural deadlines; Decree-Law No. 2020-30 (June 10, 2020) provided further economic/social relief including a pension top-up for low-income CNSS/CNRPS beneficiaries. Separately, Governmental Decree No. 2020-156 (March 22, 2020) imposed total lockdown/confinement, lifted by Governmental Decree No. 2020-411 (July 3, 2020); Presidential Decrees No. 2020-38 and 2020-54 (April 28 and May 29, 2020) invoked Tunisia's standing general state-of-emergency regime (Decree No. 78-50 of 1978) over the same period. Whether the ARP ever completed formal ratification of these decree-laws, and whether Decree-Law 2020-30's relief measures were formally repealed versus simply lapsing, could not be confirmed from available sources.

Law No. 1994-2 of January 3, 1994Elderly Persons — Rights and Protection

Enacted: January 3, 1994 | In force: 1994 | Amended: 2004
Tunisia's framework statute on the protection and rights of elderly persons (aged 60+). Recognizes the family's primary responsibility for elderly care while establishing state obligations for support. Creates licensed residential care facilities for the elderly (maisons de retraite) under Ministry of Social Affairs oversight. Establishes minimum quality standards for care facilities. Provides for home-care assistance programs for elderly persons without family support. Prohibits abandonment of elderly persons; criminalizes neglect by legal guardians or responsible family members. The 2004 amendment strengthened quality control inspections of private care facilities.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–6: Definition of elderly person; recognition of family as primary caregiver
  • Art. 7–14: State obligation to provide homes for elderly without family support
  • Art. 15–20: Licensing requirements for public and private elderly care facilities
  • Art. 21–26: Minimum standards: hygiene, nutrition, medical care, social activity
  • Art. 27–32: Prohibition of abandonment; criminal sanctions (up to 2 years)
  • Art. 33–38: Home-care assistance programs financed by CNSS/public funds

Decree-Law No. 2011-97 of October 24, 2011Martyrs and Wounded of the Revolution

Enacted: October 24, 2011 | In force: 2011 | Amended: Law No. 2012-26 of December 24, 2012
Establishes benefits, pensions, and priority employment/healthcare rights for the families of persons killed and for those wounded during the 2010–2011 revolution. The 2012 amendment broadened eligibility criteria and revised the composition of the commission responsible for determining beneficiary status. Distinct from the later Transitional Justice Law (Organic Law No. 2013-53, see Judicial Organization section), which addresses truth-seeking and accountability for a much longer historical period rather than direct revolution-era victim benefits.
