Proposition de loi n° 30/2026 (pending)Retirees' Socio-Economic Benefits & End of the Cumul Emploi-Retraite Ban (Added Run 115)

Filed by ~40 ARP deputies, early 2026 | Under review: ARP Health, Women's Affairs, Family, Social Affairs & Disabled Persons Commission (examination sessions confirmed May 8, 20, and 25, 2026) | Status: not yet enacted as of July 2026
A deputy-initiated bill responding to Tunisia's rapidly aging population (aging rate risen from 6% to roughly 16.88% in 2024, projected to reach near 20% by 2030, per Commission for Development & Strategic Planning president Sabeur Jelassi). Its centerpiece, debated at length under Article 5 of the draft, would end the long-standing prohibition on combining a retirement pension with income from another professional activity ("cumul emploi-retraite"), with deputies divided at the May 20, 2026 session over whether existing law already permits this or whether a full repeal is required, and some pressing to extend the bill's benefits to all elderly citizens rather than pensioners alone; a further incentive would give employers a 30% social-contribution exemption for hiring retired experts as consultants, mentors, or trainers. A second strand grants tariff reductions — reported inconsistently across otherwise-corroborating La Presse de Tunisie coverage as either a 30% or 40% minimum reduction on urban/regional/rail public transport (plus national airline and maritime travel outside peak periods), and either 40% or a "40–50%" discount at classified hotels and tourist establishments and on festival tickets, alongside free museum and historical-monument entry — an unresolved figure discrepancy this project flags rather than resolves without a primary bill text. Also proposes priority hospital pathways (consultations, exams, surgery) and possible exemptions from certain prevention-related contributions. Benefits would be administered via a "Carte loisirs du retraité" (Retiree Leisure Card) with terms set by decree. Distinct from the CNSS entry's two already-tracked pension bills (Proposition de loi No. 16/2026, retirement-deferral for public-sector employees, and Projet de loi No. 104/2025, easing CNSS early-retirement conditions for women) and from the 1994 Elderly Persons Law's care-facility framework (see standalone entries) — this bill targets retirees' active-life benefits and income rights rather than pension mechanics or residential care. A related but separately-numbered sign-language/hearing-impairment bill was examined by the same commission on the same May 20, 2026 date, broadening protections for persons with total or partial speech loss and mandating a unified national sign language for education, public services, and public spaces; it remains too lightly sourced (no bill number or article count located) to warrant its own standalone entry as of this run.

🏠 Land & Property Law

Real Property Registration — Law No. 65-5 of February 12, 1965 (as reformed)

Origin: 1885 (protectorate) | Major overhaul: Law No. 65-5 of February 12, 1965 | Amended: 1992, 2005
Governs land title registration (immatriculation foncière) through the Property Rights Registry (Conservation de la Propriété Foncière). Once registered, title is conclusive and indefeasible. Unregistered land may be subject to adverse possession claims. Tunisia operates a Torrens-style title system for registered properties.
LandCivil

Urban Planning Code — Law No. 94-122 of November 28, 1994

Enacted: November 28, 1994 | In force: 1995 | Amended: 2003, 2009, 2016
Governs land use planning, building permits, zoning, and urban development in Tunisia. Requires detailed urban plans (PAD — Plans d'Aménagement de Détail) for urban areas. Establishes building permit requirements, setback rules, and height restrictions. Regulates real estate development and subdivision approvals. Pending reform (Run 45): the ARP's Strategic Planning/Urban Planning Committee approved, by majority vote and in amended form, a bill reactivating and updating the separate construction-regularization statute (Law No. 2015-11) to let owners of non-compliant buildings regularize their status and obtain utility-hookup authorizations; reported June 23, 2026, the bill was headed toward a committee report ahead of a plenary vote, though its ARP registry number could not be independently confirmed and is omitted pending a primary-source citation. Detail added (Run 49): per committee-hearing coverage from earlier in its progress (the bill was first heard by the same committee on February 27, 2026, before its June 23 amended-form approval), the proposal comprises 12 articles setting out eligible categories, land-registration valuation, and the procedures for benefiting from regularization; it targets housing built without authorization or in violation of planning rules before a December 31, 2025 cutoff, with sponsors citing estimates of roughly 800,000 to one million residents across some 1,400 informal ("anarchic") neighborhoods nationwide as potential beneficiaries. Post-cutoff violations would face demolition or a fine of up to three times the land's value. These figures come from pre-committee-vote reporting (businessnews.com.tn, La Presse, African Manager) on what appears to be the same proposal tracked since Run 45 rather than a primary ARP/JORT text, and the registry number remains unconfirmed — treat the article count and beneficiary estimates as provisional until a post-vote committee report or JORT text is located. Re-confirmed (Run 96): a dedicated recheck of French- and English-language sources found no evidence that a plenary vote has occurred as of July 5, 2026 — La Presse de Tunisie, allAfrica, and African Manager's June 23, 2026 coverage all state the amended text must still proceed through a full committee report before reaching the floor, and no ARP agenda, vote outcome, or report-finalization news has surfaced since. The bill remains at the pre-report, pre-plenary stage; this is the closest watchlist item to crossing a legislative threshold and warrants rechecking again in the next run. Update (Run 83): distinct from the narrower construction-regularization bill above, a separate, broader wholesale revision of this 1994 Code itself has been underway for years — former Minister of Equipment and Housing Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri targeted completion by 2024 (announced June 20, 2023, developed via ministry workshops with UN-Habitat Tunisia, addressing climate-change resilience, energy transition, and digital-transformation planning tools), a deadline that lapsed unmet. Her successor, Minister Salah Zouari, announced in October 2025 that promulgation is now expected in 2026 (per urbanisme.fr, April 21, 2026), aiming to modernize planning tools for informal urban areas, improve state/local-authority governance coordination, and enable locally-adapted planning mechanisms — but political instability since 2021 has limited ARP debate time, creating the same institutional bottleneck reported for the Investment, Water, Environment, and Hydrocarbons codes elsewhere in this document. No draft text has been filed with the ARP as of this run.

Housing Law — Law No. 77-46 of May 30, 1977

Enacted: May 30, 1977 | In force: 1977 | Amended: 1996, 2013
Governs residential leases and tenant-landlord relations. Sets minimum lease terms, notice periods for termination, and tenant protection against arbitrary eviction. Regulates rent increases for controlled accommodation. Applies to residential leases; commercial leases are regulated separately under the COC.
LandCivil

Employee Housing Promotion Fund (FOPROLOS) — Law No. 77-54 of August 3, 1977

Enacted: August 3, 1977 | In force: 1977 | Status: in force, ongoing parafiscal levy
Creates the Fonds de Promotion du Logement pour les Salariés (FOPROLOS), financed principally by a mandatory 1% employer payroll levy on private-sector wages (collected alongside CNSS social-security contributions), dedicated to subsidized housing for salaried employees. FOPROLOS funds low-interest mortgage loans, employer/cooperative-built social housing programs, and housing-cooperative site-and-services schemes for lower- and middle-income CNSS-affiliated workers, jointly administered by the Ministry of Equipment, Housing & Territorial Planning and CNSS. Distinct from the rent-regulation framework of the Housing Law (No. 77-46, above), which governs private residential leases rather than subsidized-housing financing. (Added Run 82 — a genuine standalone gap: 81 prior runs had documented the general Housing Law but never this separate employer-levy financing statute.)
LandLaborSocial

Co-ownership Law — Law No. 77-42 of May 23, 1977

Enacted: May 23, 1977 | In force: 1977 | Amended: 1994
Governs horizontal co-ownership (apartment buildings and condominiums). Defines common areas vs. private lots, establishes the mandatory Syndicate of Co-owners (syndicat des copropriétaires), and regulates management, maintenance costs, and dispute resolution between co-owners.
LandCivil

Habous (Religious Endowments) — Decree of July 18, 1956 (as reformed)

Reform Decree: July 18, 1956 | Multiple administrative reforms since
Habous (Arabic: وقف — waqf) are religious endowments inalienably dedicated to Islamic charitable purposes. The 1956 decree reorganized habous administration under the Ministry of Religious Affairs. Public habous were progressively converted to state property for national development projects. Private habous recognized but creation of new ones restricted. Habous property cannot be sold, mortgaged, or partitioned. A historically significant category of Tunisian real property, particularly urban commercial and agricultural land.
LandCivil

Law No. 83-87 of November 11, 1983 and Law No. 2001-29 of March 19, 2001Agricultural Land Protection

Enacted: 1983, 2001 | In force: ongoing
Restricts conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural uses. Prime agricultural land (irrigated perimeters, fertile coastal plains) protected from subdivision and urbanization without prior Ministry of Agriculture approval. The 2001 law governs management of communal pastoral lands (terres collectives): partitioning, titling, and integration into the formal land registry. Essential to food security policy.
LandAgriculture

Law No. 69-56 of September 22, 1969Restriction on Foreign Ownership of Agricultural Land

Enacted: September 22, 1969 | In force: 1969 | Status: in force, subject to pending reform proposals (2025–2026)
Reserves ownership of agricultural land to persons of Tunisian nationality, agricultural cooperatives, and public legal entities (Art. 1); foreign nationals may not acquire agricultural property, a policy framed around food-security and productive-land-resource protection. Foreigners may lease agricultural land, generally capped at short renewable terms absent special authorization. As of 2025–2026 the rule on outright ownership is unchanged, but it is being debated alongside two related, separately pending legislative proposals on state-owned ("domanial") agricultural land: Proposal No. 32/2025, examined by the ARP Agriculture Committee in February 2026, would regularize and reallocate already-exploited state land — granting title to long-term informal farmers who developed neglected state plots over decades — while a second track examines long-term leasing (rather than ownership transfer) of state land to investors, including foreign investors, without altering the 1969 ownership restriction. Neither proposal had been adopted as of June 2026.
LandAgriculture

Law No. 2016-53 of July 11, 2016Expropriation for Public Utility

Enacted: July 11, 2016 | Amended: Decree-Law No. 2022-65 of October 19, 2022 (JORT No. 114, Oct. 21, 2022) | Further revision under study since Dec. 2024
Governs expropriation of private property for public utility (utilité publique), replacing the older 1976 expropriation code. Sets the procedure for declaring a project of public interest, valuing affected property, and compensating owners, with disputes heard before the Expropriation Court. Decree-Law No. 2022-65 amended the law to create a permanent "commission de reconnaissance et de conciliation" (recognition and conciliation commission) in each governorate to speed up amicable compensation settlements. A December 16, 2024 working session chaired by the Minister of State Domains and Land Affairs, Wajdi Hedhili — held pursuant to Circular No. 27 of the Presidency of Government (November 7, 2024) on accelerating public projects — launched study of a further revision intended to speed up expropriation procedures while safeguarding owners' compensation rights; the revision remained at the project/consultation stage, not yet enacted, as of mid-2026.
LandAdministrative

State Domains Code Reform & Collective Land ("Terres Collectives") Decree-Law (Run 306 addition)

Announced: July 14, 2026, at an ENA (École Nationale d'Administration) colloquium on public land and investment | Status: decree-law project and code rewrite, not yet enacted
Minister of State Domains and Land Affairs Wajdi Hedhili — the same official behind the December 2024 expropriation-procedure review above — unveiled a two-pillar land-reform roadmap on July 14, 2026: a full rewrite of outdated state-land legislation into a new State Domains Code, and complete digitization of the state's land portfolio. The draft code introduces "absolute exclusion mechanisms" barring legally disputed parcels from being assigned to investors. A companion decree-law project would grant the Real Estate Court ("Tribunal Immobilier") exceptional prerogatives and simplified derogatory procedures to definitively resolve disputes over collective/communal land ("terres collectives") — chiefly concentrated in southern governorates, where their unresolved legal status has long deterred private investment (notably in wind, solar, and industrial projects) — and to convert these land reserves into individual, transferable, bankable titles. A parallel digital land registry will map agricultural land in real time, showing exploitation status, usage-rights history, and legal status per parcel, interconnected with the Ministry of Economy's servers; of roughly 52,000 total state real-property files, audit committees have so far verified and registered 11,000 built and unbuilt assets for migration to the new dematerialized central database. Distinct from, but thematically adjacent to, the state-owned agricultural land regularization proposals above (Proposal No. 32/2025 and the long-term-leasing track), which target already-exploited state farmland specifically rather than the broader collective-land and state-domains-registry reform announced here. No decree-law text, bill number, or JORT publication had been identified as of this update.

Law No. 81-55 of June 23, 1981Real Estate Agent Profession

Enacted: June 23, 1981 | Amended: Law No. 2005-77 of August 8, 2005
Organizes the real-estate agent (agent immobilier) profession — brokerage and intermediation in property sales, purchases, and leases. Requires proof of professional competence (diploma or qualifying experience), a financial guarantee, and professional liability insurance for practice. Distinct from the Real Estate Development Law, which governs developers rather than brokers. (Run 90 addition)

Law No. 74-46 of May 22, 1974Architects Profession Organization

Enacted: May 22, 1974 | Disciplinary code: Decree No. 83-1033 of November 1983
Organizes the architecture profession — no one may use the title "architecte" or practice architecture in Tunisia without being registered in the Table of the Ordre des Architectes de Tunisie (OAT). Sets nationality, diploma, and character requirements for registration (Art. 1) and makes OAT membership mandatory (Art. 2); Decree No. 83-1033 sets out the professional code of duties and disciplinary sanctions (suspension, removal). Parallels the Urban Planning Code's building-permit regime above and the Engineers Profession Law below. (Run 90 addition)

🏢 Associations & Civil Society

Decree-Law No. 2011-88 of September 24, 2011Associations and Non-Profit Organizations

Enacted: September 24, 2011 | In force: 2011 | Replaced: Law No. 59-154 (1959)
Post-revolution statute liberalizing civil society formation. Replaced the restrictive 1959 law. Article 12: associations are legally constituted upon submission of a notification letter — no prior government approval required. Prohibits dissolution by executive action without judicial order. Enabled a rapid expansion of civil society: over 20,000 associations registered by 2015. Pending reform, updated status: a draft organic law replacing this decree-law (originally filed October 2023) is under active examination by the ARP Rights & Freedoms Commission — not merely "with the government" as previously reported — with the parliamentary bureau setting a June 24, 2026 deadline for the commission's report; as of early June 2026 the commission was still awaiting requested government agencies' opinions. Commission chair Thabet El Abed described the amended bill's foreign-funding provisions as a "disguised authorization dressed as a declaration," tightening administrative control (via Ministries of Interior and Foreign Affairs oversight and mandatory reporting of foreign transfers to the CTAF) over associational autonomy. At its June 3, 2026 session the commission was reportedly still working from a newly-received, updated version of the bill text requiring further review, had received no official government responses to its consultation letters, and had not yet scheduled civil-society hearings (Al Chourouk, June 4, 2026) — all of which suggests the June 24 report deadline was more likely missed than met, though no independent reporting has surfaced confirming whether the commission actually submitted a report by that date or what it concluded. This outcome remains unverified and should be checked again as later coverage emerges. On May 22, 2026, commission member Fatma Mseddi sent formal correspondence to the commission's president describing the file — by then covering at least twelve hearing sessions plus a dedicated study day — as effectively "blocked" despite having reached what she called an "advanced" stage, and pressed the ARP not to delay it further; this predates, and is consistent with, the June 24 deadline subsequently slipping without a confirmed outcome. Update (Run 34): as of July 1, 2026 the bill remains alive, not abandoned — the Rights & Freedoms Commission is now studying it jointly with the pending nationality-code and personal-data-protection bills (webdo.tn), with the commission publicly calling for "large concertation avec les acteurs concernés" (broad consultation with concerned stakeholders) before any adoption; no report or vote has yet followed the lapsed June 24 deadline. Civil society groups continue to warn the reform would restrict freedoms; not yet enacted as of July 2, 2026.
Key provisions
  • Art. 3: Freedom to form associations guaranteed
  • Art. 10: Founders submit notification (not seek prior approval) to the Secretary General of Government
  • Art. 12: Association acquires legal personality upon notification
  • Art. 14: Registration certificate issued within 7 days
  • Art. 26: Dissolution only by judicial order on defined grounds
  • Art. 31: Foreign associations may operate with prior authorization
AdministrativeConstitutional

Decree No. 2013-5183 of November 18, 2013 (as amended)Criteria & Conditions for Public Funding of Associations

Enacted: November 18, 2013 | Amended: Decree No. 2014-3607 (Oct. 3, 2014), Decree No. 2015-278 (June 1, 2015), Decree No. 2016-568 (May 17, 2016) | Most recent Art. 25 bis list: arrêté of July 24, 2026 (supersedes the arrêté of January 29, 2025, which itself superseded one of March 9, 2023)
The implementing decree under Decree-Law No. 2011-88 that sets the criteria, procedures, and conditions governing associations' access to public funding from the state budget and public bodies — previously undocumented in this artifact despite its direct relevance to the wave of civil-society suspensions detailed in the Administrative Suspensions & Judicial Dissolution Proceedings entry above, several of which were officially justified on grounds of "regularizing" an association's fiscal and administrative situation. Article 22 requires an association to refund public funding received under a non-complied contract, in whole or the unspent remainder, unless it regularizes its situation within three months of notice. Articles 19 and 21 impose funding-disclosure and reporting obligations on the public bodies that grant such funding; Circulaire n° 24 of September 25, 2024 specifically reminded public structures of their duty to comply with those two articles, reflecting continued enforcement focus on this decree as a compliance lever. Article 25 bis establishes a periodically updated official list, fixed by arrêté of the Head of Government, of associations subject to its special funding provisions — most recently renewed July 24, 2026 (per JORT-linked reporting), the fourth such listing on record after arrêtés of March 9, 2023, and January 29, 2025. No amendment altering the decree's substantive criteria (as opposed to the periodic Art. 25 bis list) was identified as of July 2026.
Administrative

Decree-Law No. 2011-87 of September 24, 2011Political Parties

Enacted: September 24, 2011 | In force: 2011 | Amended: 2014
Governs the formation, registration, financing, and activities of political parties. Requires notification-based registration (not prior authorization). Prohibits parties based exclusively on religion, race, gender, or region. Mandates financial transparency and annual reporting. Political party financing regulated: prohibits foreign funding, limits campaign spending. Update (Run 201): a wholly separate legislative track — a 6-article proposition de loi formally filed July 9, 2026 by deputy Fatma Mseddi — would designate Ennahdha as the Muslim Brotherhood's "political and organizational continuation" in Tunisia and classify it (along with any linked association or structure) as a terrorist organization, distinct from this decree-law's own party-dissolution mechanism; Mseddi had raised the idea informally since 2023, and this filing now formally opens the ARP's ordinary legislative examination process. No committee hearing date has yet been set (L'Économiste Maghrébin, Business News, both July 9, 2026).
AdministrativeConstitutional

Organic Law No. 2014-16 of May 26, 2014 (as amended)Electoral Law

Enacted: May 26, 2014 | In force: 2014 | Amended: 2019, 2022, September 27, 2024
Governs elections for the President of the Republic, the Assembly of People's Representatives, and the Assembly of Regions and Districts. Establishes the Independent High Authority for Elections (ISIE) as the permanent electoral commission. Sets rules on candidacy, campaigning, vote counting, and dispute resolution. The 2022 amendments (Decree-Law 2022-22) modified ISIE membership and reduced its independence according to critics. September 27, 2024 amendment: adopted by the ARP just nine days before the October 6, 2024 presidential election, it transferred jurisdiction over electoral disputes — including candidate-eligibility appeals previously heard by the Administrative Court — to the ordinary Court of Appeal of Tunis, with a 48-hour deadline to file contested-result challenges. The change followed Administrative Court rulings reinstating several candidates ISIE had excluded, and was criticized by Human Rights Watch and other observers as weakening judicial checks on election integrity at a sensitive moment. (Run 508 addition): only three candidates were ultimately approved to run in the October 6, 2024 election under this ISIE-administered framework — incumbent Kaïs Saïed, Zouhair Maghzaoui, and businessman Ayachi Zammel, who was imprisoned on electoral-fraud charges for much of the campaign itself, a circumstance widely cited alongside the September 27 amendment as evidence of the vote's constrained competitiveness (Saïed was re-elected with 90.69% on 28.8% turnout, the lowest of Tunisia's three post-2011 presidential cycles). Zammel's case reached a notable coda on July 23, 2026: marking the 69th anniversary of the Republic's proclamation, President Saïed granted a presidential pardon to 2,439 detainees and ordered the conditional release of 490 more, with Zammel among the beneficiaries, alongside former Tunisian Football Federation president Wadie Jary (Webdo, Business News, Kapitalis, La Presse, and L'Économiste Maghrébin, all July 23, 2026, cross-checked against each other) — a genuinely new development, not previously captured by any of the prior 507 runs. (Run 1072 addition): a worked example of this Law's vacant-seat by-election procedure occurred at El Kabaria (Tunis governorate) in 2026, following the death of sitting deputy Salah Mbarki. Presidential Decree No. 2026-42 of March 27, 2026 formally convened voters; ISIE (chaired by Farouk Bouasker) ran the registration, candidacy-vetting, and polling operations, holding a first round on June 28, 2026 (2,166 total votes cast, roughly 4% turnout — Mohamed Salah Salmi 663 votes/30.61% and Chaker Bouthouri 657 votes/30.33%, a six-vote margin insufficient for the absolute majority this Law requires, triggering a runoff) and a second round on July 19, 2026, again marked by very low turnout, which Chaker Bouthouri won 1,225 votes (50.14%) to Salmi's 1,218. Sourced via ISIE.tn, Business News, Tunisie Numérique, Espace Manager, and allAfrica/La Presse de Tunisie (multiply cross-checked, April–July 2026).
ConstitutionalAdministrative

Draft Law No. 027/2023 and Government Counter-Draft (2024)Proposed NGO Reform (Pending)

Parliamentary draft introduced: 2023 | Government draft reported: July 2024 | New organic law proposal: April 2026 | Status: Not enacted as of July 2026
Several competing proposals to replace Decree-Law No. 2011-88 on associations. The most advanced, presented to the ARP in April 2026, is a comprehensive organic law proposal of 45 articles across 8 chapters governing the creation, management, financing, oversight, and sanctioning of associations. Its Article 26 would ban all foreign funding of associations without prior written authorization from the Prime Minister's office (Présidence du Gouvernement), with a 2-month response deadline and implicit approval if the deadline lapses unanswered. The ARP held a dedicated study day on the bill in April 2026, and its Rights and Freedoms Committee was tasked with finalizing its report by June 24, 2026. Strongly opposed by Tunisian civil society, Article 19, ICNL, and Amnesty International as reversing the 2011 notification-based system. As of July 2026, no final law adopted; the 2011 Decree-Law remains formally in force, though see the entry below on its administrative circumvention in practice.
AdministrativeConstitutional

Proposition de loi organique (May 2026)Unified Electoral Code Proposal

Presented: May 10, 2026 (initial proposal); May 19, 2026 (expanded coverage) | Status: Under committee review, not enacted
A group of 29 Assembly of People's Representatives deputies presented an organic law proposal to consolidate Tunisia's electoral and referendum rules — currently scattered across the base 2014 Electoral Law and its many subsequent amending organic laws and decree-laws (including the 2022 ISIE reorganization and the September 27, 2024 dispute-jurisdiction amendment already documented above) — into a single unified electoral code. Transmitted to the ARP's Committee on Internal Rules, Electoral Laws, and Parliamentary Functions on May 7, 2026. As drafted, the code runs to 261 articles across three parts: (1) rules for direct elections (presidential, legislative) and referendums; (2) rules for regional/district council elections and the Conseil National des Régions et des Districts; and (3) transitional and final provisions. The proposal would centralize rules governing presidential, legislative, municipal, local, and regional elections plus referendums in one text, revise the distribution of electoral constituencies, address vacant-seat procedures in overseas electoral districts, and clarify the relationship between candidates and the Court of Accounts on campaign-finance disputes. A May 19, 2026 committee session opened debate on two contested provisions carried over from earlier electoral-law drafts: a proposed 5,000-dinar candidacy deposit (caution) and a minimum education-level requirement for candidates, both described in Tunisian press coverage as a "sensitive debate" among deputies. Distinct from, and broader in scope than, the narrower September 2024 amendment; as of July 2026 it remains under committee examination with no vote scheduled.
ConstitutionalAdministrative

Proposition de Loi Organique n°105/2025ISIE Composition & Member-Vetting Reform

Filed: July 21, 2025, by 14 deputies | ARP bureau referral: January 29, 2026 | Status: under committee review, not enacted
A 29-article, six-chapter organic-law proposal detailing the constitutional principles governing the Independent High Authority for Elections (ISIE) — council structure, member composition, election procedures, member rights/obligations, and administrative management. Distinct from, and narrower than, the 261-article Unified Electoral Code proposal above (which the same parliamentary committee is examining as a separate text) and from the 2022 ISIE reorganization already documented in the Constitutional Law section. Would expand ISIE's council from seven to nine members, with a minimum of four women, capped at six-year terms; establishes a dedicated parliamentary vetting commission to screen candidates down to 18 nominees by a three-fourths committee vote before submitting them to the full ARP for confirmation by absolute majority. Referred by the ARP bureau on January 29, 2026 to the Commission on Internal Regulations, Electoral Laws, Parliamentary Laws and Electoral Function. Not yet enacted as of July 2026.

Administrative Suspensions & Judicial Dissolution Proceedings Against Civil Society OrganizationsLTDH, ASF Tunisia, ATFD, FTDES, Al Khatt/Inkyfada & Mnemty (2025–2026)

ATFD & FTDES measures: 2025 | Al Khatt & Mnemty suspensions: October 2025 | LTDH suspension: notified April 24, 2026, for one month | Avocats Sans Frontières Tunisia suspension: notified May 5, 2026 | Al Khatt/Mnemty dissolution case opened: May 11, 2026, postponed to June 1 then split — Al Khatt to July 6, 2026 (outcome still unreported), Mnemty to August 24, 2026 | LTDH court appeal: postponed June 10, 2026, to July 15, 2026, then postponed a third time to July 29, 2026
Rather than amending Decree-Law 2011-88 itself, authorities have increasingly relied on administrative and fiscal powers to suspend prominent civil society organizations' activities. In April 2026, the Ligue Tunisienne pour la Défense des Droits de l'Homme (LTDH) — founded 1976, one of the oldest human rights organizations in Africa and the Arab world, and a member of the National Dialogue Quartet awarded the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize — was formally notified of a one-month suspension of its activities, officially justified on grounds of regularizing its fiscal and administrative situation. LTDH filed a court appeal against the suspension; the competent chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance held a hearing on June 10, 2026 but postponed examination of the appeal to July 15, 2026, leaving the matter unresolved as of this update. (Run 299 update): Kapitalis and Business News (both June 10–11, 2026) report that approximately 180 lawyers have formally constituted themselves as part of LTDH's defense team for the appeal — an unusually large collective mobilization by the bar reflecting the case's profile — with the hearing still confirmed for tomorrow, July 15, 2026, and no further postponement or early ruling reported by any outlet checked as of this update. Update (Run 313): as of this run's cutoff — the same calendar day as the scheduled hearing — no ruling or outcome has been reported by any outlet checked (Business News, Réalités, Kapitalis, Gnet), consistent with the possibility that same-day coverage has simply not yet been published or indexed. One relevant procedural note not previously flagged: Tunisian courts' annual judicial recess ("vacations judiciaires") conventionally begins July 15, which may affect whether and how quickly this appeal is actually resolved on the scheduled date; this is offered as plausible context rather than a confirmed explanation for the reporting gap, since no source directly linked the recess to this specific case. Update (Run 315): a further same-day sweep (French, English, and Arabic-language search) still found no ruling reported by any outlet, including ONAT's and LTDH's own channels — the reporting gap now spans the entirety of the hearing day itself, consistent with the judicial-recess timing noted at Run 313 rather than any indication the hearing was cancelled or further postponed. Update (Run 342): the July 15, 2026 hearing did not, in fact, produce a ruling — African Manager and Gnet (both July 15, 2026) report the Tunis Court of First Instance's correctional chamber adjourned the appeal a third time, to July 29, 2026, to allow time for a response to a report from the prosecutor general for state litigation ("rapport du procureur général auprès du contentieux de l'État"). This resolves the ambiguity Runs 313 and 315 had flagged around the judicial-recess timing: the case was formally postponed rather than silently unreported. Days later, in May 2026, Avocats Sans Frontières Tunisia (ASF Tunisia) was notified of a comparable suspension. The Tunisian Association of Democratic Women (ATFD) and the Tunisian Forum for Economic and Social Rights (FTDES) faced comparable measures during 2025, part of a wave reported by rights groups as exceeding 20 NGO suspensions since July 2025. Decree-Law 2011-88, Art. 26 requires dissolution to occur only by judicial order; rights groups (FIDH, Committee for Justice, SNJT) characterize these administrative suspensions as circumventing that judicial-order requirement and warn they set a precedent for sidelining the 2011 framework without formally repealing it. Update (Run 39): Amnesty International (May 2026) and Human Rights Watch (June 9, 2026) reports independently put the wider tally at roughly 25 associations affected by suspension or comparable administrative obstruction since mid-2025, and name additional organizations beyond the four detailed above, including Aswat Nissa, the World Organisation Against Torture's Tunisia programme (OMCT-Tunisia), I Watch (the Tunisian chapter of Transparency International), and the investigative outlet Nawaat. Both organizations frame the pattern as a coordinated use of fiscal-regularization and administrative-authorization pretexts against rights, anti-corruption, and media-adjacent groups specifically, rather than an across-the-board enforcement sweep. This remains executive/judicial practice under the existing Decree-Law 2011-88, distinct from the still-pending organic-law reform of that decree tracked in the entry above. Dissolution escalation (added Run 173): two of the suspended associations have since progressed from suspension to actual judicial dissolution proceedings — a materially more severe stage of the same Decree-Law 2011-88, Art. 26 mechanism. Al Khatt, founded December 2013 and the publisher of the investigative outlet Inkyfada since 2014 (an ICIJ partner), was notified of a 30-day suspension in October 2025 over disputed foreign-funding declaration compliance; its court challenge to that suspension failed, after which the Presidency of the Government (La Kasbah) filed a formal request for Al Khatt's judicial dissolution, announced by the association April 21–23, 2026. The Tunis Court of First Instance opened examination of the dissolution request on May 11, 2026 — jointly with an identical dissolution request against Mnemty, the anti-racism association whose president Saadia Mosbah was separately convicted on unrelated money-laundering/illicit-enrichment charges (see the Racial Discrimination Law entry) and which had itself been administratively suspended in October 2025 — with the session postponed first to June 1 and then to July 6, 2026 "to allow completion of case-file documents." No outcome has been confirmed from any source as of this run's cutoff. Update (Run 315): a dedicated search for post-July 6 coverage again found nothing beyond the same pre-hearing postponement reporting already captured — the dissolution outcome remains unreported, now nine days on. RSF, CPJ, the SNJT, and ICIJ all condemned the Al Khatt proceeding as the culmination of a multi-year pressure campaign (repeated multi-month freezes of Al Khatt's bank accounts, a January 2026 financial-crimes-unit summons) rather than a response to any single new complaint, and warned that dissolving a media outlet's publishing association achieves the same silencing effect as a direct press-law prosecution while bypassing press-specific legal safeguards entirely — see also the Decree-Law 2022-54 entry's note on CPJ's broader May 2026 "Beyond Decree 54" findings. Update (Run 186): the Intersection association for rights and freedoms' civil-society monitoring report (published via Kapitalis, July 8, 2026, and the same source underlying the Abdallah Saïd case added at Run 184) puts a first aggregate figure on the pattern's scale over its full May 2024–May 2026 monitoring window: 88 documented cases affecting civil-society organizations and activists, comprising 47 restriction/prosecution situations against associations and organizations and 41 separate judicial proceedings against individual activists and organizational leaders, of which 8 involved pre-trial detention (34 defendants prosecuted but released, 7 first-instance convictions recorded), plus 22 separate one-month administrative suspension orders against associations. The report frames the pattern as resting on four recurring mechanisms: criminalization via counterterrorism and anti-money-laundering statutes, rapid-succession administrative suspension orders, financial obstruction through frozen bank accounts, and official stigmatization branding targeted organizations as "traitors" or "foreign agents" — and documents concrete service losses from the suspensions already detailed above, including the ATFD closure eliminating four support centers for abuse victims and the loss of psychological services for refugee and migrant children. Update (Run 477): a further individual civil-society detention, previously absent from this artifact, was identified and added as a standalone entry below: the Saloua Ghrissa case (executive director of the Association for the Promotion of the Right to Difference, held over fifteen months in pretrial detention on foreign-funding allegations before her March 19, 2026 provisional release), corroborated across Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, Business News, Nawaat, and Kapitalis. Update (Run 946): the joint Al Khatt/Mnemty dissolution case, previously tracked as a single unresolved hearing since the July 6, 2026 postponement, has in fact split into two separate tracks: Kapitalis (July 29, 2026) reports that the emergency chamber ("chambre des référés") of the Tunis Court of First Instance postponed examination of Mnemty's dissolution specifically to August 24, 2026, on the request of the State's Legal Representative (Chargé du contentieux de l'État), who alleges the association committed "several breaches and violations of applicable regulations." Al Khatt's branch of the case remains separately adjourned from its own July 6, 2026 hearing with no outcome reported by any outlet as of this run. The two tracks are procedurally distinct from Saadia Mosbah's criminal conviction (see the Racial Discrimination Law entry): the dissolution case targets the Mnemty association itself as a civil-society entity, not its president individually. Confirmed via Kapitalis; not yet independently cross-checked against a second outlet as of this run, so treat the August 24 date as single-sourced pending confirmation in a future run. Update (Run 1088): a fresh sweep found no ruling reported yet on either the LTDH suspension appeal (adjourned since July 29, 2026) or the Mnemty dissolution case (adjourned since August 24, 2026); both remain open. Separately, a genuinely new development: on August 25, 2026, six international organizations — the International Commission of Jurists, Avocats Sans Frontières, No Peace Without Justice, EuroMed Rights, the World Organisation Against Torture, and Human Rights Watch — issued a joint letter (via allAfrica/ISHR) calling on UN member states to raise Tunisia's human-rights situation at the UN Human Rights Council's 63rd session (September 7 – October 9, 2026), under agenda Items 2 or 4, and to meet with Tunisian civil-society representatives. The letter cites, alongside the suspensions and dissolution proceedings documented in this entry: the dissolution of the High Judicial Council under Decree-Law 2022-11 and the 57 judges dismissed under Decree-Law 2022-35 (see the Judicial Statute entry), Decree-Law 2022-54 prosecutions of Sonia Dahmani, Khaoula Boukrim, Zied El Heni, and Haythem El Mekki (see the Decree-Law 2022-54 and Telecommunications Code entries), blocked Truth and Dignity Commission transitional-justice prosecutions and amnesty decrees, Sihem Bensedrine's 25-year conviction, electoral-candidate disqualifications, and the suspension of UNHCR refugee registration since May 2024 — a broader international-advocacy synthesis of this artifact's own documented pattern rather than a new legal instrument, so logged here as context rather than a standalone entry.

Law No. 69-4 of January 24, 1969Public Meetings, Processions & Demonstrations

Enacted: January 24, 1969 | In force: 1969 | Replaced: colonial-era decrees of 1905 and 1936
Regulates public meetings, processions, parades, demonstrations, and gatherings (réunions publiques, cortèges, défilés, manifestations et attroupements) — the base statute governing freedom of assembly in public spaces, distinct from and predating Decree-Law No. 2011-88 above (which governs the formation of associations, not the conduct of gatherings). Requires prior declaration to governorate or delegation authorities, or to the National Security Directorate in Tunis, typically 3 to 15 days before the event; authorities may restrict or ban gatherings on public-order grounds. Frequently cited in UN Special Rapporteur communications and civil-society reporting on freedom of assembly in Tunisia. No amendment or replacement bill was identified as of July 2026.

🛡️ Security & Counter-terrorism

Organic Law No. 2015-26 of August 7, 2015Countering Terrorism and Suppression of Money Laundering (as amended)

Enacted: August 7, 2015 (corrected from a previously listed July 7, 2015) | Amended: Organic Law No. 2019-9 of January 23, 2019
Cross-referenced from the Criminal Law section (see the fuller entry there for provisions and the 2019-9 amendment). Comprehensive counter-terrorism statute enacted following the Bardo Museum and Sousse beach attacks (2015). Replaced the 2003 anti-terrorism law. Defines terrorism broadly, criminalizes financing, propaganda, recruitment, and travel for terrorist purposes. Establishes specialized anti-terrorism courts and the Financial Intelligence Unit (CTAF). Criticized by human rights groups for overly broad definitions and extended pre-charge detention.
Key provisions
  • Broad definition of "terrorist act" including threats to public order
  • Criminalization of glorification of terrorism and incitement
  • Criminalizes financing of terrorism and related financial flows
  • Prohibition on travel to conflict zones for terrorist purposes
  • Specialized Terrorism Chamber at the Court of First Instance of Tunis
  • Extended detention periods for terrorism suspects
  • Asset freezing without prior judicial authorization

"Law No. 2019-73" — Correction: Citation Not Verified, Content Contradicted by ReportingInternal Security Forces Statute (Retracted)

Correction: Run 1037
Correction (Run 1037): this entry previously described a "Law No. 2019-73 of December 31, 2019" as the Internal Security Forces Statute, defining missions, hierarchy, disciplinary procedures, and — specifically — "an independent oversight body for police conduct complaints." Both the citation and that claim do not survive verification. No law numbered 2019-73 concerning internal security appears in legislation-securite.tn's own site search (which returned only an unrelated August 2019 HAICA personnel-statute decree for the string "2019-73"), in jurisitetunisie.com, or in any independent secondary source; the number and date pattern read like a plausible but unconfirmed guess rather than a checked citation. The substantive claim is independently contradicted: Tunisia has no independent external body for police-conduct complaints. Complaints against police are handled internally by the Ministry of Interior's own Inspection Générale de la Sûreté Nationale (IGSN) — not an independent authority — and civil-society and EU-funded proposals for a genuinely independent ethics/complaints commission have been advocated since shortly after 2011 without being enacted (Leaders.com.tn, Jeune Afrique); a UNDP-partnered citizen-complaints portal was only in planning for 2025–2026, not a 2019 statutory oversight body. The actual employment/organizational statute of the internal security forces is the General Statute of the Internal Security Forces, Law No. 82-70 of August 6, 1982 (as amended by Law No. 2000-58, Decree-Law No. 2011-42, and Decree-Law No. 2011-69) — confirmed via legislation-securite.tn's own amendment history, which shows no repeal or replacement by any 2019 instrument. This entry is retained, retitled, rather than deleted, so the correction is traceable; readers should treat the FSI general-statute entry as authoritative on this subject.

Law No. 2013-50 of December 19, 2013Compensation for Internal Security Force Work Accidents & Occupational Diseases (Run 120 addition)

Enacted: December 19, 2013 | Published: JORT No. 101, December 20, 2013 | Pending amendment: Proposition de loi n° 42/2025 (referred to committee May 15, 2025)
A wholly new standalone entry — despite extensive existing coverage of the Internal Security Forces Statute (Law No. 2019-73, above), this distinct compensation statute had never been documented. Establishes a special regime (régime particulier de réparation) compensating internal security force (police and National Guard) agents, cadets at their basic-training academies (per implementing Decree No. 2021-365 of May 26, 2021), or their surviving dependents, for bodily harm from workplace accidents and occupational diseases. Defines a workplace accident as any incident occurring "by reason of or on the occasion of" service duties and recognizes a schedule of presumed occupational illnesses. A dedicated medical commission establishes the causal link, sets the disability rate, and authorizes treatment. Compensation takes the form of lump-sum capital for disability rates of 5–15%, or an ongoing pension for rates of 15% and above, alongside full medical-care coverage, salary continuation during temporary incapacity, prosthetics, and survivor benefits (spouse, orphans, dependents) with enhanced allowances for dependent children and those requiring third-party care. Pending amendment: Proposition de loi n° 42/2025, referred to the ARP's Defense, Security and Armed Forces Commission on May 15, 2025, would revise Article 42 to extend the regime's benefits to agents whose disability rate was administratively determined before the law's December 2013 entry into force — closing a transitional-wording gap affecting an estimated ~400 agents, mostly retirees. Per a July 1, 2026 committee report, the bill has been finalized and transmitted to the ARP's Bureau, pending a study session ahead of plenary examination; not yet enacted as of this run.

State of Emergency Decree — Decree No. 78-50 of January 26, 1978

Enacted: January 26, 1978 | In force: 1978 | Continuously renewed since November 2015
Establishes the legal framework for declaring and managing states of emergency. Grants expanded executive powers including restriction of movement, house arrest, administrative detention, and closure of meeting places. Tunisia declared a state of emergency in November 2015 (after the Bardo Museum and Sousse beach attacks) and has renewed it without interruption since — now its tenth consecutive year. The most recent renewal, Décret n° 2026-15 of January 30, 2026 (JORT), extended the nationwide state of emergency declared by Décret n° 2025-485 of December 29, 2025 through December 31, 2026.

Arrêté Républicain n° 2013-230 of August 29, 2013 (as renewed annually)Southern/Western Buffer Frontier Zone (Run 965 addition)

Enacted: August 29, 2013 (JORT No. 2013-071) | Most recent renewal: Décret présidentiel n° 2026-206 of August 12, 2026 (JORT), extending the zone for a further year from August 29, 2026 to August 28, 2027
A wholly new standalone entry — despite extensive coverage of the state-of-emergency regime, military justice, and internal-security legislation above, this distinct, continuously-active border-security instrument had never been documented. The 2013 arrêté républicain proclaims a "zone frontalière tampon" (buffer frontier zone) along Tunisia's desert southern, southeastern, and western approaches: the southern Saharan band running south of the Lozrot–Al-Borma line to the Tunisian-Libyan border and to Borj El Khadra on the Tunisian-Algerian border, plus a strip bordering Algeria and the southeastern approach bordering Libya. Access for work or tourism requires prior authorization from the competent regional governor, with entry/exit confined to designated gates (Kambout, Al-Kamour, Al-Jbeil, Al-Matrouha, and others later created) and control/inspection points, and enforcement vested jointly in military, security, customs, and local civil authorities. The proclamation is not self-renewing: its provisions lapse unless extended by a fresh presidential decree each year, a chain unbroken (with some skipped press coverage in intervening years) since 2013, including renewals in 2015, 2016, 2017, Décret n° 2018-82 of August 14, 2018, Décret n° 2021-105 of August 18, 2021, Décret n° 2022-652 of July 21, 2022, a 2024 renewal, Décret gouvernemental n° 2025-376 of July 28, 2025 (JORT No. 96), and most recently Décret présidentiel n° 2026-206 of August 12, 2026. No underlying statute broadening or narrowing the zone's scope was identified this run — each renewal decree is a short, single-purpose prorogation of the original 2013 text.

Code de Justice Militaire — Decree No. 57-9 of January 10, 1957 (extensively amended)

Enacted: January 10, 1957 (JORT N°4, January 11, 1957) | Key amendments: Décret-loi n° 86-5 of September 16, 1986 (ratified by Loi n° 86-101 of December 9, 1986); Décret-loi n° 2011-69 of July 29, 2011; Loi n° 2024-35 of July 15, 2024
Correction (Run 134): this entry previously cited a non-existent "Law No. 86-79 of September 9, 1986" as the code's origin and asserted a "2019 amendment" restricting military-court jurisdiction over civilians. Independent, twice-corroborated research found neither claim verifiable in any Tunisian legislative database and both are now removed. The correct originating instrument is Decree No. 57-9 of January 10, 1957, subsequently amended by Décret-loi n° 86-5/1986 (ratified by Loi n° 86-101/1986), the post-revolution procedural reform Décret-loi n° 2011-69 of July 29, 2011 (created a military appeals chamber and expanded civil-party rights, but did not remove civilian jurisdiction), and most recently Loi n° 2024-35 of July 15, 2024, which narrowly amended Article 68's definition of desertion abroad in peacetime (unauthorized border crossing or absence from one's unit for 3+ days in peacetime, reduced to 1 day in wartime; also covers failure to return within 3 days after leave, mission, or training abroad ends). Military courts retain jurisdiction over civilians under Article 8 of the code, and Article 91 (criticizing/insulting the armed forces) remains actively used to prosecute journalists and activists: the 2014 Constitution's transitional provisions kept the 1957 code in force pending amendment, a November 2018 reform bill to exclude civilians from military jurisdiction stalled in the ARP and was never adopted, and civilian prosecutions have continued and increased under President Kais Saied — the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT) recorded 39+ cases against journalists before military courts since May 2023, including journalist Nasreddine Halimi's March 2025 sentencing by the Kef Military Court over Facebook posts. Confirmed by Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch (World Report 2025), the ICJ, and Tunisia's November 2022 UN Universal Periodic Review submission.

Weapons Law — Law No. 69-33 of June 12, 1969

Enacted: June 12, 1969 | Published: JORT N°23, June 13, 1969 | Implementing decree: Decree No. 70-60 of February 21, 1970
Regulates the import, trade, possession, and carrying of weapons and ammunition in Tunisia. Classifies weapons into five categories: military weapons, defensive/sporting weapons, hunting weapons, historical/collectible weapons, and air rifles. No unified "Code des Armes" exists — the framework remains this single 1969 law plus implementing decrees, with no confirmed later amendment identified.

Law No. 93-121 of December 27, 1993National Civil Protection Office (Fire & Rescue Services) (Run 81 addition)

Enacted: December 27, 1993 | Org-chart decree: Decree No. 99-2058 of September 13, 1999 | Administrative/financial-organization decree: Decree No. 94-568 of March 15, 1994
A wholly new standalone entry — despite extensive coverage of the National Police and National Guard under the Internal Security Forces Statute above, Tunisia's separate civil-defense/fire-and-rescue institution had never been documented. Creates the Office National de la Protection Civile as an établissement public à caractère industriel et commercial (EPIC) with legal personality and financial autonomy, headquartered in Tunis and placed under the supervision of the Ministry of Interior, tasked broadly with disaster and catastrophe response (Art. 2). Confirmed via legislation-securite.tn and cross-checked secondary sourcing; the primary JORT/legislation.tn text itself could not be directly reached (HTTP 503), so this entry carries medium-high rather than primary-source-verified confidence. Note: Decree No. 99-2058 only fixes the Office's organizational chart, not general implementation — Decree No. 94-568 (administrative and financial organization) is the more substantive implementing text.

Law No. 2002-81 of August 3, 2002 (as amended)Private Security, Guarding & Valuables-Transport Activities (Run 159 addition)

Enacted: August 3, 2002 | Amended: Law No. 2008-14 of February 18, 2008
A wholly new standalone entry, missed by all 158 prior runs. Regulates three categories of private security activity: property monitoring/guarding ("gardiennage"), armed transport of funds and precious metals, and physical protection of persons. Companies and their legal representatives must obtain prior authorization from the Minister of Interior (Art. 4), which is personal, non-transferable, and valid for a five-year renewable term. Licensing conditions (Art. 6) require Tunisian nationality held for at least five years, enjoyment of civil and political rights, absence of convictions for theft, fraud, forgery, or terrorism-related offenses, good conduct, commercial registration, no bankruptcy history, and no concurrent professional activity. Employees (Art. 11) must meet similar nationality/conduct standards, be at least 20 years old, hold a ninth-grade education minimum, and pass physical/mental fitness requirements; agents carry a professional card whose specimen and uniform were separately fixed by Interior Ministry orders of June 11, 2003 (professional-card digitalization introduced in 2024). Article 32 criminalizes unauthorized practice or continuing operations after suspension/revocation, punishable by three years' imprisonment and a fine of TND 50,000–100,000. Law No. 2008-14 subsequently amended several provisions, including the criminal-penalty and transitional-requirement articles. (Run 160 update) Article 15 confines licensed agents strictly to their authorized "gardiennage"/protection mission and expressly bars them from crime-prevention or suspect-pursuit acts, and from any act infringing a person's freedom of movement, physical integrity, or private life (including body/bag searches or seizure of personal effects without the owner's express consent); physical force is prohibited except in self-defense. Article 16 further confines agents to their assigned premises, with street-level intervention authorized only exceptionally, against theft or property damage. Read together, these provisions are the legal basis for the position — confirmed by the Interior Ministry's licensing framework — that private-detective and private-investigation activity (surveillance, filature, personal inquiries) is not a licensable profession in Tunisia, notwithstanding the many "private detective" services advertised online to the Tunisian market.

Law No. 82-70 of August 6, 1982General Statute of the Internal Security Forces (Statut Général des Forces de Sécurité Intérieure)

Enacted: August 6, 1982 | Amended: Law No. 2000-58 (June 13, 2000); Decree-Law No. 2011-42 of May 25, 2011 (opened the way to FSI unions); Law No. 2013-50 (December 19, 2013) | Companion text: Decree No. 2023-240 of March 16, 2023 approving the FSI code of conduct | In force as amended
The foundational employment statute of Tunisia's internal security forces, absent from this artifact until this run. Its defining legal characteristic is the classification in its opening provisions: the FSI are a civil armed force — civil, and therefore not subject to the Military Justice Code as a matter of course, but armed, and therefore not ordinary civil servants under the general civil-service statute either. That intermediate status is what the statute exists to define. It is supplemented by special statutes for each corps: the Sûreté nationale, the Police nationale, the Garde nationale, the Protection civile and the Douane. The 1982 text governs recruitment, career, transfer, hierarchy and retirement; sets obligations and incompatibilities; and establishes the disciplinary regime and the delegation of disciplinary powers, alongside the use-of-force framework. Its most consequential amendment is Decree-Law No. 2011-42 of May 25, 2011, which relaxed the original prohibition on unionisation and made the post-revolution security-union movement legally possible — a change whose consequences run through much of the policing and accountability material elsewhere in this artifact. Several 2020–2021 reform bills would have replaced the statute outright; none was enacted. Relationship to the "Law No. 2019-73" entry, resolved (Run 1037): that entry's citation does not check out — no such law is traceable in any Tunisian legal database, and its central claim (an independent police-complaints oversight body) is contradicted by reporting confirming no such body exists. This 1982 statute, as amended, is the actual, sole general employment statute of the internal security forces; the other entry has been retitled as a correction rather than left to stand as a parallel source. (Added Run 1036; relationship resolved Run 1037.)

Code of Safety and Prevention of Fire, Explosion and Panic Risks in Buildings — Law No. 2009-11 of March 2, 2009Code de la Sécurité et de la Prévention des Risques d'Incendie, d'Explosion et de Panique dans les Bâtiments

Promulgated: March 2, 2009 | Implementing regulations issued by building type (residential buildings, order of June 2, 2017; classified installations, order of September 21, 2018) | In force
An entire code that this artifact had referenced only incidentally — inside the food-safety entry, which corrects a widespread secondary-source error that misidentifies Law No. 2009-11 as a food-safety statute. It is nothing of the kind: it consolidates into a single code all rules on fire, explosion and panic safety in buildings, and it deserves its own entry both because it is a code and because it sits at the junction of three areas this artifact already covers separately — civil protection, the Urban Planning Code, and construction liability. It classifies buildings and establishments open to the public, imposes obligations on owners, operators and designers at the design, construction and operation stages, requires prior safety approval and periodic inspection by the Office national de la protection civile, and provides sanctions. It expressly abrogates the prior scattered rules it replaces, including the regulation of January 12, 1942 on theatres and entertainment venues. (Added Run 1036.)

"Sumood/Global Sumud Flotilla" Money-Laundering & Terrorism-Financing Prosecutions (Run 91 addition)

Arrests: March 6–7, 2026 | Remanded into custody: March 16, 2026 | Msahli released: April 17, 2026 | Channa released: April 23, 2026 | Bennour released: May 22, 2026 | Boughdiri release request denied: July 16, 2026 | Nawar/Chennoufi/Henchiri release requests denied: July 21, 2026 | Families' joint public appeal: August 17, 2026 | Nawar begins hunger strike: August 16, 2026 (publicly announced August 18, 2026)
A wholly new standalone entry, entirely distinct from the "state security conspiracy" cluster above — at least eight Tunisian activists linked to the Sumood/Global Sumud Flotilla coordination unit (a pro-Palestinian, Gaza-bound aid-flotilla solidarity network) — Nabil Chennoufi, Wael Naouar/Nawar, Sana Msahli (also transliterated M'hidli), Jawaher Channa, Dr. Mohamed Amine Bannour (also transliterated Bennour/Bel Nour), Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri, and Wafa Kechida — were arrested March 6–7, 2026 and remanded into custody March 16, 2026 after prolonged anti-terrorism-unit questioning, investigated by the Economic and Financial Judicial Pole under case file 2026/4010 over roughly TND 1.5 million in donations collected for the flotilla's Gaza-aid effort. Prosecutors invoke Organic Law No. 2015-26 (Countering Terrorism and Suppression of Money Laundering, see entry above) alongside general money-laundering, forgery, and aggravated-breach-of-trust provisions, charging the group with "forming a money laundering conspiracy" and misuse of funds raised through an international crowdfunding campaign tied to the first Global Sumud Flotilla's September 2025 Gaza-aid mission. Tunisian and international rights groups (Amnesty International, Middle East Monitor) have called for the activists' release, framing the prosecution as a use of counter-terrorism/AML statutes against pro-Palestinian civic activism rather than a genuine financial-crime case. (Run 635 update): the Economic and Financial Judicial Pole has since ruled on multiple release requests from within this same detained group — also including Ghassen Boughdiri (whose separate common-law protest conviction is tracked in its own standalone entry, but who is additionally a defendant in this financial-crimes case) and Ghassen Henchiri — rejecting Boughdiri's request on July 16, 2026, and separately rejecting requests from Wael Nawar, Nabil Chennoufi, and Ghassen Henchiri on July 21, 2026, prolonging those defendants' pretrial detention at Mornaguia civil prison; Boughdiri began a hunger strike July 13, 2026 protesting four months' detention without having been questioned by an investigating judge, per his defense committee. (Run 660 update): a fuller audit of this docket found that custody status for the group has diverged well beyond the "still detained" framing above — three of the eight, Sana Msahli (released April 17, 2026, per Business News and webdo.tn), Jawaher Channa (released April 23, 2026, per Business News, Kapitalis, and directinfo/WMC), and Dr. Mohamed Amine Bannour (released May 22, 2026 under judicial controls — travel ban plus a media/social-media appearance restriction — per Business News, Kapitalis, and webdo.tn; not a full charge-drop), had already been freed months before this run, while the eighth defendant, Wafa Kechida — the initiative's accountant, tasked with consolidating expenses and invoices — has a custody status that remains genuinely unconfirmed in open sources rather than simply unreported: the Soumoud coordination's own public statement says only that it "lost contact" with her following the March 2026 arrest wave, and no outlet located by this run's search has independently reported whether she was released, remains detained, or was never formally held. Confirmed via Kapitalis, Business News, webdo.tn, directinfo/WebManagerCenter, and Inkyfada's dedicated investigative piece, cross-checked against each other; still no trial date or verdict reported for this financial-crimes case as of this run. (Run 896 update): Kapitalis's August 12, 2026 report, citing the digital-rights NGO Humena, confirms Wael Nawar, Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri, and Nabil Chennoufi remain in pretrial detention at Mornaguia prison nearly five months after their March 2026 arrests, with Humena flagging deteriorating health conditions and delayed medical access specifically for Henchiri and Boughdiri amid the broader prison-overcrowding conditions documented in the INPT entry above, and calling for the four's release pending trial absent a demonstrated ongoing necessity for detention. No change to custody status, charges, or trial-date reporting from the Run 660 findings; this is a conditions/advocacy update, not a legal-status change. (Run 977 update): Middle East Monitor reported on August 17, 2026 that the families of Wael Nawar, Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri, and Nabil Chennoufi went public for the first time in their own names — rather than a rights organization appealing on their behalf, as with the Run 896 Humena statement — jointly calling on Tunisia's political and judicial authorities to release the four and drop the charges entirely, describing the case as "not merely an individual matter" but "a cause of values, a cause of freedom," and again citing harsh Mornaguia detention conditions after more than five months held. No change to custody status, charges, or trial-date reporting; this is a further conditions/advocacy update, not a legal-status change. A wholly new standalone entry, distinct from the Sumood/Global Sumud Flotilla money-laundering cluster above despite the overlapping movement name and cause — an ordinary common-law prosecution rather than a terrorism/AML case. Ghassen Boughdiri, a member of the Coordination for Common Action for Palestine and the "Al Soumoud" committee, was sentenced May 7, 2026 to seven months' imprisonment for obstructing work and violence during a protest targeting businesses perceived as linked to the occupation, part of the Palestinian-solidarity economic-boycott campaign; the Soumoud movement publicly denounced the prosecution as "harassment" of activists. Affaire Bilel Chaouachi — Terrorist-Organization Leadership Conviction (Run 152 addition)

First instance: December 11, 2025 | Confirmed on appeal: July 6, 2026
A wholly new standalone entry, distinct from the state-security-conspiracy cluster and the Secret Apparatus/Instalingo cases above — an ordinary (non-political) prosecution under the Anti-Terrorism Law (Organic Law No. 2015-26, see Countering Terrorism entry above) of a jihadist leader rather than an opposition figure. Bilel (also spelled Bilal) Chaouachi, alias Abou Yahya Zakaria, a leader of Ansar al-Charia and Daech/ISIS, was prosecuted for terrorist acts committed in Syria, planning terrorist operations inside Tunisia, and recruiting and facilitating young Tunisians' departure to conflict zones. He appeared in a video released after the November 24, 2015 bombing of a presidential security bus in central Tunis, threatening further attacks; he has been listed on Tunisia's national list of terrorist persons (with an associated asset freeze) since 2019. The Tunis Court of First Instance's anti-terrorism chamber sentenced him to 55 years' imprisonment on December 11, 2025, and the Tunis Court of Appeal confirmed the full sentence on July 6, 2026 — corroborated across Kapitalis, Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, webdo, and La Presse de Tunisie.

Affaire "Créateurs de Contenu" — Mass TikTok/Instagram Prosecution (Run 155 addition)

Justice Ministry announcement: October 27, 2025 | Verdict: July 6, 2026
A wholly new standalone entry, distinct from the state-security-conspiracy, Secret Apparatus, Instalingo, and Chaouachi cases above — an ordinary (non-political) mass prosecution of social-media "content creators." Following an October 27, 2025 Justice Ministry announcement of prosecutions targeting online content "contrary to public morals," the criminal chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance referred 18 defendants to trial and, on July 6, 2026, sentenced them to terms ranging from 1 to 27 years' imprisonment. Charges spanned production, dissemination, publication, or transmission of sexually explicit videos and images tied to TikTok and Instagram activity, alongside human trafficking, money laundering, and drug-trafficking/promotion offenses. Prosecutors relied on three statutes in combination: Organic Law No. 2015-61 of August 3, 2015 (preventing and combating trafficking in persons, see Criminal Law section), Decree-Law No. 2022-54 of September 13, 2022 (combating offenses relating to information and communication systems, see Digital Law section), and Organic Law No. 2015-26 of August 7, 2015 (countering terrorism and money laundering, see entry above) (webdo.tn, July 7, 2026). Update (Run 493): a distinct, second prosecution — not the same 18 defendants — was reported July 23, 2026: the Tunis Court of First Instance's criminal chamber referred ten further defendants (also TikTok/Instagram content creators and influencers, some detained, others at liberty pending trial) to a hearing set for September 17, 2026, on narrower morals-focused charges: publishing pornographic content and content contrary to public morals, indecent exposure, and using communication networks/systems to disseminate obscene images and videos — charges under Decree-Law No. 2022-54 and the Penal Code's public-decency provisions, without the trafficking/money-laundering counts that distinguished the July 6, 2026 verdict above. Independently corroborated by African Manager and directinfo.webmanagercenter.com (both July 23, 2026). Watch for the September 17, 2026 hearing outcome.

Proposition de loi organique (unnumbered, filed by Deputy Fatma Mseddi + 9 co-sponsors, July 9, 2026)Classification of Ennahdha as a "Terrorist Organization" (Run 400 addition)

Filed with ARP: July 9, 2026 | Status: referred, no committee hearing date confirmed as of this run
A wholly new standalone entry closing a gap in the artifact's Security & Counter-terrorism coverage: a six-article draft organic law submitted to the ARP on July 9, 2026 by Deputy Fatma Mseddi together with nine co-sponsoring deputies, presented as aimed at "protecting national security, state sovereignty, and the republican regime" and preventing "the exploitation of parties and associations as fronts for terrorist organizations." The text characterizes Ennahdha as "the political and organizational continuation of the international organization of the Muslim Brotherhood" and, on that basis, proposes formally classifying it (and any association, organization, or structure with organizational, financial, or functional links to it or to the Muslim Brotherhood) as a terrorist organization. If adopted, the bill would order the immediate dissolution of all such structures; leaders whose membership or involvement is established would lose any elected mandate and be barred from standing for election or holding public office for ten years. Mseddi had signaled the initiative in March 2026 while collecting the co-sponsor signatures required to file it. As of this run, the bill is newly filed with no confirmed referral-committee hearing date, and should be distinguished from the separate, already-adjudicated "Secret Apparatus" case above (a criminal terrorist-organization prosecution under the existing Anti-Terrorism Law, Law No. 2015-26) — this bill instead seeks a prospective, generally-applicable statutory designation rather than a case-specific criminal verdict (Businessnews, L'Économiste Maghrébin, African Manager, Le Courrier de l'Atlas, Univers News, all July 9, 2026). Watch for committee referral and hearing scheduling in subsequent runs.

Decree-Law No. 2022-20 of April 9, 2022Fidaa Foundation for Terrorism Victims & Revolution Martyrs (Run 878 addition)

Enacted: April 9, 2022 | Published: JORT, April 2022 | Amended: Loi n° 2025-1 of January 9, 2025 (JORT Issue No. 4, January 10, 2025) | Expanded benefits in force: January 1, 2026
A wholly new standalone entry — despite being in force for over four years and substantially amended in 2025, this decree-law had never been documented. Establishes the Fidaa Foundation ("Fondation Fidaa"), a public establishment with legal personality and administrative/financial autonomy placed under the supervision of the Presidency of the Republic, to provide welfare and support to victims of terrorist acts among military personnel, internal security forces, and customs agents, and to the rights-holders of the Revolution's martyrs and wounded (events of December 2010–February 2011). Organized in 39 articles across 5 chapters (general provisions; the Foundation's structure; assistance to military/security/customs terrorism victims; assistance to Revolution martyrs' and wounded's rights-holders; miscellaneous provisions). Provides continued salary payment to martyrs' families as if the deceased remained employed, funeral/medical/psychological expense coverage, and disability pensions scaled to injury severity (from minimum wage up to three times minimum wage, plus a 10% increase per dependent child, up to three). Loi n° 2025-1 substantially expanded benefits: priority social-housing access with monetary allocations where housing is unavailable, free public-facility healthcare (including psychological support, medication, and prosthetics) with private-sector coverage where medically necessary, free domestic public transport and museum/cultural-site access, automatic rank promotion and employment-priority programs for injured personnel, martyr-dependent pensions calculated on presumed career-advancement salaries, caretaker allowances for severely injured beneficiaries, university scholarships and free student housing for victims' children through age 25, and duty-free vehicle acquisition every ten years (five years for adapted vehicles) — implemented from January 1, 2026 using the 48-hour weekly minimum wage as the pension-calculation baseline. Operationalized through 2026 via phased social-housing handovers to beneficiary families (e.g., a 16-unit tranche at El Fejja, Manouba, delivered August 11, 2026, part of roughly 240 units allocated nationwide to date). Confirmed via legislation-securite.tn, Espace Manager, Mosaïque FM, WebManagerCenter/Directinfo, and L'Économiste Maghrébin, cross-checked against each other for the enactment date, JORT reference, article count, and the 2025 amendment's expanded-benefits detail.

Law No. 2004-1 of January 14, 2004National Service Law (Service national) (Run 945 addition)

Enacted: January 14, 2004 | In force: 2004 | Amended: Law No. 2008-68 of November 3, 2008; Law No. 2010-17 of April 20, 2010
A wholly new standalone entry closing a gap that had survived every prior run — this artifact had no entry at all for Tunisia's national/military service framework, despite it applying to every Tunisian citizen aged 20–35. Article 1 states national service prepares citizens to defend the homeland and contribute to national development; service obligations run from age 20 through age 35. Implementing Decree No. 2004-377 of March 1, 2004 sets conditions for deferment (sursis) — automatically granted and renewable for students and workers under 28 — and exemption (dispense), reserved for serious health conditions/disability and, for Tunisians resident or employed abroad over age 28, on presentation of a foreign work contract and residence certificate; a Ministry of National Defense order of April 22, 2004 fixes the required application file for deferment/exemption requests. Recruitment and status regularization are handled by the Direction Générale du Recrutement et de la Mobilisation in Tunis and regional recruitment offices (Tunis, Sousse, Béja, Gabès, Kasserine); failure to regularize one's situation triggers administrative sanctions, including restrictions on obtaining or renewing travel documents. Confirmed via NATLEX (ILO), legislation-securite.tn, and La Presse de Tunisie's recurring service-national explainer coverage (most recently August 11–12, 2026), cross-checked against each other for the law number, enactment date, and amendment history.
