🛂 Nationality, Immigration & Asylum

Nationality Code — Law No. 63-6 of February 28, 1963

Enacted: February 28, 1963 | In force: 1963 | Amended: 1975, 2002, 2010
Defines Tunisian nationality by birth, descent, naturalization, and reacquisition. Originally limited transmission of nationality through the paternal line; the 2010 amendment allows Tunisian mothers married to foreign nationals to transmit nationality to their children. Governs loss, renunciation, and deprivation of nationality. Naturalization requires 5 years of lawful residence. Pending reform: a bill filed at the ARP on February 27, 2026 by 36 co-sponsoring deputies (now identifiable as projet de loi n° 17/2026) would tighten naturalization by requiring proof of legal/regular entry into Tunisia plus 7 consecutive years of legal residence (up from 5), while easing rules for stateless persons born in Tunisia and creating an expedited "exceptional interest" naturalization track for high-skill foreign nationals. The ARP Rights and Freedoms Commission examined the bill at a session held May 7, 2026, which press coverage of that session also described as addressing a requirement that a stateless child's parents hold legal Tunisian residency status for the child's citizenship eligibility. Under committee review as of this update; not yet adopted.
Key provisions
  • Art. 6: Nationality by birth to a Tunisian father (jus sanguinis)
  • Art. 12: Naturalization requires 5-year lawful residence
  • 2010 amendment: children of Tunisian mother and foreign father may acquire nationality
  • Art. 30–35: Loss and deprivation of Tunisian nationality
NationalityCivil

Law No. 68-7 of March 8, 1968Entry and Residence of Foreigners

Enacted: March 8, 1968 | In force: 1968 | Amended: 1975, 2004
Governs the entry, stay, and expulsion of foreign nationals in Tunisia. Requires visa for most non-Maghreb nationals (bilateral visa exemptions apply). Establishes residence permit categories and procedures. Governs administrative detention pending deportation. Tunisia has no comprehensive asylum law; refugee status was determined by UNHCR under its mandate, but in June 2024 Tunisian authorities instructed UNHCR to suspend new registration, pre-registration, and refugee-status-determination processing (services to already-registered refugees continued); the government's stated rationale was an intent to establish a national asylum system, which had not been enacted as of Human Rights Watch's 2025 and 2026 World Report chapters on Tunisia. Update (Run 103): an Amnesty International report of July 2, 2026 quantified the suspension's effect for the first time in this artifact — UNHCR-registered refugees in Tunisia fell from 18,362 in June 2024 (when the undisclosed suspension order was given) to 7,515 by April 2026, a roughly 59% decline — and documented a government-organized "voluntary return" program for migrants operating since June 2025, alongside continued reporting of abuse against refugees and asylum-seekers left without a functioning status-determination process. (Added Run 106) See the separate Passports & Travel Documents Law entry below for the distinct 1975 statute whose border-crossing offenses (rather than this law's visa/residence-permit framework) have been used to prosecute refugee-aid humanitarian workers. Pending reform (Run 803): a 19-article, 4-chapter proposition de loi filed at the ARP in December 2024 by deputy Fatma Mseddi and co-sponsors would add a dedicated legal framework for detaining and expelling migrants in an irregular situation — migrants declining "voluntary return" would be relocated away from urban centers pending identity verification, before expulsion. Sources genuinely conflict on the bill's procedural status: a March 13, 2026 La Presse de Tunisie report states the text is under active review by the ARP's General Legislation Commission and could soon receive a hearing, while Mseddi herself, quoted by Radio Express FM, has said the ARP bureau blocked the bill outright and never referred it to committee following its filing — both accounts are given here pending a source that resolves the discrepancy. Distinct from this law's existing administrative-detention provisions and from the 2004 Irregular Migration Law below, which criminalizes irregular departure ("harraga") by Tunisians rather than addressing inbound migrants. Not yet referred to a floor vote as of this pass.
NationalityAdministrative

Passports & Travel Documents Law — Law No. 75-40 of May 14, 1975

Enacted: May 14, 1975 | In force: 1975 | Amended: Organic Law No. 2015-46 of November 23, 2015; Organic Law No. 2024-23 of March 11, 2024
Governs issuance of Tunisian passports and travel documents — ordinary passports, diplomatic/service passports, laissez-passer "B," and titres de voyage "C" and "D" for stateless persons and refugees. Articles 38, 39, and 41 criminalize facilitating, arranging, or concealing a person's irregular entry into or exit from Tunisian territory, and participating in an organization or agreement to do so — offenses distinct from the Irregular Migration Law's (2004-6) criminalization of the migrants themselves and from the 2016 Anti-Human Trafficking Law's exploitation-focused offenses. Most recently amended by Organic Law No. 2024-23 of March 11, 2024, the companion statute to that year's biometric national ID card reform (see the National Identity Card Law entry), which established the biometric passport; an earlier amendment, Organic Law No. 2015-46 of November 23, 2015, updated passport-issuance procedures. Genuinely new standalone entry (Run 106): human rights organizations have documented Articles 38/39/41 being used against humanitarian workers rather than smugglers. Tunisian authorities closed the Tunisian Council for Refugees (CTR) — a UNHCR-mandated organization providing asylum-application assistance and emergency care since 2016 — in May 2024, arresting founder Mustapha Djemali and project manager Abderrazek Krimi (plus four other staff) on charges under these articles for allegedly facilitating and harboring irregular border crossings through the CTR's refugee-assistance activities. The Tunis Court of First Instance convicted both men on November 24, 2025 (2 years, 6 months suspended; released the same day, having already served roughly 18 months in pretrial detention), and the Tunis Court of Appeal's criminal chamber upheld the conviction on May 14, 2026. Human Rights Watch (May 11, 2026) and Amnesty International characterize the prosecution as an abusive misuse of anti-smuggling provisions to criminalize refugee-aid work, consistent with this artifact's broader documentation of civil-society prosecutions (see the Associations and Judicial Organization sections). (Cross-ref, Run 213): a distinct organization prosecuted under the same articles is tracked separately at the "Tunisie Terre d'Asile" entry below.

EU–Tunisia Memorandum of UnderstandingStrategic and Global Partnership

Signed: July 16, 2023
Non-binding political declaration between the EU and Tunisia covering five pillars: macroeconomic stability, trade and investment, green energy, people-to-people contacts, and — most emphasized in implementation — migration and mobility. The EU pledged roughly €105 million for border-control capacity, €150 million in direct budget support, and a conditional €900 million in macro-financial assistance tied to an IMF program Tunisia ultimately declined to conclude. Tunisia committed to combating smuggling networks, conducting search-and-rescue operations in its territorial waters, and accepting returns of third-country nationals. The MOU bypassed parliamentary ratification on both sides. In January 2025 the European Commission overhauled its disbursement mechanism following reports of abuses by EU-funded security forces against migrants; Tunisian officials have since pushed to renegotiate the arrangement toward greater reciprocity. Update (Run 43): marking the MOU's third anniversary, a joint letter dated July 1, 2026 from Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, the International Commission of Jurists, the Committee to Protect Journalists, EuroMed Rights, and Avocats Sans Frontières was sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen calling for a full human-rights review of the partnership and conditionality on further EU funding, citing continued reports of abuses against migrants in Tunisian territory. Forms the policy backdrop to the domestic 2023–2026 migrant-policy shift above and the EU's 2026 "safe country of origin" designation below.

EU Designation of Tunisia as a "Safe Country of Origin"EU Pact on Migration and Asylum

European Parliament vote: February 10, 2026 (408–184–60) | Council approval: February 23, 2026 | Rules in force: June 12, 2026
Not Tunisian domestic law, but an EU-law development directly affecting Tunisian nationals abroad: under the EU's Pact on Migration and Asylum, the European Parliament and Council designated Tunisia one of several countries presumed "safe" EU-wide, subjecting Tunisian asylum-seekers in the EU to accelerated, presumptive-rejection border-procedure examination of their claims from June 12, 2026 onward. Distinct from, but connected to, the domestic 2023–2026 migrant-policy shift and UNHCR-registration suspension documented above and the 2023 EU-Tunisia migration MOU above. Flagged as a single-source-class finding from this run pending independent corroboration of the exact vote tallies and in-force date against a European Parliament or Official Journal of the EU primary text.

Irregular Migration Law — Law No. 2004-6 of February 3, 2004

Enacted: February 3, 2004 | In force: 2004
Criminalizes irregular emigration by Tunisian nationals ("harraga") with penalties of up to 3 years imprisonment. Criticized by human rights organizations as criminalizing movement. Used to prosecute individuals attempting to cross to Europe irregularly. Tunisia also receives migrants from sub-Saharan Africa; their status is governed by the 1968 Immigration Law and UNHCR procedure. Note: No domestic asylum law as of 2026; draft asylum law discussed since 2013 but not enacted.

Affaire Abdallah SaïdCriminalization of Migrant-Solidarity Humanitarian Work

Detained: November 12, 2024 | First-instance conviction: April 22, 2026 (Médenine Court of First Instance) | Public-prosecutor appeal: pending
Abdallah Saïd, a physician with over thirty years in public health and founding president of the Médenine-based humanitarian association "Les Enfants de la Lune" (which coordinates a network of local associations providing medical and psychological support, schooling assistance, and economic-integration programs to disabled Tunisian children, migrants, and other vulnerable groups), was placed in pre-trial detention on November 12, 2024 by the national financial-crimes investigation unit. He was initially referred to the anti-terrorism judicial unit, which found no terrorism-related basis for the case. After roughly a year and a half in provisional detention, the Médenine Court of First Instance convicted him on April 22, 2026 and sentenced him to one year's imprisonment; the public prosecutor has appealed the verdict, and Saïd remains detained. Human rights organizations, including the Committee for Justice (CFJ), characterize the case as part of the same pattern documented in the Administrative Suspensions & Judicial Dissolution Proceedings entry above and in the criminalization of migrant-solidarity work under the Irregular Migration Law framework — using provisional detention and shifting accusations (initially framed as terrorism-adjacent, ultimately prosecuted on other grounds) against humanitarian actors assisting migrants and refugees in southern Tunisia. A July 8, 2026 report by the NGO Intersection pour les droits et les libertés cited Saïd's case among 88 documented civil-society-related judicial and administrative actions recorded between May 2024 and May 2026.

Affaire "Tunisie Terre d'Asile"Criminalization of Migrant-Solidarity Humanitarian Work

Arrested: May 2024 | First-instance conviction: January 5, 2026 (Tunis Court of First Instance, criminal chamber) | Released: January 5–6, 2026
A distinct case from the Tunisian Council for Refugees (CTR) prosecution above, involving a different organization and defendants despite an identical legal theory and near-identical fact pattern. Sherifa Riahi (former director), Yadh Bousselmi, and Mohamed Joo — current or former staff of "Tunisie Terre d'Asile," the Tunisian branch of the French NGO France Terre d'Asile, which assisted asylum-seekers and migrants under a program coordinated with Tunisian authorities, local governments, and UN agencies — were placed in pre-trial detention in May 2024 alongside two former municipal officials, Mohamed Iqbal Khaled and Imen Ouardani. Initial charges of money laundering and abuse of function were dropped during proceedings, leaving prosecution solely under Passports & Travel Documents Law (No. 75-40 of 1975) Articles 38, 39, and 41 (facilitating or sheltering irregular entry, exit, or stay) and the 1968 Law on the Status of Foreigners (Law No. 68-7). After roughly 19 months (580 days) in detention, the Tunis Court of First Instance convicted all five on January 5, 2026 to two years' imprisonment with suspended execution; all were released the same or following day. Eighteen other co-defendants who remained at liberty during the proceedings were acquitted. The International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Watch, and Amnesty International condemned the conviction as criminalizing legitimate humanitarian work, consistent with this artifact's broader documentation of civil-society and migrant-solidarity prosecutions (see the Administrative Suspensions and Affaire Abdallah Saïd entries). No appeal outcome had been reported as of this run.

Amnesty International Report, July 2, 2026"Trapped in a Cycle of Abuse": Refugee & Migrant Detention Practices

Published: July 2, 2026 (Amnesty International / Amnesty International USA)
A rights-organization report (not itself a legal instrument, but documenting the administrative-practice dimension of the 2023–2026 sub-Saharan migrant policy shift catalogued across this section) that Amnesty says had not been reflected here in this level of detail. Documents Tunisian authorities' use of the Ouardia Reception and Orientation Centre in Tunis as a de facto administrative-detention facility, holding refugees and migrants indefinitely with no judicial mechanism to challenge the detention, typically pending removal — citing, among other cases, at least three women asylum-seekers from Guinea and Sierra Leone held there with four children after being arrested for begging in Djerba in May 2026. Documents officials and parliamentarians "openly advocating for racial and xenophobic hatred," which the report says has combined with reported impunity for resulting violence to make daily life increasingly untenable for refugees and migrants, particularly Black people. Also documents landlords and employers facing threatened criminal sanctions for hosting or hiring irregular migrants (consistent with the enforcement pattern under Passports & Travel Documents Law Arts. 38/39/41 and the 1968 Law on the Status of Foreigners, Law No. 68-7, already tracked via the Abdallah Saïd, Tunisie Terre d'Asile, and CTR prosecutions above), and states that the post-2024 criminalization of civil-society activity (see Administrative Suspensions & Judicial Dissolution Proceedings) has forced most independent organizations providing migrants medical assistance, legal aid, and emergency housing to suspend operations — compounding the effect of UNHCR's own 2024 registration suspension already documented in the Irregular Migration Law entry above. No Tunisian statute, decree, or JORT publication is associated with this report; it is included as a primary-source-grade account of enforcement practice under the existing legal framework, consistent with this artifact's practice of tracking how enacted law is actually being applied. (Added Run 1066.)

National Council for Tunisians Residing Abroad — Law No. 2016-68 of August 3, 2016 (reform bill pending, 2024–2026)

Enacted: August 3, 2016 | In force: 2016 | Implementing decree: Government Decree No. 2019-820 of September 10, 2019 | Reform bill: n° 2024-064, under ARP committee review since 2024 | Fully adopted at committee level: July 15, 2026 | Not yet at plenary vote
Creates the National Council for Tunisians Residing Abroad (Conseil National des Tunisiens Résidant à l'Étranger), a consultative public body with legal personality and administrative/financial autonomy, seated in Tunis and attached to the ministry responsible for Tunisians abroad. Represents Tunisia's diaspora (estimated at over 1.5 million people) before public authorities and issues an annual activity report to the President, the ARP Speaker, and the Head of Government. Government Decree No. 2019-820 (September 10, 2019) set the Council's administrative and financial organization. A reform bill (projet de loi n° 2024/064) has been under continued examination by the ARP's Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, Tunisians Abroad, and Migration Committee since 2024, with a working session held June 4, 2026 on its text, followed by a further joint hearing on June 22, 2026 with the President of the National Council for Tunisians Abroad herself. The bill would restructure the Council's general assembly, introduce individual, direct, voluntary-basis voting (including electronic voting) for diaspora representatives on a gender-parity basis — replacing the current framework's limited effective functioning since 2016 — and reposition the Council as a horizontal coordination body unifying public policy across ministries dealing with Tunisians abroad and mobilizing expatriate expertise for national economic development. Not yet adopted as of this run. Update (Run 311): per a same-day La Presse report, the ARP's Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, Tunisians Abroad, and Migration Committee adopted amendments to the bill's text on July 14, 2026, going beyond the hearing-stage status documented above — the amended text would add permanent members to the Council's general assembly (deputies elected from diaspora constituencies) alongside 60 diaspora representatives; this is a committee-level amendment adoption, not a completed committee report or plenary vote, and no bill-number change or JORT publication has been found. (Cross-ref added Run 109): separately from this reform bill, Article 83 of the Finance Law 2026 already enacted new tax and customs advantages specifically for this Council's constituency — see the Finance Law 2026 entry (Tax & Fiscal section). Update (Run 325): the same committee (Commission des relations extérieures, de la coopération internationale, des affaires des Tunisiens à l'étranger et de la migration, chaired by Riadh Jaïdane) fully adopted the bill's new version at committee level on July 15, 2026, per Tunisie Tribune's same-day report, independently corroborated by La Presse's July 14, 2026 article quoting Chairman Jaïdane — both describe the committee-level text as complete and confirm its central substantive change: reattaching the Council from its current ministry to the Présidence du Gouvernement directly, to improve cross-ministerial coordination on diaspora policy. Both sources trace to the same committee chairman's remarks (one primary account, two corroborating outlets, not fully independent reporting chains). Next step per both reports is a report to the ARP Bureau and possible plenary scheduling — still not a floor vote or enacted law as of this update. Update (Run 335): a same-day Tunisie Tribune report on the July 15, 2026 committee adoption ("Adoption en commission de la proposition de loi amendant le cadre juridique du Conseil national des TRE"), corroborated by La Presse de Tunisie and allAfrica, supplies additional membership detail beyond what Run 325 captured: the amended general assembly would seat elected diaspora-district deputies alongside the 60 diaspora representatives (each requiring at least five years' residency abroad), plus non-voting observer members drawn from concerned ministries; all seats remain on an unpaid, voluntary basis. No bill-number change, ARP Bureau referral, or plenary date has been found beyond the committee-level adoption already documented.

A member-initiated legislative proposal, not yet a government projet de loi, submitted by the Ordre des Ingénieurs Tunisiens (OIT — Tunisia's professional engineers' order) to the ARP Speaker on July 16, 2026, seeking a "loi-cadre incitative" (incentive framework law) to formalize ties with Tunisian engineers established abroad and mobilize their expertise for national development, through mechanisms for return-to-country incentives, skills transfer, knowledge-sharing, and technology-partnership/investment channels. ⚖️ Judicial Organization

Judicial Organization Law — Law No. 2013-13 of April 2, 2013 (as amended 2022)

Enacted: April 2, 2013 | In force: 2013 | Amended: 2022
Organizes the court system of Tunisia: Cantonal Courts (minor matters), Courts of First Instance (24, one per governorate), Courts of Appeal (3 — Tunis, Sousse, Sfax), Court of Cassation (apex civil/criminal court, Tunis), Administrative Court (apex administrative jurisdiction), and the Constitutional Court (established under 2022 Constitution). Specialized jurisdictions include the Terrorism Chamber at TFI Tunis.
Court structure
  • Cantonal Courts: minor civil matters, misdemeanor infractions
  • Courts of First Instance (24): civil, commercial, criminal chambers
  • Courts of Appeal (3 — Tunis, Sousse, Sfax): appellate jurisdiction
  • Court of Cassation (Tunis): reviews points of law only
  • Administrative Court: all public law disputes
  • Terrorism Chamber: specialized jurisdiction at TFI Tunis level
  • Constitutional Court: established under 2022 Constitution (Arts. 116–120)
AdministrativeConstitutional

Judicial Statute — Law No. 67-29 of July 14, 1967 (as amended)

Enacted: July 14, 1967 | In force: 1967 | Amended: 1997, 2013, 2022
Governs the appointment, promotion, transfer, discipline, and removal of judges. Establishes the Superior Council of the Judiciary (Conseil Supérieur de la Magistrature — CSM) as the body responsible for judicial governance. Post-2022, the CSM's composition was changed by presidential decree, significantly reducing judicial independence according to the UN Special Rapporteur on the Independence of Judges and Lawyers. Update (Run 40): tensions over judicial and legal-profession independence escalated in mid-2026. The Tunisian National Bar Association (ONAT) staged an escalating protest campaign — a May 13 Bar Council escalation vote, a symbolic May 18 red-armband action, then rallies at courts in Tunis (Bab Bnet), Bizerte, Béja, Jendouba, Le Kef, and Siliana — culminating in a nationwide lawyers' general strike on June 18, 2026 demanding reform of the profession's legal framework and stronger judicial-independence guarantees; Bâtonnier Boubaker Belthabet called it a success, but no government response had followed as of late June 2026, and on June 9, 2026 forty international legal and human-rights organizations issued a joint statement condemning an escalating campaign against lawyers, judges, and the Bar. Separately, judge Anas Hmaidi — president of the Association of Tunisian Magistrates (AMT), re-elected at its February 2026 congress despite government pressure — was sentenced to one year in prison on April 6, 2026, prompting condemnation from the International Union of Magistrates and the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, both linking the prosecution to the continued absence of a permanent, independent Superior Judicial Council (see the Provisional Supreme Judicial Council entry below). Update (Run 42): the Tunis Court of Appeal's correctional chamber confirmed Hmaidi's one-year sentence on July 1, 2026 in a ruling issued by default (par défaut/in absentia), this time ordering immediate execution of the sentence — a harsher procedural posture than the first-instance judgment. TAP/Diwan FM reporting confirmed the same legal qualification (Art. 136 Penal Code, obstruction of the freedom to work) tied to his conduct at a June 13, 2022 hearing in Monastir; Hmaidi continues to dispute the legitimacy of the Provisional Supreme Council of the Judiciary body that lifted his immunity on September 20, 2022. Update (Run 43): ONAT's annual general assembly was reported scheduled for July 11, 2026, a potential venue for the Bar to set conditions for renewed dialogue with the government following the unresolved June 18, 2026 general strike; no government response to the strike's demands had been reported as of this run. Update (Run 46): confirmed and refined — the July 11, 2026 assembly is not an elective session (Belthabet was already elected bâtonnier for a 2025–2028 term in September 2025); Belthabet has framed its purpose as convening the Bar Council and general assembly to "evaluate the evolution of the dispute [with the authorities] and adopt consequent measures," i.e., a strategy review on whether to escalate or seek renewed dialogue. Separately, the public prosecutor at the Tunis Court of Appeal filed an appeal challenging the quorum/procedural validity of an earlier lawyers' extraordinary general assembly, with a hearing reported set for June 10, 2026 — outcome not independently confirmed. As of this run (July 2, 2026), the government still had not proposed any official or informal mediation, per Belthabet, though ONAT says it remains open to dialogue. Update (Run 60): on July 2, 2026, UN Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers Margaret Satterthwaite publicly stated that Hmaidi's conviction "should have been overturned," a statement the AMT amplified in its own denunciation of the July 1 appeals ruling as unfair — the first UN Special Procedures reaction specifically naming this case, distinct from the broader CSM-composition criticism already cited above. Update (Run 91): a further, previously undocumented lawyer-harassment case closed a genuine gap — Ahmed Souab, a lawyer, former administrative judge, and prominent human rights defender, was arrested at his home on April 21, 2025 by anti-terrorism officers over public statements he made after representing defendants in the "state security conspiracy" case (see that standalone entry above), and was convicted at first instance to 5 years' imprisonment following a trial Amnesty International said lasted only seven minutes. On appeal, the Tunis Court of Appeal reduced his sentence to 10 months' firm imprisonment plus a 2-year suspended sentence and ordered his immediate release on February 23, 2026 (already served), also lifting the administrative-surveillance measure imposed at first instance — a rare, if partial, judicial correction amid the broader pattern of prosecutions against lawyers and judges documented in this entry. Update (Run 156): the July 11, 2026 ONAT general assembly's sourcing — flagged as unconfirmable on independent re-checks by Runs 119, 128, 131, 145, and 147 — is now corroborated by a further, previously uncited independent source: a June 30, 2026 Réalités Magazine article ("Avocats: Dans l'attente d'un dialogue") confirms the assembly "devrait avoir lieu samedi 11 juillet et pourrait faire connaître les conditions de reprise du dialogue," matching the strategy-review framing already documented above from Runs 43/46 rather than contradicting it. Update (Run 313): the July 11, 2026 general assembly's own outcome remains unreported by any outlet checked (French, English, or Arabic-language search), now 58+ consecutive runs since the assembly was held — the longest-standing unresolved item on this project's watchlist. One adjacent, single-source data point was found and is noted rather than asserted as resolution: Business News (July 13, 2026) reported Bâtonnier Boubaker Belthabet met UGTT secretary-general Slaheddine Selmi at ONAT headquarters "to discuss the general situation of the country and cooperation" — suggestive of the Bar continuing to build alliances rather than reaching an accommodation with the government, but not itself a reported outcome of the July 11 assembly and too thin (single outlet, no substantive detail on positions taken) to characterize further. Update (Run 423): the July 11 assembly's outcome remains unreported, now 62+ consecutive runs unresolved. A new false-positive trap for future runs: a distinct, earlier May 1, 2026 extraordinary ONAT general assembly — which voted a general strike/boycott of judicial-chamber hearings, with Bâtonnier Belthabet subsequently extending bar actions through the May 18 – June 18, 2026 window already documented above — is sometimes returned by search engines in place of the July 11 assembly; the two are separate events, and neither the May 1 assembly's own strike vote nor the June 18 general strike it produced is the still-unresolved July 11 assembly outcome tracked here. Update (Run 492): the Comité pour le Respect des Libertés et des Droits de l'Homme en Tunisie (CRLDHT) issued a statement dated July 19, 2026 (published by Kapitalis July 21) expressing "profound concern" over what it frames as a systemic campaign of judicial reprisals, triggered by the July 13, 2026 appellate ruling raising former Republic Prosecutor Béchir Akremi's sentence from 23 to 29 years (see the Chokri Belaïd Assassination Trial — Akremi/Ellouze entry for the ruling itself). CRLDHT frames Akremi's prosecution as retaliation for his judicial handling of the Belaïd and Mohamed Brahmi assassination files, and situates it within a broader pattern also encompassing the dissolution of the elected Superior Judicial Council (see the Provisional Supreme Judicial Council entry), the 2022 dismissal of 57 magistrates by presidential decree (see the Magistrate Dismissal Power entry), and pressure on lawyers and journalists — describing it collectively as an ongoing weakening of judicial independence since July 25, 2021. The statement also names two further magistrates alongside the already-documented Hmaidi case: Anas Hmaidi (AMT president, this entry above) and, previously undocumented in this artifact, Hamadi Rahmani — a sitting investigating magistrate prosecuted over six defamation complaints filed by former Court of Cassation president Taïeb Rached concerning Rahmani's social-media posts. Rahmani was questioned and granted provisional liberty by the dean of investigating judges at the Tunis Court of First Instance (reported December 2, 2024, tunisienumerique.com and African Manager); his defense (attorney Ayachi Hammami) contested his court appearance on judicial-immunity grounds, invoking an August 9, 2022 administrative-tribunal ruling that had suspended an earlier revocation measure against him, and requested referral to the Provisional Superior Council of the Judiciary as the sole body competent to rule on immunity waivers — the same body whose provisional, still-unreplaced status is documented in the CSM entry above. No further procedural outcome for the Rahmani case has been reported since December 2024; CRLDHT's July 2026 statement treats it as a still-live example of the pattern it describes rather than a closed matter.

Organic Law No. 2016-34 of April 28, 2016Supreme Judicial Council (Conseil Supérieur de la Magistrature)

Enacted: April 28, 2016 | First CSM seated: April 28, 2017 | Amended: Organic Law No. 2017-19 (April 18, 2017); Decree-Law No. 2022-4 (January 19, 2022) | Dissolved and replaced by Decree-Law No. 2022-11 of February 12, 2022
The baseline that the 2022 decree-laws dismantled, present in this artifact until now only as a parenthetical inside the Provisional Council entry. Recording it in its own right matters because the significance of what happened in 2022 is legible only against what existed before. This organic law created the CSM as a constitutional body guaranteeing judicial independence, structured in four parts — the Conseil de la justice judiciaire, the Conseil de la justice administrative, the Conseil de la justice financière, and an Assemblée plénière — and it moved the powers over judges' careers, appointment, promotion and discipline away from the President and the Minister of Justice and into that body. Its composition was the guarantee: two-thirds elected magistrates, one-third independent specialists. The sequence that followed is documented in the adjacent entries — amendment by Decree-Law No. 2022-4 in January 2022, then dissolution and replacement by the Provisional Supreme Judicial Council in February 2022, whose composition inverts the 2016 design by restoring executive appointment, followed by the dismissal power exercised that June. The 2022 Constitution subsequently restructured the judicial councils altogether. (Added Run 1036.)
ConstitutionalAdministrativeSuperseded

Decree-Law No. 2022-11 of February 12, 2022Provisional Supreme Judicial Council

Enacted: February 12, 2022 | Published: JORT No. 2022-016
The specific decree-law referenced above: dissolved the elected Supreme Judicial Council (created under Organic Law No. 2016-34) and replaced it with a "Provisional Supreme Council of the Judiciary," composed predominantly of senior ex officio magistrates plus members appointed by the President from candidates submitted via the Prime Ministry. Retains three specialized sub-councils (judicial, administrative, financial). Remains the operative — still "provisional" — body as of mid-2026, with no permanent council established to replace it.
AdministrativeConstitutional

Decree-Law No. 2022-35 of June 1, 2022Magistrate Dismissal Power (Completing Decree-Law No. 2022-11)

Enacted: June 1, 2022
Grants the President of the Republic power to summarily dismiss any magistrate by simple presidential decree in cases of declared "emergency," threat to public security, or harm to "the country's superior interest," based on a report from unspecified "competent authorities." Dismissal triggers automatic criminal referral; the dismissed magistrate cannot appeal until after a final criminal judgment. Used the same day to dismiss 57 judges and prosecutors, condemned by HRW, Amnesty International, and EuroMed Rights; the Tunisian Association of Magistrates continued to denounce the dismissals as unresolved injustice as of June 2026. Update (Run 263): a professional-reconversion detail, per a July 10, 2026 Business News report: six of the magistrates dismissed under this decree-law have since completed the process of registering as practicing lawyers with the Tunisian Bar, joining the profession rather than pursuing (or after exhausting) the criminal-referral track the decree-law attaches to their dismissal — illustrating one concrete downstream career outcome for the 57 dismissed magistrates nearly four years on, alongside the still-unresolved criminal referrals and appeals tracked elsewhere in this entry.
AdministrativeConstitutionalCriminal

Organic Law No. 2013-53 of December 24, 2013Transitional Justice

Enacted: December 24, 2013 | In force: 2014
Establishes Tunisia's transitional justice framework including the Truth and Dignity Commission (IVD — Instance Vérité et Dignité). Covers: truth-seeking, reparations, institutional reform, and accountability for human rights violations committed between July 1, 1955 and December 31, 2013. IVD operated from 2014–2019; issued final report in 2019 documenting systematic torture, political persecution, and economic crimes.
AdministrativeConstitutionalCriminal

Organic Law No. 2013-43 of October 2013National Authority for the Prevention of Torture (INPT) (Run 66 addition)

Adopted by NCA: October 9, 2013 | Enacted: October 21 or 23, 2013 (sources diverge on the exact day; JORT No. 85/2013) | Members elected by ARP: March 29–30, 2016
A wholly new standalone entry — despite 65 prior research runs and the extradition entry below referencing "torture risk" as a ground for refusal, no dedicated entry existed for Tunisia's National Preventive Mechanism against torture. Implements Tunisia's OPCAT obligations (ratified June 2011) via the Instance Nationale pour la Prévention de la Torture (INPT), the first such mechanism in the MENA region: 16 members elected by Parliament from human-rights associations, magistrates, doctors, and child-protection specialists, holding legal immunity and empowered to conduct unannounced visits to any place of deprivation of liberty; authorities may refuse a visit only for narrow, written, reasoned reasons. The INPT remains active as of mid-2026, distinct from the (separately documented) Truth and Dignity Commission above, which addressed historical rather than ongoing torture: it publicly criticized severe prison overcrowding in November 2024 (population risen from ~23,000 to over 32,000–33,000 against ~17,000 capacity), published a "Guide to Detainees' Rights" in November 2025, and issued a "zero impunity" statement for the UN International Day in Support of Victims of Torture on June 27, 2026. No confirmed reports of INPT defunding or leadership removal were found for 2024–2026. (Run 896 update): Kapitalis's August 3, 2026 report puts the population at roughly 33,000 detainees against an official capacity of 17,000 places — a 194.1% national occupancy rate, with some individual facilities exceeding 200% (e.g., Mahdia prison at 1,522 inmates in 850 places, ~180%) — up from ~23,000 in 2022, an incarceration rate of 267 per 100,000 residents, with slow judicial procedures and widespread pretrial detention cited as contributing causes. In response, the Ministry of Justice's 2026 plans include a new prison facility in Béja, a women's section at Monastir prison, expansion of Borj Erroumi prison, a dedicated penitentiary hospital unit at La Rabta, and expanded use of alternative sentences and electronic monitoring bracelets to ease overcrowding — confirmed via Kapitalis, cross-checked against the general figures already on file from the INPT's November 2024 statement.

"State Security Conspiracy" Prosecutions and Related 2025–2026 Convictions

Arrests from: February 2023 | Instalingo first-instance: February 5, 2025 | Case 1 sentences: April 19, 2025 | Case 1 appeal: November 27–28, 2025 | Instalingo appeal: January 14, 2026 | Case 2 appeal: February 2, 2026 | "Secret Apparatus" case verdict: June 2, 2026 | Bensedrine sentenced: June 26, 2026 | Smara appeal: July 2, 2026 | "Ramadan Evening Gathering" verdict: April 14–15, 2026 | Bhiri fraudulent-documents sentence: May 7, 2026 | Abdelli sentenced: July 7, 2026 | Ghannouchi returned to Mornaguia from hospital: August 18, 2026
A mass prosecution of dozens of opposition politicians, lawyers, and activists on charges of conspiracy against state security, prosecuted under general Penal Code state-security provisions (Arts. 72–85, see Criminal Law section) rather than a dedicated statute — added here as a standalone entry given its significance to Tunisia's post-2021 rule-of-law trajectory, previously undocumented in this artifact despite 39 prior research runs. Case 1 (defendants including Khayam Turki, Ridha Belhaj, Ghazi Chaouachi, Jaouhar Ben Mbarek, Issam Chebbi, and Abdelhamid Jelassi) produced severe sentences on April 19, 2025, described by Human Rights Watch as a "sham trial"; on appeal (Nov 27–28, 2025), 34 of 37 sentences (5–45 years) were upheld and 3 defendants acquitted (Lazher Akremi, Hattab Ben Slama, Noureddine Boutar), with several sentences increased (Chebbi, Ben Mbarek, Chaouachi, and Belhaj raised from 18 to 20 years) while businessman Kamel Ltaief's sentence was reduced from 66 to 45 years, remaining the heaviest in the case. A related but separate Case 2, focused on Ennahda party leadership, produced an appeals ruling on February 2, 2026 sentencing roughly 20 defendants to 3–35 years; Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi's sentence was raised from 14 to 20 years (56 years cumulative across his cases), and co-defendants Kamel Guizani, Rafik Abdessalem, Lotfi Zitoun, and Mouadh Ghannouchi received 35 years in absentia — Amnesty International described the ruling as deepening a "rule-of-law crisis." Separately, Sihem Bensedrine — journalist and former president of the Truth and Dignity Commission (IVD, see the Transitional Justice entry above) — was sentenced to 25 years in prison (two consecutive terms of 20 and 5 years across two cases) on June 26, 2026 by the Tunis Court of First Instance, among the most severe individual sentences of a rights defender since 2021; the case concerns "using position to gain unfair advantage," fraud, and forgery allegedly connected to an arbitral reconciliation agreement the IVD concluded with businessman Slim Chiboub during her tenure, with Bensedrine, Mabrouk Korchid, and Chiboub jointly ordered to pay a fine of roughly 1.776 billion dinars. (Run 153 addition): lawyer and fellow former IVD official Khaled Krichi — arrested June 3, 2026 on the same case — was sentenced the same day (June 26, 2026) to a cumulative 10 years (two five-year terms) and named in the same joint fine, for exploiting his position to obtain undue advantages and violating procedural regulations; the Tunisian Human Rights League (LTDH) condemned both sentences as disproportionate (Businessnews, La Presse de Tunisie, Kapitalis, Human Rights Watch, July 7, 2026). Opposition politician Abir Moussi (Free Destourian Party leader, detained since October 3, 2023, when she was arrested attempting to file a legal challenge against presidential decrees on electoral redistricting) faces at least two further parallel cases beyond this conspiracy cluster. (Run 168 update): in the "bureau d'ordre" case, concerning an incident at the Presidency of the Republic, a 12-year first-instance sentence (December 2025) was reduced on appeal to 10 years by the Tunis Court of Appeal's criminal chamber on March 13, 2026 — 9 years for "aggression aimed at disrupting the functioning of the state, incitement to violence between citizens, and public disorder," plus 6 months each for unauthorized processing of personal data and obstruction of freedom to work; PDL co-defendant Meriem Sassi received 1 year on the same two lesser counts. Separately, an ISIE-initiated complaint under Decree-Law No. 2022-54 Art. 24 ("spreading false information") produced a first-instance 2-year sentence (August 5, 2024), reduced to 16 months on appeal, then annulled and remanded by the Court of Cassation; a newly-constituted Tunis Court of Appeal panel re-confirmed the 2-year sentence on December 30, 2025 (Amnesty International, Kapitalis, Business News, cross-corroborated), replacing this entry's previously vague "ruling reported around March 2026" placeholder. Amnesty International condemned both prosecutions as unjust. (Run 593 update): Moussi's defense committee has now filed cassation appeals against all three rulings above (the "bureau d'ordre" case and both ISIE-complaint cases), reported July 28, 2026; the Cour de Cassation is expected to schedule hearings around the opening of the new judicial year (typically September–October). Press coverage gives the combined sentence across the three cases as 12 years and 6 months — a total that does not perfectly reconcile with the individual figures in this entry (9 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 2 years ≈ 12), a discrepancy in secondary reporting rather than an error in this artifact's own arithmetic (Tunisie Tribune, Réalités Magazine, African Manager, webdo, cross-checked against each other). See the Judicial Statute entry above for the related prosecution of AMT president judge Anas Hmaidi, whose one-year sentence was confirmed on appeal (with immediate execution ordered) on July 1, 2026 — Run 42 update. Update (Run 60): a related but distinct terrorism-chamber case opened July 3, 2026: the Tunis Court of First Instance's terrorism chamber rejected pre-trial release requests (June 30, 2026) for Ennahda secretary-general Ajmi Lourimi and co-defendant Mossaâb Gharbi, prosecuted under the Anti-Terrorism Law (Law No. 2015-26, see Criminal Law section) for failing to report a terrorism-related offense; no verdict has been reported as of this run. (Run 155 update): the specialized terrorism chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance delivered its verdict on July 4, 2026 — three-year prison sentences for both defendants, Lourimi for failing to report a terrorism-related offense and Gharbi for harboring, concealing, and facilitating the escape of a person involved in terrorism cases. Ennahdha denounced the case as fabricated (July 4, 2026), and the LTDH condemned the verdicts against Lourimi and Gharbi as disproportionate in a July 4–5, 2026 statement (Businessnews, webdo.tn, Mosaïque FM, Réalités, Kapitalis). (Run 190 correction/update): that same LTDH statement was previously read as naming Elyes Chaouachi a co-defendant in this Lourimi/Gharbi case; direct verification (Businessnews, Kapitalis, July 4–5, 2026) shows Chaouachi's July 4, 2026 sentence was instead handed down the same day in a wholly distinct anti-terrorism-chamber case, arising from a July 2024 arrest alongside a sought Ennahdha activist — the LTDH statement addressed both same-day verdicts together, not a shared docket, and this entry is corrected accordingly. Elyes Chaouachi — a France-based activist and son of Case 1 defendant Ghazi Chaouachi — received 15 years in that separate case, bringing his cumulative total across a long series of predominantly in-absentia convictions to more than 95 years and 8 months (up from over 80 years reported May 13, 2026, and 38 years reported November 25, 2025); he attributes the accumulating prosecutions to his public advocacy for freedoms and democracy and to his father's status as a conspiracy-case defendant, and the LTDH's July 4, 2026 statement separately denounced this sentence as "severe" and raising doubts about fair-trial guarantees and the presumption of innocence. Update (Run 63): a further related but distinct prosecution — former MP Sahbi Smara, charged not with joining the conspiracy but with fabricating one to incriminate political opponents ahead of the October 2024 presidential election — had his 11-year first-instance sentence reduced to approximately nine and a half years on appeal, July 2, 2026 (Kapitalis, Business News, Tunisie Numérique, Gnet News). Smara was separately sentenced in March 2026 to 6 months' imprisonment for assaulting Abir Moussi inside Parliament while both were sitting deputies, illustrating how this cluster of prosecutions has widened to include cases arising from, rather than merely alongside, the original conspiracy proceedings. Update (Run 81): Case 1 defendant Khayam Turki carries two further, entirely distinct convictions that should not be conflated with his conspiracy sentence above: a April 21, 2026 Tunis Court of First Instance ruling of 14 years for fraud, money laundering, and aggravated breach of trust, arising from a UAE company's complaint over a North African land-acquisition project (Kapitalis, Businessnews); and a July 3, 2026 first-instance conviction of 4 years on strictly tax-related offenses tied to his business-portfolio management, distinct from both prior cases (La Presse de Tunisie, Businessnews, allAfrica). Three separate Turki dockets are now on record: the conspiracy case (above), the April 2026 money-laundering case, and the July 2026 tax case. Update (Run 101): a wholly distinct, considerably larger and more severe case — the "affaire de l'appareil secret" ("Secret Apparatus" case) — reached a first-instance verdict June 2, 2026 from the specialized anti-terrorism criminal chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance, and should not be conflated with the Case 1/Case 2 conspiracy prosecutions above: it was opened in 2022 following a complaint by lawyers for the families of assassinated leftist politicians Chokri Belaïd and Mohamed Brahmi (killed 2013), alleging that a clandestine Ennahda security structure — directly supervised, per the prosecution, by Rached Ghannouchi — orchestrated political assassinations, conducted espionage, and infiltrated state institutions; the 35 defendants were charged under the Anti-Terrorism Law (Law No. 2015-26, see Criminal Law section) with constituting a terrorist organization, rather than under the Penal Code Arts. 72–85 state-security-conspiracy provisions underlying Case 1/Case 2. Sentences: Ghannouchi received life imprisonment plus 30 additional years; alleged mastermind Mustapha Khedher received life imprisonment plus 96 additional years (the case's heaviest sentence); former Prime Minister Ali Laarayedh received 42 years; eleven further defendants received life sentences plus additional terms, and thirteen others received 10–48 years. Ennahdha denounced the sentences as "scandaleuses" and politically motivated; rights groups (DAWN) and Ghannouchi's defense contested the verdict's legitimacy (Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, La Presse de Tunisie, businessnews.com.tn, Le Courrier de l'Atlas, Kapitalis, Middle East Eye, Middle East Monitor, all June 1–6, 2026). No appeal outcome has been reported as of this run. See the separate Chokri Belaïd Assassination Trial entry (Run 239 addition) for the distinct direct prosecution of former prosecutor Béchir Akremi and Habib Ellouze over the investigative/prosecutorial handling of the Belaïd killing itself — a different docket with no defendant overlap. (Run 256 addition): a third, distinct Belaïd-case docket — the direct prosecution of the assassination's execution/recruitment/planning groups — reached a final appeal verdict on October 14, 2025 (two death sentences upheld, four life terms, lesser terms for the remainder of 24 defendants, Ennahda's leadership not implicated); see the new Chokri Belaïd Assassination Trial — Main Case entry below. Update (Run 149): a fourth, previously undocumented distinct prosecution — the "Instalingo" case — was identified and cross-checked against 148 prior runs' coverage (no match for "Instalingo" in any prior entry). Following a September 10, 2021 raid on Instalingo, a digital-media/content-production company in Kalâa Kebira (Sousse governorate), 41 defendants including Ghannouchi were charged with conspiring against state security, seeking to alter the nature of the state, incitement to violence, and money laundering — distinct from Case 1, Case 2, and the Secret Apparatus case above, both in defendant count and in its own independent sentence track. A Tunis first-instance court sentenced Ghannouchi to 22 years, an 80,000 TND fine, and a 10-year public-office ban on February 5, 2025 (co-defendants: 5–54 years); the Tunis Court of Appeal upheld the 22-year sentence and the bulk of convictions on January 14, 2026, while reducing one female defendant's sentence and ordering her release (Anadolu Agency, Middle East Monitor, North Africa Post, corroborated against Middle East Eye's broader case-cluster reporting). No further appeal outcome has been reported as of this run. Update (Run 172): a fifth, previously undocumented distinct prosecution — the "Ramadan Evening Gathering" case (also reported as the "El-Moussamara"/"discussion circle" affair) — was identified and cross-checked against 171 prior runs' coverage (no match for "Ramadan gathering," "Moussamara," or the named co-defendants in any prior entry). The charges arise from a small political gathering Ghannouchi hosted at his home in April 2023, days before his arrest, at which he discussed the country's political situation; prosecutors relied on recordings of the gathering, which the defense contends were fabricated. On April 14–15, 2026, the criminal chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance sentenced Ghannouchi, Youssef Nouri, and Ahmed Mcharki to 20 years' imprisonment each on charges of "conspiracy to change the form of the state," with five further defendants — including Ghannouchi's son-in-law and former foreign minister Rafik Abdessalem, former MP Maher Zaid, and blogger Mohamed Samati — sentenced in absentia to 20 years; the defense stated Ghannouchi's lawyers were barred from his initial hearing for 48 hours and that counter-terrorism procedural rules were improperly applied to a non-terrorism charge (Jeune Afrique, Espace Manager, Sada News Agency, corroborated against a further wire-service report, all April 14–15, 2026). Tunisian press (Jeune Afrique, Espace Manager) reported Ghannouchi's cumulative fixed-term sentences across all five cases now exceed 60 years, on top of the separate life sentence in the Secret Apparatus case — a figure that should be read as press-reported rather than an official court tally, consistent with this entry's existing practice of flagging cumulative-total figures as approximate. (Run 305 addition): a sixth, distinct prosecution — over illegal foreign financing of Ennahda's 2019 electoral campaign via an undeclared BCW lobbying contract, resting on Electoral Law Art. 163 rather than state-security or terrorism charges — reached a "definitive" appeal confirmation on July 13, 2026 (3 years each for Ghannouchi and co-defendant Rafik Abdessalem, referred to in this case's press coverage by his fuller name, Rafik Abdessalem Bouchlaka); see the new standalone foreign-financing case entry below for the full multi-year procedural history. (Run 316 addition): a seventh, distinct prosecution — over Ghannouchi's October 2016 donation of Gandhi Peace and Tolerance Prize money to the Tunisian Red Crescent, treated by the prosecution as a tax offense rather than any state-security, terrorism, or campaign-financing charge — saw its 2-year first-instance sentence (November 14, 2025) increased to 3 years on appeal, July 13–14, 2026; see the new standalone Red Crescent donation case entry below. (Run 395 addition): former Justice Minister and senior Ennahda figure Noureddine Bhiri — previously undocumented by name in this entry despite Case 1's own "34 of 37 sentences" tally implying several unnamed defendants — was independently confirmed as one of the Case 1 defendants: sentenced April 19, 2025 to 43 years at first instance, reduced on appeal (November 28, 2025, the same Case 1 appeal date already documented above) to 25 years plus 5 years' administrative surveillance (Business News, La Presse de Tunisie, cross-checked against each other). Separately, and legally distinct from Case 1, Tunisian state media reported that a court sentenced Bhiri on May 7, 2026 to a further 20 years' imprisonment over allegations that, during his 2012 tenure as justice minister, he issued fraudulent passports and citizenship documents to foreign nationals wanted on terrorism-related charges — corroborated by Africanews and Anadolu Agency (both May 7, 2026). Bhiri and his defense have rejected both sets of charges as politically motivated; the pairing of a state-security conviction with a distinct fraudulent-documents/administrative conviction against the same defendant mirrors the parallel-prosecution pattern already documented above for Turki (money laundering/tax) and Ghannouchi (Instalingo, Secret Apparatus, foreign financing, Red Crescent). (Run 400 addition): an eighth, distinct prosecution — lawyer and 2014 presidential candidate Samir Abdelli (also transliterated Abdeli/Abdali) — reached a first-instance verdict on July 7, 2026 from the specialized anti-terrorism criminal chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance: 18 years' imprisonment on money-laundering and state-security charges, with prosecutors alleging conspiracy against the state's internal and external security; his personal driver and personal secretary received 3 and 2 years respectively on related counts. The ruling is first-instance and subject to appeal, with no appeal date reported as of this run, and no confirmed defendant overlap with Case 1/Case 2, Secret Apparatus, Instalingo, or the other dockets above (Businessnews, webdo.tn, Kapitalis, Mosaïque FM, Gnet News, North Africa Post, all July 7–8, 2026). (Run 477 addition): the "one female defendant" whose sentence was reduced and who was ordered released in the Instalingo case's January 14, 2026 appeal ruling (Run 149 addition, above) is identified by name in further reporting: journalist Chadha Hadj Mbarek, held since July 20, 2023, had her original 5-year sentence reduced to 2 years on that same ruling date after the Tunis Court of Appeal dismissed the most serious charges against her (attempted change of the form of government, incitement to violence, incitement to disorder and looting), making her immediately eligible for release; she was freed the same day and honored by the SNJT on January 16, 2026 (Kapitalis, L'Économiste Maghrébin, Le Courrier de l'Atlas, Tunisie Tribune, Espace Manager, all January 14–16, 2026). (Run 628 addition): a detention-conditions development rather than a new proceeding — Ghannouchi (85, imprisoned at Mornaguia since April 2023 and now serving the life-plus-30-years Secret Apparatus sentence atop his other convictions above) briefly lost consciousness at Mornaguia prison amid extreme heat, with witnesses (including his daughter Haifa Chebbi) citing cell temperatures of roughly 52°C (126°F) in a facility without air conditioning; incidents are reported around both July 17 and July 23, 2026, with sources not fully reconciled on which date preceded a subsequent hospital stay at an undisclosed facility (conflicting reports named either the Rabta public hospital or a military hospital in Tunis). His son Moadh Ghannouchi told Al Jazeera that family and legal counsel went 11 consecutive days without contact or confirmation of his whereabouts, with a visit request to the public prosecutor refused; the opposition National Salvation Front issued a July 27, 2026 statement citing "conflicting reports and rumours" amid the absence of an official government statement, and lawyers described his condition as "critical" as of July 25. Affaire de l'assassinat de Chokri Belaïd — Main Case (Execution/Recruitment/Planning Groups) (Run 256 addition)

Assassination: February 6, 2013 | Alleged gunman Kamel Gadhgadhi killed by security forces: February 2014 | First-instance verdict (4 death sentences): March 27, 2024 | Final appeal verdict: October 14, 2025
A wholly new standalone entry closing a gap that had eluded all 255 prior runs: the direct prosecution of the assassination itself — the execution, recruitment, and planning groups — which is a third, distinct docket within the broader Belaïd case file, alongside (but separate from) the Akremi/Ellouze direct prosecution above and the "Secret Apparatus" case's organizational-responsibility prosecution. The terrorism-specialized chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance sentenced four defendants to death at first instance on March 27, 2024 (alleged gunman Kamel Gadhgadhi had already been killed in a February 2014 security operation and was never tried). On appeal, the Tunis Court of Appeal's terrorism chamber delivered what multiple outlets reported as a final verdict on October 14, 2025, covering 24 defendants: it upheld death sentences by hanging for Mohamed Aouadi and Ezzedine Abdellaoui (plus 105 and 10 further years respectively on related counts), handed down life imprisonment to four further defendants, and lesser terms down to four years to the remainder — while explicitly not implicating the Ennahda movement or its leadership in the killing, a finding Ennahda publicly characterized (statement of October 15, 2025) as clearing it and its president "beyond any doubt" after "twelve years of false and malicious accusations." Belaïd's family criticized the ruling as leaving the case's separate organizational-responsibility file — covering the alleged clandestine security apparatus and its leadership, i.e. the docket now covered by the Secret Apparatus case above — unresolved, and questioned who was "blocking" that parallel investigation. Independently corroborated across TAP (Agence Tunis Afrique Presse), Al-Estiklal, and The Arab Weekly, all reporting the same October 14–15, 2025 verdict and sentences. This verdict predates this artifact's v4.0 baseline by several months yet had never been documented in any of the 255 prior runs' otherwise-thorough coverage of the Belaïd case file, apparently because research repeatedly focused on the still-pending Akremi/Ellouze and Secret Apparatus dockets rather than the (wrongly assumed, still-pending) main case, which had in fact already concluded.

Saber Ben Chouchane CaseDeath Sentence for Facebook Posts, Presidentially Pardoned (Run 732 addition)

Arrested: January 22, 2024 | Death sentence: October 1, 2025 (Nabeul Court of First Instance) | Presidential pardon: October 7, 2025
A wholly new standalone entry cross-checked against 731 prior runs' coverage (no match for "Chouchane," "peine de mort," or "death sentence" tied to online expression in any prior entry) — a significant gap given Human Rights Watch's characterization of the case as the first known death sentence in Tunisia for peaceful expression. Saber Ben Chouchane, a 51-year-old father of three from Nabeul governorate who ran a Facebook page ("Kaïs le misérable") with only a few hundred followers, was sentenced to death on October 1, 2025 by a five-judge criminal chamber of the Nabeul Court of First Instance. The posts underlying the conviction — published shortly before his January 22, 2024 arrest — included a photo from a Tunis demonstration calling for political prisoners' release, reposts urging Tunisians to protest the "confiscation of the revolution," and a call to demonstrate for prisoner releases on the anniversary of the 2011 uprising. The court applied Penal Code Article 72 ("attempting to change the form of government," a capital offense) and Article 67 ("offending the head of state") jointly with Article 24 of Decree-Law No. 2022-54 on cybercrime ("spreading false news," see Digital Law section) — the same decree-law underlying numerous journalist/activist prosecutions documented elsewhere in this artifact. Ben Chouchane had already spent over 14 months in pretrial detention — exceeding Tunisia's statutory maximum — before sentencing. Amid international and domestic outcry (Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and widespread Tunisian civil-society condemnation), President Kaïs Saïed granted him a presidential pardon on October 7, 2025, six days after the verdict, and he was released to his family. Distinct from the in-absentia "State Security Conspiracy" and related prosecutions documented above — Ben Chouchane was tried in person, in Tunisia, and the case did not proceed to any appeal given the pardon. Confirmed via Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Al Jazeera, allAfrica, and Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, cross-checked against each other.

Affaire du financement étranger de la campagne 2019 — Ghannouchi / Bouchlaka (Run 305 addition)

Origin: Cour des Comptes flags a 2014 BCW lobbying contract (~US$285K), renewed/expanded ~US$187K July–Dec 2019 | First-instance verdict: July 13, 2024 (3 years each) | Appeal confirmation: September 21, 2024 | Fresh first-instance verdict: January 26, 2026 (3 years, Ghannouchi) | Appeal "definitively" confirms: Monday, July 13, 2026
A sixth, distinct Ghannouchi prosecution track — resting on Electoral Law Art. 163's foreign-campaign-financing prohibition rather than the state-security-conspiracy or terrorism charges underlying Case 1, Case 2, the Secret Apparatus, Instalingo, or Ramadan Evening Gathering cases documented in the consolidated entry above — a wholly new standalone card, cross-checked against 304 prior runs' coverage (no match for "Bouchlaka" or "foreign financing"/"financement étranger" anywhere in this artifact prior to this run). The case traces to a Cour des Comptes finding that Ennahda's 2019 electoral campaign benefited from an undeclared foreign lobbying contract with the U.S. firm BCW (Burson Cohn & Wolfe), originally signed 2014 (~US$285,000) and renewed/expanded for roughly US$187,000 between July and December 2019. The economic/financial judicial pole of the Tunis Court of First Instance first convicted Rached Ghannouchi and his son-in-law and Ennahda external-relations official Rafik Abdessalem Bouchlaka to 3 years' imprisonment each on July 13, 2024, plus a fine reported at the time as roughly US$1.17 million; the Tunis Court of Appeal confirmed that sentence on September 21, 2024. Identity note: "Rafik Bouchlaka" in July 2026 press coverage of this case is the same individual as Rafik Abdessalem, Ghannouchi's son-in-law and former Foreign Minister, already extensively documented in the consolidated "State Security Conspiracy" entry above as a co-defendant sentenced in absentia to 35 years (Case 2, Feb. 2, 2026) and 20 years (Ramadan Evening Gathering case, April 14–15, 2026) — "Abdessalem Bouchlaka" is his fuller compound family name, per Kapitalis's own tag archive and multiple 2022–2025 Kapitalis reports explicitly identifying him as Ghannouchi's "gendre" (son-in-law); this entry does not describe a newly-discovered person, only a newly-discovered case against an already-tracked one. A fresh first-instance verdict was then handed down January 26, 2026 by the Tunis First Instance Court's 6th correctional chamber — again 3 years for Ghannouchi, with a fine reported by La Presse at a considerably lower ~45,000 TND, a figure not reconciled against the 2024 stage's ~US$1.17 million (the discrepancy could reflect a fine levied on Ennahda as a party versus Ghannouchi personally, a currency/reporting error, or an intervening partial-payment/settlement not described in any source found — flagged as unresolved pending a source that states the relationship explicitly). On July 13, 2026 the Tunis Court of Appeal's chamber specialized in financial-corruption cases "definitively confirmed" (Kapitalis's characterization) that January 2026 verdict — 3 years each for Ghannouchi and Bouchlaka, plus the dollar-value-equivalent fine. Independently corroborated across Kapitalis (July 13, 2024; September 21, 2024; July 13, 2026), La Presse (January 26, 2026), and Univers News (July 13, 2026), with the Mosaïque FM and African Manager July 13, 2026 headlines matching the same story. Open question for a future run: no source found explicitly bridges the September 2024 appeal confirmation to the "fresh" January 2026 first-instance verdict — the most likely explanation is a Cour de Cassation annulment-and-remand between those dates, but this has not been independently verified and should not be asserted as fact.

Businessman Maher Chaâbane — owner of Tunisia Mall, a hotel, and roughly 16 other companies concentrated in real estate, construction, and tourism — has been held in pretrial detention since a January 4, 2024 committal order issued by a Tunis Court of First Instance investigating judge, following an investigation into more than TND 240 million in public-bank credit extended to his companies without adequate collateral, which separately led to the arrest of two former public-bank directors. Affaire Taïeb Rached — "Cassations Sans Renvoi" Judicial Corruption Case (Run 103 addition)

Unauthorized chambers created: 2019 | First-instance verdict: October 27–28, 2025 | Appeal verdict: May 23, 2026
A wholly new standalone entry — distinct from the Haouas/SOREAL, Jlassi, and Mekacher financial-crime cases above, and the first prosecution of a judge of this rank in Tunisian judicial history. In 2019, as First President of the Court of Cassation, Taïeb Rached created two chambers without legal basis (Nos. 35 and 36) and appointed magistrates Abderrazek Bahouri and Marouane Tlili to sit on them; those chambers issued "cassation sans renvoi" rulings (cassation without remand for retrial) that benefited businessmen Nejib Ismaïl and Fethi Jenayah, shielding them from further prosecution and causing the Tunisian state an estimated one billion TND in losses. The Tunis Court of First Instance's specialized financial-corruption chamber convicted Rached on October 27–28, 2025 to 30 years' imprisonment, with Bahouri and Tlili (both since revoked from the magistracy) sentenced to 20 years each, alongside civil damages ordered against the judges and businessman Fethi Jenayah. On appeal, the Tunis Court of Appeal's specialized financial-corruption chamber reduced all three judges' sentences to 10 years each on May 23, 2026, while confirming roughly 935 million TND in civil damages against the three judges and Jenayah; other businessman co-defendants in the case include Adel Jenayah, Kamel Taboubi, and El Wardi Nouisri. Independently corroborated across Kapitalis, L'Économiste Maghrébin, La Presse de Tunisie, Directinfo/WebManagerCenter, African Manager, and allAfrica.

Sworn Interpreters Law — Law No. 94-80 of July 4, 1994(Run 179 addition)

Enacted: July 4, 1994 | Fee schedule: Joint Order of the Ministers of Justice and Finance, December 19, 1996 | Registration-exam rules: Ministerial Order of March 2, 2000 | Procedure manual: Ministerial Order of November 24, 1998
A wholly new standalone entry — a companion legal-profession statute to the Notaries Law (No. 94-60, above) and the Judicial Officers/Bailiffs statute, neither of which had ever been cross-referenced against this one despite both being individually documented. Organizes the profession of interprète assermenté (sworn interpreter/translator), the only category of person legally authorized to produce certified translations for use before Tunisian courts, notaries, and public administration. Establishes a roll (registre) of sworn interpreters maintained by territorial jurisdiction under the supervision of the Ministry of Justice, with admission conditioned on passing a qualifying examination whose regulations and syllabus are fixed by ministerial order (most recently the Order of March 2, 2000). A 1996 joint order of the Ministers of Justice and Finance fixed sworn interpreters' official fee schedule, and a 1998 Ministry of Justice order approved the profession's standard procedure manual. The Ministry of Justice and Tunisian consular authorities abroad (e.g., the French Consulate General in Tunis) publish official lists of registered sworn interpreters by language pair. Confirmed via ILO NATLEX's citation of the law's full title and Tunisia's Ministry of Justice site.

Mediation Law — Law No. 2002-82 of August 3, 2002

Enacted: August 3, 2002 | In force: 2002
Establishes the legal framework for civil and commercial mediation as an alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanism. Mediators must be registered and trained. A mediation agreement, once signed by parties and approved by the competent court, is enforceable as a court judgment. The Startup Act (2018) encourages mediation for commercial disputes involving labeled startups. Reduces court caseloads and offers faster, confidential dispute resolution.

Notaries Law — Law No. 94-60 of May 23, 1994(Run 44 correction)

Enacted: May 23, 1994 | Predecessor: Law No. 88-27 of July 12, 1988
Run 44 correction: prior runs cited this statute as "Law No. 67-39 of June 8, 1967" — no such law could be found in any source searched (NATLEX, jurisitetunisie.com, legislation-securite.tn), and it appears to have been a fabricated citation. The verified currently-operative statute, confirmed directly from jurisitetunisie.com's full-text reproduction and cited in the preamble of the 2011 decree-law reorganizing the lawyer profession, is Law No. 94-60 of May 23, 1994 — 65 articles across 8 chapters (registration on the professional roll; powers; legal status; rights/obligations; discipline; regional chambers and national association; transitional provisions). It separated the notarial function from that of court bailiff (huissier de justice), a split not present in the probable predecessor, Law No. 88-27 of July 12, 1988. Notaries are public officers authenticating deeds, contracts, inheritance declarations, and real property transactions; notarial acts are enforceable without court order, and all real property transfers, mortgage deeds, and company-formation documents must be notarized. Supervised by regional chambers of notaries and a national professional association.

Law No. 87-79 of December 29, 1987 (as amended)Lawyers Statute (Barreau de Tunisie)

Enacted: December 29, 1987 | In force: 1988 | Amended: 1999, 2009
Governs the legal profession and bar association in Tunisia. The Bar Association (Ordre National des Avocats de Tunisie — ONAT) is the self-regulatory body for all lawyers admitted to the Tunisian bar. Sets qualification requirements (law degree + 3-year pupillage), bar admission conditions, and continuing education obligations. Regulates fee structures, professional conduct, confidentiality (avocat-client privilege), conflict of interest rules, and disciplinary procedures. Guarantees lawyers' immunity from prosecution for oral or written statements made in the exercise of their functions before courts. 2026 ONAT–Justice Ministry standoff (added Run 170): resolves the "July 11 ONAT" watchlist item this artifact had carried unconfirmed since Run 145 — it refers to this Law's own regulatory body (avocat.org.tn), not the architects' or chartered-accountants' orders. ONAT delivered written demands for legal-profession reforms to the Justice Ministry on January 23, 2026, centered on three grievances: prosecutions targeting individual lawyers, the continued absence of a permanent Supreme Judicial Council (see the Provisional Supreme Judicial Council entry above), and the composition/appointment procedure of criminal-court chambers. An exceptional ONAT general assembly held May 1, 2026 was challenged by the Tunis Court of Appeal's prosecutor general over its procedural legality (hearing held June 10, 2026); ONAT's Council responded May 13, 2026 by approving regional strikes, red armbands, and a boycott of improperly-composed criminal chambers, culminating in a national general strike and mobilization at the Tunis Palace of Justice on June 18, 2026. ONAT president Boubaker Ben Thabet maintained the actions were lawful and did not disrupt court operations, while stating openness to dialogue. (Run 249 addition): at the June 10, 2026 hearing, some 580 lawyers filed a formal acte de constitution to defend ONAT's position against the prosecutor general's challenge; the Tunis Court of First Instance postponed examination of the case to October 28, 2026 — a date business commentary (Business News) noted risks mooting the appeal's practical effect, since the actions taken at the contested May 1 assembly (strikes, boycotts) would largely have run their course well before that hearing date. ONAT's routine annual general assembly, held Saturday July 11, 2026, was expected to set out conditions for resuming dialogue with the Justice Ministry if the dispute remained unresolved by that date; no outlet had reported that assembly's outcome as of this run's cutoff — a future run should check for its resolution. Update (Run 315): still unreported by any outlet checked in French, English, or Arabic, now well over 60 consecutive runs since the assembly convened — the longest-standing unresolved item this artifact tracks. The only adjacent item found remains Bâtonnier Belthabet's July 13, 2026 meeting with UGTT secretary-general Slaheddine Selmi (already captured at Run 313), which does not itself report the assembly's outcome. Update (Run 381): a distinct, narrower thread showed movement — Justice Minister Leïla Jaffel received the newly elected president of the Tunisian Association of Young Lawyers (Association Tunisienne des Jeunes Avocats), Montassar Nefzi, on July 16, 2026 (Business News, Réalités Magazine), and announced that a new headquarters building for ISPA (Institut Supérieur de la Profession d'Avocat, the bar's professional-training institute) had been included in the Justice Ministry's draft 2027 budget, with the ministry pledging to "favorably examine" the young lawyers' other proposals. This concerns young-lawyer-specific training-institute demands, not the main ONAT–Justice Ministry standoff described above, and does not resolve or report on the still-unconfirmed July 11 general assembly outcome — offered as an adjacent dialogue signal rather than a resolution.
Key provisions
  • Art. 1–10: Bar membership; qualification requirements; pupillage (stage) period
  • Art. 11–20: Professional rights — audience before all courts; freedom of speech in court
  • Art. 21–28: Inviolability of lawyer-client communications; prohibition of office searches without ONAT involvement
  • Art. 29–36: Professional conduct rules; prohibition of conflicts of interest
  • Art. 37–44: Fee arrangements; prohibition of contingency fees as primary arrangement
  • Art. 45–52: ONAT governance — National Council, regional bars (Tunis, Sousse, Sfax, etc.)
  • Art. 53–60: Disciplinary council; sanctions ranging from warning to permanent disbarment

Law No. 2002-52 of June 3, 2002Legal Aid (Aide Judiciaire) (Run 44 correction)

Enacted: June 3, 2002 | Amended: Law No. 2007-27 of May 7, 2007
Run 44 correction: prior runs cited this statute as "Law No. 2002-42 of April 3, 2002" — no such law could be verified in any source searched, and it appears to have been a fabricated citation. The verified statute, confirmed via legislation-securite.tn and jurisitetunisie.com's "bureau d'aide judiciaire" page, is Law No. 2002-52 of June 3, 2002, amended by Law No. 2007-27 of May 7, 2007 (extending eligibility to criminal cassation appeals). Establishes Tunisia's legal aid system for civil and criminal matters: any natural person lacking sufficient income to cover court/enforcement costs without compromising basic necessities may apply, at any stage of proceedings; non-profit legal persons and foreigners (subject to reciprocity) also qualify. Applications are decided by a Legal Aid Bureau attached to each Court of First Instance, chaired by the Republic Prosecutor with a Finance Ministry representative and a lawyer as members; decisions are not subject to appeal, though a new application may be resubmitted. A separate, older track — Decree No. 74-882 of September 26, 1974, replaced by Organic Law No. 2011-2 of January 3, 2011 — governs legal aid specifically before the Administrative Court.
