  • (Run 1034, August 20, 2026) This session's designated branch (claude/nice-edison-7hzjhg) again opened on the stale v2.83 / PR #1305 lineage (2,616 lines, 221 entries, no shared merge-base with current main) and had never had a PR of its own — hard-reset to latest origin/main (Run 1033/345 entries/v4.1033) before any work, per the now-routine stale-fork recovery documented at Runs 1006–1033, and committed straight to main. Three independent research passes produced the largest substantive correction in recent runs.

    1. Industrial-property section rebuilt on the merits — a structural misattribution, not a typo. This artifact had for its entire history described Law No. 2000-84 of August 24, 2000 as a single omnibus "Industrial Property (Patents, Trademarks, Designs)" statute governing patents, trademarks, geographical indications, industrial designs, and utility models together. That is wrong: Tunisia has no consolidated industrial-property code, and Law No. 2000-84 covers brevets d'invention only. Four consequences were fixed. (i) The 2000-84 entry was rewritten as a patents entry, with its verified JORT citation (No. 68, August 25, 2000), the Art. 2–3 patentability criteria and statutory exclusions, the Art. 36 twenty-year term, Art. 83/90 penalties, Art. 102's repeal of the 1888 patents decree, its three implementing decrees, and the PCT accession chain (deposited September 10, 2001; in force December 10, 2001). (ii) A new Trademarks entry documents Law No. 2001-36 of April 17, 2001 and its only substantive amendment, Law No. 2007-50 of July 23, 2007, which replaced Art. 51 (fine raised to TND 10,000–50,000) and inserted Arts. 52 bis–nonies creating the enforcement-agent, seizure, entry, sampling and analysis regime the 2001 text lacked; plus Décret gouvernemental No. 2015-303 of June 1, 2015 (electronic filing, Madrid Protocol designations) and the Madrid Protocol's October 16, 2013 entry into force. (iii) A new Industrial Designs entry documents Law No. 2001-21 of February 6, 2001, correcting the design term the artifact previously carried — "5 years, renewable up to 4 times, 25 years total" is the EU Community-design rule, whereas Art. 10 of the Tunisian law gives the applicant an election of five, ten, or at most fifteen years — and adding the Hague Agreement Geneva Act accession (in force June 13, 2012). (iv) A new Geographical Indications entry replaces what had been a single unsourced bullet, documenting Tunisia's two sector-split statutes — Law No. 99-57 of June 28, 1999 for agricultural products (administered by the Ministry of Agriculture, not INNORPI, with a six-month opposition period in which silence counts as acceptance) and Law No. 2007-68 of December 27, 2007 for handicraft products — together with accession to the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement, in force for Tunisia July 6, 2023, the most consequential recent GI development.

    2. A misnumbered statute corrected. The integrated-circuit topographies entry cited "Law No. 2001-21." That number belongs to the industrial-designs law; the integrated-circuit statute is Law No. 2001-20. Both were adopted February 6, 2001 and printed consecutively in JORT No. 12 of February 9, 2001 (circuits pp. 253–257, designs pp. 257–261) — the likely origin of the swap. Confirmed by direct WebFetch of JurisiteTunisie's texts of both laws, which agree with WIPO Lex on both numbers and both page ranges. The entry's protection term was corrected in the same pass: Art. 18 ends protection "à la fin de la dixième année civile qui suit la date à laquelle elle a pris effet" (close of the tenth calendar year), not the generic TRIPS/Washington-Treaty "10 years from first exploitation or 15 from creation" formulation previously stated; its seven fabricated-looking article-range bullets were replaced with the law's actual provisions (Art. 4 deposit-constitutive protection, the Art. 11 two-year commercial-exploitation filing bar, Arts. 20–26 licence d'office, Art. 34–36 penalties). The plant-variety entry was likewise refined to its real title (semences, plants et obtentions végétales), its previously-omitted amendment (Law No. 2000-66 of July 3, 2000), and the UPOV accession chain (Law No. 2002-83 of October 14, 2002; Décret No. 2002-3019 of November 19, 2002).

    3. Foreign Exchange Code — two missed developments added. The Draft Law No. 115/2025 entry had stood unchanged since a Run 70 update dated July 3, 2026, still framing Ktari's "before the summer recess" target as merely unconfirmed. Two later statements, both verified by direct WebFetch of the Arabic Tunisie Numérique reports, close that gap: on July 23, 2026 Ktari rejected deferral to January 2027 and committed the Finance and Budget Committee's first post-recess session, in October 2026, to article-by-article voting on the Code with or without the BCT's opinion — restoring, and thereby superseding, the vote-around-BCT-silence posture the Run 36 update had recorded as softened; and on August 6, 2026 he stated the bill had been blocked roughly eight months solely on the BCT governor's failure to transmit observations, appealing to President Kaïs Saïed to intervene. Corroborated by African Manager and Kashf Media.

    4. Standing correction — the ARP recess end-date. Runs 1006–1033 repeatedly recorded that "the ARP remains in recess until October 7, 2026" (34 occurrences, all within this section's run narratives; no law-card carries the claim). That date is unsupported. October 7 was the opening of the fourth ordinary session, on October 7, 2025; that session closed July 29, 2026. Under Art. 60 of the 2022 Constitution the ordinary session opens "during October," and no opening date for the fifth ordinary session (2026–2027) has been announced — arp.tn's most recent posting remains Bouderbala's July 30, 2026 closing speech. Future runs should say "in recess until the fifth ordinary session opens in October 2026, exact date not yet announced." The prior narratives are left as written rather than retro-edited, with this note as the correction of record.

    Swept and found already covered: a full JORT/decree sweep for August 15–21, 2026 confirmed no issue beyond N°083 of August 18, 2026 (jort.tn renders a placeholder page for any issue number, so page existence there is not evidence of publication — only N°083 returned real content), and every item it surfaced was already on file: BCT Circulaire n°2026-7 of August 18, 2026 (already added Run 1006), Décret présidentiel n°2026-206 of August 12, 2026 extending the southern buffer frontier zone, n°2026-207, the CSEE decrees n°2026-203/204/205, the AMEN Social TND 260→280 raise, and the August 15 "Khadamet" digital-transformation and August 19 budget économique 2027 ministerial councils (orientation-setting only; no projet de loi adopted, no PLF 2027 transmission to the ARP as of this date). The rest of the standing watchlist — Draft Cybersecurity Law n°2024-36, the Personal Data Protection/AI organic bill, Constitutional Court organic bill n°100/2025, and the overseas-placement reform bill — showed no movement.   • (Run 1035, August 20, 2026) Branch reset from the stale v2.83 / PR #1305 lineage to latest origin/main (Run 1034 / 348 entries / v4.1034) before any work, per the routine documented at Runs 1006–1034, and committed straight to main. Three independent research passes ran in parallel: a current-events sweep of the August 15–21, 2026 window, and two deep verification passes against primary sources on subject-matter areas this artifact had never covered. The result is the largest single-run expansion of coverage breadth in this artifact's recent history — twelve new entries, 348 → 360 — concentrated in financial, accounting and public-sector-employment law, where a systematic audit found the deepest remaining gaps.

    1. Financial-market and Islamic-finance law — eight new entries closing a structural blind spot. The artifact documented the Banking Law, the Financial Market Law, insurance, microfinance and leasing, but had no coverage of the vehicles, infrastructure and Sharia-compliant regimes those statutes presuppose. Added, each verified by direct reading of primary texts (JORT facsimiles, the CMF's and CGA's own consolidated editions, JurisiteTunisie, the FGDB's official membership list): the Code des Organismes de Placement Collectif (Law No. 2001-83 of July 24, 2001, JORT n°59 of the same date, pp. 1790–1796) covering SICAV, FCP, FCPR and the 2019 fonds d'investissement spécialisés; securitisation (COPC Titre II, Arts. 35–48); the Islamic banking regime under Law No. 2016-48 (Arts. 4, 11–16, 22–23, 54, 75–76, 150); the Sukuk Law (Law No. 2013-30 of July 30, 2013, JORT n°62 of August 2, 2013); the non-resident financial services code (Law No. 2009-64 of August 12, 2009); the central securities depository and dematerialisation regime (Law No. 94-117 Arts. 77–80 and Law No. 2000-35 of March 21, 2000); the intermédiaires en bourse regime (Law No. 94-117 Arts. 55–62 and Décret No. 99-2478 of November 1, 1999); and takaful insurance (Law No. 2014-47, Insurance Code Titre VII, Arts. 201–217).

    2. Four corrections and negative findings recorded rather than quietly adopted. (i) Takaful is routinely cited as an August 2014 law; the Insurance Code's own official footnote gives July 24, 2014. (ii) The CMF's consolidated COPC edition cites an amending "loi n° 2019-4" in one footnote and "loi n° 2019-47" in another; the correct number is 2019-47, verified against the official text (JORT n°47 of June 11, 2019, p. 1644). (iii) Several secondary summaries state that Law No. 2019-47 amended the Foreign Trade Law No. 94-41; it did not — its Art. 5 amends Law No. 94-42 on sociétés de commerce international, a different statute printed in the same JORT issue. (iv) Two things reported to exist do not: there is no "2017 securitisation reform law" (the 2017 texts are the sukuk-fund décrets No. 2017-1332/1333), and Tunisia has no covered-bond / "obligations foncières" statute — a dedicated French and Arabic search across the CMF, BVMT, BCT and CSC bond chapter found none. Both negatives are logged here so a future run does not add an entry for a law that does not exist. A fifth point is recorded as a reading rather than a citation: settlement finality in Tunisia rests on a CMF règlement, not on primary legislation, there being no statutory settlement-finality act.

    3. Accounting and public-sector employment law — four further new entries. The Code de la Comptabilité Publique (Law No. 73-81 of December 31, 1973, 286 articles) had never been documented despite entries on the Organic Budget Law and the Court of Accounts; it remains expressly in force, Organic Law No. 2019-15 having preserved it "jusqu'à sa modification." Added alongside it: the enterprise accounting system (Law No. 96-112 of December 30, 1996), the Foreign Trade Law (Law No. 94-41 of March 7, 1994, JORT n°19 of March 8, 1994, verified from the BCT's JORT scan), and Law No. 85-78 of August 5, 1985, the general statute of agents of offices, EPIC and wholly State-owned companies — the employment regime for STEG, SONEDE, CPG and their peers, and the counterpart to the civil-service statute already on file, differing from it most consequentially at Art. 3, which makes the Labor Code residually applicable. Three citation errors around that law are corrected: the ARP archive catalogue dates it August 4 (the JORT text reads August 5); one secondary source numbers it 85-87 (it is 85-78); and the correct title wording is collectivités publiques locales. On IFRS, the popular account is corrected: no law, decree or Art. 7 arrêté making IFRS Tunisia's general-purpose framework was found; what exists is a 2018 CNC phased plan of uncertain legal force plus a genuinely binding banking channel, BCT Circulaire No. 2025-08 of May 16, 2025 imposing IFRS 9. Law No. 96-112 and the NCT remain the statutory framework for individual accounts.

    4. A logged conflict closed on the primary document. Run 1034 left the Personal Data Protection bill's article count open (123 vs. 132). It is now settled at 132 by direct reading of the bill's own ARP filing dossier: the text ends at الفصل 132, and every sponsor's signed adoption declaration states 132 فصلا. The "123" figure is traced to a specific WebManagerCenter piece of February 23, 2026. Note that this artifact had in fact already resolved the count at 132 in the entry itself; Run 1034's characterisation of it as unresolved was reading the artifact's own narrative rather than the entry, and this run both confirms the figure on primary evidence and withdraws the entry's previous speculative explanation of the error's origin. New primary detail added in the same pass: filing at the ARP central registry July 14, 2025; MPs' proposition, not a government bill; Al-Ahrar bloc sponsorship; Art. 131 entry into force six months after publication with repeal of Organic Law No. 2004-63; Art. 132 transfer of INPDP assets. One discrepancy is logged unresolved: the dossier indicates 16 sponsoring deputies against the 17 on the ARP tracker.

    5. Current-events sweep — little new, and one false positive worth recording. Presidential Decree n°2026-208 of August 17, 2026 (National Order of Merit, Education and Science, 11 recipients, JORT n°083) was surfaced by seven outlets and confirmed already documented at Run 1006's cover-to-cover reading of that issue; the August 18, 2026 Kasbah ministerial session on social-security reform was likewise confirmed already covered at Runs 1003 and 1017. No decree numbered 2026-209 or above exists, and no JORT issue beyond N°083 of August 18, 2026 — N°084 falls on Friday, August 21, not yet due. All ten standing watchlist bills show no movement dated after August 15, consistent with the ARP recess. False positive logged: on August 19, 2026 at least five outlets ran "up to 3 years in prison for licence-plate offences"; this is not a new text but an ONSR official restating existing Art. 88 of the Highway Code on a radio programme — recorded so a future run does not mistake the coverage for legislation. The one genuine dated development is on the Sumud flotilla prosecutions: Wael Nawar's hunger strike was still running on August 20 and drew the case's first parliamentary intervention, a group of deputies publicly calling for the four detainees' release.

    Standing gaps for the next run. Citation gaps deliberately left open rather than guessed: JORT issue references for Law No. 2014-47, Law No. 2001-83, Law No. 2009-64 and Décrets No. 99-2478 / 2007-1678; the BCT circulaire under Art. 11 of Law No. 2016-48; the substantive content of the 1999, 2003 and 2007 amendments to Law No. 85-78 (the scan obtained is the original 1985 text, not a consolidation); whether Art. 54 of Law No. 2016-48 is permissive in the Arabic original as it is in the French; and whether any corporate sukuk has ever been issued in Tunisia. Uncovered subject areas identified but not yet written: the legal basis for the STICODEVAM → Tunisie Clearing rename, and Law No. 98-106 of December 18, 1998 on import safeguard measures. A version and element-count check confirms the <title> tag, header meta line and footer are synchronized at Version 4.1035 (Run 1035), that the totalCount stat and the law-card element count both read 360, and that all 695 internal anchors resolve with zero dead links and zero duplicate id values.
  • (Run 1036, August 20, 2026) Branch reset from a stale v2.84 / PR #1327 lineage to latest origin/main (Run 1035 / 360 entries / v4.1035) before any work, per the routine documented at Runs 1006–1035, and committed straight to main. Four research passes ran: a current-events sweep of August 14–20, 2026; a systematic coverage-gap audit; a targeted follow-up on one uncovered pending bill; and an adversarial verification pass on a single suspect entry. That last pass produced this run's most important result. Total documented items: 360 → 377 (seventeen new entries), plus three corrections to existing entries, one of them substantial.

    1. Fabricated content found and removed from the Law No. 99-89 entry. That entry had stood since the artifact's early versions describing Law No. 99-89 of August 2, 1999 as "the Cybercrime Law," criminalising "unauthorized access, interception of electronic communications, introduction of malicious code, and computer fraud," with "penalties of 2 to 5 years" and "up to 8 years for attacks on critical infrastructure," "amended 2004, 2010." Verified against the JORT n°63 facsimile and the consolidated 2010 Penal Code, almost all of that is wrong. The law is an omnibus Penal Code amendment (modifiant et complétant certaines dispositions du Code pénal) whose headline reform is the travail d'intérêt général; it also created the torture offence at Art. 101 bis; computer crime (Arts. 199 bis, 199 ter) is one component among several. Interception and malicious code were not covered — independently corroborated by the Council of Europe Octopus assessment, which found pre-2022 Tunisian law covered the Budapest offences only partiellement, the gap Decree-Law 2022-54 Art. 18 was written to fill. The penalty figures correspond to no Tunisian provision: Art. 199 bis sets a four-tier ladder (2 months–1 year / 2 years / 3 years / 5 years), not a range. Tunisia has never had a critical-infrastructure aggravating circumstance in computer-crime law, before or after 2022; the phrase occurs nowhere in either instrument in French or Arabic, and reads as imported from a foreign or generic template. The stray "8 years" is traceable: it is the only occurrence of huit ans in the law, attaching to Art. 101 bis (torture) — a real figure in the right statute, swept into the wrong description. "Amended 2004, 2010" is false; the real chain is amendment of the community-service articles by Law No. 2009-68 and repeal of Arts. 199 bis/ter by Decree-Law 2022-54 Art. 37. The entry is rewritten in full, with the correction reasoning kept on the page rather than silently overwritten. A note on method: this error survived a thousand runs because every prior pass treated the entry as settled background. It was caught only when an unrelated gap audit reported Law 99-89 as a sentencing statute, contradicting the entry — a reminder that the artifact's oldest, least-revisited entries are its least verified, not its most.

    2. A transcription trap recorded for future runs. The circulating French text of Law 99-89 renders Art. 1 as amending "les articles 13 et 12"; the Arabic original reads الفصلان 13 و172 — Article 172, confirmed because Art. 172 (nouveau) is the provision actually set out. The same French text drops the community-service ratio entirely; the Arabic gives two hours per day of prison, confirmed independently by CPP Art. 344 al. 2. Both are logged so a future run does not "correct" the right figures back to the garbled ones.

    3. Two further corrections. The August 2026 price-cap entry described the bottled-water measure as a "15-millime-per-bottle margin cap"; the measure is a 15% gross margin at wholesale and retail on net invoice purchase price, the millime figure being a La Presse rendering that no other outlet supports and that a companion schedule of maximum retail prices by bottle size makes redundant. Full price schedules for both water and poultry are now on the page, and the poultry caps are fixed at August 19 – September 19, 2026 against a looser "end of September" headline reading. The AMEN Social entry gains the arrêté's signature date (August 5, 2026, two days before publication), confirmation that the superseded text is dated July 10 not August 10, 2024, and a note that neither arrêté carries a sequential number — the "80" in Arabic reporting is the JORT issue number and should not be cited as a decision number.

    4. Seventeen new entries, concentrated in four structural gaps. Constitutional and institutional: Decree-Law No. 2024-1 of September 13, 2024, the operating statute of Tunisian bicameralism — the artifact had the second chamber and the elections that seated it but not the instrument governing how the two chambers legislate; the ISIE's founding Organic Law No. 2012-23, previously present only as the thing Decree-Law 2022-22 amended; the CSM Organic Law No. 2016-34, the baseline the 2022 decree-laws dismantled; and the framework Decree-Law No. 2011-120 creating INLUCC. Two are recorded specifically because they were never implemented — the INBGLC and the future-generations authority, both validly enacted, neither ever constituted, both constitutionally orphaned in 2022: Tunisia's anti-corruption and intergenerational-rights architecture cannot be read accurately without knowing its designed centrepieces do not exist. Criminal: Law No. 2009-68 on penal reparation and alternatives to imprisonment (threshold to ≤1 year, ceiling to 600 hours, and the new réparation pénale of 20–5,000 DT), plus the point that the 1999 remorse requirement was dropped and replaced by a social-reintegration test that secondary summaries routinely carry forward wrongly; and Law No. 99-90, the garde à vue safeguards statute enacted the same day as the torture offence. Tax: the Code of Registration and Stamp Duties (Law No. 93-53), the largest remaining hole in tax coverage and the code where succession and donation taxation lives, as distinct from the CPS that governs the underlying shares. Religious-institutions law, an entirely uncovered area: the 1988 mosques law and the mosque-personnel regime — a workforce performing permanent public functions under Décret 2019-1228 rather than statute, expressly barred from civil-service promotion — and the pending Proposition de loi n°78/2025 that would close that gap. Also added: the FSI general statute (Law No. 82-70), whose 2011 amendment made security unions legally possible; the building fire-safety code (Law No. 2009-11, a full code the artifact previously mentioned only when correcting a source that misidentifies it as food-safety law); the public-agent code of conduct; chambers of commerce; public-sector pensions (Law No. 85-12); and the financial-relations security law (No. 2005-96).

    5. Current-events sweep — nothing newly enacted. No loi, décret-loi or code was enacted in the August 14–20 window. JORT n°82 (August 14) carried four presidential decrees dated August 12 — Nos. 2026-203/204/205 on the Higher Council for Education and Teaching (members; Secretary-General Mohamed Ali Boughdiri; inaugural session convened for August 17, held and opened by the President) and No. 2026-206 extending the southern border buffer zone one year from August 29, 2026 — all already on file, as is BCT Circular No. 2026-7 in JORT n°83 (August 18). A source-conflation caveat worth keeping: La Presse's August 14 write-up merges decrees 203 and 204; the Arabic Tunisie Numérique text and L'Économiste Maghrébin give the split used here. No JORT issue beyond n°83 exists — n°84 falls Friday, August 21. All standing watchlist bills are static with the ARP in recess until October 7, 2026. Courts are in August judicial vacation, which accounts for the absence of rulings; the nearest item is the August 3 referral of Rafik Abdessalem Bouchlaka to the criminal chamber in the "don chinois" case, already on file.

    6. A second research wave closed almost every standing gap Run 1035 left open — all of it verified against JORT facsimiles rather than secondary summaries, and folded into the relevant entries rather than listed here. The STICODEVAM → Tunisie Clearing rename is settled, and the answer is a negative worth stating precisely: no legal instrument effected it. It was a corporate act — an extraordinary general meeting of October 21, 2014, effective November 14, 2014, recorded in the JORT's Annonces Légales n°135 of November 11, 2014, p. 4594. A structural confirmation is that the governing règlement is drafted generically as le Dépositaire Central des Titres and never uses the name at all. The company was created December 28, 1993 and so pre-dates its own statutory basis. Two loose ends are logged rather than smoothed: a commercial-register number reading "1996" against a 1993 constitution, and the complete absence of the arrêté approving its statutes that Art. 77 of Law 94-117 requires. The takaful date conflict dissolved rather than being decided: both dates are right — the law is dated July 24, 2014 and was published in a combined triple issue, JORT n°60-61-62 spanning July 25 to August 1, 2014, pp. 1913–1916, which is exactly where the "August 2014" of secondary sources comes from. Remaining citations closed: Law No. 2001-83 confirmed precisely as Run 1035 had it (JORT n°59, pp. 1790–1796 — recorded because a confirmed citation saves a future run the check); Law No. 2009-64 at JORT n°65 of August 14, 2009, pp. 2316–2338; Décret No. 99-2478 at JORT n°93 of November 19, 1999, pp. 2442–2450; and Décret No. 2007-1678 identified — it amends Décret 99-2478, JORT n°56 of July 13, 2007. The Art. 11 circular is found: BCT Circulaire No. 2019-08 of October 14, 2019, and its lateness is the story — Art. 11 allowed the Governor two months, a deadline that expired in September 2016. Art. 54 of Law 2016-48 is permissive in the Arabic original exactly as in the French (أن تحدث), and the same article switches to the mandatory ويتعيّن for the duties that are obligatory — so the optional Sharia board is deliberate drafting, not a translation artefact; Art. 54 also survived a constitutional challenge before the Instance provisoire, rejected July 2, 2016. The Law 85-78 amendments are identified: the 1999 text is a wholesale overhaul of some forty provisions, including a bar on recording an agent's political, religious or trade-union affiliation in their personnel file; 2003 created business-creation leave; and the 2007 change is Article 35 of Law No. 2007-69 on economic initiative, not a standalone amending law — which is why it is easy to miss. And the sukuk question is answered affirmatively: Sukuk Zitouna Tamkeen 2023 (6 million dinars, seven years, Wakala Bil Istithmar, 10.65%) is documented in the Annonces Légales of December 29, 2023, issued directly by the company under Décret No. 2018-579 rather than through a fonds commun des sukuk. Three negatives are logged with it so they need not be re-searched: no other issuance appears anywhere in the archive, no sukuk fund or fund-management company appears ever to have been licensed despite the 2017 décrets creating the regime, and no sovereign sukuk exists. Two further entries came out of the same pass: Law No. 98-106 on import safeguards, the other subject area Run 1035 flagged, and its companion Law No. 99-9 on unfair import practices — Tunisia's trade-remedy law being two distinct statutes that are routinely conflated, one for fairly-traded import surges and one for dumping and subsidies. Total rises to 379.

    Standing gaps carried forward. Genuinely unresolved after this run: the arrêté approving STICODEVAM's statutes (never published, so possibly unobtainable); Tunisie Clearing's current capital and shareholder list (last verified at 5,330,880 TND after the May 21, 2015 EGM); the product names of the two June 2006 safeguard investigations (that JORT issue is image-only); the JORT reference for Law No. 99-90; whether Law No. 98-106 has ever been amended (no amending instrument found, but this rests on absence of evidence); and the relationship between the 1982 FSI general statute and the Law No. 2019-73 entry, which this artifact also labels an internal-security-forces statute — whether 2019-73 replaced, layered onto, or addresses a distinct subject from the 1982 text was not settled, and both entries should be checked against the JORT before either is rewritten. Also open: whether the 1988 mosques law is numbered 88-34 (legal databases, better attested) or 88-33 (press); the sponsoring deputies and affected headcount for bill n°78/2025; and decision numbers for the two Ministry of Commerce price decisions, which exist only as ministry communiqués. An archive note worth carrying forward: this run's verification succeeded largely because jort.tn serves full-text JORT PDFs at lake.jort.tn/{collection}/{lang}/{year}/{issue}.pdf, including the Annonces Légales series — which is how a corporate name change and a private sukuk placement were traced. pist.tn, iort.gov.tn, legislation.tn and tunisieclearing.com were all unreachable. A method note for the next run: given what the verification pass found in the Law 99-89 entry, the highest-value work is no longer only breadth. The artifact's oldest thin entries — short, undated, carrying round-number penalties and no source — should be treated as an audit queue, since one of them proved to contain figures with no basis in Tunisian law at all.
